en: I bow to that son of Yamunā, by meditating upon whose lotus feet all my impurities were destroyed and I attained the state of true reality.
The Lord of Śrī,
who is solely devoted to auspiciousness that is the antithesis of all that is to be abandoned,
whose singular nature consists of infinite knowledge and bliss, and who is distinct from all other entities.
He is a great ocean of a multitude of countless auspicious qualities, such as innate, limitless, and unsurpassed knowledge, strength, sovereignty, valor, power, and splendor;

He possesses a divine form that is a treasury of infinite qualities—such as being of a single form according to His own will, inconceivable, divine, marvelous, eternal, irreproachable, unsurpassed, and radiant—with beauty, fragrance, delicacy, charm, youth, and so forth;
and He is adorned with various, diverse, infinite, wonderful, eternal, irreproachable, and immeasurable divine ornaments appropriate to Himself.
He possesses divine weapons that are commensurate with Himself, innumerable, inconceivable in power, eternal, irreproachable, and unsurpassedly auspicious;

He is the beloved Lord of the splendor of the multitude of His own infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities—such as His essential nature, form, attributes, majesty, sovereignty, and character—which are eternally, irreproachably, and commensurately suited to His own will;

and He is accompanied by immeasurable wise beings who take singular delight in being entirely subordinate to His own resolve, and who possess infinite multitudes of qualities such as eternal, irreproachable, and unsurpassed knowledge, action, and sovereignty, which correspond to His own essential nature, subsistence, and activity.

He whose essential nature and character are indefinable by speech or mind; who resides in the eternal, faultless, and imperishable supreme ether (paramavyoman), which is enriched with infinite, wonderful, and immeasurable great majesty consisting of various, diverse, and endless objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment appropriate to Himself;
whose divine play consists in the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, which is filled with various, diverse, and infinite classes of enjoyers and objects of enjoyment;
He is the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, Nārāyaṇa.
Having created the entire universe, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings,
He remains established in His own nature, beyond the reach of meditation, worship, and the like for gods such as Brahmā and for human beings;
He is a great ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous character, affection, and magnanimity.
Never abandoning His own essential nature—which is the very form and individual constitution belonging to each respective [incarnation]—He descends again and again into those various worlds.
Being propitiated by diverse beings, He bestows upon them fruits corresponding to their desires, known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Under the pretext of removing the burden of the earth, He descended to this world so that even those such as ourselves might take refuge in Him, and thus became an object of the eyes of all humanity.
Performing divine deeds that captivate the minds and eyes of all beings,
both high and low, He slew Pūtanā, Śakaṭa, the twin Arjuna trees, Ariṣṭa, Pralamba, Dhenuka, Kāliya, Keśin, Kuvalayāpīḍa, Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika,

Tośala, Kaṃsa, and others; and having done so, He nourished the entire universe with the nectar of His glances, conversations, and embraces, which were filled with boundless compassion, friendship, and affection.
By manifesting a multitude of qualities such as unsurpassed beauty and virtuous character, He made Akrūra, the garland-maker, and others supreme devotees;

and under the pretext of inciting the sons of Pāṇḍu to battle, He introduced the yoga of devotion— pertaining to Himself, as taught in the Vedānta, and supported by knowledge and action— as the means for attaining liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal.
When the battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus had commenced, that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all lords,

who acts for the benefit of the world and is overcome by affection for those who take refuge in him, made himself the charioteer and Pārtha the warrior, with all the worlds as witnesses. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Assembled on the field of dharma, at Kurukshetra, eager for battle—what did my sons and the Pandavas do, O Sanjaya? (BhG 1.1)
Even though he knew this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being blind in every respect, questioned Sañjaya out of a desire to know about Suyodhana’s victory.
Sañjaya said:
"Then, having seen the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in battle array, Duryodhana—"
Having approached the Teacher, the king spoke these words.
Behold, O Teacher, this great army of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
arrayed by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
In this [army] are heroes, great archers equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle:
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior (mahāratha).
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, and the heroic King of Kāśī;
Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, the bull among men.
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas,
as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī— all of them indeed were great chariot-warriors (mahāratha).
But as for those among us who are distinguished, learn of them, O best of the twice-born;
I shall name them to you for the sake of your information, as they are the leaders of my army. (BhG 1.7)
Yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa, who is victorious in assembly,
Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, and likewise the son of Somadatta— BhG 1.8.
And there are many other heroes who have renounced their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and all are skilled in battle.
That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient;
but this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient.
And in all the divisions, stationed according to your respective positions,
let all of you indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.

Duryodhana, having personally observed the army of the Pāṇḍavas protected by Bhīma and his own army protected by Bhīṣma, informed the Teacher that his own force was sufficient for victory over them, while his own army was insufficient for achieving victory over theirs; having reported this, he became despondent within.
Generating joy for him, the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus,
let out a loud lion’s roar and blew his conch shell.
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded; that sound became tumultuous.
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses,
Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu blew their divine conch shells.
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. (BhG 1.15)
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, has the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva have the Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
And Kāśya, the supreme archer; Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki.
Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, O lord of the earth, all blew their conchs individually from every side.
Perceiving his despondency, Bhīṣma, in order to inspire joy in him, let out a lion’s roar and blew his conch shell;
with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, he caused a proclamation to be made foretelling victory.
Then, hearing that sound, the Lord of all lords, the son of Pāṇḍu who has Arjuna as his charioteer, stood upon a great chariot that served as the instrument for conquering the three worlds;
that tumultuous noise rent the hearts of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, making both heaven and earth resound. (BhG 1.19)
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in battle array and as the clash of weapons was about to begin, the Pāṇḍava whose banner bears the monkey raised his bow.
Then, O lord of the earth, Arjuna spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies. (BhG 1.21)
Making the three worlds tremble, they blew their two divine conchs, the glorious Pāñcajanya and Devadatta.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, Vṛkodara, and the others each blew their own conchs separately.
That roar shattered the hearts of all your sons, headed by Duryodhana;
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra thought, "The army of the Kurus has perished this very day."
Thus did Sañjaya speak to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was longing for victory.
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing ready for battle, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bore the monkey that burned Laṅkā, said:
"While I observe these who stand here desiring to fight, with whom must I contend in this exertion for war? (BhG 1.22)
I behold those who have assembled here,
wishing to do what is pleasing in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for combat.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa,
having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies...
In the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth, he said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here. (BhG 1.25)

There, Pārtha saw his fathers and grandfathers standing, as well as Hṛṣīkeśa—the storehouse of knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor; who sports with the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe by His own will; and who stands presiding over every mode of control of all the internal and external organs of all beings, high and low.
Overcome by affection for his dependents, he urged his own charioteer, who stood at his side: "Station the chariot in a place from which you can properly observe those who wish to fight."
Teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends as well. (BhG 1.26)
Having beheld all those kinsmen standing there— both fathers-in-law and friends from both armies— that son of Kuntī [was overcome].
Overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, Arjuna said this: "O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle... (BhG 1.28)
My limbs fail me and my mouth becomes parched;
a trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end. (BhG 1.29)
The Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand, and my skin is burning all over;
I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to be reeling. (BhG 1.30)
And I see adverse omens, O Keśava;
nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle. (BhG 1.31)
I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. What is the use of kingdom to us, O Govinda, or what use are enjoyments or even life itself? (BhG 1.32)
For whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
these very people stand here in battle, having renounced both their lives and their wealth.
Teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers; maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives. (BhG 1.34)
Urged by him, at that very moment, he did exactly as commanded while all the kings, including Bhīṣma and Droṇa, looked on;
and he said, "Such is the state of victory for those on your side."

But that high-minded Pārtha, who is supremely compassionate, long-standing kinsman, and most righteous, does not wish to kill these men— even though they are killing him— O Madhusūdana, even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, much less for the sake of the earth. (BhG 1.35)
O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
By killing these aggressors, we would only incur sin ourselves.
Therefore, O Mādhava, we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kinsmen; for how, having slain our own people, could we be happy? (BhG 1.37)
Even though these people, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil in the destruction of a family nor the sin in betraying friends.
O Janārdana, how can we not know how to turn away from this sin, as we clearly perceive the evil resulting from the destruction of our own kin? (BhG 1.39)
Upon the destruction of the family, the eternal family traditions perish;
when the dharma is lost, unrighteousness overcomes the entire family.
O Kṛṣṇa, through the overwhelming power of unrighteousness, the women of the family become corrupt;
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, the intermixture of castes arises.
The confusion caused by those destroyers of the family leads only to hell for both the family and the lineage;
indeed, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water.
By these faults of the destroyers of the family, which cause the intermixture of castes,
the eternal laws of the classes and the laws of the families are destroyed.
O Janārdana, we have heard from tradition that for those men whose family traditions are destroyed, residence in hell is inevitable. BhG 1.44.
Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen for the sake of obtaining the pleasures of sovereignty.
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle while I am unarmed and unresisting, that would be better for me.

"Even though I have been repeatedly deceived by you most terrible slayers through the burning of the house of lac and other such means, I shall kill [them] myself with the assistance of the Supreme Person.
Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down upon the seat of his chariot.
Casting aside his bow and arrow, his mind was agitated by grief.
Beholding your men, his entire body became exceedingly dejected out of affection for his kinsmen, supreme compassion, and fear of unrighteousness; saying,
"I will by no means fight," he— his mind agitated by the grief born of separation from his kin— cast aside his bow and arrow and sat down on the floor of his chariot.
Sañjaya said:
To him who was thus overcome by compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears, and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words. (BhG 2.1)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Arjuna, whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis? It is un-Aryan, it leads away from heaven, and it brings about infamy."
Do not yield to unmanliness, O son of Kuntī; this is not worthy of you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe! (BhG 2.3)

When Pārtha had thus sat down, the Blessed Lord said: "Having censured this grief— which has arisen in an improper place, which is resorted to by the ignorant, which is contrary to the world beyond, which brings infamy, which is exceedingly base, and which is born of weakness of heart— cast it aside and arise for battle."
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, O slayer of foes, how shall I fight with arrows in battle against Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who are both worthy of honor?
For it is better to live even on alms in this world than to slay these high-souled gurus;
by slaying my gurus, who are motivated by wealth and desire, I would enjoy only blood-stained pleasures in this very world.

Again, Pārtha, agitated by affection, compassion, and the fear of dharma and adharma, not understanding that which was spoken by the Blessed One as most beneficial, said this: "How, how indeed, could I slay my gurus—Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others—who are highly venerable;
and having slain them, enjoy those very same pleasures they enjoy, sitting upon their very seats and sprinkling them with their blood?
And we do not know which of these two is better for us: whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us."
Those very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having slain whom we do not wish to live, stand arrayed before us.
My nature being overwhelmed by the defect of dejection, and my mind confused about duty, I ask you:
tell me decisively what is better for me; I am your disciple, instruct me who have taken refuge in you. (BhG 2.7)
For I do not see what could dispel this grief of mine that withers the senses—not even the attainment of unrivaled, prosperous sovereignty on earth, nor even lordship over the gods. (BhG 2.8)
"If you should say, 'Once the battle has begun in this way, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra might forcibly slay you when you have ceased from your activity,' let it be so;

yet, compared to the unrighteous victory obtained by their slaughter, it seems to me that being slain by them—who are ignorant of dharma and adharma—is indeed better. Having said this, he declared what he had determined to be for his own highest good:
"Tell that to me, your disciple who has come for refuge," he said, and with extreme supplication, he approached the feet of the Blessed One.
Sañjaya said:
Having thus spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, "I will not fight," and became silent. (BhG 2.9)
"Thinking thus: 'Since he has fallen into an unnatural state due to misplaced affection and compassion,
and since he considers even the supreme duty of warriors— battle— to be unrighteous, and since he has come for refuge out of a desire to know his duty,

his delusion will not subside without knowledge of the true nature of the Self and without knowledge that battle, when performed without attachment to its fruits, is a means to attaining the Self,' [the Lord spoke]."
The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, has composed this introduction to the inner science (*adhyātmaśāstra*).
As it has been said: “Having in view Pārtha, who was agitated by misplaced affection, compassion, and the notions of dharma and adharma, he made this introduction to the scripture. (BhG 2.9)
O descendant of Bharata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling,
spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies.
Thus, [the world] is possessed by grief caused by ignorance regarding the true nature of the body and the self,
while simultaneously propounding dharma caused by knowledge of a self distinct from the body—
thereby being endowed with mutually contradictory qualities.

Seeing Pārtha suddenly desist from his efforts in the midst of both armies prepared for battle, the Supreme Person, as if laughing and speaking words of jest, addressed him with a discourse concerning the true nature of the Self and the Supreme Self, and the means of attaining that— namely, Karma-yoga, Jñāna-yoga, and Bhakti-yoga— beginning with “Never was I not,” and ending with “I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.”
The meaning is that he spoke these words ending with this. // BhG 2.10 //
The Blessed Lord said:
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not grieve for the dead or for the living.
You grieve for those who are not to be grieved for,

and you utter such doctrines based on the ignorance of the true nature of the body and the self as, "Indeed, their ancestors fall [to a miserable state] because the rites of offering rice-balls and water have been omitted.
For those who possess knowledge of the true nature of the body and the self, there is no cause for grief whatsoever in this matter.
Those who know the true nature of the self as it really is do not grieve over bodies whose life-force has departed nor those whose life-force has not yet departed; therefore,
this contradiction is perceived in you.
The grief that "I shall kill these," and the discourse on dharma and adharma produced by the knowledge of a self distinct from the body—
therefore, you do not understand the true nature of the body.
And [He taught] the Self as eternal, distinct from that [body],
and the dharma consisting of battle and so forth as the means for attaining it;
and this battle, being devoid of attachment to fruits, is the means for attaining the true nature of the Self.
For the self does not have its existence dependent on birth,
nor does it have its destruction dependent on death,
because birth and death do not apply to it.
Therefore, that [Self] is not an occasion for grief.
The body, however, is insentient and its nature is transformation;
since its connection with birth and destruction is inherent, it too is not an occasion for grief—this is the intended meaning. (BhG 2.11)
First, listen to the true nature of the selves:
"Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men; nor indeed shall any of us ever cease to be hereafter. (BhG 2.12)
I am indeed the Lord of all; therefore, in the past, beginningless time prior to this present moment, I was not non-existent, but rather I existed.
And these individual souls (kṣetrajñas), who are subject to your control, were not non-existent; rather, they existed.
Both I and you—all of us—existed even in that subsequent infinite time.
Nor indeed shall we not exist; rather, we shall certainly exist.
Just as I am the Lord of All, the Supreme Self, and eternal—of this there is no doubt.
In the same way, sirs, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas), the selves (ātmanas), should also be considered as eternal.

Thus, it is understood that the Lord himself has stated that the difference between all individual selves and the Lord, as well as the mutual difference among the selves themselves, is ultimate (pāramārthika).
For one deluded by ignorance, at the time of the instruction on ultimate eternity for the sake of its cessation, [the words] "I," "you," "these," and "all" [are used].
Because of the designation "we" (*vayam*).

For in the doctrine that the distinction between selves is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), since the distinction between selves is not ultimately real (*atāttvika*), the mention of such a distinction at the time of teaching the truth would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, scripture also states that the distinction between selves spoken of by the Blessed One is natural (*svābhāvika*).
“Among the eternal, He is the eternal; among the conscious, He is the conscious; He is the One who ordains the desires of the many.
This means that among the many eternal and conscious beings, there is one who, being Himself eternal and conscious, ordains their desires.

However, according to the doctrine that perceives difference created by ignorance, [this occurs] through the direct realization of the true nature of the Supreme Person as the non-differentiated, immutably established, and eternally conscious Self, which is the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Since ignorance and its effects have ceased, the perception of difference caused by ignorance and the worldly activities based upon it—such as instruction and so forth—would no longer be possible.

If it is argued that this knowledge of difference is merely a persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*) for the Supreme Person who has realized non-duality, and thus, like a burnt cloth, does not cause bondage, this is not tenable; for even if the cognition of water in a mirage persists after being sublated, it is not a cause for activity such as fetching water.

In this case as well, although the cognition of difference—which has been sublated by the knowledge of non-duality—persists, it does not become a cause for engaging in instruction and so forth, because it is certain that its object is false.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the Lord, who was previously ignorant, possesses a persistence of sublated cognition due to having attained knowledge of reality through the scriptures;
for [the scripture says], "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

This is because it would contradict both Śruti and Smṛti, as in: “His power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, which is innate,” and “I know the beings that have passed away and those that are present, O Arjuna, and those yet to come; but no one knows Me.”

Furthermore, it must be explained why the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa) and the current lineage of gurus would impart the knowledge of the non-dual Self to anyone, even while the cognition of difference continues to persist, once the ascertainment of the non-dual nature of the Self has been attained.
If it is argued that [the world] arises from Arjuna and others who are perceived as being like reflections, this is not tenable;
for no one who is not insane, perceiving their own reflection in a jewel, sword, mirror, or the like,
would know those reflections to be non-different from themselves.
He teaches them something [of the truth];
yet even the persistence of what has been sublated cannot be asserted by them,
because the cause of the cognition of duality distinct from the Self— the beginningless [ignorance]— has been destroyed by the sublating knowledge of the non-dual Self.

In cases such as the cognition of two moons, however, because the ultimate defect of timira (ocular disorder) and so forth—which is the cause of the cognition of two moons—is not destroyed by the cognition of the oneness of the moon, the persistence of the sublated [cognition] is logical;
yet even though it persists, it is ineffective because it has been sublated by a stronger means of valid cognition.

In this case, however, since the cognition of difference along with its object and its cause is unreal, it is destroyed by the cognition of the true nature of reality; therefore, the persistence of the sublated is not possible in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, if the Lord of All and the contemporary lineage of gurus possess knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), then the perception of difference and the teaching of its effects and so forth would be impossible.
If they do not possess it, then because ignorance— which is the cause of that [perception]— remains, teaching is all the more impossible precisely due to their state of being ignorant.

Furthermore, since the ignorance of Brahman along with its effects has been destroyed by the teacher’s very knowledge of the non-dual Self, instruction directed toward the disciple would be purposeless.

If it is argued that the teacher and his knowledge are merely imagined (kalpita), then because the disciple and his knowledge are likewise imagined, that [instruction] too cannot bring about cessation.

If it is argued that even though [the teacher's knowledge] is imagined (kalpita), it is a remover because it contradicts what preceded it, then that is equally true for the knowledge of the Teacher (Ācārya) as well; thus, he alone would be the remover, and the instruction [of others] would be entirely useless. Enough with these improper arguments! // BhGR_2.12 //
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.

Just as an embodied being residing in a single body does not grieve, thinking "the self has perished," when it leaves the state of childhood and attains the states of youth and so forth—due to the conviction that the self is stable—even so, when there is the transition from one body to another, the wise person does not grieve, knowing that the self remains stable.
Therefore, because the selves are eternal, the self is not an object of grief. (BhG 2.13)

This much is to be done here: for those eternal selves who, due to being subject to beginningless karma, have become joined with various bodies appropriate to their respective actions, in order to bring about the cessation of bondage through those very bodies, they perform scriptural actions such as battle—conducive to their own caste and devoid of desire for fruits.
For them, the contacts of the senses with sense-objects, which produce pleasure and pain occasioned by cold, heat, and so forth, occur as unavoidable occurrences.
"But those [senses] must be endured until the completion of the scriptural duties.
He states this very point immediately thereafter:
"But the contacts with the senses, O son of Kuntī, which yield cold, heat, pleasure, and pain..."
They come and go and are impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, together with their substrata, are called *mātrās* because they are the effects of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*).
Through the ears and other senses, their contacts—such as cold, heat, softness, and roughness—become the givers of pleasure and pain.
The mention of "cold and heat" is intended as an illustration.
Endure them with fortitude until the completion of the yogic practices and other scriptural duties pertaining to battle;
for they are fit to be endured by the steadfast because they are subject to coming and going,
and they are impermanent.
The meaning is that when the karma which constitutes the cause of bondage has been destroyed, they do not exist even as things subject to coming and going.
To the question "For what purpose is that forbearance?", he says here:
"O bull among men, that steadfast man whom these [reactions] do not disturb, who is equal in pain and pleasure—he is fit for immortality. (BhG 2.15)

That man who is endowed with fortitude, who regards unavoidable suffering as pleasure, and who performs his own duty— such as battle and other actions appropriate to his caste— without regard for the fruits thereof because they are the means to immortality, is not pained by the mild or harsh touches, such as the falling of weapons, contained within those acts; he alone achieves immortality.
The meaning is that one such as you is not incapable of enduring suffering;
the meaning is that because the self is eternal, this much alone is to be done in this matter.

However, as for the statement that the eternity of the selves and the inherent perishability of bodies constitute the cause for grief— namely, "The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living"— he now begins to demonstrate its validity.
The unreal has no being, and the real never ceases to be;
the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by those who see reality.
The existence of the non-existent body is not found, nor is there non-existence of the existent Self.

Regarding both the body and the Self which are perceived, the seers of reality have seen the "end" (anta) according to their perception; since investigation culminates in a definitive conclusion, here the word "end" denotes that final determination.

The meaning is that the determination is observed that the very nature of the body, which is an insentient entity, is non-existence (asattva), whereas the very nature of the self, which is sentient, is existence (sattva);
for non-existence is indeed the essential character of destruction.
And existence has the nature of indestructibility,
as was stated by the Blessed One Parāśara: "Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of things anywhere or at any time that exists apart from consciousness."
“Thus, I have declared to you that true existence is knowledge; that which is other than it is unreal.
“The wise accept that the ultimate reality is indestructible, whereas that which is produced from perishable substances is perishable—of this there is no doubt.”

“But that which, even after the lapse of time, does not indeed undergo another designation arising from transformation and so forth—that is a real entity, O King; and what is that? To this [it is replied]:
“These bodies have an end,” and so forth.
For it is said, "But know that to be indestructible";
thus it is understood that this very [Self] is the cause for the designations of existence and non-existence.
However, since the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not the subject at hand here, this verse is not intended for that purpose.

For one who is deluded by ignorance regarding the true nature of the body and the self, it is precisely the discrimination between the two—their respective natures as perishable and imperishable—that must be taught in order to pacify that delusion.
That very point is what is introduced by the words, "the dead and the living."

And that very same point is established immediately thereafter by the statements, "But know that to be indestructible," and "These bodies have an end. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. (BhG 2.16)
Regarding how the indestructibility of the self is understood, he says here:
"But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable [self]. (BhG 2.17)
Know that this reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is indestructible;
by which conscious reality of the Self this entire insentient reality, distinct from it, is pervaded and encompassed.
Because the Self—which is incapable of destruction due to its being the all-pervading and unsurpassedly subtle—is the pervader, no entity whatsoever distinct from it can effect its destruction.
Because it is pervaded by that [destruction], due to its grossness;
for a destroyer, such as a weapon, water, fire, or wind, destroys by pervading the object to be destroyed and thereby loosening its constituent parts.
Even seals and the like destroy by generating wind through a forceful conjunction and, by means of that wind, bring about destruction.
Therefore, the reality of the self is indestructible.

But the very nature of bodies is perishability; thus he says: "These bodies are said to have an end, O Bharata, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight. (BhG 2.18)
"In this world, accumulation" (*diha upacaye*): these bodies, which consist of accumulation, are finite and have destruction as their inherent nature.
For objects such as jars, which are composed of accumulation, are seen to be finite.
For the eternal embodied soul, bodies in the form of an aggregate of elements exist for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma.
“Meritorious through merit,” and so forth—by such scriptural passages, [the body] is said to perish at the conclusion of its karma.
But the Self is imperishable; why?
Because it is immeasurable.
For the self is not apprehended as an object of cognition, but rather as the cognizer;
and so it will be stated later.
“Those who know that [reality] call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).

Nor is the self perceived as consisting of a manifold accumulation; for throughout every body, there is the perception in a single form—as the subject—that “I know this,” whether it be the body or something else.
Furthermore, unlike the body and so forth, no difference in form is perceived in the knower despite differences in location;
therefore, because it is of a single nature, because its essence is non-increasing, because it is the subject of cognition (*pramātṛ*), and because it is all-pervasive, the self (*ātman*) is eternal.
The body, however, is [non-eternal] because its essence is increasing.
Because it exists for the sake of embodied beings experiencing the fruits of their karma,
because it possesses manifold forms,
and because it is all-pervasive, it is subject to destruction.
Therefore, since the body is by nature perishable and the Self is eternal, neither constitutes a ground for grief.

Having endured with fortitude the unavoidable contacts with persons—such as the falling of weapons—whether occurring within yourself or from others, undertake the action called battle, which has no intended fruit, for the sake of attaining immortality;
for he who thinks this [Self] is a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain, [both lack knowledge].
Both of them do not understand this: that it neither kills nor is killed.
Regarding this Self whose nature has been thus described,
whoever considers it to be a slayer— that is, any cause of killing— or whoever considers it to be slain by any cause whatsoever;
Both of them do not understand;
for by the reasons already stated, because this [Self] is indeed eternal, "this" (the weapon) does not kill "this" (the Self), meaning that this [weapon] is not the cause of its destruction.
And for this very reason, this Self is not killed.
The verbal root *han* also has the self as its object and expresses the act of causing separation from the body;
this is evident in such [scriptural injunctions] as "One should not harm any living beings" and "A Brahmin is not to be killed."
The scriptures concern themselves with the means for bringing about the dissolution of the body in a manner not [ordinarily] prescribed.
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be again. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (BhG 2.20)

By the very reasons already stated, because the self is eternal and unchanging, it is said that birth, death, and all such states are merely attributes of the insentient body and do not exist [in the self].
In this regard, birth and death— which are experienced by everyone in all bodies as occurring in the present tense— never touch the self at any time.
The meaning is this: having existed, it will not cease to exist hereafter; having existed at the beginning of the kalpa, it will not fail to exist again at the end of the kalpa.
The point is that the birth at the start of the kalpa and the death at its end—perceived through scripture in certain bodies such as those of Prajāpati and others—do not touch the Self.
Therefore, the Self residing within all bodies is unborn;
for that very reason, it is eternal.
It is everlasting, not subject even to the subtle and continuous transformations characteristic of primordial nature (prakṛti).
"Old yet ever new" means that he is to be experienced as if always unprecedented;
therefore, when the body is slain, this Self is not slain.
O Pārtha, how can that person—who knows this Self to be imperishable, eternal, unborn, and undecaying—cause anyone to be slain, or slay anyone? (BhG 2.21)
Thus, the person who knows this Self to be eternal— by virtue of its indestructibility, its birthlessness, and its incapacity for decay—
how can that person cause any Self to be slain among the Selves abiding in the bodies of gods, humans, animals, and stationary beings?
Or how can he slay any [Self]?
The meaning is: how does he cause destruction, or how does he become the instigator of that?
The intention is that this lamentation—"I am destroying these, I am killing them"—is rooted solely in ignorance regarding the true nature of the self.

Even though for eternal selves only the separation from the body is effected, nevertheless, since bodies—which are the means for experiencing pleasant enjoyments—are perishing, there certainly exists a cause for grief consisting in the loss of them.
Thus: "Just as a person, having cast off worn-out clothes, takes up other new ones;
so the embodied self, having cast off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones. (BhG 2.22)

From the scriptures it is understood that for those who cast off their bodies in a righteous war, they assume a body of even greater auspiciousness than the one they have abandoned; therefore, just as those discarding worn-out garments take up new and beautiful ones, only a cause for joy is found here.

Furthermore, in order to facilitate easy comprehension, [the Lord] clarifies and reinforces the indestructibility previously stated in the words, "But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded":
"Swords do not cut it; fire does not burn it.
Water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (BhG 2.23)
This Self is neither cut, nor burnt, nor moistened, nor dried away;
it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
Weapons, fire, water, and wind are unable to perform cutting, burning, moistening, or drying upon the Self.

This is because the Self is all-pervading, having by its very nature the quality of permeating all principles (*tattva*); furthermore, because it is subtler than all principles, it cannot be reached by them, and because cutting, burning, moistening, and drying are actions that must be performed upon something that is pervaded.
Therefore, the Self is eternal, fixed, immovable, and ancient; it is of a stable nature, unshakable, and primordial.
This is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable;
therefore, knowing it to be so, you ought not to grieve.

This self is unmanifest (*avyakta*) because it is not manifested by those means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which objects suitable for cutting and so forth are manifested; therefore, it is of a different nature from things such as those subject to being cut.
And it is inconceivable, because, being of a nature distinct from all things and endowed with their respective individual essences, it is not even fit to be an object of thought;
and for this reason, it is unchangeable, meaning it is incapable of undergoing modification.
Therefore, having understood this Self characterized as described, you ought not to grieve on its account.
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, even if you consider this [self] to be constantly born or constantly dying, even so,
you ought not to grieve in this manner.
If you consider this very body— which is constantly born and constantly dying— to be the Self,
and not something distinct from the body as previously described,
even so, you ought not to grieve excessively in this manner.
Because the arising and destruction of the body, which is by nature subject to transformation, are unavoidable.
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore, you ought not to grieve over this inevitable matter.
The destruction of what has arisen is certain and observed to be unavoidable;
likewise, the birth of what has been destroyed is also unavoidable.
How, then, is this possible: that there is the arising of what has been destroyed?
Because that which exists is perceived arising, and that which does not exist is not perceived;
arising, destruction, and so forth are specific states of an existing substance.
For substances such as threads, when endowed with a particular arrangement, are indeed called cloth and so forth;
even by one who maintains the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavāda), only this much is perceived,
for no other substance is cognized there apart from the specific configuration of the threads.

Since the specific linguistic conventions regarding the adoption of different names for the operations of causal factors (kāraka) are sufficiently accounted for by this alone, it is not reasonable to postulate a separate substance.
Therefore, arising, destruction, and so forth are merely particular states of an existing substance.
When a substance has reached the state designated as "arising," its transition to another state that is incompatible with the former is called "destruction."

Just as clay substance undergoes a succession of transformations such as being a lump, a jar, potsherds, or powder, it is inevitable that a transforming substance (*pariṇāmidravya*) undergo a series of transformations.
In this process, the attainment of a subsequent state by a substance in its prior state is its destruction; that very same [attainment] is the arising of the substance in that [subsequent] state.
Thus, this succession of transformations known as arising and destruction is unavoidable for a substance that is subject to change; therefore, you ought not to grieve over it.

Since even that slight sorrow which arises from observing the transition of an existing substance from one state to another state that contradicts its previous condition does not occur among beings such as humans, he says:
"O Bhārata, beings have an unmanifest beginning and a manifest middle."
Their dissolution is indeed unmanifest; what cause for lamentation is there in that?

Beings such as humans certainly exist as substances that have not previously been perceived in their prior state, are perceived in their intermediate state as humans and so forth, and will not be perceived in their subsequent state; they simply abide in their own respective natures. Therefore, there is no ground for lamentation in this regard. (BhGR 2.28)

Having thus stated that there is no cause for grief even in the doctrine that the body is the self, [the Lord] says that one who perceives the Self—which is distinct from the body and of a wondrous nature—as the seer, the speaker, and as that which attains certainty regarding the Self through hearing, is rare:
"Someone beholds this as a wonder; likewise, another speaks of it as a wonder;
and yet another hears of it as a wonder; and even having heard it, no one at all truly knows it" (BhG 2.29).

Thus, its nature being described as such, it exists in a wondrous manner, being of a different genus from all other things whatsoever; some person among infinite beings— whose sins have been exhausted by great austerity and whose merit has been accumulated— perceives it, while another such as that speaks of it to others,
and likewise, only someone else hears it.
Even having heard this as it truly exists, no one knows it according to reality;

by the use of the word "also" (ca), it is implied that even among the seer, the speaker, and the hearer, seeing according to reality, speaking according to reality, and hearing according to reality are difficult to attain.
This embodied self in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible, O Bharata;
therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings.
Even when the body of every embodied being, beginning with the gods, is being slain, this indwelling Self (dehin) must be understood as eternally indestructible.
Therefore, all beings—from the gods down to the stationary objects—though they possess diverse forms, are equal in their essential nature and eternal according to the aforementioned intrinsic nature;
it is only the diversity and impermanence residing in the body that exist.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve for all beings, beginning with the gods;
it is not only for Bhīṣma and the others that you should do so.
Moreover, having regard for your own duty, you ought not to waver;
for there exists nothing better for a Kṣatriya than a righteous war.

Moreover, even though this commenced war involves the killing of living beings, you ought not to waver when considering it as your own duty (svadharma), like the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others. Indeed, for a Kṣatriya, there exists no greater good than righteous war conducted according to justice.
"Valour, majesty, fortitude, skill, and not fleeing in battle—"
Generosity and lordship are the duties of a kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
For it will indeed be stated thus:
"In the Agniṣomīya and other sacrifices, there is no killing of the animal,
because [the animal] first casts off its inferior body, such as that of a goat."

For it is heard in scripture that the ritual of immolation (*saṃjñapana*) leads to the attainment of a more excellent body, heaven, and so forth; indeed, it is declared: "Verily, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm; you go to the gods by auspicious paths, where the doers of good deeds go, and not the doers of evil—there may the god Savitṛ place you."
Moreover, in this context, it has been stated that those who die in battle attain a more auspicious body,
as in the passage beginning, "Just as one casts off worn-out clothes and takes up new ones. Therefore, [this act] is like the work of a physician or a surgeon for the sake of a patient.
In the Agniṣomīya and other sacrifices, the very act of protecting this [vital essence] is what constitutes the ritual slaughter.
O Pārtha, happy are the Kṣatriyas who, by chance, obtain such a battle as this— an open door to heaven.
Fortunate and meritorious Kṣatriyas obtain such a battle—effortlessly attained, serving as a means to unsurpassed happiness, and free from obstacles. (BhG 2.32)
But if you will not engage in this righteous battle,
then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you will incur sin.

Now, if you do not engage in this commenced battle, which is the very nature of a Kṣatriya’s duty, out of delusion, then by failing to perform the duty you have undertaken, you will abandon the fruit of your own duty—supreme happiness—and the unsurpassed fame resulting from victory, and instead incur supreme sin. (BhG 2.33)
And beings will also speak of your undying infamy;
for one who has been highly esteemed, infamy is worse than death. (BhG 2.34)
It is not merely that you will suffer the loss of your unsurpassed happiness and fame;
rather, all beings—whether capable or incapable—will proclaim your imperishable infamy, pervading all places and times, saying, "Pārtha fled when the battle had begun.
If you ask what follows from this, it is that for one who is esteemed by all for his heroism, vigor, prowess, and so forth, infamy born of such a reversal exceeds even death itself.
The meaning is that for one who has incurred such infamy, death alone is better for you.
Regarding the thought, "How will infamy come upon me, a hero who has desisted from battle out of affection for kinsmen and compassion? he says here:
"The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the fight out of fear; and having been highly esteemed by them, you will incur their contempt. (BhG 2.35)
Those great chariot-warriors such as Karṇa, Duryodhana, and others, for whom you were previously esteemed as a heroic enemy,
will now, when battle has arrived, perceive you as being easily grasped due to your lack of activity; those great chariot-warriors will consider you to have desisted from the fight out of fear.
For among heroes, cessation from battle—except out of fear of an enemy—is not possible unless it arises from affection for kinsmen or similar reasons.
Moreover, your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, censuring your prowess; what indeed could be more painful than that? (BhG 2.36)
"In our presence, how could this son of Pṛthā endure even for a moment?
For his capability exists only elsewhere, away from us. Thus, your enemies, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, will disparage your prowess and utter many unspeakable insults against you, the heroes.
What grief could be greater than that for you?
Upon hearing such unspeakable things, you yourself will surely think that death alone is better. (BhG 2.36)
Therefore, he says that for a hero, both the slaying of others by oneself or being slain by others oneself leads to the highest good:
"Either slain you shall attain heaven, or victorious you shall enjoy the earth."
Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle.
If you are slain by others in a righteous war, you will attain supreme beatitude from that very act; or, having slain your enemies, you shall enjoy a kingdom free from thorns.
Since the dharma known as battle, which does not have its fruit preordained, is a means to the supreme good (*paramaniḥśreyasa*), you shall attain that supreme good;
therefore, having resolved that exertion for battle is the means to liberation characterized by the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), rise up for that purpose.
The intention is that this alone is appropriate for you, the son of Kuntī. (BhG 2.37)
He describes the manner of engaging in battle for one who desires liberation:
"Having made pleasure and pain equal, as well as gain and loss, victory and defeat, then engage in battle; thus you shall not incur sin. (BhG 2.38)

Thus, having known the Self to be distinct from the body, eternal, and untouched by the nature of all bodies, engage in battle with an unchanging intellect amidst the unavoidable experiences of pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat caused by the falling of weapons and other such factors—free from desire for fruits such as heaven, and motivated solely by the sense that this is one's duty.
By acting in this way, you will not incur sin; you will not attain the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which is of the nature of suffering.
The meaning is that you will be liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra.
Having thus taught the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, He begins to describe the yoga of action (karmayoga), which is the means to liberation preceded by that knowledge:
"This wisdom has been declared to you according to Sāṅkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, endowed with which you shall cast off the bondage of action. (BhG 2.39)
*Sāṅkhya* is the intellect (*buddhi*);
*Sāṅkhya* is the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*) which is to be determined by that intellect.

Regarding the true nature of the self that is to be known, the intellect intended for its knowledge is the subject matter [of this work], beginning with the words "But indeed, I am not... and ending with "...therefore, you ought not to grieve for any beings. This very [intellect] is [the subject].
They were addressed as follows:

"The application of the intellect (buddhi-yoga) that must be taught regarding the performance of rituals— which serve as the means to liberation preceded by self-knowledge— is what is expressed here by the word 'yoga'."
"For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom"— this will indeed be stated later.
In that regard, listen to this wisdom concerning yoga which is now being declared.
"Endowed with that intellect by which you shall cast off the bondage of action—
the 'bondage of action' (karmabandha) meaning the bondage of saṃsāra through action. (BhG 2.39)
He speaks of the greatness of action when it is endowed with the wisdom about to be described:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a very small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear. (BhG 2.40)
In this yoga of action, there is no loss of the forward step;
"forward step" means the undertaking,
and "loss" means the destruction of the efficacy of the means toward the fruit.
There is no fruitlessness even for that which has been commenced but not completed, or even interrupted.
When there is an interruption of what has been commenced, no transgression occurs either.
Even a very small portion of this dharma called *karmayoga* protects one from great fear—that is, from the fear of *saṃsāra*.
This is the meaning:
"O Pārtha, neither here nor in the hereafter does destruction exist for him"—this will be elaborated upon later.
For other means, whether worldly or Vedic, when interrupted, do not lead to their fruit.
And they lead to transgression. // BhGR 2.40 //
He distinguishes the intellect whose object is action performed for the sake of desire from the intellect whose object is action that serves as a means to liberation:
"In this world, O joy of the Kurus, the resolute intellect is one;
for the intellects of those lacking resolve are many-branched and indeed infinite. (BhG 2.41)
In all this scriptural action, there is but one resolute intellect (*vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ*).
The intellect directed toward the action to be performed by one seeking liberation is the resolute intellect;
"resoluteness" (*vyavasāya*) means certainty.
For that intellect is preceded by the ascertainment of the true nature of the Self;
however, the intellect whose object is action performed for the sake of desire is of the nature of non-resolution.
For in that context of the qualification for desire, only the knowledge of the existence of a Self distinct from the body is required.

There is no determination of the true nature of the self's own essence; for even in the absence of such a determination, the desire for fruits such as heaven, the performance of the means thereto, and the experience of those fruits are possible, and there is no contradiction [between this and the pursuit of liberation].
This resolute intellect is "single" because it has as its object the means to a single result;
for all actions are prescribed for one who desires liberation solely for the sake of that one result called liberation.
Therefore, since the purpose of the scripture is one, the intellect regarding all actions is indeed one.

The meaning is as follows: just as the six rites beginning with the Āgneya sacrifice—which possess their respective procedures (itikartavyatā)—constitute a single scriptural purpose by virtue of achieving a single result, and thus the cognition regarding them is one;

in the same way, the cognitions of those lacking resolve—who are entitled to perform actions that achieve results such as heaven, sons, cattle, and food—are infinite because of the infinity of those results.
In that regard as well, there are many branches;
for even though a ritual such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa is enjoined for a single result,
it possesses a multiplicity of branches due to the distinction between intermediate results understood from [mantras] such as "May you obtain long life."
Therefore, the intellects of those lacking resolve are infinite and many-branched.

What is meant by this is as follows: having abandoned all principal and intermediate fruits that are heard of in connection with obligatory and occasional rites, one should perform all actions with liberation as the sole fruit, treating them as the single purpose of the scripture.

And those actions performed out of desire that are appropriate for one's own caste and stage of life should be practiced according to one's capacity, having abandoned their respective fruits and unified with the obligatory and occasional rites as means to liberation. // BhG 2.41 //

Now, he censures those who are entitled to perform rites for specific desires: "O Pārtha, those unwise ones who delight in the talk of the Vedas and assert that there is nothing else, utter this flowery speech. (BhG 2.42)

Those whose nature is desire and who look toward heaven follow that [Vedic teaching] which yields birth as the fruit of action, abounds in various ritual performances, and leads toward the attainment of enjoyment and power. (BhG 2.43)
For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [desire],
the intellect characterized by resolute determination is not established in meditative concentration.

That speech which the unwise— those of little knowledge who are devoted to the ritualistic declarations of the Vedas and attached to those Vedic doctrines that proclaim fruits such as heaven— proclaim, being intent upon the attainment of enjoyments and power, is like a flowering tree that bears fruit only in appearance and is delightful only at first sight.

Those who maintain that there is nothing else—asserting that apart from the attainment of those [pleasures], there is no further fruit such as heaven; whose souls are possessed by desire, meaning their minds are inclined toward desire; and who are intent on heaven, meaning they have heaven as their ultimate goal.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: those who utter this flowery speech—which, at the conclusion of fruits such as heaven, yields the fruit known as rebirth and karma; which abounds in specific ritual actions, being rich in particular rites due to its lack of knowledge of reality; and which leads toward the attainment of enjoyments and power.

For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose knowledge has been stolen away by that speech concerning enjoyments and power, the intellect characterized by the aforementioned resolve is not established— that is, it does not arise— in the mind fixed in meditative concentration.
The mind (*manas*) is called *samādhi* because self-knowledge is concentrated (*samādhīyate*) therein.
The meaning is that in their minds, no cognition ever arises regarding actions—which are the means to liberation—preceded by the ascertainment of the true nature of the Self.
Therefore, one who desires liberation must not form an attachment to actions performed for the sake of desired fruits.
Why do the Vedas—which produce rebirths yielding such meager fruits and which are engaged in sustaining one's own life out of a greater affection than even thousands of parents—declare these things?
Or how can that which is proclaimed by the Vedas be said to be renounced? To this, He says:
"The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna."
Free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the desire for acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self.

The three qualities (*guṇa*) are the triad (*traiguṇya*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Persons who abound in *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are designated by the term "triadic" (*traiguṇya*). The Vedas have them as their object; indeed, out of a desire for their welfare, the Vedas instruct those abounding in *tamas*, those abounding in *rajas*, and those abounding in *sattva* on what is beneficial.

If these [beings] do not understand that their own welfare consists precisely in the means for attaining heaven and so forth, which correspond to their own respective qualities, then— being dominated by *rajas* and *tamas*, turned away from liberation which is the fruit of *sattva*, and failing to know the means for attaining the fruits they themselves desire— they will, being helpless under the sway of passion, enter into what is unworthy of pursuit through the delusion of taking it to be worthy, and thus go to ruin.
Therefore, the Vedas have the three qualities (guṇas) as their domain;

you, however, become free from the three qualities now. You are currently abounding in sattva, so increase that very quality; do not become one who abounds in the three qualities mutually intermingled.
The meaning is that one should not increase the abundance of those [qualities].

"Free from dualities" (*nirdvandva*) means having emerged from all the worldly nature. "Ever established in purity" (*nityasattvastha*) means be ever established in a state of purity that is free from the other two qualities and constantly increasing.
If it is asked how, [the answer is]:

being free from acquisition and preservation (*niryogakṣema*), abandon the acquisition (*yoga*) of objects external to the nature of the Self and the means for attaining it, as well as the preservation (*kṣema*) of those already attained; become possessed of the Self (*ātmavān*), intent upon the investigation of the nature of the Self.
Acquisition (*yoga*) is the attainment of what has not been attained; preservation (*kṣema*) is the guarding of what has been attained.
For you who conduct yourself in this way, the abundance of rajas and tamas will perish,
and sattva will increase.
Whatever purpose there may be in a small reservoir when there is water overflowing everywhere,
just so much purpose is there in all the Vedas for a Brahmin who possesses true knowledge.
Nor is everything proclaimed in the Veda to be accepted by everyone;

just as when there is a well overflowing with water on all sides for one who has imagined every possible need, a thirsty person takes from it only as much as is useful— that is, only as much as serves his purpose.

Not everything; thus, among all the Vedas, for a learned Brāhmaṇa who is a seeker of liberation according to the Veda, only that which is the means to liberation is to be adopted, and nothing else. BhG 2.46.
Therefore, for one established in goodness who seeks liberation, only this much is to be adopted; thus He says:
"Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits.
Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. (BhG 2.47)

Regarding actions that are heard in scripture as being connected to some specific fruit— whether they be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)— the seeker of liberation who is established in eternal *sattva* has authority only over the action itself.
He never has authority over the fruits understood to be connected to it,
because a fruit accompanied by [desire] is of the nature of bondage, whereas the fruitless, solitary [action] consisting of my worship is the cause of liberation.
And do not become the cause of [attachment to] action and its fruit;
even while performing action, you who are established in constant sattva and seek liberation must also maintain the realization of your own non-agency.
It should also be reflected upon that you are not the cause even of the fruit, such as the cessation of hunger;
whether both of these [the action and its result] are to be attributed to the qualities (guṇas), or to Me, the Lord of all, will be explained later.
Having reflected thus, perform your work.
Regarding inaction— that is, non-performance—
let there be no attachment on your part to what you have declared, namely, "I will not fight."
The meaning is that, in the manner described, let there be attachment only to actions such as battle.
He clarifies this very point:
"Established in yoga, O Dhanañjaya, perform actions, having abandoned attachment;
becoming the same in success and failure—this equanimity is called yoga. (BhG 2.48)

Having abandoned attachment to kingdom, kinsmen, and the like, perform actions such as battle while established in yoga; perform them having become equanimous toward success or failure, such as victory, which are inherent within those actions.
This very equanimity regarding success and failure is what is expressed by the word "yoga" in the phrase "established in yoga."
Yoga is the concentration of the mind characterized by equanimity toward both success and failure.
To the question, "For what purpose is this stated repeatedly?", he says:
"For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in wisdom; those motivated by fruits are pitiable. (BhG 2.49)

This yoga of the intellect— which has as its object the renunciation of the primary fruit and which has as its object equanimity toward the attainment or non-attainment of intermediate results— is vastly superior to other action performed apart from it.
This discrepancy between the two, consisting of excellence and deficiency, is great.
Action performed while endowed with the aforementioned yoga of wisdom dispels all the miseries of worldly existence and leads to liberation, which is characterized as the supreme goal of man;
other action, however, results in the cycle of birth and death consisting of immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, while performing action, seek refuge in the aforementioned wisdom.
"Refuge" means a place of dwelling;
the meaning is: "Abide in that very intellect.
Those who are wretched—performing actions out of attachment to results and the like—are wretched transmigrators. // BhG 2.49 //
One endowed with wisdom casts off both good and evil deeds in this very world;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in actions. (BhG 2.50)
But one who performs action joined with the yoga of the intellect abandons both good and evil deeds—accumulated since beginningless time, infinite, and serving as the cause of bondage.
Therefore, apply yourself to the aforementioned yoga of the intellect.
Yoga is skill in actions; this yoga of the intellect is skill, that is, supreme proficiency, while actions are being performed.
The meaning is that it is to be accomplished through extreme effort.
For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action,
are liberated from the bondage of birth and go to the state that is free from all suffering.

Those who, joined with the yoga of discernment, perform action having renounced the fruit born of action, thereby become completely liberated from the bondage of birth and go to the state free from suffering; for this is well-known throughout all the Upanishads—this is the meaning.
When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion,
then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.

When, by acting in the manner described through that practice, your impurity has been shaken off, then your intellect will itself attain—will reach—a state of detachment (*nirveda*) regarding both what was previously heard from us as something to be abandoned, such as the fruits [of action], and what is yet to be heard hereafter. This "muddied state" (*kalila*) of delusion is of the nature of delusion itself, caused by attachment to extremely meager results. At that time, you will go to a state of world-weariness.

He now describes the fruit called Yoga, which is the defining characteristic of the practice of dharma that is preceded by knowledge of the true nature of the Self and refined by a particular state of the intellect, as taught in the passage beginning with "But listen to this regarding yoga":
"When your intellect, confused by the scriptures, shall stand unshakable and immovable in meditative concentration (samādhi), then you will attain Yoga. (BhG 2.53)
"Śruti" means hearing.

When, through hearing from us, there arises a cognition specifically directed toward the Self—which is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things, eternal, unsurpassed, subtle, and real—and which is itself unwavering and uniform; when that cognition shall stand immovable in the mind purified by the performance of unattached action; [then...]
Then you will attain yoga, which is the self-realization.

This is what is meant: the yoga of action (karmayoga), preceded by the knowledge of the Self produced from the scriptures, brings about the culmination in knowledge known as the state of one whose wisdom is steady;
it takes the form of the culmination in knowledge.
But the state of one whose wisdom is established accomplishes the self-contemplation known as yoga. // BhGR 2.53 //

Having been told this— the nature of the state of one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajñatā), which is to be accomplished through the yoga of action consisting in the performance of disinterested action, and which serves as the means for yoga—
Arjuna asks about the manner in which one of steady wisdom performs his practice: Arjuna said:
What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, O Keśava, when he is established in samādhi? What does the man of steady intellect speak, how does he sit, and how does he move? (BhG 2.54)
What is the description of one who is established in samādhi, whose wisdom is steady?
That is to say, what is his defining characteristic?
And what does the one of steady wisdom do, such as speak and so forth? // BhG 2.54 //
Since the essential nature [of the Self] is also expressed by describing its specific mode of functioning, that specific mode of functioning is now stated;
the Blessed Lord said:
"O Pārtha, when one abandons all desires dwelling in the mind..."
But when one is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is said to be of steady wisdom.

When one is content with the Self alone, by means of the Self through the mind, relying solely upon the Self, and by virtue of that contentment thoroughly abandons all desires of the mind other than that [Self],
then he is called "one whose wisdom is steady.
This is the pinnacle of steadfastness in knowledge.
Immediately following that, the state of one established in knowledge, which is neither far removed nor close to the preceding stage, is described:
"One whose mind is unperturbed amidst sorrows, who is free from longing amidst pleasures, and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed—he is called a sage of steady wisdom. (BhG 2.56)
When causes of suffering such as separation from loved ones arise, one whose mind is undisturbed does not become sorrowful;
being free from longing for pleasures, one remains free from longing even when beloved objects are present;
and being devoid of passion, fear, and anger—wherein passion is longing for things yet to come—[one is established in equanimity].
He is free from that;
he is free from suffering and fear caused by the sight of reasons for separation from the beloved or the arrival of the unpleasant.
Anger is a modification of one’s own mind caused by suffering residing within another conscious being, which arises from the cause of separation from the beloved or the arrival of the unpleasant;
one who is free from that, such a sage (muni) whose nature is self-contemplation is called "steadfast in wisdom" (sthitadhīḥ). // BhG 2.56 //
The state prior to that is now described:
he who has no attachment anywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering various things, whether auspicious or inauspicious—his wisdom is firmly established. (BhG 2.57)

He who is everywhere without attachment to dear things and remains indifferent; who, having encountered the auspicious or inauspicious—consisting of union with or separation from the beloved—is free from both rejoicing and aversion; he too is one whose wisdom is established.
Then he describes the state prior to that:
"When one withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established. (BhG 2.58)
When the senses are intent on contacting their respective objects, he withdraws them from those objects in every way— just as a tortoise draws in its limbs— and establishes the mind within the Self.
He too is one whose wisdom is established.
Thus, there are four stages of perfection in knowledge,
each preceding one being brought to completion by the succeeding one.
Now, he speaks of the difficulty of attaining steadfastness in knowledge and the means for its attainment:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food, with the exception of taste;
but even that taste turns away from him upon seeing the Supreme. (BhG 2.59)
The objects of the senses are their nourishment;

for the embodied being who abstains from food—whose senses have been withdrawn from objects—the objects, upon turning away, turn back with the exception of taste (*rasa*); "taste" here means attachment (*rāga*).
The meaning is that attachment to sense objects does not cease.
Even attachment ceases once one has perceived the nature of the Self as being far more blissful than sense objects.
For even of a wise man who strives, O son of Kuntī,
the turbulent senses violently carry away the mind.
Without the vision of the Self, attachment to sense objects does not cease;
and as long as attachment to sense objects has not ceased, the turbulent and powerful senses forcibly carry away the mind of even a wise man who is striving.
Thus, mastery over the senses depends upon the vision of the Self, and the vision of the Self depends upon mastery over the senses; therefore, steadfastness in knowledge is difficult to attain.
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent on Me;
for his wisdom is firmly established whose senses are under control.

Desiring to abandon all this, one should restrain the senses—which are difficult to conquer due to their attachment to sense objects—and, having fixed the mind upon Me, who am the auspicious refuge of the heart, remain composed in meditation.
When the mind is directed toward Me, it becomes purified by the burning away of all impurities; thus, freed from attachment to sense objects, the mind brings the senses under its own control.
Then, the mind with its senses subdued becomes capable of perceiving the Self.
As it has been said: "Just as a fire with rising flames burns dry wood when fanned by the wind, so Viṣṇu, established in the mind, burns away all the impurities of yogis."
Thus it is said:
"For he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established" (BhG 2.61).

Thus, one who proceeds toward the conquest of the senses through the pride of his own effort without having fixed the mind upon Me perishes; so it is said: "For a person dwelling on sense-objects, attachment to them arises. From attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger is produced. (BhG 2.62)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory, the destruction of intelligence; and from the destruction of intelligence, one perishes.

For one whose attachment to sense objects has not been cast off, even if the mind is not fixed upon Me and he remains with his senses restrained, meditation on sense objects will be unavoidable due to the beginningless latent impressions of evil.
As a person meditates on sense objects, attachment arises once again, greatly intensified;
from attachment, desire is born.
Desire (kāma) is the state of fruition of attachment;
it is that state which, having reached it, a person is unable to remain without experiencing sense objects—that is desire.
From desire, anger is born;
when desire is present,
yet the object is not at hand.
Toward those persons present before him,
the thought arises, "They have performed what we desired"; from that anger,
delusion (saṃmoha) arises.
Delusion is the state of being devoid of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
by means of it, one performs everything [inappropriately].
Consequently, there occurs a lapse of mindfulness regarding the effort already undertaken, such as the conquest of the senses.
From the loss of mindfulness comes the destruction of the intellect; that resolve which was made toward self-knowledge would be destroyed.
From the destruction of the intellect, one becomes submerged once again in saṃsāra and is ruined. (BhG 2.62–63)
But one who moves among sense objects with the senses free from attachment and aversion, self-controlled and having a disciplined mind, attains serenity.

Having fixed the mind on Me, the Lord of all, who am the auspicious object of refuge in the manner described, one whose every impurity has been burnt away moves among sense objects with senses that are free from attachment and aversion and brought under self-control—meaning, acting while disregarding sense objects; such a person, being self-governed and having a disciplined mind, attains serenity, which means he becomes pure in his inner heart. // BhG 2.64 //
In serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises for him;
for the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established.
When this person’s mind attains serenity, the abandonment of all sufferings caused by contact with material nature occurs.

For one whose consciousness is serene and whose mind is free from defects that obstruct the perception of the Self, the intellect immediately becomes established in the subject of the isolated Self. Therefore, when there is serenity of mind, the abandonment of all sufferings necessarily follows. 65.
For one who is not disciplined, there is no discernment; for one who is not disciplined, there is no meditative cultivation.
For one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; for one who lacks peace, how can there be happiness? (BhG 2.66)
For one who has surrendered the mind to Me but proceeds to restrain the senses by his own effort alone, the intellect directed toward the isolated Self will never succeed;
for that very reason, the contemplation of it is impossible for him.
For one who does not contemplate the isolated Self, the cessation of longing for sense objects does not occur.
For one who is not tranquil and is possessed by longing for sense objects, how can there be the attainment of eternal, unsurpassed happiness?
Furthermore, he describes the misfortune that befalls one who does not exercise restraint over the senses in the manner previously stated: "For when the mind follows after the wandering senses,
it carries away one's wisdom, just as the wind sweeps away a boat upon the waters" (BhG 2.67).

When the mind is directed toward and follows the movement of the senses as they range over their objects, that mind carries away a person’s wisdom— which is otherwise inclined toward the solitary Self— and makes it inclined toward sense-objects;
just as a contrary wind forcibly carries away a boat being steered upon the water.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him whose senses are completely withdrawn from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established.
Therefore, for one whose mind is established in Me as the auspicious refuge in the manner described, and whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses,
it is that very person’s wisdom that becomes firmly established in the Self.
Thus, for one whose senses are restrained and whose mind is serene, he declares the attainment of perfection:
