"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (BhG 2.69)
That cognition which has the Self as its object is night, as it were, for all beings, being unilluminated like night;
in that cognition whose object is the Self, one who has restrained the senses remains awake with a serene mind, meaning he stays observing the Self.
In that cognition which has sound and other sense-objects as its objects, all beings are awake, meaning they are fully conscious.
That cognition whose objects are sound and so forth becomes as if night—unmanifest—to the sage who perceives the Self.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires. (BhG 2.70)

Just as the waters of rivers enter the ocean— which is of a single form and being filled by its own nature— and yet the ocean undergoes no change whatsoever whether those waters enter it or not; even so, he who is self-restrained, into whom all desires— the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest— enter, attains peace.

The meaning is that he who does not undergo any modification— whether sounds and other objects have entered the range of the senses or not— by means of the very satisfaction of beholding his own Self, he alone attains peace;
not one who desires objects of desire.
He who is transformed by sound and the other sense objects never attains peace.
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing,
without the sense of "mine," and without egoism, attains peace.
They are called "desires" (kāmāḥ) because they are desired; these are sound and the other sense objects.
That person who, having abandoned all objects such as sound, is free from longing for them and devoid of the sense of "mine" regarding them—
He moves about free from the conceit of self in the body, which is not the self;
having seen the Self, he attains peace.
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, one is no longer deluded.
Established even at the time of death in this state, one attains the liberation of Brahman.
This steadfastness in unattached action, preceded by the knowledge of the eternal Self, is characterized by a steady intellect and is *brāhmī*—that which leads to Brahman.
Having attained such a state in action, one is no longer deluded and does not undergo rebirth in *saṃsāra*.
Abiding in this state even in the final stage of life, one attains *brahmanirvāṇa*; that is, one goes to Brahman, which consists of liberation.
The meaning is that he attains a self that is solely intent upon bliss.

Thus, for one who does not know the true nature of the self (*ātman*) and that action known as battle is the means for attaining it—being deluded by the notion that the body is the self—and who has consequently desisted from battle due to that delusion, the *Sāṅkhya* intellect concerning the eternal self was taught in the second chapter as a means for the pacification of delusion. Furthermore, the intellect concerning the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), which consists in the performance of disinterested action and is preceded by that [Sāṅkhya] intellect, which serves as the means for the yoga of one whose wisdom is steady (*sthitaprajña*), was also taught there. As it has been said:

“The wisdom of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, whose sphere of activity is action performed with detachment from the eternal Self, is declared in the second chapter as the characteristic of one whose intellect is steady, for the sake of pacifying that delusion. (BhG 2.72)

Thus, in order to describe that exclusive and absolute devotion—which is denoted by such terms as "knowledge," "meditation" (upāsana), and "contemplation" (dhyāna)—and which serves as the means for attaining the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, who is free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance and possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, and who is to be attained by those seeking liberation;

[the author first describes] the nature of the self that is the attainer, as declared in the Prajāpati discourse beginning with, "The Self which is free from evil... and so forth, which constitutes a limb of that devotion.

The vision of reality (*yāthātmya-darśana*) has been described as being accomplished through the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), which is produced by action performed without attachment and preceded by the knowledge of its eternity.

For, in the discourse of Prajāpati, following the statement "he who, having discovered that Self, knows it," the vision of the essential nature of the Self—the seeker—is presented as a supplement to the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) taught in the *Dahara* section; after this, the nature of the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), which is bodiless and transcends waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, is established.
“Even so, this serene being, having risen from this body and having attained the supreme light, manifests in its own true form”— thus [the text] concludes with the fruit of the Dahara-vidyā.

Likewise, in other passages such as, “Having known God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind joy and sorrow,” after enjoining the knowledge of the inner self (pratyagātma-jñāna) by the phrase “through the attainment of internal yoga” as a subordinate element of the supreme knowledge (paravidyā) being enjoined by the words “having known God,” [it proceeds].
Having purified the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) with the passage beginning, “The wise one is neither born nor dies,” and starting from, “Subtler than the subtle,” [the text proceeds].
“Having realized the Self as great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve.
“This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
but by whomsoever this Self chooses, by him it is attained. To him, this Self reveals its own form.”
Having established the nature of the Supreme, the meditation upon It, and the fact that such meditation takes the form of devotion through these and other passages, [the text continues]:
"But that man who has discernment as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind,
he reaches the end of the journey— that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
Thus [the Lord] concluded with the fruit of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*).
Hereafter, with the next four chapters, Arjuna speaks as he elaborates upon this very vision of the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—the one who has attained it—along with its means.
Arjuna said:
If you consider intelligence to be superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava? (BhG 3.1)
With these seemingly contradictory words, you are, as it were, confusing my intellect.
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one path by which I may attain the highest good. (BhG 3.2)
If it is your view that knowledge alone is superior to action,
for what reason then do you urge me toward this terrible deed?
What is meant by this is that steadfastness in knowledge alone is the means for the realization of the Self.
However, it has been stated that the perfection of action (*karmaniṣṭhā*) is the means for accomplishing that [perfection of knowledge],

and that the perfection of knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*), which serves as the instrument for the vision of the Self, is to be accomplished by the cessation of the activity of all the senses and the mind toward objects such as sound.
If the vision of the Self, which is to be accomplished by the cessation of the activity of the senses, is what one desires to establish, [then...]
"I should be directed toward steadfastness in knowledge preceded by the cessation of all ritual action.
For what purpose do you enjoin me to this terrible action, which consists of the activity of all the senses and is opposed to the realization of the Self?"

Therefore, it appears to me that you are, as it were, confusing me with these mixed statements. For, on the one hand, there is the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*), which consists in the cessation of the activity of all the senses and serves as the means for the realization of the Self; and on the other hand, there is action (*karman*), which is the opposite of that. To say "perform that very [action]" regarding such a steadfastness is a contradictory and indeed confused statement.
Therefore, speak a single, unambiguous statement, by which statement I may determine what is to be performed and thereby attain the highest good. (BhG 3.12)
The Blessed Lord said:
O sinless one, in this world a twofold path was declared by me of old:
the path of the Sāṅkhyas through the yoga of knowledge, and the path of the Yogins through the yoga of action.
What was previously stated has not been correctly understood by you.

For in this world, which is filled with various types of qualified persons, I have previously declared that the two-fold culmination— pertaining to knowledge and action— is indeed unmixed according to one's qualification.

For not every worldly person who has conceived a desire for liberation is immediately capable of exercising authority over the yoga of knowledge; rather, one becomes qualified for steadfastness in knowledge only when the impurities of the mind have been destroyed by action performed as a mere means of propitiating the Supreme Person without regard for its fruits, and when the senses are no longer distracted.

“From whom the activity of beings proceeds, by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him with one’s own duty, a human being attains perfection. Thus, it will be stated that actions have as their sole purpose the propitiation of the Supreme Person.
Here too, by prescribing that action should be performed without aiming for its fruit in such passages as “Your right is to action alone,” and so forth, [the Lord teaches the same].

For one whose intellect has transcended the delusion consisting of agitation regarding sense objects, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is proclaimed by such passages as, "When he abandons desires...
Therefore, it is stated that the steadfastness of the Sāṅkhyas alone is through the yoga of knowledge,
whereas that of the Yogins is through the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
*Sāṅkhya* is the intellect (*buddhi*); those endowed with that are *sāṅkhyas*. Those who are connected to the intellect whose sole object is the Self are *sāṅkhyas*;
those who do not deserve that [intellect] are *yogins*, who are qualified for the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
The qualification for the yoga of action belongs to those whose intellects are occupied with sense-objects.
However, since it has been stated that those of unconfused intellect have the qualification for the yoga of knowledge, nothing contradictory or confused has been said here.
When the desire for liberation has arisen in any worldly person, the yoga of knowledge is suddenly difficult to practice; thus he says:
"A person does not attain freedom from action through the non-commencement of actions, nor does he achieve perfection merely through renunciation. (BhG 3.4)
A person does not attain *naiṣkarmya*— the steadfastness in knowledge— merely by not undertaking scriptural actions,
nor by abandoning those scriptural actions already undertaken.
Since that [perfection] is the accomplishment of action performed as a mode of worshiping the Supreme Person without aiming for its fruit,
one cannot attain it without that [devotion].

For those who have not propitiated Govinda through actions devoid of aimed-at fruits, and whose accumulated stores of infinite sins proceeding from beginningless time remain undestroyed, self-abidance preceded by the non-distraction of the senses is difficult to achieve.
He establishes this very point:
"For no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
indeed, everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature. (BhG 3.5)
For no person existing in this world ever remains at any time without performing action;

even one who is resolved that "I do nothing," every person is helplessly impelled and driven toward their own appropriate action by the qualities (guṇas) born of material nature— sattva, rajas, and tamas— which have increased in accordance with past actions.

Therefore, having destroyed the previously accumulated store of sins through the yoga of action characterized as described above, and having brought the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest under control, the yoga of knowledge is to be accomplished by one whose internal organ is stainless.

Otherwise, he who sets out for the yoga of knowledge but remains with his organs of action restrained while dwelling on objects with the mind becomes a hypocrite; thus [the Lord] says: "He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell on them with the mind... (BhG 3.6).
One whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called a hypocrite.

One whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) remains unsubdued because his sins have not been destroyed, who has set out for the knowledge of the Self but whose mind is turned away from the Self due to its inclination toward sense objects, and who remains dwelling only on those very objects—
thinking one way but acting otherwise— he is called "one of false conduct" (*mithyācāra*).
The meaning is that one who is intent upon the knowledge of the Self but acts contrarily becomes ruined.
But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind,
engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached— he is preeminent.

Therefore, one who— having restrained the senses by means of the mind directed toward the vision of the Self— commences the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) through those very senses which are naturally inclined toward action, performing it without attachment in a scriptural rite that belongs to the same class as objects previously practiced,
excels even a person established in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭha*), because for him negligence is rendered impossible. (BhG 3.7)
Perform your prescribed duty, for action is superior to inaction;
even the maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction.
It is fixed and pervasive;
for action is pervaded by its union with *prakṛti*.

You, being joined to *prakṛti* through beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), are bound by necessity, because action is easily performed and because negligence is impossible [for one so situated].
Perform action alone;
even compared to *akarma*—which here refers to steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*)—action alone is superior.
This is because, based on the introductory statement, "A person attains freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*)," the word *akarma* denotes precisely that steadfastness in knowledge.

Even for one qualified for steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*), steadfastness in knowledge is more difficult to achieve because it is not previously practiced, is therefore uncertain, and is prone to negligence; thus, steadfastness in action (*karmaniṣṭhā*) alone is superior.
Furthermore, while performing action, the contemplation of the self’s non-agency through the knowledge of the self’s true nature will be explained immediately hereafter.
Therefore, since even the knowledge of the Self is included within the yoga of action, the meaning is that this [action] alone is superior.
The statement regarding the superiority of action over steadfastness in knowledge is only possible when one has the qualification for steadfastness in knowledge;
for if there were qualification for steadfastness in knowledge alone by abandoning all action, [the comparison would not hold].
In that case, for one who is inactive and established in knowledge, even the maintenance of the body—which assists that state of being established in knowledge—will not be accomplished;
yet, until the completion of one's spiritual practice, the sustenance of the body must necessarily be maintained.
One should sustain the body only by eating the remnants of the *mahāyajña* and other rites performed with wealth acquired through righteous means.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "When food is pure, the nature (sattva) becomes pure; when the nature is pure, there is steadiness of memory," and so forth;
and because it will be stated later, "But those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin.
Therefore, even for one established in knowledge, if he does not perform action, even the maintenance of his body will not be accomplished.

Since even for one established in knowledge who still maintains a body, obligatory and occasional duties such as the great sacrifices must necessarily be performed until the completion of their spiritual practice;
since even within the yoga of action, the contemplation of the true nature of the Self through the realization of the Self's non-agency is included;
and since the yoga of action is both easily practiced and free from negligence for one who is still joined with material nature.
Therefore, even for one who is fit for steadfastness in knowledge, the yoga of action is superior to the yoga of knowledge;
thus, the intention is: "For that reason, you should practice only the yoga of action. (BhG 3.8)

If that is so, then since actions such as the acquisition of wealth are inherently filled with the agitation of all the senses—including egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*)—this person will surely be bound by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma; to this he replies:
"Other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by karma.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for its sake, free from attachment. (BhG 3.9)
When one performs actions that are not remnants of scriptural duties such as sacrifice—namely, actions performed for the sake of one's own personal purposes—one becomes bound by karma in this world.
Therefore, perform actions such as the acquisition of wealth for the sake of sacrifice;
perform them while being free from that attachment which consists in regarding them as means for achieving one's own personal ends.

Thus, when action is performed by one who is free from attachment for the sake of sacrifice and so forth, the Supreme Person, propitiated by those actions such as sacrifice, cuts away his latent impressions (vāsanā) of karma that have been active since beginningless time and grants him the vision of His own undisturbed Self; this is the meaning.
He states that those who are intent on accomplishing all human goals must maintain their bodies solely with the remnants of sacrifice,
whereas there is fault for those who maintain their bodies with what is not the remnant of sacrifice:
"Having created beings together with sacrifices, Prajāpati spoke of old."
By this you shall procreate; let this be the cow of plenty that grants your desired objects.

The word *Prajāpati*, when used in its unconditioned sense, refers to Nārāyaṇa—the Lord of all, the creator of the universe, the soul of the universe, and the ultimate refuge—based on such scriptural passages as "the Lord of all.

In ancient times, at the moment of creation, that Blessed Lord Prajāpati, being supremely compassionate, beheld the creatures who were subject to the power of association with insentient matter (*acit*) since beginningless time; whose distinctions of name and form had been withdrawn; who were dissolved within Himself; who were unworthy of any human goal; and who were like non-sentient beings.
Desiring to revive them and for the sake of accomplishing sacrifices which constitute their own worship, He created those [beings] together with sacrifices and spoke thus:
"By this sacrifice, you shall propagate yourselves; bring about your own increase."
May this sacrifice of yours be the fulfiller of the desire known as liberation, which is characterized by the supreme goal of man, as well as of those desires that are conducive to it.
How so?
"By nourishing the gods with this [sacrifice], let those gods nourish you in return;
nourishing one another, you shall attain the supreme good. (BhG 3.11)
By this act, which consists of propitiating the deities, you should propitiate the gods who have become my very body and whose essence is myself;
for it will be said later: "I am indeed the enjoyer and also the lord of all sacrifices.
Propitiated by sacrifice, those gods, whose essence is myself, shall nourish you with the food, drink, and other offerings required for their own propitiation.
Thus, cultivating one another in this way, you shall attain the supreme good known as liberation.
For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you the enjoyments you desire;
he who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is verily a thief.

The gods, who are nourished by sacrifice—that is, propitiated by sacrifice—and whose nature is centered in Me, will grant you your desired objects; that is to say, they will grant all those enjoyments sought after by you who strive for liberation characterized as the supreme human goal, as well as those enjoyments which have been overlooked due to your subsequent worship, provided they were previously nourished by successive sacrifices. This is the meaning.

He who enjoys the enjoyments given by them for the purpose of their own propitiation, without returning them to them, is indeed a thief. For "theft" consists in nourishing one's own self by forming the notion of ownership over an object intended for another's use, even while it was prepared solely for that other's purpose.
Therefore, this [act] entails not merely an unfitness for the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
Rather, the intention is that one will also go to hell.
He explains that very point:
"The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake eat only sin. (BhG 3.13)

Those who, having taken up materials solely for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Person abiding in the form of Indra and others, and having worshipped the Supreme Person as He truly is with those [materials], sustain their bodily existence by eating what remains from that [offering], are liberated from all the sins accumulated since beginningless time which obstruct the perception of the Self's true nature. But those who, taking up materials given by the Supreme Person in the form of Indra and others for the sake of His own worship, cook and eat them for their own sake—
Those of evil nature consume only their own sin; because they have transformed themselves into sin, they are called "sin.
Averse to the vision of the Self, they are cooked solely for the sake of hell.

Furthermore, having demonstrated through both worldly perspective and scriptural perspective that everything has sacrifice as its root, [the Lord] declares the necessity of following sacrifice and the fault in not following it:
"From food all beings come into being; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice comes rain; and sacrifice originates from action. (BhG 3.14)
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (akṣara).
Therefore, Brahman is omnipresent and eternally established in sacrifice.
O Pārtha, he who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion lives in vain; he is of sinful life and delights only in the objects of the senses.
“From food all beings arise, and from rain comes the production of food”—this is witnessed by the whole world;
and that rain arises from sacrifice is understood through scripture:
“An oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun.”
"From the Sun rain is born," and so forth.
Furthermore, sacrifice arises from action, which consists of the activities of the agent such as the acquisition of materials;
and action, in turn, originates from Brahman.
And here, the body—which is a transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti)—is indicated by the word "Brahman.
For in the passage, "From that, this Brahman, name-and-form, and food are born," primordial nature is indicated by the word "Brahman.
Here too, it will be said: "My womb is the great Brahman."
Therefore, by the statement "action originates from Brahman," it is meant that action arises from the body, which is a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
In the phrase "originating from the Imperishable Brahman" (*brahmākṣarasamudbhavam*), the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to the individual soul (*jīvātman*).

Since the body, presided over by the Imperishable soul when satisfied by food, drink, and so forth, is capable of performing action, the body—which serves as the instrument for action—is said to "originate from the Imperishable."

Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is all-pervading, the body resides within all qualified beings, and it is eternally established in sacrifice, having sacrifice as its root. Thus, this wheel set in motion by the Supreme Person consists of bodies endowed with life— referred to by the word "beings"— which arise from food, and food arises from rain.
From sacrifice comes Parjanya;
sacrifice comes from action in the form of the agent's activity; and action comes from the body together with the living soul.

The living body, moreover, arises again from food; thus, revolving like a wheel through this mutual relationship of cause and effect, he who is entitled to the path of action (karmayoga) or the path of knowledge (jñānayoga) and does not follow or engage in it—
failing to maintain his body with the remnants of sacrifice— becomes one whose life is sinful.
One whose life is for the sake of initiating evil, or is transformed by evil, or is of both natures, is one with a life of evil (aghāyu).
For this very reason, he delights in the senses and does not delight in the Self; the senses themselves become his gardens.

With his body and mind nourished by what remains from non-sacrificial acts, his *rajas* and *tamas* are intensified; being averse to the vision of the Self, he finds delight solely in the enjoyment of sense objects.
Therefore, O Pārtha, even though he strives in the yoga of knowledge and other such practices, his efforts are fruitless, and thus he lives in vain.

For one who perceives the Self as independent of any means of accomplishment, there is no undertaking of rituals such as the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) appropriate to one's caste and stage of life, just like that of a liberated person; thus he says: "But for the man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone—for him there exists no duty. (BhG 3.17)
For him there is no purpose whatsoever served by action here, nor any by inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire.
But he who is independent of the means of the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action, who by his very nature delights in the Self, is directed toward the Self,
is satisfied by the Self alone and not by food, drink, or other things distinct from the Self,
and is contented in the Self alone—
For one for whom the garden, garlands, sandalwood paste, song, instrumental music, dance, and so forth— all that is to be maintained, nourished, and enjoyed— is the Self alone,
there remains nothing further to be done for the realization of the Self.
Because its own nature as the Self is always perceived by itself, there is no purpose— meaning no utility— whatever in the means for realizing the Self that have been performed;
nor is there any disadvantage whatsoever from not performing the means for realizing the Self.
Because its vision of the self is not dependent upon any means of realization,

this [self], which is by its very nature averse to all insentient objects distinct from itself, finds no purpose or means of attainment whatsoever among any of the specific transformations of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), such as space and the rest, along with their effects; therefore, there is no undertaking of a means for the sake of turning it away from those.
For he is indeed already liberated.
Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains the Supreme.
Because the engagement in the means [of knowledge] occurs only for one whose vision of the Self is not dependent on such means;

and because even for one engaged in the means, since it is easy to perform, since it is free from negligence, since it involves an internal inquiry into the true nature of the Self, and since even the practitioner of knowledge (*jñānayogin*) requires a certain degree of continuity with action, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) alone is superior for the fulfillment of the vision of the Self.
Therefore, until the attainment of the Self, you should always perform action preceded by non-attachment;

indeed, by performing action without attachment and with the constant contemplation of the absence of agency as will be described, a person attains the Supreme through the yoga of action—that is, he attains the Self.
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone.
Since even for one qualified for the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of action alone is superior for the realization of the Self;
for this very reason, Janaka and other royal sages, who were the foremost among the knowers, attained perfection and reached the Self through the yoga of action alone.

Thus, having first stated that for one who desires liberation but is unfit for the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) and is instead qualified for the yoga of action (karmayoga), only the yoga of action is to be performed; and having further explained with reasons why even for one qualified for the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of action is superior to the yoga of knowledge, it is now stated that for one designated as "cultured" (śiṣṭa), the yoga of action alone must be performed under all circumstances.
Even considering the welfare of the world, you ought to act.
Whatever a great man does, that very thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. (BhG 3.21)
Even while perceiving the need for the welfare of the world, you ought to perform action alone.
For whatever a preeminent person— renowned both for his knowledge of the entire scripture and for his own practice— performs, that very same thing people who lack complete understanding also perform.

Even when performing an action, whatever authority the best man follows and whatever auxiliary factors he employs, even those who do not possess complete knowledge follow that very same practice with those same auxiliaries.
Therefore, for the sake of protecting the world, the best man—renowned for his refinement—must always perform in its entirety the duties appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*);
otherwise, the sin arising from the destruction of the world would cause him to fall away even from the yoga of knowledge.
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by Me;
nor is there anything unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.

For me—the Lord of all, whose desires are fulfilled, who is omniscient, whose resolve is true, and who moves at my own will in the three worlds in the forms of gods, humans, and others—there is nothing whatsoever to be done;
for there is nothing unattained that remains to be attained through action.
Nevertheless, I engage in action solely for the protection of the world.
For if I were not to engage tirelessly in action at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action; I would be the author of confusion and would destroy these beings. (BhG 3.24)
I am the Lord of all, whose resolve is ever true, who performs the play of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe by His own will;

though born among men as one who benefits the world at His pleasure, having descended into the house of Vasudeva— the foremost of the virtuous— I would not, even for a moment, fail to remain unweariedly engaged in the duties appropriate to that lineage.

The disciplined ones follow the path of my son Vasudeva—the foremost among the cultured—even though they themselves do not possess complete knowledge, thinking in every way that "this alone is dharma.
If they fail to perform their own duties, they will fail to attain the self due to the sin of non-performance and will become destined for hell.
If I, however, do not perform the action appropriate to my lineage, [the world would perish].

In this very way, all the cultured people (*śiṣṭaloka*), whose determination regarding dharma is dependent upon my conduct, would perish and be destroyed simply by my failure to act. By not maintaining the conduct prescribed by the scriptures, I would become the cause of the confusion of castes (*saṃkara*) for all the families of the cultured,
and thus I would bring ruin upon these creatures.

In the same way, even you—being the son of Pāṇḍu, the foremost among the cultured, and the younger brother of Yudhiṣṭhira, Arjuna—if you were to qualify for steadfastness in knowledge, then the cultured seekers of liberation who follow your conduct, being themselves of incomplete knowledge and unaware of their own qualification, would not qualify for steadfastness in action and would thus perish.
Therefore, by a learned man who is a public exemplar, action alone must be performed. (BhG 3.23–24)
O Bhārata, just as the ignorant act while attached to action,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.
The wise man, acting with disciplined composure, should not cause confusion of mind among the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, he should encourage them to perform all actions himself.
The ignorant— those who know the Self incompletely—

are attached to action, having an unavoidable connection with it; because they do not know the Self completely, they are not qualified for the yoga of knowledge consisting of its practice, and thus, being qualified for the yoga of action,
they perform the yoga of action itself for the sake of perceiving the Self.

Likewise, one who possesses complete knowledge of the Self, being unattached to action, though capable of being designated as qualified for the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), should nevertheless practice only the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) for the sake of protecting the world; desiring to establish the determination of dharma among the cultured through his own conduct, he should act thus.

This is for the sake of those seekers of liberation who are ignorant, who lack complete knowledge of the Self, who are unable to undertake the yoga of knowledge due to their attachment to action, and who are bound by the beginningless latent impressions of karma (*vāsanā*).

One should not cause confusion of intellect by suggesting that for those qualified for the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), there exists a means for perceiving the Self other than the yoga of action, given that action itself is mandatory.
What then? Even one who is capable of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) through complete understanding of the Self, according to the manner previously described—

With the understanding that "the yoga of action alone, independent of the yoga of knowledge, is the means for the vision of the Self," one who is disciplined should perform only action and thereby generate delight among those who know all actions only partially. (BhG 3.25–26)

Demonstrating the distinction between the wise and the ignorant who both practice the yoga of action, the Lord teaches the manner of contemplating the self's lack of agency, which is required for karma-yoga:
"Actions are performed in every way by the qualities of nature;
he whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer. (BhG 3.27)

But the knower of truth, O mighty-armed one, having understood the divisions of the qualities and their functions, does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities that move among the qualities. (BhG 3.28)
One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer," with regard to actions being performed in accordance with the qualities of nature, such as sattva and the rest;
he is one whose self (ātman) is deluded by egoism (ahaṅkāra).
Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) means the conceit of "I" with respect to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is not the true object of the "I.
By means of this, one whose true nature is unknown imagines oneself to be the agent among the qualities and their functions; such is the meaning.

One who knows the truth regarding the divisions of the qualities and their functions—that is, regarding the division of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and regarding the division of their respective functions—[is not affected by egoism].
Thinking that the qualities—sattva and the others—operate within their own respective effects, one does not become attached to the actions of the qualities, thinking "I am the doer."
Those who are deluded by the qualities of material nature become attached to the actions performed by those qualities;
one who knows the Whole should not disturb those dull-witted people who do not know the Whole.

Those who possess incomplete knowledge, having set out for the vision of their own Self, are deluded regarding the Self as it truly is because they are conjoined with *prakṛti* and thus by the qualities (*guṇas*) of *prakṛti*. They become attached only to the activities of the qualities—that is, to actions—and not to the nature of the Self which is distinct from them.
Therefore, since they are not capable of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), their qualification lies solely in the yoga of action (*karmayoga*).
One who knows the whole should not cause those dull-witted people, who are such as they are and lack complete knowledge, to waver from their state established in the yoga of knowledge.
For those dull-witted ones, following the conduct of superior persons, might—upon seeing him risen above the yoga of action—become unsettled in mind regarding the yoga of action.
Therefore, the superior one himself, remaining in the yoga of action while contemplating his own lack of agency through the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, [should not unsettle them].
Having shown that karma-yoga alone is the independent means for the vision of the Self, the meaning is that one should cause those who do not know the whole to take pleasure in it.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that even for one qualified for the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga), this [karma-yoga] is superior to jñāna-yoga.
Therefore, though he may be designated as such, he should perform this very [karma-yoga] for the sake of the welfare of the world.

By defining the nature of the self as distinct from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the manner of performing action was explained by superimposing agency upon the *guṇas*. This contemplation of agency within the *guṇas* is not inherent to the self’s own essential nature; rather, this agency is produced by contact with the *guṇas*. Now, through the discrimination between what is attained and what is not attained, the following contemplation is presented: that this agency is produced by the *guṇas*.

By defining the essential nature of individual selves as being subservient to Him because they constitute the body of the Supreme Person, and by superimposing upon the Lord— the Puruṣottama who is the Self of all— the agency produced by the qualities (guṇas), the performance of action is thus enjoined:
"Having surrendered all actions to Me with a mind fixed on the Self..."
Free from desire and free from the sense of "mine," fight, rid of all feverish anxiety.

Having renounced all actions with a mind directed toward the inner self (adhyātmacetas) in Me— the Lord of All who has become the inner Self of all beings— perform every enjoined action, such as battle, free from desire for rewards, free from the sense of "mine," and devoid of distress.
That which is the consciousness within the Self is "adhyātmacetas."
The meaning is: by means of knowledge concerning the true nature of the Self, which is established by hundreds of scriptural texts.

[As it is said: "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all... "This one who has entered within as the agent... "Abiding in the self, yet being internal to the self, whom the self does not know; whose body is the self; who rules the self from within."

Scriptural passages such as, "He is that Self, the inner controller, the immortal," declare this Self— which is the body of the Supreme Person— to be directed by Him, and the Supreme Person to be the director;
likewise, Smṛti texts such as, "The ruler of all," and so forth, convey the same.
“I am seated within the heart of all, and from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
“The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.”

Thus it will be said [in the following verse]. Therefore, by contemplating the nature of the self as being impelled by Me because it has Me as its body—thinking, "All actions are being performed by Me alone"—one should surrender them to Me, the Supreme Person;
and regarding those very actions as solely for My propitiation, one should be free from desire for their fruit.

Therefore, being free from the sense of "mine" regarding that action, perform the battle and other duties with your own self as the agent and your own instruments as the means, remaining free from feverish anxiety; do so by reflecting that the Supreme Person— the possessor of all, the Lord of all— Himself causes His own actions to be performed solely for the purpose of His own worship.

The meaning is: perform the yoga of action with ease, being free from the sense of "mine" regarding actions, liberated from the internal fever of thinking, "How shall I fare with this prior accumulation of infinite sins extending from beginningless time?", and [realizing] that the Supreme Person alone, when propitiated by these actions, will release you from bondage.

His status as the Lord of all and His being the ultimate remainder (the supreme object of dependence) are indeed established by such scriptural passages as: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords; Him, the supreme deity among deities," "The Lord of the universe," and "The Lord of lords."
Sovereignty is the state of being a controller; it is the state of being the master and the lord.
"This very point is the direct essence of the Upaniṣads," he says:
"Those men who constantly practice this teaching of mine, full of faith and free from carping, they too are liberated from the bonds of action. (BhG 3.31)

Those men who are qualified to study the scriptures, having determined that "this alone is the meaning of the scripture" according to my teaching, act accordingly; and those who, though not acting upon it, have faith in this scriptural meaning;
and even those who lack such faith yet do not harbor malice toward this great virtue, thinking, "This scriptural meaning is not possible"—[all these attain the goal].
The meaning is that they do not manifest any fault in the meaning of the scripture. They are all liberated from all karmas—the causes of bondage—which have been commenced since beginningless time.
The word "api" (also) in the phrase "they also" indicates their separation from the others.

The meaning is that even those who do not practice this meaning of the scripture at present, if they have faith and are free from malice toward it, their sins are destroyed by that faith and lack of malice; and having practiced this very meaning of the scripture before long, they are liberated.
He states the fault of those who do not practice the meaning of the Upanishads favored by the Blessed One, being faithless and envious:
"But those who, finding fault with this, do not follow my teaching—know them to be deluded in all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of sense. (BhG 3.32)

But those who do not practice all this— that everything pertaining to the self is my body, supported by me, subservient to me, and impelled solely by me— and who, having failed to reflect thus, do not perform all actions accordingly,
and those who have no faith;
And those who persist in being envious— know them to be especially deluded regarding all forms of knowledge, and for that very reason ruined; they are "without consciousness" (*acetasaḥ*),
for the function of consciousness is indeed the ascertainment of the true nature of things.
Due to the absence of that [knowledge], they are mindless;
they possess perverted knowledge and are utterly deluded in all respects. (BhG 3.32)

Thus, having reflected that agency belongs to one associated with *prakṛti* and is produced by the predominance of its qualities (*guṇa*), and that this [agency] is dependent upon the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), one who is fit for either the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) or the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) should practice *karmayoga* alone. This is because *karmayoga* is easier to perform, less prone to negligence, and independent as it contains within itself the knowledge of the Self; whereas the other [path] is difficult to perform, prone to negligence, and dependent on action for the sake of maintaining the body and so forth.
It has also been stated that for one who is designated [as a seeker], that very [practice] must be performed specifically.

Henceforth, in the remainder of this chapter, it is declared—along with its potential for negligence—that the yoga of knowledge is difficult to accomplish: "Even the man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature."
Beings follow their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?

The scriptures teach that such a nature of the Self is distinct from *prakṛti*, and that this alone should always be contemplated; nevertheless, even one who possesses knowledge acts only toward worldly objects in accordance with his own *prakṛti*—that is, according to his ancient latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"Beings follow their nature": sentient creatures, being conjoined with the non-intelligent, follow nothing other than the impressions set in motion since beginningless time.
Since those elements follow one's latent impressions (vāsanā), what can the restraint imposed by the author of the scriptures accomplish?
He describes the manner in which one follows one's nature:
"Lust and hatred are seated in each sense-organ toward its respective object;
one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries" (BhG 3.34).

Regarding the objects of the cognitive organs such as hearing—namely sound and so forth—and the objects of the active organs such as speech—namely speaking and so forth—there exists an unavoidable attachment (*rāga*) consisting of the desire to experience them, which is produced by prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
and there exists an unavoidable aversion (*dveṣa*) when that experience is obstructed.
These two, having brought under their control one who strives for the yoga of knowledge with all senses restrained, forcibly engage him in their own respective functions.
Consequently, this person becomes averse to the experience of his own true nature and is destroyed.
By undertaking the yoga of knowledge, he should not fall under the sway of attachment and aversion;
for those two, attachment and aversion, are his invincible enemies that obstruct the practice of knowledge.
Better is one’s own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed.
Death in one’s own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear.

Therefore, because it is easily performed, one's own duty (*svadharma*), which is the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), is superior—even if deficient in quality—to the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which is another's duty (*paradharma*) and thus difficult for one entangled in nature to perform; even if the latter is endowed with qualities, it is practiced for only a short time and is fraught with negligence.
For one who abides in the yoga of action, which is their own duty and fit to be undertaken by themselves, even death is better than failing to attain the fruit in this very life.
Because one who is free from obstacles can, even in the immediately following birth, undertake the practice of yoga with unconfused action;

whereas for one already entangled in material nature, it is impossible to adopt [the path] by oneself, and thus the yoga of knowledge—which has become a duty belonging to another—is fraught with danger due to its inherent potential for negligence.
Arjuna said:
Then by what impelled does this man commit sin,
O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force?

Now, the Blessed Lord said: "If this person, having set out for the yoga of knowledge, does not desire to experience sense objects himself, by what impelled does he act as if forcibly constrained toward the sin consisting of the experience of sense objects? It is this desire, it is this anger, born of the quality of rajas."
One who eats much and commits great evil—know him here to be your enemy.

For this [individual], who exists in a state of union with the *prakṛti* composed of the qualities (*guṇas*) through the process of emergence and suppression, and who has begun the pursuit of knowledge, there arises from the quality of passion (*rajas*) a desire for objects such as sound, born of past latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This desire, which is a great consumer, is the enemy; it draws him toward sense-objects.

When its course is obstructed, this very [desire] transforms into anger toward those sentient beings who cause the obstruction, becoming a great evil that impels one toward violence against others and similar acts.
Know this innate enemy, born of the quality of passion (rajas), which is an adversary to the yoga of knowledge.
As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust,
and as an embryo is enveloped by the womb, so is this [perception] covered by that.
Just as fire is obscured by smoke,
just as a mirror is obscured by dirt, and just as an embryo is enveloped by the fetal membrane.
In that same way, this multitude of living beings is enveloped by that desire.
He describes the manner of this obscuration:
"Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise, O son of Kuntī—by that which takes the form of desire, which is insatiable and like a fire. (BhG 3.39)

The knowledge regarding the Self of this living being—who is wise and whose nature is knowledge—is covered by this eternal enemy, which acts according to its own will and generates delusion regarding sense-objects; it is insatiable, seeking objects that ought not to be attained, and like fire, it knows no satisfaction. (BhG 3.39)
By what instruments does this desire preside over itself? To this he says:
"The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
through these it deludes the embodied soul by veiling its knowledge. (BhG 3.40)
"This desire presides over itself by means of these"—thus, the senses, mind, and intellect are its seat.

By means of these—the senses, mind, and intellect—which serve as its seat and are directed toward sense-objects, desire veils knowledge and deludes the embodied being who is joined with material nature; that is to say, it deludes him in various ways, turning him away from self-knowledge and making him intent on the experience of sense-objects.
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restraining the senses,
abandon this evil which destroys knowledge and realization.

Since this enemy in the form of desire causes aversion toward the Self by directing one toward sense objects for one who is engaged in the yoga of knowledge— which consists of the cessation of the activity of all the senses— therefore, you, who are inclined toward the activity of the senses due to being joined with material nature, must first, at the very time of commencing the means to liberation,
restrain the senses within the yoga of action, which consists of the activity of the senses.

Abandon—destroy—this enemy in the form of desire, which is sinful and the destroyer of knowledge and discernment; that is, the destroyer of the knowledge concerning the true nature of the Self and the knowledge concerning the discrimination between the Self and the not-Self.
Regarding those things that oppose knowledge, he says: "They say the senses are superior, and the mind is superior to the senses. (BhG 3.42)
The intellect is superior to the mind, but that which is beyond the intellect is He.
They say that the senses are the primary obstacles to knowledge, because when the senses are occupied with their objects, knowledge does not arise in the self.
Higher than the senses is the mind; even when the senses have ceased their activity, if the mind is inclined toward sense-objects, knowledge of the self is not possible.

The intellect (*buddhi*) is superior to the mind (*manas*); for even when the mind is turned away from other modifications (*vṛtti*), if there occurs the activity of erroneous determination (*viparītādhyavasāya*), knowledge does not arise.

Even when everything up to the intellect has ceased, if desire—which is synonymous with longing (*icchā*)—arising from *rajas*, persists, that very desire, having set these [faculties] beginning with the senses upon their own objects, obstructs the knowledge of the Self.
This is what is being said:
"But he who is beyond the intellect.
The meaning is that he who is even beyond the intellect is desire (kāma). BhG 3.42.
Thus, having understood that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by means of the self,
O mighty-armed one, slay the enemy in the form of desire, who is difficult to overcome.

Thus, having understood that desire— which is even beyond the intellect, which opposes the yoga of knowledge, and which is an enemy— establish the self (the mind) by means of the self (the intellect) in the yoga of action, and slay, that is, destroy, this difficult-to-overcome enemy in the form of desire.

In the third chapter, it was stated with supporting reasons that for one seeking liberation who is still bound to material nature (prakṛti), karma-yoga alone must be practiced because such a person lacks immediate qualification for jñāna-yoga; furthermore, even for one qualified for jñāna-yoga, karma-yoga preceded by the contemplation of non-agency (akarta-tva-anusandhāna) is superior.
It was also stated that for one designated as a "refined" (śiṣṭa) person, karma-yoga specifically must be performed.

Now, by means of the fourth [chapter], having established the necessity of this very yoga of action— since it was taught at the beginning of each Manvantara for the sake of uplifting the entire world— the true nature of this yoga of action, along with its divisions, is presented through its internal essence of knowledge.
In the yoga of action (karmayoga), it is stated that the element of knowledge alone holds primacy;
and as an incidental discussion, the true nature of the Lord’s incarnations is described.
The Blessed Lord said:
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat told it to Manu; and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku. (BhG 4.1)
Thus, this [yoga] was known by the royal sages, handed down through tradition;
but over a long period of time, O scorcher of foes, that yoga was lost here on earth.
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today, for you are My devotee and My friend; indeed, this is the supreme secret.
You should not think that this yoga which has been taught by me now is intended merely for the purpose of inciting you to battle;

rather, at the very beginning of the Manvantara, for the sake of uplifting the entire world, I myself taught this yoga to Vivasvat as a means to liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal,
and Vivasvat [taught it] to Manu.
"Manu [taught it] to Ikṣvāku"—
thus did the ancient royal sages know this yoga, which had been obtained through a succession of traditional transmission.
Over a long period of time, due to the dullness of the intellects of various listeners, it became almost lost.

This very same ancient Yoga, whose essential nature is unerring, has been declared by Me to you— who have taken refuge in Me alone with friendship and excessive devotion— along with its ancillaries and in full detail; that is to say, it is impossible for anyone other than Me to know or speak it, because this is the supreme secret knowledge proclaimed in the Vedāntas.
In this context, in order to know the true nature of the Lord’s incarnations as it really is, Arjuna said:
"Arjuna said:
Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier."
How may I understand this, that you spoke [this] in the beginning? BhG 4.4.
In terms of the calculation of time, your birth is at least as old as our own;
furthermore, the birth of Vivasvat is calculated by the count of twenty-eight cycles of four yugas.
Since you yourself declared this at the beginning, how can this be considered impossible? May I understand it according to its true meaning?

Surely it can be said that [this knowledge] may have been acquired in another birth, and for great beings, the recollection of what was done in another birth is indeed appropriate; thus there is no contradiction here.
Nor does he fail to recognize this speaker as the son of Vasudeva, the Lord of All.
For he will say thus:
"You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest purity;
the eternal, divine Person, the primal God, unborn and all-pervading."
"All the sages, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have said this to you;
and you yourself have told it to me," as has been heard repeatedly from Bhīṣma and others during King Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice and other occasions.
"In Kṛṣṇa alone indeed is the origin and also the dissolution of the worlds;
for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, exists"— in such passages as these,
[the phrase] "for the sake of Kṛṣṇa" [is used].
The meaning is that this entire world is a remnant of Kṛṣṇa.
To this it is replied: Pārtha indeed knows the Blessed One, the son of Vasudeva.

Even though he knows him, his intention in questioning as if he did not know is this: [he wonders] how the Lord of All, who is the sole embodiment of auspiciousness opposed to every form of evil, who is omniscient, whose will is ever-true, and who has attained all desires—could He be of the same nature as gods, humans, and others who are subject to the power of karma?
Is birth false, like a magical illusion and the like, or is it real?
If it is real, what is the manner of its occurrence? And of what nature is this body?
And what is the cause of birth? When is there birth?
And for what purpose is there birth?
The meaning of the question is understood through the manner of its resolution.
The Blessed Lord said: Many births of mine have passed away, as well as yours, O Arjuna.
I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe. (BhG 4.5)
By this, the truth of his birth is stated,
because of the statement "many births of mine have passed," and because [the word] "and yours" is employed as a corroborative example. (BhG 4.5)
He describes the manner of his descent, the true nature of his body, and the cause of his birth.
Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, and though I am the Lord of all beings,
yet by presiding over my own material nature, I manifest myself through my own creative power.
Without ever abandoning any of the supreme divine attributes, such as being unborn, imperishable, and the Lord of all, I manifest by presiding over my own nature through my own *māyā*.
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means one's own inherent being; the meaning is that I manifest by presiding over my very own nature, in my own form, and by my own will.
For my own essential nature is...
“He who has the color of the sun, beyond the darkness”; “Dwelling in the distance of this space”; “This golden person who is within the sun.”
“In him is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden”;
“All moments of time were born from the luminous Person.”
“Having light as his form, whose will is truth, whose self is space, possessing all desires, containing all desires, possessing all fragrances,
possessing all tastes,” and “a garment of saffron dye,” as established by such scriptural passages;
[He exists] by means of His own *māyā*, that is, by His own illusory power.

The word *māyā* here is a synonym for knowledge (*jñāna*), as in the expression “*māyā*, *vayuna*, and *jñāna*. Accordingly, there is the usage of an authority: “By means of *māyā*, he constantly knows the auspicious and inauspicious [deeds] of living beings.”
"By my own knowledge" means by my own volition.

Therefore, without abandoning my own essential nature— which consists of all auspicious qualities such as being free from sin and so forth— yet assuming through my own volition a form belonging to the same class as gods, humans, and others,
I manifest in the form of gods and so on.
Regarding this, the Śruti says: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways.
The meaning is that, while not undergoing birth in the manner common to other persons, he is born in the form of gods and others through his own volition by the process described above.

And because there is no contradiction between the preceding and following passages: "Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna; all of them I know," "Then I manifest myself," and "He who knows thus in truth my divine birth and action."
He states the time of His birth:
"Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bharata, and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest Myself. (BhG 4.7)
There is no fixed rule regarding the time of my manifestation.

Whenever there is a decline of Dharma— established according to the system of the four castes and the four stages of life as proclaimed in the Veda and consisting of duties to be performed— and whenever there is an uprising of its opposite, Adharma, then I myself, by my own resolve, manifest myself in the manner described.
He states the purpose of his birth:
"For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evil-doers, and for the sake of establishing dharma, I manifest myself age after age. (BhG 4.8)

The saintly ones (*sādhavaḥ*), whose character is defined by the dharma already described, who are the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas, and who have set out to take refuge in Me— finding that My name, activities, and true nature are beyond the reach of speech and mind, and thus unable to sustain or nourish their own selves without the sight of Me— they would perceive even a mere moment as a thousand kalpas, with all their limbs utterly relaxed, through the granting of the vision of My form, My movements, and My conversation.

For their protection and for the destruction of those opposed to them, and for the re-establishment of the diminished Vedic dharma— which consists of my own worship— by manifesting my nature as the object of worship, I appear in the form of gods, humans, and so forth, age after age.
The meaning is that there is no fixed restriction to specific ages such as the Kṛta or Tretā.
He who knows in truth thus my divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me, O Arjuna. (BhG 4.9)

Thus, he who knows in truth my divine, non-material, and unique birth and activity— which are free from birth in the form of contact with the three qualities of *prakṛti* rooted in karma that is to be abandoned, and which are endowed with all auspicious attributes such as sovereignty over all, omniscience, and the power of true resolve; and whose sole purpose is the protection of the righteous and taking refuge in Me— [he knows Me].
Having abandoned his present body, he does not undergo rebirth;
he attains Me alone,
for by means of the knowledge of the true nature of My divine births and activities, all sins that oppose taking refuge in Me have been utterly destroyed.
In this very life, by taking refuge in me in the manner described, he who is my sole beloved and whose mind is fixed on me alone attains me.
Regarding this, he says:

"Those who are free from passion, fear, and anger, who are absorbed in Me, and who have taken refuge in Me—many such as these, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state of being. (BhG 4.10)
Many have become thus purified by the austerity known as the knowledge of the truth of my birth and deeds;
and so says the Śruti:
"The wise fully comprehend its source."
The wise, who are the foremost among the intelligent, know his manner of birth in this way; such is the meaning.
In whatever way people approach me, in that same way do I reward them;
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.

I do not merely provide protection for those who seek refuge in me by descending in the form of gods, humans, and so forth; rather, for those who, seeking refuge in me, approach and take shelter of me by conceiving of me in whatever manner accords with their own expectations—
in that very way, according to their intended mode, I favor them, meaning I reveal myself to them.

What need is there for much here? All human beings, with their sole desire being to follow me, perceive my path and my entire nature— even though it is beyond the reach of the speech and mind of yogis— through their own respective instruments, such as the eyes and so forth, in every way and according to all their needs.
Having experienced it, they continue accordingly.

Now, having concluded this incidental discussion, in order to explain the manner in which the subject at hand—karma-yoga—assumes the form of knowledge, the Lord speaks of the rarity of those qualified for such karma-yoga:
"Desiring success through action, people here worship the deities;
for in the world of men, success born of action is quickly attained. (BhG 4.12)

All men indeed, desiring the fruits of their actions, worship and propitiate only deities such as Indra; none, however, worships Me, who am the very self of the deities like Indra, the enjoyer of all sacrifices, and free from any desire for results.
Why is this so? Because in this very human world, the accomplishment of sons, cattle, food, and other such things arises immediately from ritual action.

The term "human world" is intended to indicate [all worlds], including heaven and so forth. All worldly persons, being undiscriminating due to an inexhaustible accumulation of infinite sins proceeding from beginningless time,
and desiring immediate results, perform all actions— aimed at sons, cattle, food, heaven, and the like— as mere propitiation of deities such as Indra.
But no one whose heart is weary of saṃsāra and who desires liberation would undertake the yoga of action as described above, which consists in my worship; this is the meaning.
He states the cause for the destruction of the evil that obstructs the undertaking of the application of action as it has been described:
"The fourfold order of society was created by Me according to the divisions of qualities and actions;
know Me to be its author, yet also its non-author and immutable. (BhG 4.13)

The entire world, beginning with the four castes and extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has been divided by me and created according to the distribution of qualities such as *sattva* and according to the distribution of actions such as tranquility (*śama*) corresponding to those qualities.
The mention of "creation" is for the sake of illustration;
[the world] is also protected by me alone.
And it is withdrawn by me alone.
Know me to be the non-agent even of that agent who performs the manifold creation and so forth.
To the question "How so?", he says here:
"Actions do not smear me, nor do I have a longing for the fruit of action;
he who thus understands Me is not bound by actions. (BhG 4.14)
Since these various acts of creation and so forth do not smear me— that is, they do not bind me—
those diversities of gods, humans, and others are not instigated by me; rather,
the meaning is that they are instigated by the specific merits and demerits (puṇya-pāpa) of the beings to be created.
Therefore, by distinguishing between what is already attained and what is not yet attained, I am not the agent of the manifold creation and so forth;

for the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) who have been created—having received the instruments and bodies necessary for creation—enjoy the various objects of experience obtained through creation in accordance with their own karma, which is motivated by attachment to results and other such factors;
and since it is they alone who have a longing for the fruits of their actions regarding creation and the like, I have no such longing.

Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "There is no partiality or cruelty [on the part of the Lord], because He takes [other factors] into account. And likewise the Blessed Parāśara states: "He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating the things to be created, since the powers of the things to be created are indeed the primary causes."
O best of those who shine, apart from this mere sign, nothing else is required; a thing is led to its state of being a real entity by its own power.
Thus [it is said]:
this Supreme Person is merely the cause of the creation of the objects to be created—the individual souls (kṣetrajña) such as the gods and others;
however, regarding the diversity of the gods and so forth, the primary cause is the power of the past karma of the individual souls who constitute the created beings.

Therefore, apart from the mere material cause and apart from the Supreme Person who is the creator of the creation, this entity known as the *kṣetrajña* does not depend on anything else for its diverse states as gods and so forth;
the meaning is that it is led to the state of being a god or other such entities solely by the power of its own past karma.

In the manner thus described, he who fully knows Me—Me who am the creator of creation and so forth, yet am in fact a non-creator, and who am free from attachment to the fruits of actions such as creation—[attains liberation].
He is not bound by past actions—the causes such as attachment to results—which are opposed to the undertaking of the yoga of action; the meaning is that he is liberated. (BhG 4.14)
Knowing this, even those seekers of liberation in the past performed action;
therefore, you too perform action, as it was performed by the ancients in times of old.

Knowing Me thus, those ancient seekers of liberation, freed from sins, performed actions characterized as described above. Therefore, you— having shaken off sin through knowledge of Me in the manner stated— must perform that very same ancient action, performed by the ancients such as Vivasvat, Manu, and others, which was spoken by Me at that time and will now be described.
He speaks of the difficulty of discerning the action about to be described:
"Even the wise are deluded as to what is action and what is inaction;
therefore I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil. (BhG 4.16)
What is the nature of the action to be performed by one desiring liberation, and what is inaction?
"Inaction" refers to the knowledge of the true nature of the agent, the Self.
Regarding the nature of the action to be performed and the knowledge contained within it— on both these points even wise sages are deluded and do not know them as they truly are.
Therefore, I shall declare to you that action which has knowledge inherent within it.
Having known and performed that, you shall be liberated from the bondage of the impure cycle of existence;
for the fruit of performance is indeed the knowledge of the action to be done.
To the question, "Why is this so difficult to understand? he says:
"For one must understand action, and one must understand what is contrary to action;
and one must understand inaction as well—profound is the way of action. (BhG 4.17)
Because there is something to be understood regarding the nature of action that serves as the means to liberation, as well as regarding prohibited action (vikarman),
in the form of obligatory, occasional, and desire-driven rites.
Action that has taken on various forms, such as the acquisition of materials for its performance, is *vikarman* (mis-action).
Furthermore, it must be understood in relation to *akarman* (inaction) and in relation to knowledge (*jñāna*).
The course of action for one seeking liberation is profound and difficult to comprehend.

Regarding "what is to be understood in action" (*vikarmani*): in actions such as the acquisition of materials for obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, one must abandon the diversity created by differences in results and instead contemplate the fact that they all have liberation as their sole fruit, because they constitute the single purpose of the scripture.
This very point was stated in the verse, "The intellect characterized by resolve is one," and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
He now states what is to be understood regarding both action and inaction:
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. (BhG 4.18)
By the word "akarma" (inaction) here, the knowledge of the Self under discussion— which is other than action— is meant.
He who sees the knowledge of the Self even while action is being performed,
and he who sees action even while abiding in the knowledge of the Self [is a sage].
What is meant by this?
It is said that one who perceives an action being performed as having the form of knowledge through the investigation into the true nature of the Self,
and perceives that very knowledge as having the form of action because it is contained within the yoga of action— that is what is meant.
For when an action is being performed, if there is a contemplation of the true nature of the Self as its agent, both of these [requirements] become fulfilled.
Thus, he who perceives action as having within it the core of contemplation on the true nature of the Self is wise and a knower of the entire meaning of the scripture.
Among men, he is disciplined and worthy of liberation; he alone is the performer of all duties and the fulfiller of the entire purpose of the scriptures.
Regarding how the action being performed through direct perception can possess the form of knowledge, he says here:
"The wise call him a sage whose every undertakings are free from desire and purposeful intention, and whose actions have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge. (BhG 4.19)

For that seeker of liberation whose undertakings of all ritual acts— whether obligatory, occasional, or optional— are preceded by worldly activities such as the acquisition of wealth, are free from desire for rewards,
and are devoid of mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*);
wherein a "mental construct" is defined as the identification with the Self through its association with the qualities of *prakṛti*.
Those who are devoid of that [action] are those engaged in the contemplation of the true nature of the Self as distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti).

The knowers of reality say that a wise man who performs action in this manner—his former actions having been burnt by the fire of knowledge regarding the true nature of the Self inherent within action—is such a one.
Therefore, it is logically established that action takes the form of knowledge.
He explains this very point:
"Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever content and dependent on nothing, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all. (BhG 4.20)

Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented— meaning contented in his own eternal Self— and without dependence, meaning devoid of the notion of a support in the unstable material nature,

he who performs actions— even though engaged in them with outward intent— does not perform any action at all; the meaning is that under the guise of action, he performs only the practice of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is precisely the cognitive nature of action that is being purified:
"Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action only for the body, one incurs no sin. (BhG 4.21)

Free from desire—that is, devoid of the intention for results—one whose mind and self are controlled, whose thoughts are restrained, and who has renounced all possessions; being free from the sense of "mine" regarding material objects and their constituent elements because the Self alone is his sole purpose, and performing throughout his life only such action as pertains to the body, he incurs no sin—that is, he does not incur the cycle of transmigration—and through this very form of Karma-yoga, which is unimpeded by a lack of steadfastness in knowledge, he perceives the Self. Furthermore, one who is content with whatever comes by chance, who has transcended the pairs of opposites, and who is free from envy...
Being equal in success and failure, even after acting, he is not bound.
Content with whatever means for sustaining the body come to him by chance,
he has transcended the pairs of opposites, enduring cold, heat, and other unavoidable conditions until the completion of his practice;
and being free from envy, he is devoid of malice toward others through the recognition that their own past actions are the cause of the misfortunes they encounter.

He who is equanimous in success and failure—that is, one whose mind remains the same regarding the attainment or non-attainment of victory and so forth in actions such as battle—is not bound even after performing action, and despite lacking steadfastness in knowledge, he does not enter into transmigratory existence. (BhG 4.22)
For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge,
and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, all karma is entirely dissolved.

For a person whose mind is established in knowledge regarding the Self, who has emerged from attachment to anything other than that, and who— consequently liberated from all possessions— is engaged in the performance of sacrificial and other rites characterized as previously described, his entire prior karma, which is the cause of bondage, completely dissolves and is exhausted without remainder.
It has been stated that action takes the form of knowledge because it is conjoined with the contemplation of the true nature of the Self as dissociated from primordial matter (prakṛti);

now, he declares that all action, along with its accessories, takes the form of knowledge because it is conjoined with the contemplation of the Supreme Person, who is the Supreme Brahman, as the essence of everything:
"The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman."
Through that meditative absorption in the work of Brahman, one must go to Brahman alone.
In the phrase "the offering is Brahman" (*brahmārpaṇam*), the oblation (*havis*) is qualified.
That by which something is offered is the "offering-vessel" (*arpaṇa*), such as the ladle (*sruc*) and so forth;
because it is an effect of Brahman, it is Brahman.
That oblation whose offering is Brahman is "brahmārpaṇam"; Brahman is the oblation, and the offering of that oblation is "brahmārpaṇam.
And he himself has become Brahman.
