He who reflects that "it has been offered into the fire of Brahman"—that is, into the fire which has become Brahman—by the agent who is Brahman, such that every action consists of Brahman and is permeated by Brahman because its nature is Brahman;
he is one whose concentration is on action as Brahman (*brahmakarmasamādhi*).
By means of that concentration on action as Brahman, Brahman alone is to be reached; that is, the true nature of the self, which has become Brahman because its nature is Brahman, is to be attained.

Action performed by one desiring liberation, being accompanied by the realization that it is essentially the Supreme Brahman itself, takes the form of knowledge and is a direct means for the perception of the Self; the meaning is that it does not stand as an intermediary between action and steadfastness in knowledge.
Having thus established that action possesses the form of knowledge, he speaks of the different varieties of the yoga of action:
"Some yogis perform sacrifice solely to the divine;
others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman. (BhG 4.25)

Other karma-yogins practice and serve the sacrifice consisting of the worship of the gods— that is to say, they establish their firm resolve in that alone. Others offer the sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman by means of the sacrifice itself.
Here, the word *yajña* refers to the implements of sacrifice such as the oblation (*havis*) and the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*);
according to the principle that "the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman," they bring the sacrifice and the fire-oblation (*homa*) to completion.
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses.
Some strive for the restraint of the senses, such as hearing and the rest;
other yogis strive to prevent the senses from being inclined toward sound and other objects.
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.
Others offer all the activities of the senses and the activities of the vital breaths into the fire of the yoga of mental restraint, which is kindled by knowledge.
This means that they strive to prevent the mind from being subject to the activities of the senses and the vital breaths.
Others perform sacrifices with material substances, sacrifices of austerity, and likewise sacrifices of yoga;
and others, ascetics of firm vows, perform sacrifices of Vedic study and sacrifices of knowledge.
Some practitioners of action-performing yoga are performers of material sacrifices; having acquired materials in accordance with justice, they strive in the worship of deities,
some in acts of giving,
and some in sacrificial rites.
And some [perform] oblations;
all these are sacrifices of material substances (dravyayajña).
Some perform sacrifices of austerity (tapoyajña), reaching their culmination in such practices as the kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa, and fasting.
And others, performing the sacrifice of yoga, apply themselves to reaching sacred fords and holy places.
Here, the word "yoga" refers to that [sacrifice], because the context concerns the different types of dedication to action (*karmaniṣṭhā*).
Some are devoted to the practice of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*).
Some are intent on the practice of knowing that goal; they are ascetics (yatayaḥ), characterized by constant effort,
firm in their vows, and resolute in their determination.
Others offer the outgoing breath into the incoming breath, and likewise the incoming breath into the outgoing;
having restrained the movements of both the outgoing and incoming breaths, they are devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Others, restricted in their food, offer the vital breaths into the vital breaths; others, practitioners of action, establish themselves in the yogas of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
which are of three kinds according to the divisions of inhalation (pūraka), exhalation (recaka), and retention (kumbhaka).
"One offers the prāṇa into the apāna" refers to inhalation (pūraka);
"the apāna into the prāṇa" refers to exhalation (recaka);
and "having blocked the movements of the prāṇa and apāna... they offer the prāṇas into the prāṇas" refers to retention (kumbhaka).
The phrase "those who are restricted in diet" applies to all three [stages] as well, those who are devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma).
All these, too, are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice.
Those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman.

These individuals, engaged in the various forms of *karmayoga*—beginning with the sacrifice to the gods (*daivayajña*) and ending with *prāṇāyāma*—which they have undertaken according to their own inclination, are knowers of sacrifice in the form of obligatory and occasional rites preceded by the "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*), as declared in the verse: "Having created all beings together with sacrifices... (Gītā 3.10).
Devoted to that [Brahman] and having their impurities destroyed by that very means, while sustaining their bodies with the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice,
they remain engaged in the yoga of action and attain the eternal Brahman.
This world does not exist for one who performs no sacrifice; how much less another, O best of the Kurus?

For one who does not perform sacrifices—that is, for one devoid of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites preceded by the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and so forth—this world does not exist; that is, the worldly human goals (*puruṣārtha*) known as dharma, artha, and kāma, which pertain to the natural world, are not accomplished.
How much less, then, can there be the other human goal known as liberation (*mokṣa*)?
Since liberation has been introduced as the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha), this world is pointed out as a human goal other than that;
for it is merely natural (prākṛta).
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices have been spread forth at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action. Knowing this, you shall be liberated.

For thus, many kinds of karmayogas are spread out at the mouth of Brahman, existing as means for attaining the true nature of the Self; know all those karmayogas—characterized as described and divided as stated—to be born of action. Know them to be born of the obligatory and occasional rites performed day after day. Having understood this and practicing in the manner described, you shall be liberated. (BhG 4.32)
It has been stated that action possesses the form of knowledge because knowledge is internal to it;
regarding that action in which knowledge is internal, he declares the primacy of the very portion consisting of knowledge:
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice performed with material objects."
O Pārtha, every action in its entirety culminates in knowledge.
In action which possesses both forms, the aspect consisting of knowledge is superior to the aspect consisting of material substance;

for all action and everything else that is to be adopted reaches its completion in knowledge. That very knowledge, which is the goal to be attained through all means, is practiced as being inherent within action;
and that very knowledge, when practiced, gradually attains the state of being the goal itself.
Learn that by humble prostration, by inquiry, and by service;
the wise who have seen the truth will instruct you in that knowledge. (BhG 4.34)
That knowledge concerning the Self was taught by Me, beginning with the words, "But know that to be indestructible," and ending with, "This has been declared to you.

Know that abiding in action conjoined with that [knowledge] becomes clear in form from time to time through prostration, inquiry, service, and so forth, in accordance with its maturation, by means of those who possess knowledge.

However, those knowers who have directly realized the nature of the Self, when served through prostrations and the like, will perceive your disposition as you inquire thoroughly out of a desire for knowledge and will impart that knowledge to you.
He states the definition of the knowledge regarding the true nature of the Self, which consists of direct realization:
"Knowing which, O Pāṇḍava, you will not again fall into such delusion;
by which you will see all beings without exception in yourself, and then in Me" (BhG 4.35).

That knowledge, knowing which you will no longer fall into such delusion— consisting of the egoistic conceit of being a god or other [beings], and the resulting locus of "mineness" and so forth— and by which you will see all beings, conceived in the forms of gods, humans, and so on, as being nothing but your own Self;
for there is equality between yourself and other beings when they are divested of their material nature, insofar as they possess the single form of consciousness.
It will also be stated that the nature of the Self is entirely equal and free from the defects arising from contact with primordial matter (*prakṛti*):
"For Brahman is faultless and equal; therefore, they are established in Brahman.
Furthermore, you shall see all beings without exception in Me.

Because of the identity of nature with my own self, for every purified reality of the Self, it will indeed be stated: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own state" (Gītā 14.2).

Likewise, in such passages as, "Then the wise man, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3), the identity of nature with the Supreme is understood for the reality of the Self when it is liberated from name and form.
Therefore, every essential reality of the self, when liberated from primordial nature (prakṛti), is mutually equal and equal to the Lord of All.
Moreover, even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone.
Even if you are the most sinful among all sinners, you shall cross over the entire ocean of previously acquired demerit by means of the very raft that is the knowledge of the Self as its object.
Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.
Just as a fully kindled fire consumes a heap of fuel,

so the fire consisting of the knowledge of the true nature of the self reduces to ashes the infinite accumulation of karma residing in the individual soul that has been active since beginningless time.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
Since there exists no other thing in this world as purifying and cleansing as the knowledge of the Self,
therefore the meaning is that the knowledge of the Self destroys all sin.

Such knowledge, perfected through the yoga of action characterized by knowledge— which is practiced day after day according to instruction— one attains within one's own self by oneself in due course of time.
He states that very point clearly:
"The man of faith, who is devoted to it and has his senses restrained, gains knowledge;
having gained knowledge, he attains supreme peace without delay. (BhG 4.39)

Having thus obtained knowledge through instruction, one who possesses faith and is devoted to the increase of the instructed knowledge, with a mind fixed solely upon it and senses restrained from other objects, attains in a short time that knowledge which has reached the state of maturation as described; having attained such knowledge, he quickly reaches supreme peace— he attains the ultimate Nirvana.
The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. (BhG 4.40)

The ignorant person— thus devoid of the knowledge obtained through instruction, lacking faith in the means for increasing that instructed knowledge, and being slow to act— possesses a doubting nature, a mind full of doubt, and perishes; he becomes ruined.
When this knowledge concerning the true nature of the Self has been taught, even for one whose mind is full of doubt, this world does not exist, nor does the next;
the human goals consisting of dharma, artha, and kāma are not accomplished, so how much less liberation? This is the meaning.
Since all human goals consist in the accomplishment of scriptural duties,
and since the success born of scriptural action is preceded by the certainty that the self is distinct from the body,
it is impossible for one who doubts the self to partake even in a fraction of happiness.
O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced actions through yoga, whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge, and who is self-possessed.

By means of the yoga as instructed, one who has renounced action— having transformed action into the form of knowledge— and whose doubts regarding the Self have been severed by the knowledge of the Self as taught, being self-possessed and wise with a mind firmly established in the taught meaning, are not bound by past, endless actions that serve as the cause of bondage.
Therefore, having severed with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart, which has arisen from ignorance, take refuge in yoga and arise, O Bharata!

Therefore, having severed with the sword of self-knowledge taught by Me the doubt concerning the Self that resides in the heart and has arisen from beginningless ignorance, take recourse in the yoga of action taught by Me; for that purpose, arise, O Bhārata!

In the fourth chapter, the distinction in the nature of karma-yoga based on its preliminary form as knowledge was stated, as well as the primacy of the cognitive element; furthermore, it was stated in the third [chapter] itself that even for one qualified for jñāna-yoga, karma-yoga is superior because it includes self-knowledge, because it is free from negligence, because it is easier to perform, and because it is independent. Now, having established the swiftness of steadfastness in knowledge regarding the attainment of the Self through the means of karma-yoga, and the manner of contemplating the absence of agency inherent within karma-yoga, [the author will explain] the knowledge that is its root.
It is purified.
Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions and again you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better. BhG 5.1.
You praise the renunciation of actions (*karma-saṃnyāsa*), the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), and again the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).

What is meant by this is as follows: having established in the second chapter that for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) the yoga of action must first be performed, and that for one whose impurities of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-kaṣāya*) have been worn away by the yoga of action, the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana*) must be achieved through the yoga of knowledge; then, in the third and fourth chapters, it is shown that even for one who has reached the stage of eligibility for the yoga of knowledge, steadfastness in action (*karmaniṣṭhā*) alone [is required].
Since that very steadfastness in knowledge, independent [of action], is the means for attaining the Self, you praise steadfastness in action;
therefore, between these two—steadfastness in knowledge and steadfastness in action—which one is more excellent as a means for attaining the Self, being determined by its greater ease and swiftness?
Tell me that. (BhG 5.1)
The Blessed Lord said: Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good;
however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action. (BhG 5.2)
Renunciation is the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of action is also the yoga of knowledge; for one capable of the yoga of knowledge, both are independently conducive to the supreme good.
Yet, between these two, the yoga of action is indeed superior to the yoga of knowledge consisting in the renunciation of action. (BhG 5.2)
To the question "Why?", he says here: "He should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires;
for, O mighty-armed one, being free from the pairs of opposites, he is easily liberated from bondage. (BhG 5.3)
The practitioner of action who is satisfied by the experience of the Self contained therein desires nothing apart from that,
and for that very reason hates nothing; and for that very reason, he is a bearer of the pairs of opposites.
He should be known as one who is eternally renounced and eternally established in knowledge;
for by being established in the yoga of action, which is easy to perform, he is easily liberated from bondage. (BhG 5.3)
Regarding the fact that the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action are both means for attaining the Self, He states their mutual independence:
"The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
one who is properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both" (BhG 5.4).

Those who proclaim that the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action exist as separate entities due to a difference in their fruits are fools whose knowledge is unperfected; they are not wise, for they lack complete understanding.
The yoga of action indeed brings about the yoga of knowledge alone.

The meaning is that those who claim a distinction between the two on the grounds of a difference in their fruits—arguing that the yoga of knowledge alone accomplishes the vision of the Self—are not wise.
Since both have the singular fruit of the vision of the Self, one who is established in even one of them obtains that very same fruit.
He explains this very point: "The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by the followers of Yoga as well;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees. (BhG 5.5)
That very fruit which is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya who are established in knowledge— consisting in the perception of the Self—
is likewise attained by those established in the yoga of action.
Thus, he who perceives Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, being optional alternatives because they have the same fruit—he alone sees; that indeed is the meaning of "he is wise. // BhG 5.5 //
He said: "This is the distinction:
renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
but the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman without long delay. (BhG 5.6)
Renunciation, however, is the yoga of knowledge; it cannot be attained without yoga—that is, without the yoga of action.

One who is disciplined in yoga, that is, engaged in the yoga of action, becomes a sage (*muni*) by nature—one whose habit is to contemplate the Self—and having accomplished the yoga of action with ease, he attains Brahman, that is, the Self, before long, in a very short time.
But one who is engaged in the yoga of knowledge accomplishes that yoga with great difficulty;
the meaning is that because it is difficult to accomplish, he attains the Self after a long time.
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, such a one is not tainted.

But one who is engaged in *karmayoga*, abiding in the pure action prescribed by the scriptures in the form of the worship of the Supreme Person, becomes pure-minded through that; having conquered the self (*vijitātmā*) because his mind is occupied with the action he has practiced, he easily conquers the mind, and for that very reason conquers the senses. By being steadfast in the investigation into the true nature of the self as the agent, he becomes one whose self has become the self of all beings—that is, one whose self has become the self of all beings, such as gods and others.
For one who investigates the true nature of the Self, the Self of the gods and others, as well as one’s own, is of a single form;
this is because the distinctions of gods and so forth, being merely specific transformations of *prakṛti*, cannot possibly possess the form of the Self.

Being dissociated from *prakṛti*, it is of a uniform form everywhere within the bodies of gods and others by virtue of having knowledge as its sole form. This will be stated immediately thereafter: "Brahman is indeed faultless and equal."
Being thus, even while performing action, he is neither smeared nor bound by the conceit of a self in what is not-self;
therefore, the meaning is that he attains the Self before long.
Since karma-yoga is superior both because of its ease and its swiftness,
therefore listen to what is required for it:
"The disciplined knower of truth should think, 'I do nothing at all.'"
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing;
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, and even closing them—
he who maintains the conviction that it is merely the senses operating upon their objects.

Thus, the knower of the reality of the Self, maintaining the connection that the organs of knowledge such as hearing, the organs of action such as speech, and the vital breaths operate within their respective objects, should think, "I do nothing at all," [realizing] that for me, whose sole nature is knowledge, [the sense of agency] is produced by the connection with the organs and vital breaths which are rooted in karma.
The meaning is that one should consider such agency to be [the result of] mental construction, and not something inherent to one's own nature.
He who performs actions by dedicating them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (BhG 5.10)
By the word "Brahman," primordial nature (prakṛti) is meant here; for it will be stated later: "My womb is the great Brahman.

Since the senses are specific modifications of the transformation of primordial nature, one performs actions by means of primordial nature abiding in the form of the senses, in the manner described by the words "seeing, hearing," and so forth.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits [of action],
he who performs actions thinking "I do nothing at all"—
even while existing as one joined with *prakṛti*— is not tainted by the evil that is the cause of bondage, which consists in the identification of the self with *prakṛti*.
Just as a lotus leaf is not smeared even when in contact with water, so too [the sage] is not smeared; this is the meaning. // BhGR 5.10 //
With body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone,
yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits such as heaven, yogis perform action—which is accomplished by the body, mind, and senses—for the sake of self-purification;
the meaning is that they act for the destruction of the bonds of past karma residing within the self. (BhG 5.11)
The disciplined one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains peace that is final;
the undisciplined one, acting under the impulse of desire and attached to the fruit, is bound.

The disciplined one—who is steady regarding fruits other than the Self and whose inclination is solely toward the Self—having abandoned the fruit of action and performed action merely for the purification of the Self, attains the steadfast peace that consists in the experience of the Self; he attains the eternal bliss of liberation. The undisciplined one—who is restless regarding fruits other than the Self, who is averse to the vision of the Self, and who is attached to the fruit through the impulse of desire—while performing actions, is perpetually bound by those actions and remains eternally subject to saṃsāra.

Therefore, it is stated that one who is free from attachment to the fruits of action should perform actions solely for the sake of liberating the self from bondage, having renounced those actions within *prakṛti* as it has transformed into the form of the senses.

Now, the renunciation of agency within *prakṛti* as it has transformed into the form of the body is described: "Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled one dwells in happiness."
In this city of nine gates, the embodied self neither acts nor causes others to act.

This agency regarding actions belongs to the self because of its connection with a body rooted in past karma, and not because it is inherent to its own nature. With a mind focused on this discrimination, the embodied one, being self-controlled, renounces all actions within the city of nine gates and dwells in happiness—neither making effort for the sustenance of the body himself, nor causing the body to act. (BhG 5.13)
He declares the true, natural form of the Self:
"The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is nature that acts. (BhG 5.14)

This Lord—the Self, who abides in His own natural state and is not subject to karma—does not create nor produce the agency that is unique to each class of beings among gods, animals, humans, and stationary objects existing through contact with material nature (prakṛti), nor does He produce their respective specific actions, nor the connection with the fruits of those actions, such as birth as a god and so forth.
Who then? It is nature (svabhāva) that operates.
"Nature" (*svabhāva*) means innate disposition (*prakṛti-vāsanā*).

It refers to all such things as agency and so forth, which are produced by dispositions generated by the conceit of being this or that self (*ātma-abhimāna*), arising from contact with natures in the form of gods and so on, produced by successive past actions since beginningless time;
the meaning is that these are not caused by one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). (BhG 5.14)
The Lord does not take upon himself the sin or even the merit of anyone;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded. (BhG 5.15)
He does not take away the evil or suffering of anyone whom he regards as his own, such as a son, nor does he remove it;
nor does he take away or remove the merit or happiness of anyone whom he regards as hostile.
For he is all-pervading (vibhu).
It is not localized;
it does not have a specific location such as the body of a god or other beings;
for this very reason, it belongs to no one.
And nothing is disagreeable to anyone;
all this is produced by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
How can such a perverse predisposition arise for one whose nature is thus?

Knowledge is veiled by ignorance, which is the opposite of knowledge; that is, its knowledge is veiled and contracted so that it may become fit for the experience of the fruits of each preceding action.

By means of that karma, which consists in the obscuration of knowledge, there arises union with bodies such as those of gods and the like, as well as delusion in the form of the ego-identification with each of those [bodies]. And from that, there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of such ego-identification with the self.
And there is the latent impression (vāsanā) of actions appropriate to that [birth];
from such impressions, the conceit of a self contrary [to reality] and the undertaking of action arise. (BhG 5.15)

“By the boat of knowledge alone one shall cross over all evil,” “The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes,” and “There is indeed nothing as purifying as knowledge”— these previously stated [scriptural passages] are brought into harmony with their respective contexts.
But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun. (BhG 5.16)

When all selves are thus engaged, for those selves whose ignorance—in the form of an accumulation of beginningless and infinite karma that veils knowledge—is destroyed by that knowledge concerning the self; which is produced by the instruction on the true nature of the self according to the definition stated above; which is unsurpassedly pure; and which acquires excellence through daily practice.
For them, that innate, supreme knowledge—immeasurable and uncontracted—illumines everything exactly as it exists, like the sun.

Regarding the phrase "for them": because they have destroyed ignorance, their plurality is merely a conceit arising from the notion of multiplicity; however, the fact that the nature of the Self is not multiple—as understood from the opening statement, "Never was I not," etc.—is here stated even more clearly.
Nor is this plurality caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
because for those whose ignorance has been destroyed, there is not even a trace of a limiting adjunct.

By the statement, "Their knowledge is like that of the sun," the fact that knowledge is an attribute inherent to its own nature (*svarūpānubandhidharma*) is expressed through the use of a distinction (*vyatireka*).
And by the analogy of the sun, the existence of the knower and knowledge is like that of light and its source;
from this very fact, it is logically established that in the state of saṃsāra, knowledge undergoes contraction through karma, while in the state of liberation, it undergoes expansion.
With their intellects fixed on That, with That as their self, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal,
they go to the state of no-return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge.
Those whose intellects are such, who have reached a firm conviction through the vision of the Self as being of that nature, whose very selves are that, whose minds are directed toward that object,
and who are established in that— meaning those devoted to its constant practice.

Devoted to that, considering that alone to be the supreme goal, they— having shaken off their ancient impurities through such practiced knowledge— attain such a Self from which there is no returning again. From that state of the Self, rebirth does not exist.
That Self is one from which there is no return;
the meaning is that they go to the Self abiding in its own essential nature. (BhG 5.17)
The wise look with an equal eye upon a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste.
Among those endowed with learning and humility,
as well as among mere Brahmins,
and among cows, elephants, dogs, outcastes, and others who appear in extremely diverse forms, the wise— those who know the true nature of the Self— [perceive them all as equal].

The meaning is that those who perceive equality everywhere because the Self has the single form of knowledge alone, [see that] the diverse forms belong to Prakṛti and not to the Self; for the Self is equal everywhere due to having the single form of knowledge alone.
Even here, heaven is won by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is faultless and equal, therefore they abide in Brahman.

Right here, even at the very stage of practicing the means, they have conquered creation; they have conquered saṃsāra—those whose minds, according to the manner described, abide in equanimity toward all selves.
For Brahman is indeed faultless and equal.
Indeed, the reality of the Self is Brahman, for it is equal, being free from the defects of association with primordial nature (prakṛti).
If you remain established in that equality with the Self, you are indeed established in Brahman;
for establishment in Brahman alone is the conquest of saṃsāra.
The meaning is that those who contemplate the very equality [of all beings] through the fact that their own selves possess the single form of consciousness are indeed liberated.
He teaches that manner in which the maturation of knowledge— consisting of equal vision— comes to a Karma-yogin who is established [in yoga]:
"One should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor should one be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant."
Steady in intellect, undeluded, the knower of Brahman abides in Brahman.

Whatever is pleasant and whatever is unpleasant to one abiding in such a body and in such a state, according to the impressions of past karma— one should encounter both of these without experiencing joy or agitation.

How so? One of steady intellect (*sthirabuddhi*) is one whose intellect is fixed upon the stable Self; he is undeluded (*asaṃmūḍha*). Delusion (*saṃmoha*) consists in identifying the stable Self with the unstable body;
he is free from that.
And how is that so?
One who knows Brahman is established in Brahman;
being a knower of Brahman through instruction, he is engaged in the practice of that very Brahman.

This is what is meant: having come to know the true nature of the self through the instruction of those who know reality, and striving in that very state, one should abandon the conceit of identifying the body with the self; established in the beloved experience of perceiving the self as stable in form, one should not give way to joy or agitation upon encountering the unstable, material likes and dislikes. (BhG 5.20)
He whose self is unattached to external contacts finds happiness within the Self;
with his self united in yoga with Brahman, he enjoys imperishable bliss.

In the manner thus described, he whose self is unattached— that is, whose mind is unattached— to external contacts, which are experiences of objects distinct from the self, finds and obtains happiness within the inner self alone;

such a person, having abandoned the practice of material nature, with his self united in yoga with Brahman— his mind engaged in the practice of Brahman— attains the imperishable happiness that consists in the experience of Brahman.
He speaks of the extreme difficulty of renouncing worldly enjoyment: "For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the wombs of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them. (BhG 5.22)
Those enjoyments born from the contact of the senses with their objects are sources of suffering and result in suffering;
for they are perceived to have a beginning and an end, existing only for a brief time.
One who knows the true nature of things does not take delight in them.
He who is able here, even before liberation from the body,
to endure the impulse arising from desire and anger— that man is disciplined, that man is happy.

Even before the liberation of the body, while still in this very state of practicing spiritual discipline, he who is able to endure and restrain the impulse arising from desire and anger through the joy of self-realization is "yukta" (steadfast), fit for the experience of the Self.
Only such a person shall, after the liberation of the body, attain the singular bliss of experiencing the Self.
He who finds happiness within, whose delight is within, and likewise whose light is solely within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the bliss of Brahman.
He who, having abandoned all experience of external objects, finds internal happiness and finds joy solely in the experience of the Self;
he whose pleasure is increased by his own qualities through the Self alone, being one for whom the Self is the very garden;
and likewise, he who exists as one whose light is internal, possessing knowledge of the Self alone—such a person is described thus.
That yogi, having become Brahman, attains the bliss of self-realization, which is the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
The sages, whose taints are destroyed, who have severed all doubts, who are self-controlled, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa.
With their doubts severed, they are liberated from the dualities of cold and heat; self-controlled, with their minds restrained within the Self alone;
and devoted to the welfare of all beings, being intent on the well-being of all creatures as if they were themselves.
The seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*) are those who behold; they are devoted to the contemplation of the Self.
Those who are thus become free from all impurities that obstruct the attainment of the Self, and they attain the extinction into Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇam*).
He states that Brahman is extremely easy to attain for those characterized as described above:
"For ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained, and who have conquered their selves, the extinction into Brahman exists on every side. (BhG 5.26)

For ascetics who are free from desire and anger, who are habituated to effort, whose minds are restrained, whose thoughts are disciplined, and who have conquered themselves— that is, mastered their own minds— the extinction of Brahman (brahmanirvāṇa) lies all around them;
the meaning is that for those who have become such, the extinction of Brahman is as if held in the palm of their hand.
He concludes the teaching on the yoga of action, which culminates in its own specific goal, with these words:
"Having turned outward the external points of contact, and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils... (BhG 5.27).
The sage who has restrained his senses, mind, and intellect, who is devoted to liberation,
and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed— he is indeed always liberated.

Having cast aside external contacts with sense objects and withdrawn all activity of the external senses, sitting with the body straight upon a seat suitable for yoga, fixing the eyes between the eyebrows or on the tip of the nose, equalizing the inward-moving *prāṇa* and outward-moving *apāna* breaths by making the inhalation and exhalation even in their movement, one whose senses, mind, and intellect are no longer inclined toward anything other than the contemplation of the Self—
Therefore, he whose desire, fear, and anger have departed,
who is intent on liberation— meaning for whom liberation is the sole purpose—
and who is a sage, characterized by the habit of beholding the Self;
The meaning is that he is indeed eternally liberated; just as he is liberated in the state of realization (*sādhyadaśā*), so too is he liberated even in the state of practice (*sādhanadaśā*).
He declares the ease with which this Karma-yoga—described as having the performance of obligatory and occasional rites as its procedure and being crowned by Yoga—is accomplished:
"Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. (BhG 5.29)
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the well-wishing friend of all beings, one attains peace;
indeed, one attains happiness through the very performance of the yoga of action.
"The Great Lord of all worlds" means the Lord even of all the lords of the world.
For it is heard in scripture: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among the lords.
The meaning is that, having known Me as the Great Lord of all worlds and the friend of all, one engages easily in Karma-yoga, which consists of My worship;
for everyone exerts themselves for the sake of worshipping a friend. (BhG 5.29)
The Blessed Lord said:

He who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not one who merely maintains no sacred fire, nor one who merely abstains from action.
The yoga of action (karmayoga) has been explained along with its ancillaries;
now the method for practicing yoga—which consists of the contemplation of the Self and is accomplished through both the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga) and the yoga of action—is being described.
In this context, the yoga of action, which takes the form of knowledge and is crowned by yoga, is restated in order to reinforce its status as an independent means of achieving yoga.
Not depending on the fruit of action, such as heaven and so forth;
"what is to be done" means the performance of action itself is what must be done;
since it consists in the worship of the Supreme Person who is my friend in every respect, action alone is my purpose.
He who performs action with the understanding that nothing is to be accomplished by it is both a renunciant established in the yoga of knowledge and a yogi established in the yoga of action.
The meaning is that he is established in both, having as his means of yoga the practice of self-contemplation.
He is neither devoid of sacred fires, nor inactive, nor unengaged in prescribed rites such as sacrifices,
nor is he established in knowledge alone.
For his [the one established in knowledge] there is only steadfastness in knowledge, whereas for the one established in the yoga of action, both exist; this is the intended meaning.
Since knowledge also exists in the application of action characterized by the previously mentioned marks, he says:
"O Pāṇḍava, know that which they call renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to be yoga;
for no one becomes a yogi who has not renounced his mental resolves (saṅkalpa). (BhG 6.2)
Know that very thing which they call renunciation, the yoga of knowledge, and the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, to be indeed the yoga of action.
He establishes this: for no one indeed becomes a yogi without having renounced their sankalpa.

One by whom the sankalpa regarding the self—namely, the notion of "self" directed toward Prakṛti, which is not the self—has been renounced or abandoned through the investigation into the true nature of the Self (ātma-yāthātmya), is one whose sankalpa has been renounced (saṃnyasta-saṅkalpa);
one who is not thus is one whose sankalpa has not been renounced (asaṃnyasta-saṅkalpa).
For among those practitioners of action described above, there is no practitioner of action who is not of such a nature;
for it has been said: "He whose undertakings are all free from desire and volition. (BhG 6.2)
It is said that it is indeed the yoga of action that accomplishes yoga through heedfulness:
"For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. (BhG 6.3)
For the seeker of liberation who desires to attain yoga, which is the vision of the Self, karma-yoga alone is said to be the cause;
for that very person who has ascended to yoga— that is, for one whose yoga is firmly established—
tranquility, the cessation of action, is said to be the cause.
The meaning is that one must perform actions until the attainment of liberation, which consists in the vision of the Self.
Regarding the question of when one becomes established in yoga, it is said here:
"When one is indeed attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitional thoughts, then one is said to have ascended to yoga. (BhG 6.4)

When this yogi, by virtue of having the nature of experiencing only the Self, does not become attached to— nor deserves attachment for— the objects of the senses (which are material entities distinct from the Self), nor for the actions associated with them,
then he is called one who has renounced all volitional thoughts and is established in yoga.

Therefore, for one who desires to ascend [to yoga], because of the fitness for experiencing sense objects, the practice of non-attachment to them—namely, *karmayoga* alone—is the cause for the accomplishment of yoga.
Hence, one who desires to ascend should perform *karmayoga* itself, which consists in the practice of non-attachment to sense objects. (BhG 6.4)
He says that very thing: "One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not let the self sink down.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. (BhG 6.5)
With one's own mind,
being unattached to sense objects, one should uplift oneself;
with a mind contrary to that, one should not cause oneself to sink.
The self alone is indeed the friend of the self;
that very same self is the enemy of the self.
The self is the friend of that self by which the self has been conquered by the self;
but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would act as an enemy in the state of enmity.
The mind of that man by whom his own mind has been conquered from sense objects is his friend; however,
for one who is not self-possessed and whose mind is unconquered, his very own mind would act as an enemy— meaning it would act as an adversary to his own welfare.

As it was said by the Blessed One, and also by Parāśara: “The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, the mind leads to bondage; free from sense objects, the mind leads to liberation. (BhG 6.6)
The state suitable for the commencement of yoga is described as follows:
for one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is composed;
likewise, amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor.

In one who has conquered the self—that is, one whose mind is mastered and free from modification—and who is tranquil, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is perfectly established (samāhita) within the mind.
Here, the inner self (pratyagātman) is called the "Supreme Self" because it is that very self which is the subject under discussion. It remains established in its own essential nature.
For even that [self] is the supreme self in relation to its preceding states;
or rather, the grammatical connection is: "the self is supremely composed."
One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is steadfast, whose senses are conquered,
and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same— he is called a yogi who is disciplined.

One whose self is satisfied by knowledge and discernment— that is, whose mind is contented by knowledge regarding the nature of the Self and by knowledge regarding the form of the Self as being of a different class from Prakṛti— is immovable (kūṭastha), remaining established in that single-natured Self which persists through all common states such as those of gods and others;
and for that very reason, he has conquered his senses.

One for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal—because, by being established in his own nature which is distinct from material nature, he lacks the sense of an object of enjoyment toward specific worldly things and thus finds them all of equal utility—that practitioner of karma-yoga is said to be "yukta" (steadfast);
that is, he is said to be fit for the practice of yoga consisting in the vision of the Self.
And so it is said:
"One who possesses an even mind toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen—as well as toward the virtuous and the sinful—is preeminent. (BhG 6.9)
Those who desire one's welfare without regard for differences in age are friends (*suhṛd*);
those of equal age who desire one's welfare are companions (*mitra*); and enemies (*ari*) are those who, due to some cause, wish one harm.
Those devoid of both causes are neutral;
those devoid of both from birth are impartial;
and those who, from birth, lack desire and possess aversion are hateful.
By birth alone, relatives are well-wishers;
the virtuous are of righteous character; and the wicked are of evil character.

Because there is no purpose served by friends, allies, and others when one’s sole aim is the Self— and because there is an absence of conflict— one who maintains an even-mindedness toward them is distinguished as being fit for the practice of yoga.
The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline the self.
The yogi, established in the practice of karma-yoga as described, should constantly— day after day, during the time of yoga— yoke himself; that is, he should make himself disciplined,
meaning he should make himself established in his own vision [of the Self].

Staying in a secluded place, devoid of people and free from noise, alone— even there not accompanied by another— with his mind and self controlled, that is, with his mind and internal organ restrained.

Free from desire, he is indifferent toward the entire world of objects distinct from the Self; free from possessiveness, he is devoid of the sense of "mine" regarding anything whatsoever other than that.
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass, one over the other— BhG 6.11.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained,
let him sit upon his seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
In a clean place— not occupied by impure persons, nor possessed by them, untouched by impure objects, and being a sanctified spot—
one should prepare a seat made of wood or other materials, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass;

having settled upon that seat which is conducive to mental clarity and provides support, one should sit with the mind focused one-pointedly on yoga, restraining the activities of the mind and the senses.
Withdrawing the activities of the mind and senses with his whole being, he should practice yoga for the purification of the self and the cessation of bondage;
he should effect the vision of the Self.
Holding the body, head, and neck erect, motionless and steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in any direction. (BhG 6.13)

With a tranquil self, free from fear, established in the vow of celibacy, and having restrained the mind, let him sit disciplined, with his thoughts fixed on Me, making Me his supreme goal. (BhG 6.14)
Holding the body, head, and neck straight, motionless, and steady by means of a support,
without looking around at the directions,
and gazing at the tip of his own nose;

With a tranquil self and a mind of ultimate peace, free from fear and devoted to the life of purity, having restrained the mind and fixing it on Me, disciplined and attentive, regarding Me as the supreme goal, he should sit meditating upon Me alone. (BhG 6.14) / 14 /
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in Nirvana and abides in Me.

Thus, always yoking the self—the mind—to Me, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Person, the auspicious refuge for the mind, one whose mind is restrained and whose mind has become motionless through being purified by My touch, and meditating on Me alone, attains the peace that culminates in liberation, which is established in Me; he attains that peace established in Me, which is the very pinnacle of liberation.

Having thus described the mind’s abiding in the Blessed One, the auspicious refuge—which serves as the cause for the purity of the mind of one who has begun the practice of yoga—He speaks of another requisite for yoga:
"Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all; nor for him who is habituated to excessive sleep, nor for him who is ever awake, O Arjuna. (BhG 6.16)
For one who is disciplined in diet and recreation, disciplined in performing actions,
and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
Excessive eating and fasting are opposed to yoga; likewise are excessive indulgence and lack of activity, as well as excessive sleep and wakefulness,
and similarly, excessive exertion and lack of exertion.
For one whose food and conduct are moderate, whose exertion is moderate, and whose sleep and waking are moderate, yoga—which destroys all suffering and severs the bonds—becomes perfected.
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be "yoked" (in yoga). (BhG 6.18)

When the mind, which has purpose as its object, is restrained within the Self alone— specifically restrained because it finds no higher purpose, remaining fixed and motionless therein— then, being free from longing for all desires, one is said to be "yoked" (yukta) and said to be "fit for yoga" (yogārha).
"Just as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker—this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices yoga of the self. (BhG 6.19)
Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker or move,
but remains steady with its light,
such is the simile for the nature of the Self of the yogi who is self-controlled, whose mental fluctuations other than [the one-pointed state] have ceased, and who is practicing yoga within the Self.
The meaning is that, like a steady and radiant lamp placed where there is no wind, the Self remains motionless with all mental fluctuations ceased, shining with the light of knowledge.
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds contentment within the Self. 20.
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and transcends the senses—he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; (BhG 6.21).
Having gained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering.
One should know that disjunction from the union with suffering is designated as yoga;
that yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency.
By means of the practice of yoga as the cause, the mind, restrained everywhere, comes to rest in that yoga; one delights therein, thinking, "This is supreme bliss.
And in that yoga, seeing the Self by means of the self—the mind—one finds satisfaction in the Self alone, independent of anything else.
Furthermore, in that yoga, one knows—that is, experiences—that ultimate bliss which transcends the senses and is perceivable solely by the intellect of the Self.
And that yoga in which one established remains unshakable from its true nature due to an abundance of bliss because of being absorbed in it;
having attained which yoga, one who has desisted from other yogas longs for that alone and does not consider any other gain to be superior to it;
and established in which yoga, even when desisting, one is not moved by even heavy suffering such as the loss of a virtuous son.

One should know that [yoga] is the separation from the union with suffering, characterized by being the opposite of the union with suffering, and denoted by the word "yoga. Yoga of this nature must be practiced at the stage of its commencement with a mind free from despondency and with a joyful heart, through firm resolve.
Having abandoned all desires born of volition without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses on all sides by means of the mind alone— BhG 6.24.
Little by little, one should achieve stillness through the intellect held with firmness;
having fixed the mind upon the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
Desires are of two kinds: those born of contact and those born of mental construction.
Those born of contact are cold, heat, and so forth;
those born of mental construction are children, fields, and so forth.
In that regard, those [objects] which arise from mental construction can be abandoned by their very nature;

having abandoned all of them through the mind alone by means of reflecting upon their transitory nature, and having abandoned the joy and agitation caused by them regarding unavoidable sense-contacts born of touch, one should gradually restrain the entire collection of senses from every object on all sides.

Having withdrawn from everything other than the Self by means of an intellect held firm by fortitude and directed toward the domain of discernment, and having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all.
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away,
from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under the control of the Self alone.
Since the mind is unstable within the self due to its flickering nature, and since it wanders outward toward various objects because of its inclination for them,
one should restrain the mind with effort from each such object and bring it under control within the self alone through the cultivation of supreme bliss.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is tranquil,
whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint.
With a mind tranquil within the Self, with a mind motionless within the Self,
with the mind dissolved in the Self, and thus having all impurities burnt away by that very means,
he is one whose passion has been stilled, having destroyed the quality of *rajas*.
From that very state, supreme bliss—consisting of the experience of the nature of the Self—approaches this yogin who has become Brahman and abides in his own true form.
The word "hi" (for) indicates a reason; the meaning is that the nature of the Self consists of supreme bliss. (BhG 6.27)
Thus constantly disciplining himself, the yogi, freed from all taints,
easily attains the infinite bliss of contact with Brahman.

Thus, by uniting the self in the manner described, one becomes free from all former impurities through that very practice and easily, without effort, eternally enjoys the infinite bliss consisting of the touch of Brahman— that is, the experience of Brahman.
Now, the fourfold state of the maturation of yoga is described:
"One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere. (BhG 6.29)

Because of the equality of his own self and other beings— whose essential nature is free from material nature— insofar as they consist solely of the form of knowledge, and because any inequality resides in material nature, one whose self is disciplined in yoga perceives with equal vision everywhere, through the single form of knowledge, among all selves freed from material nature; he beholds his own self abiding in all beings and all beings within his own self, seeing them as having the same form as all beings.
The meaning is that one perceives one's own self and all beings as having a form identical to one's own self.
When the single Self is seen, because of its equality with it, the entire reality of the Self becomes seen; this is the meaning, as indicated by the statement: "one who sees the same everywhere."
This is also evident from the restatement, "This yoga which has been declared by you as equality," and from the statement, "For Brahman is faultless and equal. (BhG 6.29)
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—I am not lost to him, nor is he lost to Me. (BhG 6.30)
Furthermore, one who has entered the state of fruition (vipāka-daśā) attains a similarity to me;

as it is said, "The stainless one attains supreme equality. Seeing this equality with me—which belongs to every self-substance that has shaken off merit and demerit and abides in its own essential nature—he who sees Me in every self-substance [sees truly].
He perceives my entire essential nature within himself; through mutual similarity, by perceiving one, he perceives that the other is also like this.
For him who perceives my own true nature, I do not perish because of that similarity, nor do I become invisible; and for me as well, it is the same for one who perceives me.
Beholding his own self as equal to me because of its equality with me, he does not go to non-perception.
Furthermore, he describes the state of the fruition:
"The yogi who, established in oneness, worships Me as abiding in all beings, even while acting in every way, dwells in Me. (BhG 6.31)

The yogī who, during the state of yoga, abides in oneness—having abandoned ordinary distinctions and firmly devoted himself to Me as dwelling in all beings, by virtue of My being of a single form consisting solely of uncontracted knowledge—even when he is in the state of emergence (vyutthāna), however he may conduct himself, seeing his own self and all beings, he abides in Me; that is, he sees Me alone.
The meaning is that he always perceives my very same identity within his own self and in all beings.

Beyond that, he states the ultimate goal: "O Arjuna, he who, by means of self-comparison, looks upon everything with equanimity—whether it be pleasure or pain—that yogi is considered supreme. (BhG 6.32)

Because his own self and the selves of others are of a single form consisting of non-contracted knowledge, he who— by way of this analogy— sees the happiness arising from the birth of a son and so forth, as well as the suffering arising from their death and so forth, as equal in himself and in others, meaning that he sees the birth and death of his own son as equal to the birth and death of another's son due to the equality of their lack of connection [to a separate self].
That yogi is considered supreme; he is considered to have reached the pinnacle of yoga.
Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by you,
I do not perceive its steady endurance because of the mind's restlessness.
For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (BhG 6.34)

This yoga which you have taught consists of seeing with equanimity everywhere— in all selves that have been experienced for so long as being absolutely distinct through the divisions of gods, humans, and so forth, and through the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)— yet which, by virtue of having knowledge as their sole form, possess mutual equality, and by virtue of not being subject to karma, possess equality with the Lord.
I do not see a stable state for this yoga, because of the fickleness of the mind.

Even regarding objects practiced incessantly, the mind—which is inherently fickle—is impossible for a person to establish in one place; it forcibly overcomes the person and wanders elsewhere with great persistence.

I consider it extremely difficult to restrain that mind—which, despite being accustomed to its own objects, is by nature fickle—and to fix it upon a self whose form is the opposite of those objects; for it is like trying to stop a great wind blowing against one with a fan or the like. The intention is that the means for restraining the mind must now be explained. (BhG 6.33–34)
The Blessed Lord said:
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control through practice and dispassion.
"Yoga is difficult to attain for one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my view.
But it can be attained by one who has mastered the self through effort and by means of the proper method. (BhG 6.36)
There is no doubt that the mind is indeed difficult to restrain due to its restless nature;

nevertheless, it can somehow be controlled through a focused inclination produced by the practice of regarding the Self as a mine of virtues, and through the absence of craving produced by seeing everything other than the Self as a mine of defects.
Yoga is difficult to attain even with great strength by one whose self is uncontrolled and whose mind is unsubdued.

However, by means of the previously mentioned method—consisting of the worship of Me, characterized by self-control and internalized knowledge—one who has conquered the mind through effort can attain this very yoga which consists of equal vision.
Now, Arjuna asks so that he may hear correctly the majesty of yoga as it was heard at the outset in the words, "In this, there is no loss of effort";
for it was in that context that the majesty of Karma-yoga was proclaimed, owing to its inclusion of self-knowledge and its being headed by Yoga.
And that is indeed the majesty of yoga.
Arjuna said:
"One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-restraint, whose mind has strayed from yoga—"
O Kṛṣṇa, failing to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does one go to?
O mighty-armed one, I hope that he, being without support and bewildered on the path of Brahman, does not perish like a scattered cloud, fallen away from both and lost.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely; for indeed, no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt. (BhG 6.39)

Having set out in yoga with faith, but failing to attain perfection in yoga due to a deficiency in effort characterized by more intense practice, and thus having a mind fallen from yoga—does such a person, fallen from both, perish like a scattered cloud?
Just as a fragment of a cloud, severed from a great cloud in the east and failing to reach another great cloud, perishes in mid-air; [does he likewise perish?]
In that very way, may it not perish. How is there a falling away from both?
It is being without a foundation.
"Confused on the path of Brahman":

for this person who is free from desire for rewards, ritual action—which exists as the means for attaining heaven and so forth—does not serve as a firm foundation by way of producing its own fruit; thus he is "without support. He is "confused on the path of Brahman," meaning he has fallen away from that path.
Therefore, having fallen away from both, does he simply perish, or does he not perish?
You ought to sever this doubt of mine completely.
For there is indeed no one other than you— who perceives everything at all times simultaneously through direct perception by its own nature— who could be the dispeller of this doubt.
The Blessed One said: "O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him.
For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state. (BhG 6.40)

For one who has set out in yoga with faith, there is no destruction either here or hereafter; that is to say, there is no destruction consisting in the failure to obtain desired objects—whether in the experience of ordinary heavenly rewards or in the experience of Brahman—nor is there any attainment of the undesirable known as "obstruction" (pratyavāya). Indeed, one who practices yoga, which is of the nature of unsurpassed excellence, never goes to a state of woe at any time throughout the three periods.
"How will this person fare? To this he says:

"Having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for eternal years, one who has fallen from yoga is reborn in the home of the pure and the prosperous. (BhG 6.41)
Having fallen from yoga through longing for the enjoyments of a certain kind,
he reaches worlds attainable by those who have performed great merit; there, by the very majesty of yoga, he enjoys enjoyments of that same kind which are exceedingly auspicious,
dwelling there for eternal years until the end of his thirst for those enjoyments, becoming free from craving for that enjoyment.
One who has fallen from the practice of yoga is born into a family of pure and prosperous people who are fit for the undertaking of yoga, by virtue of the greatness of yoga.
Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in this world.
If one whose yoga is fully matured should waver, he is born into a family of great beings who are wise yogis practicing yoga and who are themselves capable of teaching yoga.
Thus, birth in either of these two kinds of families— among those fit for yoga or among yogis— is extremely difficult to attain in this world for ordinary people.
But this is brought about by the greatness of yoga.
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his previous body;
from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection.
For by that very same prior practice, he is drawn [toward it] even against his will;
in that birth, he regains that very same connection of the intellect with the object of yoga belonging to his previous body.
Then, like one who has awakened from sleep, he strives again for perfection so that he is not struck down by obstacles.
He strives in such a manner;
by that former practice, by his previous habituation to the object of yoga, even though he has fallen from yoga and is no longer in control, he is drawn back toward yoga itself.
For this greatness of yoga is well known—this is the meaning. (BhG 6.43)
Even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Brahman of sound.

One whose yoga has not yet commenced, even though desiring to know yoga, may have a mind that wavers from it; yet, having once again attained that very desire to know and having practiced yoga such as the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), he transcends the *śabdabrahman*.
*Śabdabrahman* refers to *prakṛti* (primordial nature), which is the Brahman capable of being designated by words such as "god," "human," "earth," "intermediate space," and "heaven.

The meaning is that, liberated from the bondage of *prakṛti*, he attains the Self, which is incapable of being designated by words such as "god" or "human," and which is solely composed of knowledge and bliss.
But the yogi who strives with effort, having been purified of all taints and perfected through many births, then attains the supreme goal.

Since the majesty of yoga is thus, therefore, one whose sins have been thoroughly purified by the accumulation of merit acquired over many births attains perfection; and the striving yogi, though he may falter despite his efforts, surely reaches the supreme goal once again.
By stating that the yogi is superior to all because of his dedication to the highest human purpose, [the Lord] declares his excellence over everyone else.
The yogi is superior to the ascetics, and he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge;
the yogi is also superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.
That human goal which is accomplished through mere austerities, that which is accomplished through forms of knowledge other than the knowledge of the Self,
and that which is accomplished through mere rituals such as the horse-sacrifice;

Because yoga is the means for accomplishing a human goal superior to all those [others], the yogi is superior to the ascetics, the men of knowledge, and the men of action; therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.

Thus, the vision of the inner self (pratyagātma-darśana), which is a constituent part of supreme knowledge (paravidyā) and was declared in the discourse of Prajāpati, has been explained; now, he introduces supreme knowledge itself: "By all yogis as well, with their inner self absorbed in Me..."
He who, endowed with faith, worships Me, is considered by Me to be the most disciplined of all.
The genitive case in the word *yoginām* is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*).
By the verse beginning with “the Self abiding in all beings,” four kinds of yogis have been presented;
since the yogi who is about to be described is not included among them, the genitive cannot here be understood as expressing a selection from a group (*nirdhāraṇe*).
"Even among all"—those indicated by the word "all," beginning with ascetics and so forth;
even there, the meaning of the ablative case is to be understood according to the logic already stated:
"compared to yogis—even compared to all [others], the yogi to be described hereafter is the most disciplined."
The meaning is that, in comparison with that [supreme state], there is no distinction whatsoever between ascetics and the like and yogis,
just as mustard seeds are inferior in relation to Mount Meru.
Even though among the mustard seeds themselves there exists a mutual relationship of being lesser or greater, nevertheless, their designation as "inferior" remains the same when compared to Meru.

With an inner self and mind absorbed in Me through an excess of love for Me, having a nature that cannot be sustained by anything else; full of faith because of an extreme love for Me and thus unable to endure even a moment’s separation, he who worships Me with haste toward the attainment of Me— Me, whose play consists in the arising, expansion, and dissolution of the entire universe filled with various and infinite classes of enjoyers, objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment.

[He is] the treasure-house of an immeasurable multitude of auspicious qualities—such as knowledge, power, sovereignty, heroism, capacity, and splendor—which are untouched by any defect and possess limitless excellence;

[He is] the divine form which is a treasury of infinite qualities such as inconceivable, divine, marvelous, eternal, irreproachable, unsurpassed brilliance, beauty, fragrance, delicacy, charm, and youth, all of which are uniform, according to His own will, and matchless;
[He is] whose essential nature and intrinsic being are beyond the comprehension of speech and mind.

To the great ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous conduct, affection, and magnanimity; the refuge for the entire world without discrimination; the remover of the suffering of those who bow before him.
The sole ocean of affection for those who depend on him,
who has become an object of sight for the eyes of all people,
and who does not abandon his own essential nature.
He had descended into the house of Vasudeva,
illuminating the entire world with His infinitely superior splendor and refreshing the universe with His own radiance.

"He worships, serves, and attends upon [Me]"—this is the meaning. "He is considered by Me to be the most disciplined" means that he is the most excellent of all; thus, I consider him so because he directly perceives everything at all times exactly as it is, by his own nature.
By the first six chapters, [the nature] of the Supreme Brahman—the ultimate goal to be attained, the boundless, the sole cause of the entire universe—[has been established].

In order to explain the worship of the glorious Nārāyaṇa— who is omniscient, the soul of all beings, whose resolve is truth, and who possesses great majesty— as the means for attaining Him, there has been stated the vision of the true nature of the individual self (pratyagātman), which is to be accomplished through the performance of ritual action preceded by the knowledge of the Self, as that constitutes an ancillary part of such worship.
Now, by means of the middle group of six verses, the nature of the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman and His worship—which is denoted by the word *bhakti*—is described.
This very point will be stated further on:
"From whom the activity of beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded..."
By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection.
Beginning with "Thus," up to:
"Having become free and devoid of the sense of 'mine,' being tranquil, he is fit for becoming Brahman.
Having become Brahman, his self serene, he neither grieves nor desires."
Being equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me.

The knowledge expressed by such passages as, "One who knows this thus becomes immortal here," and "Verily,

“When there is purity of being, there is constant mindfulness;

“The knot of the heart is rent asunder, and all doubts are cut away.”

Because of the consistency with such passages as, "And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen," it is understood that [the practice] denoted by the terms *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (worship) consists of a continuous stream of mindfulness (*smṛti-santāna*) that takes on the same form as direct perception (*darśana*).
Furthermore, this is confirmed by the qualification in the passage: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
only by whomsoever He chooses is He attained, and for him this Self reveals His own form. This refers to the Supreme Self.

It is determined that the very continuum of mindfulness— which, being the cause of the state of being worthy of attainment, is itself of an exceedingly dear form due to the fact that what is remembered is exceedingly dear— is precisely what is denoted by the term "upāsana" (meditative worship).
For that alone is called "bhakti" (devotion).
Because of such statements as, "Devotion is defined as contemplation preceded by affection," and so forth;
therefore, [the scripture says]: "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here;
there is no other path for the journey."
“Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity,
nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen me.”

In that regard, in the seventh chapter, first, the true nature of the Supreme Person who is the object of worship is presented; then His concealment by *prakṛti* is shown, followed by surrender (*prapatti*) to the Blessed Lord for the sake of removing that concealment.
The classification of the types of lay practitioners (upāsaka) and the superiority of the knower (jñānin) are stated.

O Pārtha, listen to how you shall know Me in My entirety and without doubt, with your mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me. BhG 7.1.

With his mind directed toward me and unattached [to anything else], because of his excessive love for me, he has his mind firmly bound to me through my true nature, my qualities, my activities, and my divine manifestations;

such that at the very moment of separation from them, his own being would dissolve, he is thus deeply attached to me. Likewise, having me as his refuge, he himself would dissolve without me, and thus he takes refuge in me, making me his sole support.

And being solitary, I shall, along with that knowledge whose object is the solitary, declare the knowledge whose object is my own essential nature.
What need is there for much? Having known that knowledge—
Furthermore, for me, nothing else remains to be known.

He speaks of the difficulty of attaining the knowledge that is about to be described: "Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (BhG 7.3)
Human beings are qualified for the study of the scriptures;
among thousands of them, only a rare few strive until they reach perfection.
Among thousands who strive until they reach perfection, only a rare few, having known Me, strive for perfection through Me.
Among thousands of those like me, perhaps only one knows Me truly as I am, according to My actual state;
the intention is that no one does.
"That great-souled one is very rare."
For it will be said later: "But no one knows me. (BhG 7.3)
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus is my nature divided eightfold. (BhG 7.4)

Know that this is My nature (prakṛti), which exists as this world consisting of manifold and infinite objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment; it is divided eightfold in the form of earth, water, fire, air, and ether—possessing qualities such as smell—and in the form of the mind and other senses, as well as in the form of the intellect (mahat) and the ego (ahaṃkāra). BhG 7.4.
O mighty-armed one, know that this nature of Mine is inferior; but know that there is another, higher nature of Mine, which is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained.

This is my other nature; but know that there is another, distinct from this insentient nature which exists as the object of experience for the sentient, a supreme nature consisting of the individual soul (jīva), which is of a different class in form from that [insentient nature], and which is of the nature of consciousness, being my own nature as its primary experiencer.
By which this entire insentient world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world.

Understand that all these beings of mine— consisting of a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, existing in high and low states from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and originating from my two natures (prakṛtis)—
