are indeed mine, for they have their source in my two natures.
Likewise, because the entire world has its origin in the two primal natures (prakṛti),
and because both of those have me as their source and belong to me,
understand that I alone am the origin of the entire world, I alone am its dissolution, and I alone am its sovereign.

The fact that even *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which constitute the aggregate of the conscious and the unconscious, have their source in the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) is established by both Śruti and Smṛti:
"The Great Principle (*mahat*) dissolves into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*);
the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (*akṣara*)."
“The Imperishable dissolves into darkness;
darkness becomes one with the supreme deity.
And: “O sage, two forms arise beyond the essential nature of Viṣṇu: Pradhāna and Puruṣa.”
“The primordial nature (prakṛti) which I have described, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest,
and the person (puruṣa)— both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self. And the Supreme Self is the support of all, the Supreme Lord.”
He is celebrated by the name Viṣṇu in the Vedas and in the Vedāntas.
For such are the Śruti and Smṛti passages beginning with "BhG 2.1" and so forth. //76//
O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing else whatsoever higher than Me.

Just as I am supreme by virtue of being the cause of even the two *prakṛtis*—which are the causes of all things—and by virtue of being the sovereign over all insentient objects as well as the sentient soul which remains as their substratum; likewise, I alone am supreme through My possession of attributes such as knowledge, power, and strength.
Other than me, there is nothing whatsoever else that is superior, possessing any other qualities such as the power of knowledge and so forth, distinct from me.
All this is strung upon me, like clusters of gems upon a thread.

All this multitude of sentient and insentient entities, in both their states of effect and cause, constitutes My body; like a cluster of gems on a string, they are strung upon and supported by Me, who abide as the Self.
As it is said: "He whose body is the earth," and "He whose body is the self."
"He is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"—
thus it is established in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and other texts that the world and Brahman exist in the relationship of body and self.

Therefore, since everything is a mode (*prakāra*) of the Supreme Person who constitutes its very self by being His body, the Supreme Person alone exists in every mode; thus, He alone is denoted by all words. This he expresses through various instances of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):
"I am the taste in water, O son of Kuntī; I am the light in the moon and the sun."
The syllable Om among all the Vedas, the sound in space, and the virile power in men.
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the radiance in the fire;
I am the life-force in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
Know me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.
And among the powerful, I am strength devoid of lustful passion;
O bull of the Bharatas, I am desire that is not contrary to righteousness toward all beings.
All these diverse entities have arisen from Me alone; they subsist in Me as My own remains, existing within Me as My very body;
therefore, it is I alone who abide in each and every form.
Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.

What is being specified? Know that all those states of being— whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)— which exist in the world as bodies, as sense organs, as objects of enjoyment, and as their respective causes, have arisen from Me alone.
And because they are attached to me through their possessiveness, they remain in me alone;
yet I am not in them, nor have I ever been dependent on them for my existence,
even though the body's existence is otherwise dependent upon the self.
Even though the Self remains by means of the body, there is still benefit [derived from it];
however, for me, no such benefit exists through them,
and my sole purpose is mere sport— this is the meaning.
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
Thus, this entire universe, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, which is mine, arises from me alone at various times,
dissolves into me,
and remains established in me alone.
"I am indeed that which has become the body of envy and is composed of pride; thus, in both the state of cause and the state of effect, I alone exist in every way as the body of all.

Therefore, by virtue of being the cause, by virtue of being the sovereign remainder, and by virtue of my multitude of countless auspicious qualities such as knowledge and so forth, I alone am supreme in every respect."

There exists nothing else superior to me by any collection of auspicious qualities. Such as I am, I am beyond the three states consisting of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* qualities; yet I, who am supreme and imperishable—remaining eternally of one form—am [perceived] through those very same three qualities which are inferior, momentary in their destruction, and through my own unique collections of auspicious qualities and various modes of being experienced.

Deluded by objects that exist as bodies, senses, and objects of enjoyment in accordance with past karma, this entire world— abiding in the forms of gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings— does not recognize [the Self].

How is it that, even though You— who are by Your very nature infinite, unsurpassed bliss, eternal, always of one form, and most excellent compared to all worldly objects of enjoyment and their modes— remain present, the entire class of enjoyers conceives the notion of enjoyability toward objects that are extremely inferior, composed of qualities (guṇas), and unstable? To this, he says:
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the qualities, is difficult to overcome.
This illusion of Mine, consisting of the qualities—that is, composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—is divine because it was created by Me alone, who am the Divine engaged in play;
therefore, it is difficult for all to overcome, meaning it is hard to transcend.

Its designation by the term "māyā" is due to its capacity to produce diverse effects, just like the weapons of the Asuras and Rākṣasas; and as it is said: "Then, for his protection, the supreme discus Sudarśana, garlanded with flames, arrived as commanded by the Blessed One."
"By him, moving swiftly, that thousand illusions of Śambara were each individually destroyed while protecting the body of the boy"— thus it is said in such passages.
Therefore, the word *māyā* does not denote a false object.

Even in the case of magicians and the like, the term "māyāvī" (illusionist) is used because they produce a cognition that has a false object as its content through certain mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, which is indeed ultimately real [in its own nature].
Likewise, in that context, the mantra, medicinal herb, and so forth, are themselves "māyā";
for in all usages, the referent of a word must be a single entity that is common to all instances.

In this context, the application of the word "māyā" to false objects is metaphorical, because they are the objects of a cognition that perceives them as the effects of *māyā*, just as one says, "The galleries are shouting. O Blessed One, this [world] consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*) is indeed the ultimate *māyā* itself.

In such passages as, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā," it is stated that its effects are the obscuration of the Lord's true nature and the notion that one's own nature is an object of enjoyment.
Therefore, O Blessed One, the entire world, deluded by māyā, does not recognize the Blessed One, whose essential nature is infinite and unsurpassed bliss.
He states the means for liberation from Māyā:
"Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this Māyā. (BhG 7.14cd)

Those who take refuge in me alone—me, whose will is truth, who am supremely compassionate, and the shelter of the entire world without distinction—they cross over this *māyā* of mine consisting of the qualities; the meaning is that, having cast off *māyā*, they worship me alone.
To the question of why all do not resort to surrender to the Lord—which leads to the worship of the Lord—the Lord says:
"The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in Me;
their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, and they have embraced a demonic nature. (BhG 7.15)
Those who commit evil deeds and perform sinful actions do not take refuge in Me;
according to the degree of their wickedness, those deluded ones are of four kinds: the lowest among men, and so forth.
"Those whose wisdom has been carried away by illusion, having resorted to a demonic nature"—
the deluded are those who possess perverted knowledge.

In the manner previously described, they regard themselves as having the single essence of being subservient to the Lord, and they consider the entire range of objects of enjoyment to be subservient to themselves.
These lowest of men, though their true nature is known in a general sense, are unworthy of being oriented toward Me.

Their knowledge regarding Me and regarding My divine sovereignty has been stolen away by deceptive arguments that produce doubts concerning those very subjects, for they have had their wisdom snatched away by Māyā.
Thus addressed,
those who have resorted to a demonic nature possess a very firm conviction regarding my domain and the domain of my sovereignty that leads only to hatred;
they are those who have resorted to a demonic nature.
Each subsequent one is more sinful than the preceding.
O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. (BhG 7.16)
Those who have performed good deeds and meritorious actions, having come to me for refuge, worship me alone;

and they are of four kinds according to the gradations of their merit, becoming progressively superior to one another due to the excellence of their practice resulting from the greater weight of their good deeds.
The "afflicted" (ārta) is one who lacks a stable foundation and has fallen from his power, desiring its restoration;
the "seeker of wealth" (arthārthin) is one who, not having attained power, desires it.
Between these two, there is merely a difference in their orientation.
Because they are one in their scope as objects of sovereignty, there is only a single qualification.

The seeker (jijñāsu) is one who desires to attain the true nature of the self as liberated from primordial matter (prakṛti). It is said that he is a "seeker" because knowledge itself is his true nature.

And the wise one is one who knows his own essential nature as having its sole essence in being subservient to the Blessed One, as declared in the passage beginning, "But know my other nature, higher than this" (BhG 7.5); not finding final rest in the isolated self dissociated from material nature, he desires the Blessed One and considers the Blessed One alone to be the supreme goal to be attained. (BhG 7.16)
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is ever-disciplined, and whose devotion is single-minded, excels.
For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me. (BhG 7.17)
Among them, the man of knowledge is distinguished.
Why? Because it is said, "ever-disciplined and single-mindedly devoted. For the man of knowledge, whose sole goal is Me, his union with Me is constant.
But for the other two, their yoga consists in attaining whatever they themselves desire;
likewise, the wise one has devotion toward Me alone,
whereas the other two have devotion toward Me as well as toward their own desired objects and the means to attain them.
Therefore, he alone is distinguished.
Furthermore: "For I am exceedingly dear to the knower. The word *artha* here signifies that which is denoted.
The meaning is that just as I am dear to the knower, so it cannot be described even by me, who am omniscient and omnipotent; for dearness is devoid of any measurable limit.
As it was said of Prahlāda, the foremost among the wise:
"Though being bitten by great serpents, his mind remained attached to Kṛṣṇa; established in the joy of remembering Him, he did not perceive his own body."
In that very same way, he too is dear to me.
All these are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge is My very Self; this is My opinion.
For he, being disciplined in soul, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
"All these indeed worship Me alone"— thus [they are] noble and generous;
for those who take even the slightest thing from Me are indeed givers of My very self.
But the man of knowledge, I consider, is my very self; for I believe that my own sustenance depends upon him.
Why is this so?
Because, since he cannot conceive of sustaining himself without me, he has taken refuge in me alone as the unsurpassed goal to be attained.
Therefore, without him, even my own maintenance of selfhood is not possible;
hence, he is indeed my very self.
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge attains Me, realizing, "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled person is very rare.
This is not the fruit of births meritorious in small measure, namely,
my surrender preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of the Self, whose sole essence is the remainder of Me;
rather, it occurs at the end— after the conclusion— of many births meritorious in their merit.

Having become possessed of knowledge that "I am one whose sole essence is being a remnant of Vāsudeva, and whose very nature, existence, and activity are dependent upon Him; and He, moreover, is supreme by virtue of His countless multitudes of auspicious qualities," [one realizes] that Vāsudeva alone is my ultimate goal to be attained and the means of attainment.
Whatever else exists within his heart's desire, he approaches me with the thought, "All that is mine," and he worships me.
That high-souled one of great mind is very difficult to find; he is rarer than the rarest in the world.
This is precisely the meaning of the statement, "Vāsudeva is everything."
For it follows from the context: "I am exceedingly dear to the knower" (Gītā 7.17), and "for he, being disciplined in soul, is established in Me alone as the supreme goal" (Gītā 7.18);
and this "possessor of knowledge" is indeed one who possesses the characteristics just described.
Because he possesses the aforementioned state of being a knower,
[it is said]: "Beginning from 'Earth, water...,' up to 'Egoism— thus is My material nature divided eightfold.'"

"Know that this lower nature of Mine is one thing, but distinct from this is another, higher nature, which is the soul (jīva). Thus, the fact that the two natures—the sentient and the insentient—have as their sole essence their subservience to the Supreme Person is stated.
[And: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe."
Beginning with, "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya," [the Lord says]:
"Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me."

Thus, it has been stated that the two natures (prakṛti)—in their states as both cause and effect—have their essential nature, existence, and activity dependent upon the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), and that the Supreme Person is superior to everything in every respect;
therefore, He alone is here called the "knower" (jñānin). //719//
He demonstrates the very rarity of such a knower:
"Those whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities, adhering to their respective rules, constrained by their own nature. (BhG 7.20)

For all worldly persons are constrained and eternally accompanied by their own nature—the latent impressions of sin—which consists of objects related to the modes of material nature; their knowledge of their own true nature and its objects is carried away by various desires corresponding to those impressions, which are themselves composed of the modes and serve as the objects of their longing; thus, for the sake of fulfilling those respective desires, they worship other deities distinct from Me, namely the deities such as Indra alone.

Adopting this or that specific rule— having adopted the particular rule that is not common [to all] for the sole purpose of pleasing a specific deity— they resort to those very [deities] and worship them.
Whatever form a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his firm and unwavering. (BhG 7.21)
Those deities as well are My own bodies, established by such scriptural passages as: "He who dwells in the sun... whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is," and so forth.

Even though one may not know that they are My own bodies, whichever devotee desires to worship whichever particular form of Mine—such as the sun and others—with faith; [I grant him unswerving devotion].
Even for one who does not know this, I establish that very same faith—unwavering and free from obstacles—by reflecting that "this is faith directed toward my own form."
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that deity;
and from him he obtains his desires, for they have indeed been ordained by Me alone.
Endowed with that unimpeded faith, he strives toward the propitiation of Indra and the other deities.
Then, through the propitiation of those very deities who have become my own body, he obtains precisely those desired objects of his longing which have been ordained by me alone—
even though this occurs at the time of propitiation.
"Indra and the others are my own forms;
therefore, their worship is indeed my own worship"—one who does not know this, nevertheless, because that object is in fact my own worship, I alone fulfill the desire of the worshipper.
(BhG 7.22) But for those of small intelligence, that fruit is finite.
Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; my devotees, however, come to me as well.

For those of small intellect and limited understanding, who sacrifice only to Indra and other deities, the fruit of that worship is meager and it is finite. Why? Because "the worshippers of the gods go to the gods"; since those who sacrifice to them go to the gods, such as Indra and others.
For even Indra and the other gods possess limited enjoyments and exist for a limited duration of time;
consequently, those who attain union with them fall away along with them.
My devotees, however, recognizing that those very same actions constitute worship of Me, abandon attachment to limited fruits and, making my gratification their sole purpose, attain Me.

Furthermore, they do not return; for it will be said: "But having come unto Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist. (BhG 8.16) [Note: The verse cited here corresponds to BhG 8.16, though the provided text number 7.23 appears to be an editorial or typographical error.]
But others, however, thinking that even my descent among humans and other beings is of no consequence for the sake of being sought as a refuge by all, say:
"The unintelligent think of me, who am unmanifest, as having attained manifestation, not knowing my supreme, inexhaustible, and unsurpassed nature. (BhG 7.24)

I, the Lord of all, whose essential nature and character are beyond the reach of speech and mind, am to be propitiated by all actions; out of supreme compassion and affection for those who take refuge in me, I have descended as the son of Vasudeva with my true nature unaltered, so that I may be sought as a refuge by all.
Yet, ignorant of this, my supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed state, they regard me from here as being like an ordinary mortal prince.
The intellects consider me— who was previously unmanifest, but who has now attained manifestation by reaching a particular birth through the power of karma— to be [merely that];
therefore, they do not take refuge in me.
And they do not propitiate [the gods] with ritual actions.
To the question, "Why then is it not revealed in this way? he says here:
"I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā;
deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable. (BhG 7.25)
Enveloped by the *māyā* known as the conjunction with the specific human form and so forth belonging to the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), I am not manifest to everyone.

Because of this, this deluded world—merely perceiving my human form and such—regards me, though I am perceived, as being subject to birth and decay; whereas I am beyond the deeds of Vāyu and Indra, possess a splendor exceeding that of the Sun and Fire, unborn, undecaying, the sole cause of the entire universe, and the Lord of all.
He does not recognize me as having assumed a human form for the sake of being a refuge for all.
I know all beings that have passed away and those that are present, O Arjuna, as well as those yet to come; but no one knows Me.
I know—that is, I am aware of—all beings, past, present, and future.

But no one knows me; the meaning is that among all beings existing in the three periods of time who are being perceived by me, not a single person is found who, having recognized me as Vāsudeva in this manner—descended for the sake of being the refuge of all—takes refuge in me alone.
Therefore, the man of knowledge is indeed very difficult to find.
For thus,
O Bhārata, scorcher of foes, at the time of creation all beings fall into delusion through the confusion of dualities arising from desire and hatred.

By means of delusion—known as the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat—which arises from desire and aversion, all beings fall into confusion at the very time of creation, that is, at the moment of birth.

This is what is meant: in the pairs of opposites consisting of the *guṇas*, such as pleasure and pain, there are desire and aversion directed toward specific objects that were practiced in previous births;

through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of those, at the time of birth once again, that very same thing known as a pair of opposites arises as the object of desire and aversion, thereby causing delusion for living beings.
Through that delusion, all beings fall into confusion;
they come to have the nature of desire and aversion toward their objects,
rather than having the nature of pleasure and pain arising from union with or separation from Me.
But the man of knowledge has as his very nature the pleasure of union with Me and the pain of separation from Me;
no being whatsoever is born that does not possess this same nature.
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end—
they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites and firm in their vows, worship me.

But for those whose accumulated store of preeminent merit, earned over many births, has brought to an end their sin— which has persisted since beginningless time, which is the cause of likes and dislikes regarding pairs of qualities consisting of the *guṇas*, and which inclines one toward intoxication— they, having taken refuge in Me according to the gradations of their previously mentioned good deeds, are liberated from the delusion consisting of the *guṇas* for the sake of release from old age and death, and for the sake of great sovereignty.
And for the sake of attaining Me, those of firm vows and firm resolve worship Me alone. BhG 7.28.
In this regard, he introduces the specific qualities to be known and the factors to be adopted by those three who strive for liberation from old age and death by taking refuge in Me:
"Those who, having taken refuge in Me, strive for liberation from old age and death—they know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action in its entirety. (BhG 7.29)
Those who, having taken refuge in Me, strive for liberation from old age and death— that is, for the realization of the true nature of the Self as distinct from primordial matter—
they know that Brahman;
they know the entirety of the inner self (adhyātma).
And they know all action to be such.
Those who know Me as being together with the elemental beings and the divine, and as being together with the sacrifice—
even at the time of departure, they, with disciplined minds, know Me.

Because of the re-specification here with the word "those who," it is understood that other qualified persons (adhikārin) previously mentioned are intended; the statement, "Those who know Me as possessing the elements and possessing the gods, seeking sovereign power," although appearing to be a restatement (anuvāda), is indeed prescriptive (vidhāyaka) because its meaning was not previously established;
likewise, the phrase "possessing the sacrifice" is also prescribed without distinction for all three types of qualified persons.
This is due to the very nature of things.
For the performance of the three types of sacrifices—the obligatory, the occasional, and the great sacrifices—is unavoidable.
And even at the time of death, they know Me in accordance with what is conducive to their own attainment.

By the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "te ca," those who previously strove for liberation from old age and death are included as being known [by Me] at the time of departure; by this it is stated that even the possessors of knowledge, due to the very nature of their goal, know Me along with the sacrifice, and they know Me at the time of departure in accordance with what is to be attained by them.
In the seventh [chapter], the status of the supreme Brahman Vāsudeva as the object of worship, his sovereignty over all sentient and insentient entities, his causality,
and his nature as the substratum are [established].
Because it constitutes the entire body [of all things], it is denotable by the word "all" in every respect;
it is the controller of all,
and by virtue of its multitude of auspicious qualities, it alone is the supreme.

The concealment of that [Self] occurs through entities composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which exist as the body and the senses and as objects of experience, and which are caused by the stream of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) proceeding from beginningless time.

Through the surrender to the Lord (*bhagavat-prapatti*) caused by exceedingly excellent merit (*sukṛta*), and through the gradations of such merit, there arises a distinction among worshippers based on the excellence of their realization with respect to sovereignty, the true nature of the Imperishable (*akṣara-yāthātmya*), and the attainment of the Lord.

Having established the superiority and the rarity of one who seeks the Blessed One through constant application, single-minded devotion, and an extreme love for the Supreme Person, [the author] introduced the distinctions between what is to be known and what is to be adopted among these three;
now, in the eighth [chapter], he distinguishes the specific categories of what is to be known and what is to be adopted that were introduced.

Arjuna said: What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma), O Supreme Person? And what is declared to be the elemental (adhibhūta)? What is called the divine (adhidaiva)? BhG 8.1.
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, and how? And at the time of departure, how are You to be known by those of self-restraint, O Madhusūdana?
For those striving for liberation from old age and death by taking refuge in the Blessed One, what is that which is declared as "to be known" regarding Brahman and the Adhyātma (the inner self)?
What is to be known by those seeking sovereign power regarding the Adhibhūta (the elemental) and the Adhidaiva (the divine)?
And who is that which is designated by the term Adhiyajña (the sacrificial), to be known by all three?
And how does he possess the nature of being present at the sacrifice?
And at the time of departure, how are You to be known by these three who have restrained their selves? // BhG 8.1,2 //
The Blessed Lord said: The supreme, imperishable Brahman is called the Self (adhyātma) by its very nature;
the creative emission that brings about the origin of the existence of beings is designated as action (karma).

That which is designated as Brahman is the supreme imperishable; it is called "akṣara" because it does not perish, and it is the collective totality of all individual knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
Thus says the Śruti:
"The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable; the imperishable dissolves into darkness," and so forth.
The supreme imperishable is the essential nature of the self, liberated from primordial matter (prakṛti).
This intrinsic nature is called the "inner self" (adhyātma).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

That which is not the self, yet is connected to the self— consisting of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth— is declared in the *Pañcāgnividyā* as that which is to be known.
Both of these must be understood by those seeking liberation—one as that which is to be attained, and the other as that which is to be abandoned.
"Visarga," known as action (*karma*), brings about the manifestation of the states of beings;
"the state of beings" refers to the condition of being human and so forth.
The emission (*visarga*) that causes its arising—
produced by connection with a woman and established by the Vedic scripture, "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"—
is designated as *karman*.
And all of that, together with its consequences, should be understood by those seeking liberation as something to be dreaded and avoided;
and it will be explained immediately below as something to be avoided.
“Desiring which they lead the life of celibacy. BhGR 8.3.
The perishable state is the *adhibhūta*, and the *puruṣa* is the *adhidaivata*;
I alone am the *adhiyajña* here in this body, O best of embodied beings.

That which is designated as the *adhibhūta* (the objective field) for those seeking sovereignty is the perishable state (*kṣaro bhāvaḥ*), which exists within the elements beginning with space; it is a specific transformation of those elements, characterized by perishability, and consists of distinct objects with their respective substrates—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. These distinct objects with their substrates, which are to be attained by those seeking sovereignty, are what must be contemplated by them.
And the Puruṣa is the "adhidaivata"; the Puruṣa designated by the term *adhidaivata* is that which exists above the deities (*devatopari*).

Existing above all deities beginning with Indra and Prajāpati, the Puruṣa is the enjoyer (*bhoktā*) of the objects of enjoyment—such as sound and so forth—which are distinct from the objects of enjoyment belonging to Indra, Prajāpati, and the others.
And that state of being the enjoyer is to be contemplated as something to be attained by those who seek sovereignty.
"I alone am the Adhiyajña"— that is, I exist as the one to be propitiated through sacrifices.

In this regard, during the performance of the great sacrifices and other daily and occasional rites, the three classes of qualified persons should reflect: "I myself, abiding as the Self within Indra and the others who have become my body, am the one to be propitiated by these sacrifices. This is what is to be meditated upon. (BhG 8.4)
And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, attains My state; there is no doubt about this. (BhG 8.5)
This also applies equally to the three [castes]:
"And at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone,
he attains My state— that is, he attains My own nature (svabhāva)."
The meaning is that at that time, he takes on such a form as corresponds to how one contemplates him;
just as Ādibharata and others were produced at that time from forms belonging to the same species as the deer being remembered.
It is stated very clearly that it is the nature of the final cognition to produce the form of something belonging to the same class as its own object:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when one finally leaves the body,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly permeated by that state" (BhG 8.6).
Whatever state of being one remembers at the time of death when casting off the body, to that very state one goes immediately after death;
for the final impression arises only with respect to an object previously cultivated. (BhG 8.6)
Therefore, at all times remember Me and fight;
with your mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt. (BhG 8.7)
Since the final cognition arises only with respect to an object practiced during previous times,
therefore, until your departure from this life, remember Me day after day;
and perform the daily and occasional duties enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti, such as battle and other acts connected to your caste and stage of life, which serve to effect that daily remembrance.
Thus, with your mind and intellect dedicated to me through this means, and remembering me alone at the time of death in whatever manner you desire, you shall attain me;
there is no doubt in this. (BhG 8.7)

Having thus stated in general that the attainment of one's own goal depends upon the final cognition, he begins to explain the different modes of meditation for those three [classes of aspirants] for that purpose;
therein, he describes the mode of meditation for those seeking sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), as well as the mode of the final cognition according to that meditation:
"With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice, not wandering elsewhere..."
Contemplating the supreme divine Person, O Pārtha, he goes to Him.

By means of the yoga of daily practice and through being disciplined with a mind that does not wander elsewhere, one who contemplates Me— the supreme, divine Person in the manner about to be described— at the time of death, goes to Me alone; like the case of [the sage] Ādibharata attaining the state of a deer, he becomes My equal in form, distinguished by sovereignty.

Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the constant cultivation of the object of meditation by the mind at all times that are not incompatible with obligatory or occasional duties; yoga, however, is the meditation characterized as previously described, performed day after day at the specific time designated for yoga.
One should meditate upon the ancient Seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtle, the sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who is resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness. (BhG 8.9)

At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga, having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person. (BhG 8.10)
The Seer, the Omniscient, the Ancient, the Primeval, the Instructor, the Ruler of the universe, subtler than the subtlest— more minute even than the individual soul (jīva)—
the Sustainer of all, the Creator of all,
whose form is inconceivable, having a nature entirely distinct from everything else.

[He is] sun-colored, beyond darkness, possessing a divine form that is non-material and uniquely His own; having fixed and stabilized the vital breath (prāṇa) between the eyebrows at the time of departure with an unwavering mind— due to the strength of yoga practiced daily with devotion and the resulting cultivated impressions— one should [behold] the divine [form] there, in the center of the brows.
Whoever should recollect the Puruṣa, he approaches Him alone, attains His state,
and becomes equal to Him in sovereignty— this is the meaning.

Now, he describes the manner of remembrance for those seeking isolation (kaivalya): "That imperishable which those who know the Vedas declare, which ascetics free from passion enter, and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy—that goal I shall proclaim to you in brief. (BhG 8.11)

That Imperishable which those who know the Vedas describe as having qualities such as being neither gross nor subtle, that Imperishable into which the passionless ascetics enter, and that Imperishable desiring to attain which they practice celibacy— [that is Brahman].
I shall declare that state to you in brief.
It is called a "state" (*pada*) because it is reached and understood by the mind;
it is my own nature, the imperishable (*akṣara*), which is to be known through all the Vedāntas and is to be meditated upon as follows:
The meaning is: "In that way, I shall explain it in brief."
Having restrained all the gates of the senses and fixed the mind within the heart,
placing the vital breath in the head, he remains established in the practice of yoga-concentration.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me, he who departs, leaving the body, attains the supreme goal. (BhG 8.13)

Having restrained all the senses, beginning with the ears— which serve as gateways for cognition— having withdrawn them from their respective functions, and having fixed the mind upon Me, the Imperishable, seated within the lotus of the heart, he remains established in that which is called yoga, maintaining a steady state of being fixed solely upon Me.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om," which denotes Me, and remembering Me— the one denoted by that syllable—

who departs casting off the body after placing his vital breath in the crown of the head, he attains the supreme goal; the meaning is that he reaches the Self, which is free from material nature, identical in form to Me, and from which there is no return.
“He who does not perish when all beings perish.”
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; him they call the supreme goal.
This will be stated immediately thereafter [in BhG 1.46]. //812, 13//
Thus, the method of worshipping the Blessed One has been described for those seeking sovereignty and those seeking isolation (kaivalya) according to what is appropriate for their respective goals;
now, He describes the method of worshipping the Blessed One and the manner of attainment for the man of knowledge (jñānin):
"He who, with an undistracted mind, remembers Me constantly and perpetually..."
I am easily attained, O Pārtha, by that yogin who is constantly disciplined.

To him who constantly remembers Me from the time of his exertion onward— at all times, with a mind focused on no other, remembering Me intensely because of My supreme dearness, unable to sustain himself without the remembrance of Me, and practicing that unsurpassed remembrance— to that ever-steadfast yogi who desires constant union, I am easily attained; I alone am to be reached.
My state, consisting of sovereignty and so forth, is not easily attained;
yet, unable to endure separation from it, I myself choose that very state.
For it is heard in scripture: "He alone is to be obtained by whom He is chosen."
The meaning is this: I alone bestow the ripening of the meditation that is conducive to attaining Me, the destruction of its opposites, and such qualities as extreme dearness to Me;
for it will be said: "To those who are ever steadfast and worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me."
"Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. (BhG 10.11) //814//
From this point on, with the remainder of the chapter, the Lord speaks of the non-return of the man of knowledge and the seeker of liberation, and the return of those who seek power:
"Having come to Me, the high-souled ones, having attained the supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is an impermanent abode of suffering" (BhG 8.15).

Having attained Me, they do not undergo birth again—that abode of all suffering, which is impermanent and unstable—because these high-souled ones possess great minds; having known My true nature as it actually exists, through their extreme love for Me, they find no sustenance for themselves apart from Me. With their minds absorbed in Me and taking refuge in Me, by worshipping Me, they attain the state of supreme perfection.
They have reached me. // BhG 8.15 //
Immediately after [discussing] those who have attained the state of sovereignty and those who have reached the Blessed One, [the Lord] stated the cause for returning and for not returning:
"O Arjuna, from the world of Brahmā downwards, all worlds are subject to return;
but having come unto Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist. (BhG 8.16)
All worlds existing within the interior of the cosmic egg, extending up to the realm of Brahmā, are abodes of enjoyment and sovereignty, yet they are subject to recurrence and destruction.
Therefore, for those who have attained the state of sovereignty, destruction is unavoidable due to the perishability of the place they have reached.

However, for those who have attained Me—the omniscient one whose will is ever-true, who sports in the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, who is supremely compassionate, and who is eternally uniform—there is no possibility of destruction; thus, there is no rebirth for them.
It does not exist.

He describes the regulation of the times of creation and destruction for the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā and for those contained within them, which are brought about by the volition of the Supreme Person:
"Those people who know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas are the ones who truly understand day and night. (BhG 8.17)
At the arrival of day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very same thing known as the unmanifest.
This very same multitude of beings, having come into existence again and again,
dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha, and comes forth at the arrival of day.

Those people who understand the arrangement of day and night as established by my own volition for all beings from humans up to the four-faced Brahmā, know that the day of the four-faced Brahmā lasts for a thousand cycles of the four ages (caturyuga),
and his night is of the same duration.

There, at the arrival of Brahmā’s day, the manifest world—consisting of bodies, senses, objects of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment existing within the three worlds—proceeds from the unmanifest state, which is the body of the four-faced one.
At the arrival of his night, it dissolves back into that very same unmanifest state, the body of the four-faced one.
This very group of beings, subject to karma, having come into being again and again at the arrival of the day, dissolves at the arrival of the night.
Again, at the arrival of day, [the world] comes into being; likewise,

at the end of a thousand yugas in the form of the conclusion of the rainy season, the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā and Brahmā himself dissolve into me alone, according to the sequence beginning with "the earth dissolves into water, and the waters dissolve into fire," until reaching the unmanifest, the imperishable, and darkness.

Thus, since everything other than myself originates from me through the regulation of time and dissolves back into me, it is inevitable that they are subject to birth and destruction; consequently, for those who have attained states of sovereignty, a return [to worldly existence] is unavoidable. However, for those who have come unto Me, there is no possibility of returning again.
Now, he says that for those who have attained isolation (kaivalya), there is no returning again:
"But beyond that unmanifested state is another, unmanifested, eternal being, which does not perish even when all beings perish. (BhG 8.20)
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they speak of him as the supreme goal, attaining which they do not return—that is my supreme abode.

Therefore, from that unmanifest (avyakta), which is of the nature of insentient primordial matter (prakṛti), there is another, superior (para) and more excellent state (bhāva)—distinct from it by virtue of having the single form of pure consciousness.
It is "unmanifest" (avyakta) because it is not manifested by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); the meaning is that its unique aspect is self-cognized.

The eternal (*sanātana*) is that which is constant by virtue of being incapable of origination or destruction; though situated here and there within all elements beginning with space—both those possessing causes and their effects—even as they perish, it does not perish.
That is called the unmanifest (*avyakta*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*), as in:
"But those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest... (Gītā 12.3).
In passages such as "The immutable is called the immovable," those who know the Veda declare that to be the supreme goal.

This very same [Self] is what is meant here by the term "supreme goal" in the verse, "He who departs, leaving the body, goes to the supreme goal"; the meaning is that the Self exists in its own essential nature, dissociated from contact with primordial matter (prakṛti).
Having attained that which exists in such a state, established in its own essential nature, they do not return;
that is my supreme abode, my supreme place of governance. While insentient *prakṛti* is one place of governance, [this is another].
The nature of the individual soul (*jīvaprakṛti*) when conjoined with that [matter] is the second state of governance;
the liberated nature, established in its own essence and separated from contact with non-consciousness (*acit*), is the supreme state of governance—this is the meaning.
And that is of the nature of non-return.
Alternatively, the word *dhāma* signifies light;
and here, "light" is intended to mean knowledge.

The supreme *dhāma* is the liberated essential nature of the Self, characterized by unlimited knowledge, as distinguished from the Self whose nature is limited knowledge due to its association with primordial matter (*prakṛti*). (BhG 1.20–21)
But that which is to be attained by the wise is therefore utterly distinct from that; thus he says:
"That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion alone—he within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded. (BhG 8.22)
“O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread.”
That Supreme Person— who has been indicated by the words "Me, the supreme and imperishable," and so forth, within whom all beings abide, and by whom this entire universe is pervaded—
that Supreme Person is attainable through undivided devotion, as expressed in the phrase "with a mind focused on nothing else, constantly. //822//

Now, he describes the common path beginning with light for both the knower of the true nature of the Self and the one devoted to the Supreme Person: "The path beginning with light is heard in the Śruti for both;
and that is characterized by non-return, as in the case of the Pañcāgni-vidyā."
In such passages as, "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity,
they pass into the light; from the light, into the day," etc.,
it is taught that for one who has traveled by the path beginning with light, there is attainment of the supreme Brahman and non-return.
"He leads them to Brahman; those who proceed by this path do not return to this human whirlpool.

Furthermore, this scriptural mention of the journey—namely, "Those who know thus"—does not have as its object the attainment of the Self which is a subsidiary part of the higher knowledge (paravidyā), as found in the Prajāpati discourse and other such passages.
Because the separate scriptural mention, "And those who in the forest worship with faith, [saying] 'Austerity is [Brahman]'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1), would otherwise be purposeless;
and because in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, it is stated: "Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.1).

Having stated the distinction between consciousness and matter—that the state of being humans and so forth is caused by merit and demerit and belongs to the waters themselves when mixed with other elements, while for the Self it is merely an embrace by them—[the text continues]:
“Now, those who know thus... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1].

"They enter the flame... they do not return to this human whirlpool"—from this it is understood that it has been stated that those who thus know the two distinct entities, the conscious and the unconscious, as things to be abandoned and as the goal to be attained, proceed by way of the flame and the like and do not return.

For one who knows the true nature of the Self and is devoted to the Supreme Person, there is the statement regarding the attainment of Brahman: "He leads them to Brahman. Thus, the reality of the Self, when separated from the unconscious matter, is of the nature of Brahman, having the single essence of being subservient to Brahman.
Thus it should be understood;
and this is also due to the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).
Furthermore, the state of having a single flavor as a subordinate part of the Supreme is established by such scriptural passages as, "He who dwells in the self... and "Whose self is the body."
I shall now declare that time, O bull of the Bharatas, departing at which yogis go either to non-return or to return.
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—
departing there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman.

Here, the word "time" (kāla) is intended to indicate the path by virtue of its being predominantly presided over by deities who identify with the time periods beginning from the day and ending with the year.
The meaning is: "I shall describe that path upon which departing yogins attain non-return, and those of meritorious deeds attain return.
The passage beginning with "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course" serves as an illustration of the year and so forth.
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun’s southern course— attaining the lunar light during that time, the yogin returns.
And this is an illustration of the world of the ancestors and so forth situated on the path beginning with smoke;
here, the word "yogi" refers to one who is connected with meritorious karma. (BhG 8.25)
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are indeed considered eternal.
By the one, a person goes to non-return; by the other, he returns again.
The bright path begins with light and so forth, while the dark path begins with smoke and so forth;
by the bright path, one goes to non-return.
But by means of the dark path, one returns again.
These two paths—the bright and the dark—are declared in the eternal Śruti for various types of wise men and those of meritorious deeds:
"Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they pass into the light."
“Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, ‘Sacrifices, works of public utility, and gifts [constitute the path],’ they pass into the smoke. (BhG 8.26)
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogi whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.
Knowing these two paths, a certain yogi is not deluded at the time of departure;
rather, he proceeds by his own path of the gods.
Therefore, day after day, remain engaged in yoga known as the contemplation of the long-term courses of existence.
Now he states the fruit of knowing the meaning of the scripture taught in the two preceding chapters:

"Whatever meritorious fruit is declared to come from the Vedas, from sacrifices, from austerities, and from charity—all that transcends the yogi who has understood this; he attains the supreme, primordial abode. (BhG 8.28)
Whatever fruit is prescribed for all meritorious acts—such as the study of the Vedas in the form of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva*; sacrifices; austerities;

and gifts—all that is surpassed by knowing this majesty of the Blessed One proclaimed in these two chapters. Because of the excellence of the bliss arising from this knowledge, one regards all those other fruits as mere straw.
Having become a yogi and a man of knowledge, he attains the supreme, primordial abode which is the goal of the wise. (BhG 8.28)

The specific distinctions based on the types of lay devotees (*upāsaka*) have been explained. Now, having clarified the majesty of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), who is the object of worship, as well as the distinction among those possessed of knowledge (*jñānin*), the essential nature of worship in the form of devotion (*bhakti*) is being described.
The Blessed Lord said:
I shall declare this most secret knowledge, together with realized wisdom, to you who are free from malice—knowledge by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil. (BhG 9.1)

But this most secret knowledge—consisting of devotion, known as worship, accompanied by realization (vijñāna), that is, accompanied by the specific knowledge pertaining to worship—I shall declare to you who are free from malice; the meaning is: I shall declare it to you who, having heard of My majesty—which is of an infinite variety and distinct from everything else—think, "It is exactly so."
Having known that knowledge which culminates in practice, you shall be liberated from all inauspiciousness that stands as an obstacle to attaining Me.
This is the royal science, the royal secret, this supreme purifier;
it is directly perceivable, consistent with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable.
It is the king of sciences among sciences, the king of secrets among secrets;
or, it is the science of kings, hence "rājavidyā."
For kings possess vast and unfathomable minds;
the meaning is that this knowledge belongs to those of great mind.
Indeed, it is only those of great mind who are skilled in concealing what must be concealed; therefore, it is their own secret.
This is the supreme purifier, which removes all impurities that obstruct the attainment of Me;
it is a matter of direct perception.
"Avagama" means that which is understood; thus, it refers to the object [of knowledge].
That knowledge whose object is an understanding that has become manifest is "pratyakṣāvagama.
The meaning is: when I am worshipped through worship in the form of devotion, I then and there come to be directly perceived by the worshipper.
Furthermore, it is "dharmyam," which means not departing from dharma.
For "dharma-ness" consists in being the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

The meaning is that, by its very nature as something exceedingly dear, and by bringing about my vision at that very moment, it is itself the form of the supreme good, yet it is the means for attaining my state— which is the ultimate and unsurpassed form of the supreme good.
Therefore, it is very easy to perform and very easy to undertake;
it is to be adopted because of its extreme dearness;
it is imperishable, meaning inexhaustible.
Even after bringing about my attainment, he himself is not diminished;
the meaning is that for one who performs such worship, even when the gift of myself has been bestowed, it appears to me as if something has been done by him for me.
O scorcher of foes, those persons who have no faith in this dharma do not reach me, but return to the path of the cycle of death.

Regarding this dharma known as worship—which has Me, the unsurpassedly beloved, as its object; which is itself of the nature of the unsurpassedly beloved; which is the means for attaining Me, the supreme liberation; and which is imperishable—those persons who, while in a state fit for its undertaking, fail to have faith in it—that is, who lack the eagerness preceded by conviction—fail to attain Me and remain perpetually on the path of worldly existence, which is of the nature of death.
The meaning is: "Aha! This is a great marvel. BhGR 9.3.
Listen now to my inconceivable majesty, which has become the object of attainment:
by me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded;
all beings abide in me, yet I do not abide in them. (BhG 9.4)
Yet the beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the sustainer of beings and the source of all beings, does not abide within the beings.

This entire world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, is pervaded by me—the inner controller (antaryāmin)—who am of unmanifest form and whose true nature is not revealed; that is to say, I have pervaded it as its presiding lord for the sake of supporting and governing this world.
As it is said in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa:

“Abiding in the earth... whom the earth does not know,” and “abiding in the self... whom the self does not know”—thus, the pervasion by the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), who is unseen by the entire range of sentient and insentient entities, has been stated in various places. Therefore, “all beings abide in Me”: all beings abide in Me, the Inner Controller.
In that very same Brāhmaṇa, it is stated:
"He whose body is the earth... who controls the earth from within;

he whose body is the self (ātman)... who controls the self from within. Thus, by establishing [the elements and the self] as bodies, their state of being governed is demonstrated, and consequently, their maintenance and regulation are shown to be dependent upon Him.
And as for their being residual:
I do not abide within them, nor am my own existence dependent upon them; the meaning is that they provide no assistance whatsoever toward my own abiding.
Nor do the elements abide in Me; I do not possess the quality of being a support for them, as water is for a jar or other objects.
How so? By My volition (*saṅkalpa*).
Behold My divine power (*yoga*); behold this wondrous power, unique to Me, which is impossible to conceive elsewhere.

What is that yoga? "My Self, the sustainer of beings and the source of all beings, supports all beings but does not dwell within them; I am the sustainer of all beings, yet no benefit whatsoever is rendered to me by them."
My very self is the creator of beings; my mind-made resolve alone is the nourisher, the sustainer, and the controller of all beings.
To provide an illustration for the fact that the existence and activity of all this depend upon His own volition, He says:
"Just as the great wind, moving everywhere, is eternally situated in space, even so, understand that all beings abide in Me. (BhG 9.6)

Just as a great wind, having no support, abides in space and moves everywhere— yet that wind, being without support, must necessarily be admitted to abide dependent on me— even so, understand that all beings abide in Me, who am unseen by them, and are supported by Me alone, as the knowers of the Veda have declared.

“The rising of clouds, the ebbing of the ocean, the division of the moon, the quivering of the wind, the flashing of lightning, and the course of the sun—these are the manifold illusions (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu. This means that these are the great wonders unique to Viṣṇu. Scripture also states: “Under the governance of this Imperishable (*akṣara*), O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart.”
“From fear of Him the wind blows;
from fear of Him the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra [tremble],” and so forth. (BhG 9.6)

It has been stated that the maintenance and activity of all things proceed from the volition of the Blessed Lord, who is independent of everything else; likewise, it is said that their origination and dissolution also result from His volition alone: "O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa, all beings go to My own nature;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth. (BhG 9.7)
All beings, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, [enter] my own nature— which is the body of Myself,
denoted by the word "tamas," and which is unfit for the differentiation of name and form.
At the end of the eon, at the time of the dissolution of the Four-faced One, they go [to their source] through my resolve;
those very same beings I emit again at the beginning of the eon.
As Manu has said: "This was then enveloped in darkness... he, having meditated, [emitted it] from his own body."
Scripture as well [affirms this], such as: "He whose body is the unmanifest," and "The unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable; the Imperishable dissolves into Darkness."
And [it is said]: “In the beginning, that was hidden by darkness, without a distinguishing mark. (BhG 9.7)
Taking hold of My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature.

Taking hold of my own nature, which is manifold and subject to transformation, I cause it to transform in eight ways; and by the power of my deluding nature, composed of the *guṇas*, I repeatedly emit at various times this multitude of beings—consisting of four classes: gods, animals, humans, and immovable things—rendering them powerless.
If that is so, then actions such as the creation of an unequal world would bind you by giving rise to cruelty and other such faults; to this he replies:
"And those actions do not bind Me, O Dhanañjaya, for I remain as if indifferent, unattached to those actions" (BhG 9.9).
And those acts, such as the creation of inequality and so forth, do not bind me, nor do they produce qualities such as cruelty in me;
for it is solely the previously performed actions of the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) that are the cause of their diverse states as gods and others.
I, however, am unattached to that inequality, remaining there like one who is indifferent.

As the author of the Sūtras has said: "Inequality and cruelty [do not apply to the Lord] because He takes account [of other factors]; if it is argued that [karma] cannot exist because there was no prior division [of beings], we say no, because [the cycle of existence] is beginningless. (BhG 9.9)
Under my supervision, Nature gives birth to the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world indeed revolves.

Therefore, my nature, impelled by the karma of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and overseen by me whose will is ever-true, gives birth to the world of moving and non-moving beings. By this reason—namely, my oversight in accordance with the karma of the Knower of the Field—you should behold my divine yoga, which consists of my sovereignty, my possession of a true will, and my freedom from defects such as cruelty;
behold this yoga of mine, the son of Vasudeva.
As the Śruti says:
"The Illusionist creates this entire universe, and within it another is held fast by illusion;
one should know illusion to be Nature (prakṛti) and the Illusionist to be the Great Lord (maheśvara). (BhG 7.14) //910//
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form, not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. (BhG 9.11)

Thus, those deluded by their own evil deeds disregard me— the Great Lord of all beings, the omniscient one whose will is truth, the sole cause of the entire universe— who, out of supreme compassion, have assumed a human form so as to be accessible to all; they consider me to be like an ordinary man.

The meaning is that they disregard me by regarding me as belonging to the same class as other humans merely because of my assumption of human form, while remaining ignorant of this supreme state of mine— which consists in assuming human form— being rooted in my boundless compassion, magnanimity, good character, and affection for all beings, and in which I am the Great Lord of all creatures.
Futile their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and bereft of discernment,
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.
In their human state, they have resorted to a deluding nature— demonic and asuric— which conceals their supreme compassion and other divine qualities;
thus they are those whose hopes are futile, whose desires are vain and fruitless, and whose actions are in vain and whose undertakings are useless.

Possessing vain knowledge— meaning their knowledge is fruitless due to a perverted understanding regarding all my objects, whether moving or unmoving— and being devoid of consciousness, meaning they lack true knowledge of the reality of everything everywhere, they regard me, the Lord of All, as equal to others; and whatever they desire to do toward me, and whatever undertakings they initiate for that purpose, [is in vain].
The meaning is that all of that becomes futile.
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings.

But those great-souled ones who, having approached me for refuge through their own accumulated stores of merit, have shaken off all bonds of sin and have taken recourse to my divine nature— they, knowing me as the imperishable source of beings, whose name, action, and form are beyond the reach of speech and mind, and who have descended in human form out of supreme compassion for the protection of the virtuous— worship me with undistracted minds.

Out of an excess of love for Me, being unable to sustain their minds, their selves, and their external senses without worshiping Me, they worship Me with the sole purpose of My service. Constantly glorifying Me, striving with firm vows,
and bowing down to Me with devotion, they worship Me, ever-disciplined.
Because of their extreme love for me, they are unable to sustain themselves even for a moment or a fraction of a moment without chanting my praises, reciting my names, and bowing down to me;
remembering my names which express my specific qualities, with all their limbs bristling with horripilation and their throats choked with joy,
they constantly chant such names as Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, and so forth.

Likewise, striving with firm resolve in my works such as worship and the like, as well as in services to them such as the creation of pleasure gardens and groves, they prostrate themselves like a staff upon the ground— regardless of dust, mud, gravel, and so forth— with their eight limbs, including their two feet, two hands, head, mind, intellect, and ego, all bowed down by the weight of devotion.
Constantly disciplined, longing for eternal union with Me, and resolved upon self-surrender as their ultimate goal, they worship Me.
Others also, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as the one,
as the distinct, and manifoldly as the one whose face is everywhere.
Other great-souled ones also worship Me, sacrificing with the previously mentioned acts such as chanting and with the sacrifice known as knowledge.
How so? By means of multiplicity—that is, through the distinctness of the world-form—and by means of unity, they worship Me who am established as the universe-faced one, existing in every form.

This is what is meant: the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva himself, whose body consists of the extremely subtle sentient and insentient entities that are not yet fit for the differentiation of name and form, and who possesses true resolve, forms the volition, "May I exist with a gross body consisting of sentient and insentient entities differentiated into various names and forms";
and thus intending this, he alone remains as the body of the manifold world known as gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings. Those who reflect in this manner [attain liberation].
"And they wait upon me. (BhG 9.15)
For thus I alone abide as the body of the universe; so he says:
"I am the ritual act, I am the sacrifice, I am the ancestral offering (svadhā), and I am the medicinal herb;
I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter (ājya), I am the fire, and I am the oblation. (BhG 9.16)
I am the sacrifice; I am the sacrifice such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others;
I alone am the great sacrifice;
I alone am the Svadhā that nourishes the hosts of ancestors.
I alone am the medicine and the oblation;
I alone am the mantra; and I alone am the clarified butter.
This is for the sake of illustration: the meaning is that the oblation consisting of Soma and so forth is myself alone;
I am the fire such as the Āhavanīya and others;
and the act of offering (homa) is also myself alone. (BhG 9.16)
I am the father of this world, the mother, the sustainer, and the grandfather;
I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable Om, and also the Rig, Sama, and Yajur Vedas.
Of this world consisting of the stationary and the moving,
[He exists] here and there in the form of fatherhood and motherhood.
"I alone exist as the sustainer and as the grandfather.
Here, the word *dhātṛ* refers to a specific conscious being distinct from the mother and father who is the cause of one's birth.
Whatever is to be known through the Vedas, whatever is pure and purifying—
that is indeed I;
and I alone am the knower and the sacred syllable *praṇava*, which is the seed of the Vedas.
And I alone am the Veda, consisting of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus.
I am the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the dwelling, the refuge, and the friend;
I am the source, the place of dissolution, the repository, and the imperishable seed. (BhG 9.18)
It is called "gati" because it is gone to (*gam-yate*); the meaning is the place to be reached in various instances;
the "bhartṛ" is the sustainer (*dhārayitṛ*).
The Lord is the ruler; the witness is the direct observer; the abode is the place of residence, such as a house and so forth.
Refuge:
A conscious being who is to be relied upon for the attainment of the desired and the warding off of the undesired is a refuge;
and that is indeed myself.
I am the well-doer who seeks the welfare [of all],
and I alone am the source, the place of dissolution, and the locus for the birth and destruction of anyone whatsoever, wherever that birth or destruction may occur.
It is called a "nidhāna" because it is deposited (nidhīyate);
the meaning is that I alone am that which is to be produced and that which is to be withdrawn.
It is the imperishable seed, the cause which is devoid of decay in each respective instance.
That is indeed myself. BhGR 9.18.
I heat up; I withhold the rain and I send it forth. I am both immortality and death, and both being and non-being, O Arjuna. (BhG 9.19)
In the form of fire, the sun, and so forth, I alone give heat;
in the summer season and other times, I alone withhold the rain, and likewise, during the rainy season, I alone release it.
Both immortality and death;
that by which the world lives and that by which it dies— both of these are indeed myself.
What is the use of saying more here?
Both the existent and the non-existent are I alone; that which exists is I.

The meaning is that whatever is non-existent— namely the past and the future— I myself exist as its very mode, because I abide as the body of all things, both conscious and unconscious, in all their various states. Likewise, by means of the knowledge of unity, those who do not fail to perceive that I alone exist as the mode of the entire universe— which stands divided into manifold names and forms through distinctness— worship me.

Having thus described the conduct of those great-souled knowers who have as their sole enjoyment the experience of the Blessed Lord, [the Lord] speaks of the conduct of the ignorant who desire objects of sense, in order to show their distinction from them: "Those who possess the three Vedas, the drinkers of Soma, whose sins are purified, having worshipped me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven. Having attained the holy world of the lord of the gods, they enjoy divine celestial pleasures in heaven. (BhG 9.20)
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and desiring objects of desire, they obtain the state of going and returning. (BhG 9.21)
The three sciences (*trividyā*) consist of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas;
those who are devoted solely to these three sciences are called *traividyas*,
but they are not devotees of the end of the three (*trayyantaniṣṭhāḥ*).

For those who have reached the culmination of the three Vedas, having known Me alone— the one to be known by all the Vedas— in the manner previously described, worship Me alone through the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) and through chanting and other acts performed with supreme devotion, for whom I am the sole goal to be attained.
But the followers of the three Vedas (*traividyāḥ*), on the other hand, drink the remnants of the Soma from sacrifices dedicated solely to Indra and others as propounded by the Vedas.
"Purified of sins" means cleansed of those sins that obstruct the attainment of heaven and other such realms;

by means of sacrifices— which are mentally conceived as being solely for deities such as Indra, though in reality they are of My nature— they worship Me, yet not knowing Me as I truly am, they pray for the path to heaven.
Having attained the world of the Lord of the Gods—a realm of merit unmixed with suffering—they enjoy divine celestial pleasures here and there.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, once the merit that served as the cause for that experience is exhausted, they enter the mortal world once again.

Thus, those who are devoid of the knowledge established in the Vedānta, who desire heaven and other such rewards resulting from rites, and who have merely resorted to the dharma of the three Vedas, [attain this].
The meaning is that they obtain what has been gone to and returned from—experiencing such things as the heavens, which are meager and unstable—and they turn back again and again.

But for those great-souled ones who, having meditated upon Me as the form most dear and unsurpassed, attain Me—consisting of infinite and supreme bliss—they do not return; thus [the Lord] shows their distinction: "Those people who worship Me, thinking of no other, for those who are ever-devoted, I carry the burden of their acquisition and preservation. (BhG 9.22)
"Non-different" means having no other purpose;

because they cannot maintain themselves without thinking of Me, they have the sole purpose of thinking of Me. Those great-souled persons who, thinking of Me—who am endowed with all auspicious qualities and possessed of all sovereign powers—wait upon Me, attend upon Me from every side.
To those who worship me without deficiency— those who are constantly devoted and who long for constant devotion toward me—
I [grant] yoga, characterized by attainment of myself.
And I carry that security which consists in the state of non-return.
But those who, devoted to other deities, worship them endowed with faith— even they, O son of Kuntī, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule.

But those who are devotees of deities such as Indra, being solely devoted to the Triple Veda and endowed with faith, worship Indra and the others— they too, by the logic previously stated, because everything has Me as its self since it is My body,
and because the words "Indra" and so forth actually denote Me, worship Me alone in reality.
However, they sacrifice without prior adherence to the prescribed rules;

for they regard Indra and the other deities as objects to be propitiated through ritual action, rather than as the ultimate reality as the Vedānta texts enjoin— such as the passage beginning, "Where the four officiating priests attain union with the gods."
They do not worship that [deity] as being primary;

for the collection of Vedāntic passages, by establishing Indra and others— who exist as bodies of the Supreme Person— as objects of worship, establishes that the Supreme Person alone, who is their very self, is the direct object of worship.
The *caturhotṛ* sacrifices refer to rituals such as the *agnihotra*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and others.
When the Supreme Self is established as the very self [of the sacrificer], these rites proceed toward identification with the deities such as Indra who constitute His body;
the meaning is that these rituals reach this state of identification, in that they become acts of propitiation for Indra and the other deities.

Therefore, those who possess the threefold knowledge (traividyā) do not recognize that these ritual acts are the means of propitiating the Supreme Person whose body consists of Indra and the other deities, and that He alone is the one to be propitiated; consequently, they partake only of limited fruits and are subject to the nature of transmigration. Thus it is said:
For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall.
And the meaning is that I alone am the Lord and the bestower of fruits in each respective case.
"Oh, how great is this diversity!
For while engaged in the very same action, some, through a mere difference in intention, become partakers of extremely small fruits and are subject to the nature of falling away;
whereas others become partakers of the fruit consisting in the attainment of the Supreme Person, which is infinite, unsurpassed bliss, and do not return again. Thus he said.

Those who follow the vow of the gods go to the gods; those who follow the vow of the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me as well. (BhG 9.25)

The word *vrata* denotes a resolve (*saṅkalpa*). Those who possess the "vow to the gods" (*devavrata*)— namely, those who have the resolve to worship Indra and the other deities through rituals such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices—
they go to the gods, Indra and the rest.
Those who have the intention of sacrificing to the ancestors, thinking, "We sacrifice to the ancestors through ancestral rites and the like," go to the ancestors.
And those who have the intention of sacrificing to elemental spirits, thinking, "We sacrifice to yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and other such beings," [go to those beings].
Those beings go [to those respective states].
Those who, by means of those very sacrifices, worship me with the thought, "We worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, whose body consists of the gods, ancestors, and elemental beings"—
those sacrificers to me go to me alone.
Those who observe vows dedicated to the gods and others, having attained those deities and enjoyed limited enjoyment with them, perish along with them at the time of their destruction.

But those who worship Me—Me, who am without beginning or end, omniscient, whose will is ever true, a great ocean of an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, and of unsurpassed, unsurpassable bliss—do not return again; this is the meaning. (BhG 9.25)
He says that there is this further distinction even for those who sacrifice with wine:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering of devotion from one of purified soul, I accept. (BhG 9.26)

Whoever offers me with devotion even a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— being exceedingly dear to Me, such that one cannot sustain oneself without the offering of these— I accept what he gives. To him,
