whose soul is disciplined and whose mind is endowed with the purity of having the offering of those very things as his sole purpose, I grant the fulfillment of his desires.

That which has been offered with such devotion— though I am the Lord of all, who has attained all desires through the play of the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of the entire universe, whose resolve is infallible, who possesses an infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, and who abides in the experience of my own innate, unsurpassed, and infinite bliss; [I accept it].
I eat only upon attaining that beloved one who is far beyond the path of desire,
as it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*:
"Those actions which are performed by those whose intellects have attained single-minded focus..."
"The Lord himself indeed accepts all of them with his own head. (BhG 9.26)

Since this distinction is beyond the reach of the speech and mind of even great-souled knowers (*jñānin*), therefore, having become a knower yourself, with your self bowed down by the weight of devotion characterized as previously described, and constantly performing your own duties such as chanting, circumambulation, worship, and prostration,
you should likewise perform worldly and Vedic obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites; thus he says:
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away,
and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me.
Whatever worldly action you perform that is necessary for the maintenance of the body, whatever you eat for the sake of sustaining the body,
and whatever Vedic rites— such as burnt offerings, gifts, and austerities— you perform as obligatory or occasional duties; [all these are done by Me].
Offer all that to Me.
"Arpaṇa" means that which is offered; act in such a way that the agency, the enjoyment, and the status of being the object of worship for all actions—both worldly and Vedic—become surrendered to Me.
This is what is meant: [surrender] those deities and others who are perceived as the objects of worship in sacrifices, gifts, and so forth, to the agent of the action.

And for you, the enjoyer, because you belong to me and because your nature, existence, and activity are dependent upon my will, you exist in me alone— the supreme subordinate and the supreme agent; thus, I am both you as the agent, enjoyer, and worshipper, and the entire host of deities who are to be worshipped.

Offer up the entire collection of rites of propitiation, preceded by your own state of being directed by Me, with the single flavor of absolute non-remainder; and, filled with intense love, contemplate this as being the very essence of the nature of the Object of Propitiation. // BhG 9.27 //
In this way, you shall be liberated from the bonds of action through their very fruits, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
with your self disciplined by the yoga of renunciation, being fully liberated, you shall come unto Me.

Thus, with your mind disciplined by the yoga called renunciation, contemplating yourself as subservient to Me and having the single flavor of being under My control, and contemplating all action— both worldly and Vedic— as worship of Me, you shall be liberated from all the endless bonds of past actions consisting of good and evil fruits, which are obstacles to attaining Me.
Released from those, you will come to me alone.
Hear from me this supreme, world-transcending nature of Mine: I am equal toward all beings; to Me there is none hateful and none dear.
But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I am also in them. (BhG 9.29)

Among all beings existing in the forms of gods, animals, humans, and immovables— whether they exist as extremely superior or inferior in terms of birth, appearance, nature, and knowledge— I am equal in my being a refuge for all. This one is not to be disliked by me because he is inferior in birth, appearance, nature, knowledge, and so forth, nor is he to be abandoned because he is a cause of agitation.

Because they have taken refuge [in Me] solely out of extreme affection for Me— rather than because they consider Me superior due to My birth and other such attributes— there is no one among those who take refuge in Me by virtue of such qualities who is "dear" or "to be won over.
On the contrary, those who worship Me with the sole purpose of worshipping Me, since they find no means of sustaining themselves without My service out of their extreme love for Me,
abide in Me alone as they please, just like those of equal virtues to Me, regardless of whether they are high-born or low-born.
I, too, abide among them as if I were superior to them.
Even there,
if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion,
he is indeed to be regarded as righteous, for he has rightly resolved.
In whatever specific caste one is born, there are certain customary practices that are to be adopted and others that are to be avoided;

even if one has transgressed those, if they worship Me according to the manner described— being devoted to no other and making My worship their sole purpose— then such a person is indeed virtuous, indeed the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas.
"He should be honored and highly esteemed" means he is equal to those previously mentioned.

Why is this so? Because his resolve is perfectly right; for his determination is most excellent: "The Blessed One, the sole cause of the entire universe, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, my Master, my Guru, my friend, my supreme [deity]... [and so forth].
"This resolve, which is to be enjoyed [only by the steadfast], is difficult for all others to attain; therefore, he has undertaken it.
Furthermore, his devotion to that task—which has no other purpose—is constant; thus, he is indeed excellent and should be highly esteemed."

When this resolve and its fulfillment—namely, the distribution in the manner described—have been accomplished, any transgression of his conduct is merely a slight deficiency; it does not warrant disregard, but rather, the meaning is that he is indeed to be highly esteemed. (BhG 9.30)

But is it not said: "Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain this through wisdom"?
Because of such scriptural passages as these, [the Lord] says here that the transgression of right conduct obstructs the continuous flow of the arising of successive births:
"O son of Kuntī, declare with certainty: he whose mind is fixed on dharma quickly attains eternal peace; my devotee never perishes" (BhG 9.31).

By worshipping Me alone with the motive of loving Me, one shakes off all sins and thereby eradicates the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* from their very root; thus, one quickly becomes righteous (*dharmātmā*) and swiftly becomes single-minded in the worship of Me, free from all obstacles and accompanied by [all favorable] requisites.
Indeed, such a form of worship is what was designated by the word "dharma" at the outset in the passage beginning, "O scorcher of foes, this is the dharma."
"He attains eternal peace"—he attains that which is perpetual and non-returning, namely, the cessation of conduct opposed to the attainment of Me.
O Kaunteya, you yourself should make this promise regarding this matter: one who has begun devotion to Me does not perish even if mixed with opposing conduct;
rather, through the majesty of my devotion, having destroyed every kind of opposition and attained the eternal cessation of such opposition, he quickly becomes one whose devotion is perfected.
For even those who may be of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras—by taking refuge in me, O Pārtha, they too attain the supreme goal. (BhG 9.32)
How much more so, then, O Brahmins, meritorious ones, and royal sages—having reached this transient and unhappy world, do you worship me! BhG 9.33.
Indeed, even women, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of sinful birth attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in me;
how much more so, then, the Brāhmaṇas and royal sages of virtuous birth who are established in devotion to me!
Therefore, you, a royal sage, having reached this transient world which is full of misery due to being afflicted by the threefold suffering, worship me.
He declares the nature of devotion:
"Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. (BhG 9.34)
Fix your mind on Me, the Lord of all lords,
who is the sole embodiment of auspiciousness opposed to every form of evil,
and who is omniscient.
In the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama, whose resolve is truth and who is the sole cause of the entire universe;
To him whose eyes were as pure, large, and like the petals of a white lotus;
who resembled a clear, dark-blue cloud;
and whose splendor was like that of a thousand suns risen simultaneously.
In the great ocean of the nectar of loveliness,
with four noble and stout arms, and wearing exceedingly radiant yellow garments;

Fix your mind without interruption, like a continuous stream of oil, upon the Lord of All—the one adorned with a crown of *āmala* fruit, makara-shaped earrings, necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; an ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous conduct, beauty, sweetness, profundity, magnanimity, and parental affection; the refuge of the entire world, who regards no distinction among its inhabitants.
He specifies that very point: "My devotee" (madbhaktaḥ) means one who is endowed with an extreme degree of love for Me; the meaning is, "be one whose mind is fixed on Me.
He specifies it further: "Sacrificing to Me" (madyājī) means become intent upon sacrificing to Me, which is brought about by the experience of Me as the object of limitless and unsurpassed love.
As for "sacrifice" (yajana), it refers to a state of complete and exclusive devotion.
For sacrifice consists in the bestowing of all enjoyments, such as those that are metaphorical, tactile, or consumable.
Thus, it is said: "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me," meaning: "Become intent on the production of wine, which brings about an unsurpassed and inexhaustible joy born from my own experience."

Furthermore, He qualifies that very same [instruction]: "Bow down to Me. Make a firm resolve for the utmost humility within Me, your inner self—Me who am the object of experience for you as one whose exceeding love is caused by My own experience of being infinitely superior and most dear—and do so until your entire mode of existence becomes exclusively devoted to Me, never ceasing. "Devoted to Me" (*matparāyaṇaḥ*) means one for whom I alone am the supreme refuge (*param ayana*).
The meaning is: "by me" (mayā), that is, as my refuge, because of the impossibility of sustaining oneself without me.
Having thus disciplined yourself and being solely intent on me, having attained a mind capable of experiencing me through such boundless and ever-increasing love, you shall come to Me alone;
for here the word *ātman* refers to the mind.
The meaning is: having meditated upon Me with such a mind, having experienced Me, having worshipped Me, and having bowed down to Me, being devoted to Me alone, you shall attain Me alone.

Thus, worldly actions for the sake of maintaining the body, as well as Vedic obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karmāṇi*), have been performed by Me alone for My pleasure, with their sole essence consisting in being subordinate to Me.

Acting thus constantly— performing with love my glorification, prostrations, salutations, and so forth, while contemplating that the entire world is under my governance and has as its sole essence being subservient to me— and further contemplating my own multitude of most beloved qualities, you shall attain Me alone by practicing this worship characterized as described above day after day.
The yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) has been described along with its auxiliary elements.
Now, for the sake of generating and increasing that devotion, the infinite multitude of the Lord’s auspicious qualities— such as His absolute sovereignty (*niraṅkuśaiśvarya*) and so forth—
and the fact that the entire world is His very self because it constitutes His body and is impelled by Him, are elaborated.
The Blessed Lord said:
O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word, which I shall speak to you, who are dear to Me, out of a desire for your welfare. (BhG 1.101)

Having heard of my greatness, you are filled with joy; therefore, out of a desire for your welfare—consisting in the generation and increase of devotion to me—I shall speak further supreme words concerning the expansion of my own majesty. Listen to that with an attentive mind. (BhG 1.101)
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin;
for I am, in every respect, the source of the gods and the great seers.

Even the hosts of gods and the great seers—who perceive objects beyond the senses and possess superior knowledge—do not know my origin or my power; they do not know my name, my actions, my essential nature, or my true being.
This is because I am the source of all those gods and great seers in every respect; I am the source of their very nature, as well as their knowledge, power, and so forth.
The knowledge granted to them by me is limited, corresponding only to the merit that serves as the cause for their status as gods or great seers.
Therefore, those of limited knowledge do not know my true nature and so forth as they truly are.
Thus, this knowledge concerning the inconceivable true nature of the Divine and so forth is declared to be the means for liberation from the sins that obstruct the arising of devotion:
"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins. (BhG 10.3)
"It is not born" means "unborn" (*aja*);

by this, its heterogeneity from insentient, transformative matter (*vikāridravya*), as well as from the transmigrating conscious being (*saṃsāricetana*) conjoined with that [matter], is stated. For the birth of the transmigrating conscious being consists in its conjunction with non-consciousness (*acit*) caused by karma.
By the word "beginningless" (*anādi*), the fact that the liberated self (*muktātman*) is of a different nature from that which has a beginning is stated.
For the state of being unborn (*ajatva*) of the liberated self is indeed possessed of a beginning;
since its connection with that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) occurred previously, it possesses the fitness for such abandonment.
Therefore, by the term "beginningless," its unfitness for that [bondage] is expressed through its being the opposite of it; and this is also shown by such scriptural passages as "faultless.

Thus, he who knows Me—the Lord of the world, the Lord even of the lords of the worlds, who am unfit for that [bondage] because My essential nature is the opposite of any connection with what is to be abandoned—is undeluded among mortals.

Delusion (*moha*) is the state of identifying [the Self] with that which belongs to the same class as other things; one who is free from that is "undeluded" (*asaṃmūḍha*). Such a person is liberated from all sins that are obstacles to the arising of devotion to Me.
This is what is meant: in the world, a king among men is of the same species as other men, having attained his sovereignty through some particular action.
Likewise, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) is also such;
likewise, the Lord of the Egg (Brahmā) is also of the same nature as other transmigrating beings,
because he too is included within the three types of cultivation.
And from the Vedic scripture, "He who ordains Brahmā," as well as others who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth;
yet this one is the Great Lord of the world, [distinguished] from the insentient in the states of cause and effect, and from the sentient who are subject to his rule, whether bound or liberated.

He who knows Me as distinct from all others—being of a nature entirely opposed to everything that is to be abandoned, being solely intent upon infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, and having as His sole essential nature the act of governing—is free from the delusion of similarity with other things;
such a person is liberated from all sins. (BhG 1.103)
Having thus established that the removal of sins— which are obstacles to the arising of devotion— occurs through the contemplation of one's own true nature,

and that the arising of devotion follows as a matter of course from the removal of those obstacles, [the Lord] now describes the manner in which devotion increases through the contemplation of the expansion of His own sovereignty and the multitude of His auspicious qualities:
"Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, and tranquility..."
Happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence, as well as fear and fearlessness.
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—
these various states of beings arise from me alone.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the mind’s capacity for discernment;
knowledge (*jñāna*) is the certain determination regarding the specific characteristics of conscious and unconscious objects;
and non-delusion (*asaṃmoha*) is the cessation of the perception of similarity toward an object such as mother-of-pearl, which is of a different class from the previously grasped silver.

Forbearance (kṣamā) is the state of an unaltered mind even when there is a cause for mental agitation; truth (satya) is speech that corresponds to reality as it has been perceived and is beneficial to living beings.
Here, what is intended is a mental disposition that accords with that [truth].
Because this is a section concerning the fluctuations of the mind:
*dama* is the restraint of the external organs from objects that lead to harm; *śama* is the restraint of the internal organ in the same manner.
Pleasure is an experience agreeable to oneself; pain is an experience disagreeable to oneself;
existence is the process of coming into being.
The arising of the mind caused by the experience of the agreeable is *bhava*;
its non-arising caused by the experience of the disagreeable is the dejection of the mind (*avasāda*);
and fear is the suffering born from perceiving the cause of future suffering.
The cessation of that [desire] is fearlessness;
non-violence is the state of not being a cause of suffering for others;
equanimity is the state of having an equal mind regarding oneself, one's friends, and one's enemies, as well as regarding gain and loss.
Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is the state of being satisfied when all [objects] are perceived as one's own self;
austerity (*tapas*) is bodily exertion consisting of the scriptural reduction of enjoyments;
and charity (*dāna*) is the bestowing of one's own objects of enjoyment upon another.
Fame is the renown of possessing virtues;
infamy is the renown of lacking virtues.
Both of these should be understood as two types of mental activity corresponding to those [qualities].
Because of that context;
and likewise with austerity and charity.
Thus, all these states of being of all creatures—the mental functions that are the causes of their engagement and withdrawal—proceed from Me alone, being dependent upon My volition.
And the initiators of the creation and maintenance of all living beings proceed dependent upon my will; thus he says:
"The seven great seers of old and likewise the four Manus—born of my own nature and mind, from whom these creatures in this world have descended. (BhG 1.106)

The seven great sages of the past, namely Bhṛgu and the others who were the seven great sages born from the mind of Brahmā for the purpose of perpetuating the eternal creation; and those four Manus known as Sāvarṇikas who exist for the purpose of perpetuating the eternal maintenance of the world,
from whose lineage all these creatures in this world are born— these are the progenitors of offspring at every moment until the final dissolution.
And those protectors, Bhṛgu and the others, as well as the Manus, are "of my nature" (madbhāvāḥ); that is, they whose nature is the very same as my own nature— they are of my nature,
established in my thought.
The meaning is that they follow my own volition.
He who knows in truth this glory and this yoga of Mine is united with unshakable yoga; of this there is no doubt. (BhG 1.107)
Vibhūti is sovereign power.

He who knows in truth this manifestation of mine—consisting in the fact that the origin, maintenance, and activity of everything are dependent upon me—and also my yoga, which consists of the multitude of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all things to be abandoned; [he knows Me in truth].
He is joined with an unwavering and unshakable yoga of devotion;
of this there is no doubt.
The intention is that you yourself will see that knowledge concerning My manifestations and concerning My auspicious qualities increases the yoga of devotion.
He demonstrates the increase of devotion through the form that is the ripening of the knowledge of His manifestations:
"Thinking, 'I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds,' the wise, endowed with such realization, worship Me. (BhG 10.8)
"I am the source—the cause of the origin—of the entire manifold expansion of the diverse sentient and insentient universe;

everything proceeds from me alone. Realizing this, which is my natural and unimpeded sovereignty, as well as my endowment with a multitude of auspicious qualities such as good character, beauty, and affection, the wise and the enlightened, filled with devotion, worship me, who am endowed with all auspicious attributes.
"Bhāva" refers to a particular modification of the mind;
the meaning is that those who long for me worship me. (BhG 1.108)
How so?
With their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they are contented and they rejoice. (BhG 1.109)
"With minds fixed on Me" means having their thoughts centered on Me;
"with life gone to Me" means having their very existence dependent on Me— the sense being that they are unable to sustain themselves without Me.

Mutually informing one another of My qualities as they have each experienced them personally, and recounting My divine and beautiful deeds, the speakers are satisfied and delighted; the speakers are satisfied by those words which have no other purpose, and the listeners are delighted by hearing them, which are supremely dear beyond measure. (BhG 1.109)
To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love,
I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
To those who are constantly disciplined, who aspire to constant union with Me, and who worship Me, I—out of compassion—grant that very yoga of discernment which has reached its state of fruition;
by means of which they come to Me.
Moreover,
out of compassion for them alone, I, abiding within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance by means of the radiant lamp of knowledge.
For the sake of favoring them alone, I,
abiding within their own being and established as an object within the activity of their minds, manifest my own multitude of auspicious qualities;

and by means of the radiant lamp known as knowledge regarding me, [I dispel] that state of being inclined toward objects previously practiced other than myself, which is born from ignorance in the form of past karma that opposes knowledge.
I destroy darkness.
Arjuna said:

Having thus heard of the Lord’s unique possession of a multitude of auspicious qualities— which is of a nature entirely distinct from all else and which generates unsurpassed bliss for those who hear it— and having heard of the extent of His sovereignty,
Arjuna, desiring to hear its further details, spoke.
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Supreme Purifier;
for you are indeed that whom the Vedas declare as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Supreme Purifier.
“From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; and into which they enter when they depart.”
“Seek to know that; that is Brahman,” “The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme,” and “He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself.”
Likewise, "the supreme abode" (paraṃ dhāma);
the word *dhāma* signifies light; it is the supreme light, as in: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven."
"Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form," and "The gods [worship] him as the light of lights.
Likewise, it is the supreme purity, the supreme purifier.
It causes the wise man to be free from the clinging of all impurities and brings about their destruction.
As it is said: "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus."
"Just as a tuft of cotton wool thrown into a fire is utterly consumed, even so are all his evils consumed.
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self"—thus indeed do the Śrutis declare. (BhG 1.1012ab)
The eternal, divine Person, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading.
"All the sages say this of you, as do the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa; and you yourself tell it to me. (BhG 1.10)
And all the sages, who know the true nature of the higher and lower reality, declare you alone to be the eternal, divine Person, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading;
likewise do the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa.
"Those brahmins who know the gods, and those people who know the supreme self—"
They speak of the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa as the eternal Dharma.
Govinda is indeed said to be the supreme purifier among all purifiers;
he is the merit among merits and the auspiciousness among auspicious things.
The lotus-eyed one, the eternal god of gods, is the three worlds themselves.
Therein indeed dwells Hari, the slayer of Madhu, whose nature is inconceivable.
“This glorious Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk,
has left his serpent-couch and come to the city of Mathurā.”
“Dvāravatī is meritorious, for there dwells Madhusūdana;
he is the ancient God himself, for he is the eternal Dharma.
Likewise: “Where the divine Nārāyaṇa, the supreme self, the eternal one, resides...”
In that regard, O Pārtha, the entire world consists of sacred fords and sanctuaries.
That is merit, that is the supreme Brahman, that is the sacred ford, and that is the grove of asceticism;
there dwell the celestial rishis, the perfected ones, and all those whose wealth is their austerity.
Where the primordial god, the great yogi Madhusūdana, resides—that is the holiest of all holy places; let there be no doubt in you regarding this.
“Kṛṣṇa alone is indeed the origin and the dissolution of the worlds;
for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings exists.”
Thus [it is said].
And likewise, you yourself declare:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and indeed ego."
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.
From the passage beginning with "BhG 7.6" up to the end of "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds" (BhG 10.8).
I consider all this that you tell me, O Keśava, to be the truth;
for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.
Therefore, I consider all this to be a statement of things as they truly exist,
not intended for praise or the like;
for you speak of my sovereignty— which is unique, unsurpassed, infinite, and innate— as well as the infinity of your auspicious qualities.
Therefore, O Blessed One, treasury of unsurpassed wisdom, power, strength, sovereignty, heroism, and splendor,
neither the gods nor the dānavas— whose knowledge is limited— comprehend Your manifestation or the manner of Your manifesting forms.
O Supreme Person, O Creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the world, You alone know Yourself by Yourself.
O Supreme Person,
you yourself know yourself by yourself alone, through your own knowledge.
The creator of beings;
the progenitor of all beings;
the lord of beings, the controller of all.
O God of gods, the supreme deity even among deities;
just as you exist surpassing humans, animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth by means of a multitude of auspicious qualities such as beauty and virtuous conduct,
so too do you exist surpassing all those deities by various such qualities.
O Lord of the world, O Sovereign of the universe!
You ought to speak in full of Your divine self-manifestations,
by which manifestations You abide pervading these worlds.
Those divine manifestations which are unique to you,
you alone ought to describe them in their entirety;
the meaning is that you yourself must reveal them.
Endowed with those infinite manifestations and those particular modes of governance, you abide pervading these worlds as their ruler.
How may I, as a yogi, know you by constantly meditating upon you?
And in what various states, O Blessed One, are you to be contemplated by me?

Being a yogi established in the yoga of devotion, I have set out to constantly contemplate You through devotion; yet, how am I to contemplate You—the object of contemplation, whose multitude of auspicious qualities such as perfect sovereignty and the like transcend the aforementioned states of intellect, knowledge, and so forth—in which various other states am I to contemplate You as the Controller? // BhG 1.1017 //
O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of Your yogic power and majesty; for there is no satiety for me as I hear this nectar.

“I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds”—thus has Your connection with the status of creator and so forth, as well as Your majesty and governance, been stated in brief. Speak of these again in detail.
For me, there is no satiety in hearing the nectar of Your majesty as it is being spoken by You;
indeed, my lack of satiety is known by You alone—this is the intended meaning.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Behold, O best of the Kurus, I shall declare to you my auspicious manifestations (vibhūtis) according to their preeminence; there is no end to my full extent."
O best of the Kurus,
I shall describe to you my auspicious manifestations according to their preeminence.
By the word "preeminence," excellence is intended.
For it will be said: "And me, the chief among household priests.
I shall describe certain supreme manifestations in the world;
however, they cannot be fully told in detail, nor can they be heard.
Because they are infinite.
"Mastery" (vibhūtitva) means the state of being that which is governed;
for it has been stated that the various distinct states of all beings, such as the intellect and so forth, arise from Me alone.
This is because it is established [in the scripture] by the statement: “He who knows this majesty (vibhūti) and yoga of Mine in their true essence.

Likewise, it has been stated there that what is indicated by the word *yoga* is the power of creation and so forth, while what is indicated by the word *vibhūti* is the state of being impelled by that [power]; and furthermore:
“I am the source of all; from Me everything proceeds.”
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship me. (BhG 7.19)

In this regard, he has very clearly stated the following meaning— which is designated by the word "yoga" (discipline)— namely, that the governance consisting of the impelling of all beings exists as his own self, and that he is the creator, protector,
and destroyer of everything: "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings."
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.
I am established as the Self within the heart— the inner seat— of all beings who constitute my own body;
for the so-called "Self" is indeed the support, the controller, and the sovereign of the body in its entirety.
Thus it will be said:
"And I am seated in the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss," and "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna."
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of his illusory power.
Thus it is said.
And it is heard [in scripture]: "He who, dwelling within all beings, is distinct from all beings; whom all beings do not know;
whose body all beings are; who, dwelling within, controls all beings."
"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal";

and also: "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, who controls the self from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal."
Thus, abiding as the Self of all beings, I am their beginning, middle, and end; that is to say, I am the cause of their origin, maintenance, and dissolution.

Having thus established that the Blessed One’s abiding as the self within all things that constitute his own manifestations is the reason for their designation through grammatical coordination with various terms, he now designates specific manifestations by way of such coordination.
For when the Blessed One abides as the self, all words find their ultimate resolution in him alone.

Just as words such as "god," "man," "bird," and "tree," while denoting bodies, ultimately terminate in their respective selves (ātman), so too the Lord's abiding as the self of each [entity] is the very basis for His grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with those various words; this He will state in the conclusion of the section on manifestations (vibhūti): "There is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without Me," because of this statement that all things are inseparable from Himself.
And inseparable connection [is established] by way of being governed [by Me];
this was stated at the outset: "Everything proceeds from Me.
"Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminaries I am the radiant Sun."
Among the Maruts I am Marīci; among the stars I am the Moon.
Among the twelve Ādityas who are numbered as twelve, I am that most excellent Āditya named Viṣṇu;
among the luminaries that illuminate the world, I am the radiant Sun, the host of Ādityas;
and among the Maruts, I am Marīci, the most excellent.
“I am the moon among the constellations. This is not a genitive used for specification (nirdhāraṇa), as in the expression “I am consciousness among living beings.”
I am that very Candra, who is the lord of the stars. BhGR 1.1021.
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava;
among the senses, I am the mind; and among beings, I am consciousness.
Among the Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva—I am the Sāmaveda, which is the most excellent.
Among the gods, I am Indra. Among the eleven sense organs, I am the mind-organ, which is the most excellent.
"That I am"—
this [particle] "api" is not used in the sense of selection;
it refers to that consciousness which belongs to sentient beings who possess consciousness.
Such am I.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among peaked mountains, I am Meru.
Among the eleven Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am Vaiśravaṇa;
and among the eight Vasus, I am Pāvaka.
Among the peaked mountains, those beautified by their summits, I am Meru.
And know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the chief of the household priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean.
I am that Bṛhaspati who is the most excellent among domestic priests; I am Skanda among the leaders of armies, that is, the generals.
Among lakes, I am the ocean.
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation; among immovable things, I am the Himalayas.
Among the great seers, such as Marīci and others, I am Bhṛgu;
among words that express meaning, I am speech, and of those, I am the single syllable, the Praṇava.
Of sacrifices, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) am I;
of the mountains, I am the Himavat.
Among all trees, I am the Aśvattha; among divine sages, Nārada;
among Gandharvas, Citraratha; and among perfected beings (siddhas), the sage Kapila.
Know me as Uccaiḥśravas among horses, born from the nectar;
as Airāvata among lordly elephants, and as the king among men.
Among weapons, I am the thunderbolt; among cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow;
I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and among serpents, I am Vāsuki.
Among the Nāgas I am Ananta, and among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa;
among the ancestors I am Aryaman, and among those who exercise restraint I am Yama.
Among trees, I am the venerable Aśvattha;
among divine sages, I am Nārada; and [among cows] I am the divine Surabhi, the yielder of all desires.
I am Kandarpa, the cause of procreation;
the sarpas have a single head,
while the nāgas have many heads.
Among aquatic creatures dwelling in the water, I am Varuṇa;
among those who wield the rod of punishment, I am Vaivasvata.
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who mete out time, I am Time;
among beasts I am the king of beasts; and among birds I am Vainateya.
Among those who calculate with a desire for what is harmful, I am Time, which is death.
Among purifiers I am the wind; among those who bear weapons, I am Rāma;
among fish I am the makara; and among flowing rivers, I am the Gaṅgā.
Among those whose nature is to move, I am the wind;
among those who bear weapons, I am Rāma.
Here, the state of being a weapon-bearer is my manifestation.

Because there is no other entity [besides Him], the sun and others are the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) who exist as the body of the Blessed One abiding as the Self; thus, they stand in the position of being those who bear His attributes.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna; among sciences, I am the science of the Self, and among those who debate, I am the debate.
"Creations" (sarga) are those things that are created; their "origin" (ādi) is their cause.
The meaning is: "I alone am the creator, in each respective case, of all living beings who are being created at all times."
Likewise, I alone am the one who withdraws those things that are always being withdrawn here and there;
and similarly, "the middle" refers to preservation—I alone am the preserver of all things that are always being preserved. This is the meaning.
I am that debate which is undertaken for the sake of determining the truth by those engaged in sophistry, cavil, and the like.
Among letters, I am the letter *a*; among compounds, I am the copulative (*dvandva*).
I alone am inexhaustible Time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.

Among letters, it is established by the Vedic revelation that "the letter *a* is indeed all speech"; thus, I am the letter *a*, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all phonemes. Among compounds, I am the collective whole (*sāmāsika*), the aggregate of compounds;
among those, I am the copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*), for it is preeminent because both constituent members are equally predominant.
I alone am inexhaustible time, consisting of units such as *kalās* and *muhūrtas*;
I am Hiraṇyagarbha, the four-faced creator of all.
I am death that carries away all, and I am the origin of those things yet to be; I am fame, fortune, speech among women, as well as memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.
I am death, the snatcher of all life-breaths;
I am the karma called origination for those who are about to be born;
I am prosperity; and I am fame.
I am speech, and I am memory, and I am intelligence.
I am fortitude, and I am forbearance.
Among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among meters, I am the Gāyatrī;
among months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and among seasons, I am the flower-bearing spring.
Among the Sāmans, I am the Bṛhat-sāman;
among the meters, I am the Gāyatrī;
and among the seasons, I am Vasanta, the maker of flowers.
Of those who practice deception, I am gambling; of the radiant, I am splendor;
I am victory; I am resolve; and of those possessed of goodness, I am goodness.
Among those who practice deception, I am the gambling with dice and other implements upon the grounds for deception;
among victors, I am victory; among the resolute, I am resolve.
I am the courage of the courageous;
I am the courage that is great-mindedness.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among the poets, the poet Uśanas.
In this context, being the son of Vasudeva is my manifestation,
precisely because there is no other meaning [to the name];
among the Pāṇḍavas, I am Dhanañjaya, Arjuna.
The sages (*munayaḥ*) are those who, through contemplation (*mananena*), perceive the true nature of the Self (*ātma-yāthātmya*);
among them, I am Vyāsa.
The poets (*kavayaḥ*) are the wise ones (*vipaścitaḥ*).
Of those who seek to subdue, I am the rod of punishment; of those who desire victory, I am statesmanship.
Among secrets, I am silence; and among the wise, I am knowledge.
I am the punishment for those who transgress the rules;
I am the policy that serves as the means of victory for those seeking conquest;
and I am silence regarding the concealment of secrets among those connected to them.
And among those possessed of knowledge, I am knowledge itself.
Moreover, O Arjuna, I am that which is the seed of all beings;
there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me.
That which exists as the seed of each respective state for all beings situated in all their various conditions— whether it be perceived or unperceived—
that is indeed myself.
There is nothing that could exist apart from me, who am established as the very self of the entire collection of beings.

Because of the introductory statement, “I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings,” even here in the verse, “There is no being, moving or unmoving, that can exist without Me,” what is intended is precisely the state of abiding as the Self.
The meaning is that the entire collection of entities, in all their states, would be joined with Me, who have become their very Self.
By this, it is made manifest that the very reason for this entire designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is its abiding as the Self (*ātmatā*).
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
this extensive detail of my manifestation has been declared by me only in brief.
There is no end to my divine and auspicious manifestations;
however, this detailed expansion of my manifestations has been declared by me in brief through certain specific attributes.
Whatever being possesses greatness, or is endowed with beauty, or is even possessed of power—
know that very thing to have arisen from a fragment of my splendor.
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, endowed with lordship, glorious— that is, radiant—
or prosperous with wealth and grain, or powerful— that is, intent upon auspicious undertakings;
Understand that each of those is produced from a portion of my own splendor (*tejas*).
"Splendor" means the capacity for overcoming others;
the meaning is that it arises from a single part of the power of governance belonging to me, whose power is inconceivable.
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge to you, O Arjuna?
Pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I stand as the world.
What is the purpose of speaking at such length regarding this knowledge?

This entire world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, whether in its state as an effect or its state as a cause, and whether gross or subtle, exists in its own essential nature and persists [therein].
And so that she might not transgress my resolve regarding the diversity of her activities, I remain established there, pervading her with a ten-thousandth of a ten-thousandth part of my own majesty,
as stated by the venerable Parāśara:
“In a fraction of a fraction of ten thousand times ten thousand of whom this power of the universe resides. (BhG 10.42)

Thus, for the sake of the accomplishment and further increase of *bhakti-yoga*, it has been stated that the Lord is the Self of all, characterized by His own natural and unique collection of auspicious qualities which distinguish Him from everything else; and that, for that very reason, the entire multitude of things consisting of the sentient and the non-sentient— which are distinct from Him— constitute His body, such that their essential nature, existence, and activity are dependent upon Him.

Having heard from the Blessed One regarding this unique nature of his, which is not shared by others, and how the entire universe depends upon him for its very essence, existence, and activity, Arjuna— thinking "it is exactly so"— and desiring to directly perceive the Blessed One as he truly and eternally is, spoke. And indeed, immediately thereafter, through the grace of the Blessed One, he shall behold him in that very way.
“For the God who consists of all wonders, who is infinite and whose faces are everywhere... there the entire universe, divided in many ways, is situated as one”—this indeed will be said.
Arjuna said:
"For the sake of my grace, [you have spoken] the supreme secret known as the Adhyātma."
By those words which were spoken by you, this delusion of mine has vanished.

For my sake— who am deluded by the ignorance consisting of the conceit that the body is the self— your supreme secret, the supreme mystery known as the inner self (*adhyātma*), which is the speech to be spoken concerning the Self,
beginning with “Never indeed was I not” and ending with “Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi,” has been spoken for the sole purpose of showing me favor.
Therefore, this entire delusion of mine concerning the self has vanished and been cast far away.
And likewise,
O lotus-eyed one, the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from you, as has your imperishable majesty. (BhG 11.2)

O lotus-eyed one, from the seventh chapter up to the end of the tenth, I have indeed heard in detail from you how the origin and dissolution— birth and destruction— of all beings other than yourself occur from you, the Supreme Self;

and that your sovereignty over all conscious and unconscious entities is eternal and imperishable, as are your multitude of auspicious qualities such as knowledge and power, which belong to you alone.
Your supreme transcendence, your status as the support of all, and your alone being the impeller in all activities such as thinking and blinking—
thus have your immeasurable majesties been heard.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to indicate the desire to see [these qualities] which is about to be described.
"It is even so as you have said of yourself, O Supreme Lord.
I desire to see your divine form, O Supreme Person."
O Supreme Lord,
this is indeed so, as you yourself declare of your own self.

O Puruṣottama, ocean of affection for those who take refuge in you, Your divine sovereignty— which is unique to You— manifests in the capacity of being the ruler, the protector, and the creator of all.
In its capacity as the destroyer and the sustainer,
in its being a mine of auspicious qualities, and in its state of supreme transcendence.
I desire to see, that is, to directly perceive, the form established as being of a nature entirely distinct from all other things.
If you think it is possible for me to see that, O Lord,
then, O Master of Yoga, show me Your imperishable Self.
If you think that my form— which is the creator of all, the ruler of all, and the substratum of all— is capable of being seen by me, then...
Therefore, O Lord of Yoga, yoga is the union with auspicious qualities such as knowledge;

for You will say, "Behold My divine yoga. O treasury of knowledge, power, sovereignty, heroism, strength, and splendor—qualities impossible for anyone other than You—reveal Your own imperishable Self to me.
"Indestructible" (avyayam) is an adverbial modifier;
the meaning is: "Show yourself to me in your entirety."

The Blessed Lord said: Thus requested by Pārtha, whose throat was choked with joy and who was filled with curiosity, the Blessed Lord said: "Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and by the thousands."
Of various kinds, divine, and of diverse colors and forms.
Behold all my forms abiding in every place—
then by the hundreds and thousands, diverse and of various kinds,
divine and extraordinary.
Behold those of various colors and forms— of various colors such as white, black, and so forth, and of various shapes.
Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts;
behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before! (BhG 11.6)
Behold within my single form the twelve Ādityas,
the eight Vasus,
and the eleven Rudras.
The two Aśvins and the forty-nine Maruts;
this is mentioned for the sake of illustration.

In this world, behold all those things perceived through direct observation and those seen in the scriptures, as well as many other wonders never before seen in any world or in any scripture. (BhG 11.6)
Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings gathered here in one place within my body, and whatever else you wish to see.
Behold here, within this single body of mine— and even there, situated in one place, in a single part— the entire world with its moving and unmoving beings;
and whatever else you wish to see.
Behold that also as being merely a single part of a single body.
But you shall not be able to see Me with these very eyes of yours;
I give you divine vision—behold My sovereign yoga. BhG 11.8.

I shall show the entire universe within one part of my own body; however, you will not be able to see me in such a state— entirely distinct from all else and immeasurable— with these ordinary eyes of yours, which perceive only limited and finite objects.
"I give you a divine, non-ordinary eye, the means for seeing Me.
Behold My sovereign yoga—behold My yoga that is not shared by others;
the meaning is: behold My yoga of infinite knowledge and so forth, and My yoga of infinite majesty. (BhG 11.8)
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great Lord of Yoga,
then revealed his supreme sovereign form to Pārtha.

Having spoken thus, Hari— the son of Pṛthā’s maternal uncle, the Great Lord of Yoga, the Sovereign of most wondrous yogic powers, Nārāyaṇa who has become the Supreme Brahman— standing as the charioteer, revealed to Pārtha, the son of his paternal aunt Pṛthā, His own supreme, divine, and unique form.
That form is the substratum of the entire world in all its manifold variety, and it is the ruler of the universe;
and such is that form, possessing many mouths and eyes and displaying many wonders.
Adorned with many divine ornaments and wielding many uplifted divine weapons.
Wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with celestial perfumes and unguents,
the God consists of all wonders— Ananta, whose faces are everywhere.
The radiant Lord,
infinite, existing throughout the three periods of time; because He is the substratum of the entire universe, He is incapable of being delimited by space or time.
Having faces on all sides, with faces turned toward every direction,
he was endowed with divine garments, perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and weapons appropriate to himself.
He further specifies that very radiance indicated by the word "divine":
"If the light of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky, that might be similar to the splendor of that Great-Souled One. (BhG 11.12)
This is for the purpose of showing that splendor is immeasurable;
the meaning is that its nature is inexhaustible splendor.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu beheld the entire universe, divided into many parts, situated within the body of the God of gods.
Therein, he is infinite in length and breadth,
possessing infinite arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes,
and endowed with immeasurable splendor.
Endowed with immeasurable divine weapons,
adorned with immeasurable divine ornaments appropriate to himself,
and wearing divine garlands and garments.

Upon the divine body of the God of gods— anointed with celestial perfumes and full of infinite wonders— there exists a manifold division consisting of the various classes of experiencers, such as Brahmā and other diverse deities, animals, humans, and immobile beings; as well as the distinctions between the places of enjoyment, the objects of enjoyment, and the instruments of enjoyment, including the earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the subterranean realms of Pātāla, Talātala, Vitala, and Sutala.
The entire world consists of both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa); as it is said:
“I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds,” and “Come, I shall declare to you my auspicious manifestations.”
“I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings,” and “Of the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu,” and so forth,
up to: “There is no being, moving or unmoving, that exists without Me.”
This was declared by the verse ending with, "Having pervaded all this universe, I remain with but one part," meaning situated in one place or in a single location;
the Pāṇḍava, having obtained divine vision suitable for that vision through the grace of the Blessed One, beheld it. (BhG 11.13)
Then Dhananjaya, overcome with wonder and his hair standing on end, bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence. (BhG 11.14)

Then Dhanañjaya, having beheld the Lord—who is the support for the entire universe of great wonders with but a single portion of His own body, the impeller of all things, and the possessor of a multitude of most wonderful and infinite auspicious qualities such as knowledge—was overcome with amazement; his hair standing on end, he prostrated himself like a staff with his head and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke. (BhG 11.14)
Arjuna said:
O God, I see all the gods in Your body, as well as all the various classes of beings; I see the Lord Brahmā seated upon his lotus throne, and all the ṛṣis and the radiant serpents. (BhG 11.15)
O Lord, I see all the gods within your body; likewise, I see all the various hosts of living beings,
as well as the four-faced Brahmā, the lord of the cosmic egg.
Likewise, he saw the Lord seated upon the lotus-throne, the Lord established within Brahmā who is seated on the lotus-throne, and likewise all the sages headed by the divine seers (devarṣis),
as well as the radiant serpents, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the rest.
I see You with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms on all sides;
O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form, I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning.
I see you everywhere with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms; O Lord of the Universe, controller of the universe, O Universal Form, whose body is the universe!
Since you are infinite, therefore I perceive neither your end, nor your middle, nor again your beginning.

I see You wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus— a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to behold from every direction, with the brilliance of a flaming fire and the sun, immeasurable.

I behold You as a mass of splendor, blazing on all sides, difficult to gaze upon from every direction, with the radiance of a flaming fire and the sun, immeasurable, wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus.
You are the supreme imperishable to be known; you are the ultimate refuge of this universe.
You are the undecaying protector of the eternal dharma; I consider you to be the ancient Puruṣa. (BhG 11.18)
In the Upaniṣads,

in such passages as "Two sciences are to be known," you alone are that supreme Imperishable (akṣara) designated as the object to be known; you alone are the supreme repository of this universe, the ultimate support of all this world.
You are imperishable, devoid of decay;
in whatever nature, with whatever qualities, and with whatever power You exist, You remain forever in that very same form.

You alone are the protector of the eternal dharma—of the eternal, constant Vedic dharma—through such incarnations as these. You are considered by me to be the Sanātana Puruṣa; I have known you to be that very Sanātana Puruṣa who is declared in such passages as, "I know this great Puruṣa," and "The Puruṣa beyond the highest."
The meaning is: "That you, the ornament of the Ukkala clan, have now been thus directly perceived by me."
I behold You, who are without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite power and infinite arms, with eyes like the moon and the sun;
I see Your face like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with Your own splendor.
It is without beginning, middle, or end, being devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
It possesses infinite vigor, meaning vigor that is without limit or superior degree;
the word "vigor" (vīrya) is used for the sake of illustration.
The meaning is: a treasury of infinite, unsurpassed excellence in knowledge, power, sovereignty, vigor, capacity, and splendor.
"With infinite arms" means with innumerable arms;
this too is for the sake of illustration.
[The deity] possesses infinite arms, bellies, feet, faces, and so forth;

his eyes are like the moon and the sun, and all his eyes are endowed with grace (*prasāda*) and majesty (*pratāpa*). Grace is [the disposition] toward gods and others who are favorable and perform acts such as prostration.
His majesty is directed toward those who are the opposite of that, such as the asuras and rākṣasas;
for it will be said: "The rākṣasas flee in fear to all directions, and all the hosts of siddhas pay him homage.
His face is like a blazing fire, with a mouth resembling the kindled fire of universal destruction (kālānala), a mouth suited for the act of withdrawal.
I behold You, the creator of all, who are scorching this entire universe with Your own splendor— that is, with that power of brilliance capable of overwhelming others. Such as You are, I see You.

The meaning is: "I directly perceive You, who are the support of all, the ruler of all, the destroyer of all, an ocean of immeasurable qualities such as knowledge, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and possessing such a divine body, exactly according to the instruction.
[An objection is raised: "How can there be many bellies and so forth within a single divine body?"
Thus it is logically established:
from a single region of the waist, which is of infinite extent, there emerge upwards the aforementioned belly and other parts,
and downwards the aforementioned divine feet.
In that regard, there is no contradiction in having two eyes within a single face.
"Seeing You in such a state, the gods and others, as well as I, are deeply distressed," he said:
"For this space between heaven and earth, and all the directions, are pervaded by You alone;
having seen that wondrous and fierce form, O Great-Souled One, the three worlds are thus shaken with fear. (BhG 11.20)
The word *dyu* (heaven) and the word *pṛthivī* (earth) both serve to indicate the worlds above and below;
the space between heaven and earth is the intermediate region (*avakāśa*),
within which all the worlds abide.
This entire space and all the directions have been pervaded by you alone.

Having seen this wondrous, fierce form of yours—endless in extent, vast, most marvelous, and most terrible—the three worlds are terrified. This occurs while the hosts of gods led by Brahmā, asuras, ancestors, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, who have come desiring to witness the battle, look on.
The entire three worlds— consisting of those who are hostile, favorable, and neutral— were utterly distressed and extremely terrified.
O Great-Souled One, whose mental activity is unfathomable,
the Blessed One granted to Arjuna alone a divine eye as the means for the direct realization of the form that is the refuge of the universe, even for these beings.
If it is asked for what purpose,
it is in order to manifest His entire sovereignty to Arjuna;
therefore, this is said:
“Having seen this wondrous and formidable form of yours, O Great-Souled One, the three worlds have been thrown into utter confusion. (BhG 11.20)
For these hosts of gods enter into you; some, filled with fear, praise you with joined palms;
and the assemblies of great seers and perfected beings, having cried "Hail!", extol you with abundant hymns of praise.
These hosts of gods, the most excellent, having beheld you, the refuge of the universe, enter into your presence with joyful minds.

Among them, some, beholding your exceedingly fierce and wondrous form, become terrified; with palms joined in reverence, they utter words in the form of praise according to their own capacity for knowledge.

Other hosts of great seers and hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), who know the true nature of the higher and lower reality, say "May it be well! and praise you with abundant hymns befitting your majesty.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas—all behold you and are filled with wonder.
The ancestors are those who drink warmth,
for according to the Vedic revelation, "the ancestors indeed partake of warmth.
All these, having fallen into a state of wonder, gaze upon you.
O mighty-armed one, having seen your vast form with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs, and feet, many bellies,
and terrifying with many tusks, the worlds as well as I am deeply distressed.

With its many fangs, it is of an exceedingly terrifying form; all the worlds previously mentioned—those who are hostile, those who are favorable, and those who are neutral, making three kinds in total—and I myself, having seen such a form as this, have become extremely distressed.
O Viṣṇu, seeing You touching the sky, blazing, multicolored, with Your mouth wide open and Your large eyes aflame, my inner self is deeply distressed; I find neither fortitude nor peace.
The word "namas" [is applied] to that which is described in the verses: "In that supreme firmament," "Of solar hue, beyond darkness," and "Dwelling in the far distance of this space."

The term "supreme ether" (paramavyoman), established by such scriptural passages as "He who is its overseer in the supreme ether," denotes that which transcends the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa);
[it refers to the Lord] in relation to both the principle of primordial nature along with its modifications and the Person (puruṣa) in all his states.

Because of the statement that it "touches the sky by being the support of the entire [universe]," and because it was previously stated that "this space between heaven and earth is indeed pervaded [by it]";

having seen You— blazing, multicolored, with wide-open mouths and blazing, wide eyes— I am distressed in my inner self, my mind utterly terrified, and I find no steadiness, I do not obtain the ability to sustain this body.

"O Viṣṇu, O Pervasive One! Having seen You—who are all-pervading, immeasurable, most wonderful, and most terrible—I find no peace for my mind or my senses; the meaning is that I become one whose every limb is relaxed and whose senses are agitated. (BhG 11.24)

Having seen Your mouths, terrible with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, I no longer know the directions nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of gods, Abode of the Universe! (BhG 11.25)
Having seen your mouths, which are exceedingly terrible and engaged in the destruction of all things like the fire at the end of an eon, I know not the directions and find no peace.
O Abode of the worlds, Lord of gods, Supreme Maheśvara even of the lords such as Brahmā!
"Be gracious toward me;
act in such a way that I may return to my natural state"—this is the meaning. (BhG 11.25)

Thus, demonstrating that the stability and activity of the entire world are dependent upon him, Pārthasārathi revealed to Pārtha his own intended purpose— the removal of the earth's burden— by means of the destruction of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who were disguised in royal attire, and of those portions of the Asuras who had infiltrated the followers of Yudhiṣṭhira; he showed that this would be accomplished by himself alone.

And that Pārtha, having directly perceived the Lord’s sovereignty consisting of his status as the creator and so forth, and seeing— even though it had not yet occurred— the destruction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons and others within that very Lord, the Self of all, by means of the divine eye obtained through His grace, spoke this.
And here are these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with all the hosts of kings—Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karna), along with our own foremost warriors as well. (BhG 11.26)
They are entering your mouths, which are terrifying and formidable with tusks;
some are seen caught between the teeth with their heads crushed to powder. (BhG 11.27)

These sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and all the others, along with Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Karṇa the Sūta’s son, together with all the hosts of kings on their side and even some of our own chief warriors, are entering in haste your terrifying mouths, which are formidable with tusks, for their destruction; therein, some are seen with their heads crushed, clinging to the gaps between your teeth.
Just as the many currents of rivers flow toward the ocean alone, so do these heroes of the world of men enter Your blazing mouths. (BhG 11.28)
Just as moths enter a blazing fire with full force for their own destruction,
even so do these worlds enter your mouths with full force for their destruction.
These royal persons,
like many currents of river water flowing toward the ocean,
or like moths rushing into a blazing fire, [have perished].
Your faces, blazing forth of their own accord, enter [the mouth] in haste for their own destruction.
Devouring all the worlds on every side with thy flaming mouths, thou art licking them;
filling the entire universe with thy splendors, thy fierce radiance scorches it, O Viṣṇu.

Devouring the entire assembly of kings with your flaming mouths, you lick again and again—repeatedly performing the act of licking—the lips and other parts of your mouth which are drenched in their blood.
Your most terrible splendors, your rays, having filled the entire world with your own powers of light, scorch it.
Tell me who you are, O one of fierce form; salutations be unto you, O best of gods, be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primeval One, for I do not comprehend your manifestation.
“Reveal yourself, the Imperishable. Thus requested by you to manifest your unobstructed sovereignty, you have displayed this form of extreme terror while revealing that unobstructed power.
I wish to know who you are, possessing such a terrifying form, and what you intend to do.
I do not know your intended course of action;
tell this to me.
Homage be to you, O best of gods!
"Be gracious; let there be salutation unto you, O Lord of All!
Having said, 'It was for this purpose that you manifested this form as the Destroyer in order to act thus,' become gracious in appearance. (BhG 11.31)

When asked, "What is Your intention in manifesting this terrible form while You, out of an excess of affection for those who depend on You, were displaying Your universal sovereignty? the Blessed Lord, the Charioteer of Pārtha, declared His own purpose:

"My manifestation of this terrible form is for the purpose of making it known that I alone am engaged in slaying the entire world of kings, headed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, even without the exertion of Pārtha;
and the purpose of making that known is to incite Pārtha to action."
The Blessed Lord said:
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown mature; I have begun here to sweep away the worlds.
Even without you, all these warriors stationed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.
He who measures and calculates is *kāla* (Time).

Calculating the end of the lifespan of all these kings, headed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I have grown into a form of terrible aspect and am here engaged in bringing about their destruction— that is, in proceeding toward the total withdrawal of the world of kings.

Therefore, by my will alone—even without your effort and even without you—these warriors headed by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who stand in your opposing ranks, all of them shall cease to exist; they shall perish. (BhG 11.32)
Therefore, arise and win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone; be merely the instrument, O Savyasācin.
Therefore, rise up against them for battle;
having conquered those enemies, obtain glory,
and enjoy a prosperous kingdom in accordance with dharma.

"These very ones, having already committed offenses, were previously slain by me alone; they have been assigned to their destruction. You, however, become merely the instrumental cause (nimitta) in their killing;
become like a weapon or similar tool for those being slain by me."
*Savyasācin*: from the root *ṣac*, meaning "to join together"; one who is habitually accustomed to joining arrows with the left hand is *savyasācī*.
"With the left hand also he effects the joining of the arrow"; the meaning is that he is capable of fighting with both hands.
Slay Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna, and likewise the other chief warriors, who have already been slain by me; do not be distressed. Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle.
"Kill Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, and the others, whom I myself have already designated for slaughter because they have committed offenses; you shall kill them.

Do not be distressed by thinking, 'How shall I kill these elders, kinsmen, and others who are attached to worldly enjoyments? Do not feel pain on their account out of fear of merit or demerit, nor out of affection for your kin, nor out of compassion."
Since those who have committed offenses against you have been assigned by me alone to be slain,
therefore fight without hesitation;
you shall be the victor, you will conquer your enemies in battle.
In their slaughter there is not even a trace of cruelty;
rather, the meaning is that victory itself is obtained.
Sañjaya said:
Having heard these words of Keśava, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, trembling with joined palms,
bowed down again and spoke to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice, prostrating himself in utter fear.

Having heard these words of Keśava, who is an ocean of affection for those who have taken refuge in him, Arjuna— having bowed to him, trembling with great fear, and prostrating before him again with joined palms— Kirīṭin spoke with a faltering voice.
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by the proclamation of Your glory the world rejoices and is filled with devotion;
the demons flee in fear to every quarter, and all the hosts of perfected beings offer You homage. (BhG 11.36)
It is fitting and appropriate that this entire world— including the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, kinnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, and others— who has come here desiring to witness the battle,
rejoices upon seeing you, the Lord of All, through your grace and by the proclamation of your glory.

And it is because you are so beloved that the *rākṣasas*, upon seeing you, flee in fear in all directions, and all the hosts of *siddhas*—the assemblies favorable to the *siddhas* and others—pay homage; all this is fitting, such is the connection with what precedes. (BhG 11.36)
He establishes this very propriety [of your being worshipped]:

"And why, O Great Soul, should they not bow down to you, who are greater even than Brahmā, the primordial creator? O Great Soul, for what reason would Hiraṇyagarbha and the others not offer salutation to you, who are greater than Brahmā—that is, Hiraṇyagarbha—and who are the original creator? (BhG 11.37ab)
O Infinite One, Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe, You are the Imperishable, that which is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.

O Infinite Lord, Abode of the World, You alone are the Imperishable (akṣara). It is called "imperishable" because it does not decay; for the reality of the individual self (jīvātmatattva), established by such scriptural passages as "The wise one is neither born nor dies," indeed does not decay.

You alone are both the existent and the non-existent; You alone are the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*) designated by the words "existent" and "non-existent," abiding in the relationship of cause and effect.

That which is in the state of an effect, possessing the differentiation of name and form, is designated by the word "existent"; and that which is in the state of a cause, being unfit for such [differentiation], is designated by the word "non-existent"—You alone are both.

Furthermore, that which is beyond—that which is other than and superior to this primordial nature and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) associated with primordial nature—is the reality of the liberated self (*muktātmatattva*). You are that.
But even that, you yourself [know]. BhGR 11.37.
You are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe.
Therefore, you are the primordial god, the ancient Puruṣa.
"You are the supreme repository of this universe.
This means that because the entire universe is deposited within you, you are the supreme repository of this universe;
the sense is that you alone are the ultimate substratum by virtue of being the Self of the universe, which constitutes your body. (BhG 11.37)
You are the knower and the object to be known, and the supreme abode; by You, O Lord of infinite forms, the entire universe is pervaded.
In this world, you alone are every knower and everything that is to be known.
Thus, abiding as the self of all, you alone are the supreme abode— the meaning being the state to be attained.
By you, O one of infinite forms, the universe is pervaded;
by you, as the Self, the entire world, consisting of a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious, is pervaded and permeated. (BhG 11.38)
Therefore, he says that you alone are denoted by such words as "wind" and so forth:
"You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, and the Great-Grandfather. You alone are the Great-Grandfather of all.
And the Grandfather and others:
the ancestors are the progenitors (prajāpati) of all creatures;
the father of the progenitors is Hiraṇyagarbha, the grandfather of all creatures.

The meaning is: you are the father even of Hiraṇyagarbha, the great-grandfather of all creatures; since you exist as the very Self (ātman) of the Grandfathers and others, you alone are what those respective words denote.
Having beheld the Blessed One of such most wondrous form, his eyes wide with joy and bowed down by extreme awe, he pays homage in every direction.
Homage, homage be to You a thousand times; and yet again, further still, homage, homage to You!
Salutations to You from the front, and salutations to You from behind; let there be salutations to You from every side, O All!
You possess infinite power and immeasurable prowess; You pervade all, and therefore You are the All.
O Amitavīrya, you of immeasurable prowess, you pervade all things by being their very self;
therefore, you are everything.

Since you pervade the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient entities by way of being their self, therefore—because the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient entities is a mode of yours by virtue of being your body—you alone, as the possessor of all modes, are the referent of the word "all.
This is the meaning: "You are the imperishable, both being and non-being."

It has been very clearly stated that the reason for the designation of complete grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—as in “Wind, Yama, Fire,” and so forth—is precisely the pervasion [of the Self] as the Self: “By You the universe is pervaded, O You of infinite forms,” and “You encompass all, therefore You are everything. (BhG 11.40)

Whatever was said by me rashly, thinking "O friend"—saying "O Kṛṣṇa," "O Yādava," or "O friend"—because I did not know this greatness of Yours, whether through negligence or even out of affection; [for that, I seek Your forgiveness]. BhG 11.41.
And whatever disrespect you have suffered from me for the sake of derision— whether in matters of dwelling, bedding, seating, or food—
whether alone or even in your presence, O Acyuta, I beg forgiveness of you, the immeasurable one.

By me, who was ignorant of this majesty of yours— consisting of your infinite power, immeasurable prowess, being the inner self of all, your status as the creator, and so forth— and who, out of negligence or delusion,
thought "He is my friend" due to affection or long-standing acquaintance, thinking "He is my companion," [I have acted].
O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava,
O friend— whatever was thus spoken to you impetuously and devoid of humility, [forgive that].
And whatever was done out of jest, or whenever you— who are always worthy of honor—

were treated with disrespect; whether in monasteries, on beds, on seats, or at meals, when we acted together, whether in private or in your presence, that all I ask forgiveness of you, who are immeasurable.
You are the father of this world of the moving and the unmoving; you are its worshipful one and its most venerable teacher.
There is no one equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior, even in the three worlds, O You of incomparable power?
O you of incomparable power,
you are the father of this entire world, both moving and unmoving;
you are also the teacher of this world.
Therefore, you are the most venerable and the most worthy of worship in this world of the moving and the unmoving.

There is no one equal to you; how could there be anyone else superior? Even within the three worlds, there is no one other than you who is your equal in any quality such as compassion; how then could there be anyone superior? // BhG 11.43 //
Therefore, having bowed down and prepared my purpose, I seek to propitiate you, the adorable Lord.
O God, as a father for his son, a friend for a friend, or a lover for his beloved, it is right for you to forgive me.

Since you are the father of all, the most worshipful, the teacher, and preeminent among all in qualities such as compassion, therefore, having bowed down to you, the Lord worthy of praise, and having prostrated my body, I seek your grace— just as one would toward a son who, though he has committed an offense, [remains dear].
And just as a father or a friend, when entreated with prostrations by a companion, becomes gracious;
so you, who are supremely compassionate, ought to forgive everything for the sake of my beloved.
I am thrilled at seeing what has never been seen before, yet my mind is distressed with fear;
therefore, O God, show me that very same form again. Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe! (BhG 11.45)
Having seen your form, never before seen, most wonderful and most fierce, I am thrilled and filled with joy;
yet my mind is distressed by fear.
Therefore, show me that very same form of yours which is so serene.
Be gracious, O Lord of gods, O Abode of the universe; show favor toward me, O Sovereign even of the gods beginning with Brahmā, O You who have become the refuge of the entire world.
I wish to see You likewise as the one wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and with the discus in hand;
