O thousand-armed one, O universal-formed one, become manifest in that very four-armed form.
In that very same way as before, I wish to see you wearing a crown, holding a mace, and with a discus in hand;
therefore, be endowed with that very same previously established four-armed form.
"O thousand-armed one, O universal form! Now, you who are seen in the form of having a thousand arms and a universal body—remain endowed with that very form. This is the meaning. (BhG 11.46)
The Blessed Lord said: O Arjuna, being pleased with you, I have through my own yoga shown you this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primordial— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.
That which is my mass of splendor, consisting of brilliance;
the universe, which has become the self of the universe; infinite, without interior.
This is for the sake of illustration;
it is devoid of beginning, middle, and end;
it is the "first" (ādi), being the primordial source of everything other than myself.
This form has never before been seen by anyone other than you; it has been shown to you, my devotee, by me out of grace, through my own yoga—that is, through the power of my own true resolve.
He says that I, as I truly am, cannot be seen by any means whatsoever other than exclusive devotion:

"O hero of the Kurus, in this world of men, I, who am of such a form, cannot be seen by anyone other than you, not by the study of the Vedas and sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities. (BhG 11.48)

Established in such a form as it truly is, I cannot be seen by anyone other than you who possesses devotion toward Me—by any person devoid of exclusive devotion—even through the Vedas, sacrifices, and the like.
Let there be no distress for you, nor any state of delusion, upon seeing this terrible form of Mine;
with fear dispelled and a joyful mind, behold once again that very same form of Mine.
May both that distress which arises from seeing such a terrible form and this state of delusion that exists within you not come to pass.
I shall show you that very same gentle form which you have previously practiced; behold this very form of mine.
Sañjaya said:
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed him his own form once again;
and the Great-Souled One, assuming once more a gentle body, comforted him who was terrified. BhG 11.50.
Having spoken thus to the son of Pāṇḍu, the Blessed One, the son of Vasudeva, again displayed his own four-armed form;
and when the prince was terrified by the sight of this unfamiliar form, the Great-Souled One, whose resolve is truth, reassured him once more by assuming his familiar and gentle appearance.
The four-armed form alone is the inherent nature of this Supreme Person, the Lord of all, the Supreme Brahman, who acts for the benefit of the world and is the son of Vasudeva.
Out of fear of Kaṃsa, at the request of Vasudeva, two arms were withdrawn until the slaying of Kaṃsa, after which they were manifested again.
[As it is said: "O God, Lord of gods, you have been born, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace."
O Lord, by your grace, withdraw this divine form.

"...O Soul of the Universe, assume this four-armed form"— thus was it prayed for. Even for Śiśupāla, though he was an enemy, the object of his constant meditation was precisely that four-armed form of Vasudeva’s son,
described as "possessing noble, thick, four arms, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace."
Therefore, it is said here by Pārtha that [the Lord] is four-armed in that very form.
Arjuna said:
O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours,
I am now restored to my senses and have returned to my natural state.

Having now beheld this exceedingly gentle form of yours— endowed with limitless, unsurpassed beauty, delicacy, and charm, unique to you alone, and established in the human form— I have regained my senses and returned to my natural state.
The Blessed Lord said: You have seen this form of mine which is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
This form which you have seen—standing under my command, the support of all, and the cause of all—is extremely difficult to behold; it cannot be seen by anyone.
Even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
But they did not see it.
To the question "Why?", he says here:
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen me. (BhG 11.53)
But by undivided devotion alone, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe. (BhG 11.54)
By means of the Vedas— through their teaching, exposition, study, hearing, and recitation— as well as by sacrifices,

gifts, oblations, and austerities, when these are performed solely and devoid of devotion to Me, it is impossible to see Me as I truly abide. But through unswerving devotion alone, one may know Me in truth according to the scriptures, and realize Me in truth through direct perception.
And it is possible to enter [it] in its true nature;
thus says the Śruti:
"This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing."
"He is to be attained by whomsoever He chooses; to him this Self reveals His own form. (BhG 11.53–54)
O Pāṇḍava, he who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as the supreme goal, who is devoted to Me, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward any living being— he comes to Me.
He who performs all actions, such as the study of the Vedas and so forth, in the form of worship of Me, is one who works for Me (matkarmakṛt).
He for whom I alone am the supreme goal in all undertakings is one who has Me as his highest aim (matparamaḥ).
He is one for whom I am the supreme goal;

he is my devotee who, because of his extreme love for me, finds no sustenance for himself without the chanting of my names, my praise, meditation on me, worship of me, prostration to me, and so forth, and who, having me as his sole purpose, performs these acts constantly.
He is my devotee.
"Free from attachment" means being unable to endure any other association because of the singular love for Me alone.

"Without enmity toward all beings" means that, because one's own nature consists solely of pleasure and pain arising from union with or separation from Me, and because one reflects upon how one's own suffering is caused by one's own transgressions, and because one reflects upon how all beings are dependent upon the Supreme Person, there is no cause for enmity toward any beings; thus, one is without enmity toward them.

He who has become thus attains me— me as I truly exist; the meaning is that he becomes one whose slightest trace of defects such as ignorance has been cast away, and who experiences nothing but me alone.

To Arjuna, who desired to directly perceive the unimpeded sovereignty of the Supreme Brahman, Lord Nārāyaṇa— the goal to be attained by those established in the yoga of devotion— the Lord, an ocean of qualities such as limitless compassion, magnanimity, and gentleness, and whose resolve is ever true,
revealed His sovereignty exactly as it exists.
And it has been stated that, in reality, the attainment of the Blessed One’s knowledge and vision is obtainable exclusively and absolutely through devotion (*bhakti*) to the Blessed One alone.

Immediately thereafter, the superiority of the worship of the Blessed One in the form of devotion—over the worship of the self (*ātma-upāsana*), which is the means for attaining the self—is established because it more swiftly accomplishes its own goal and is easier to practice;
furthermore, this is the means for the worship of the Blessed One.
For one who is incapable of that, there is steadfastness in the Imperishable (akṣara-niṣṭhā),
and those [paths] required for it are now described.
Furthermore, the excellence of the worship of the Blessed One follows from the excellence of the object of worship, which is the goal to be attained.
“Of all yogis as well, he who worships me with his inner self absorbed in me and possessed of faith— he is deemed by me to be the most disciplined.”
Thus it has been said here:
"Of those who, being ever-devoted, worship You with devotion, and those who worship the Imperishable and the Unmanifest—of these, which are the best knowers of yoga? (BhG 12.1)

In this manner, by the way described in the verse beginning with "mat-karma-kṛt," those devotees who are constantly disciplined (satatayuktāḥ), regarding You, the Blessed One, alone as the supreme goal to be attained,

worship You— the one endowed with all glories, a boundless ocean of infinite qualities such as unsurpassed beauty, amiability, omniscience, and the power of true resolve— You who are perfectly complete.

And those who worship that very Imperishable, which is the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and which is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)—its true form not being manifested by the instruments such as the eyes and so forth—for both of these groups, who are the most proficient in yoga? The meaning is: who are the swifter in reaching their respective goal?
For it will be made clear later [in verse 18] with the words "I shall come to them without delay, O Pārtha" that the state of being most proficient in yoga pertains to this swiftness.
The Blessed Lord said: Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined.

Those who, with supreme faith, having fixed their minds on Me because of My being exceedingly dear to them, worship Me—being ever-steadfast and desiring constant union—the meaning is that they worship Me by fixing their minds, which are the objects of attainment, upon Me; they are the most disciplined, and the meaning is that they attain Me easily and without delay. (BhG 12.2)
But those who worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, all-pervading, inconceivable, immovable, unchanging, and eternal; BhG 12.3.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses and possessing equanimity toward all things,
those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone.
The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater;
for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings.

But those who [know] the Imperishable, which is the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is indefinable because it cannot be designated by words such as "god" and so forth due to its distinctness from the body, and for that very reason unmanifest to the instruments of perception such as the eyes;

which is all-pervading and inconceivable— meaning that although it exists everywhere within the bodies of gods and others, it is unfit to be conceived in any of those forms because it is of a different nature from them.

The meaning is that it is "immovable" (*kūṭastha*) for that very reason— being common to all, yet unconnected with the specific forms of various things such as gods and so forth— and because it does not move or deviate from its own unique form due to its changelessness,
it is therefore "fixed" (*dhruva*), eternal.
Having properly restrained the entire collection of senses, such as the eyes and others, from their respective functions, [one should remain].

They possess an equal intellect everywhere; that is, they have an equal intellect because the Self, though abiding in bodies of diverse forms such as gods and others, is of a single form consisting solely of knowledge.
For this very reason, they are devoted to the welfare of all beings and have desisted from what is harmful to all beings.
Indeed, the state of being devoid of harm toward all beings is [the result of] abandoning the conceit of diversity in forms such as gods and others regarding the Self.
Those who thus worship the Imperishable (akṣara) also certainly reach Me; the meaning is that they indeed reach the Self which is of the same nature as Myself and is not subject to saṃsāra.
For it will be stated later: "They have attained a state of similarity with Me."
And it is heard [in scripture]: "The stainless one attains supreme equality.

Likewise, the distinction of the Supreme Brahman from the immutable (akṣara) designated by the word "immutable"—that which is the unchanging (kūṭastha)—will be stated: "The unchanging is called the immutable."

"But the Supreme Person is another" (Gītā 15.17); and in the Akṣaravidyā, "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is apprehended" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5), that which is indicated by the word "Imperishable" is indeed the Supreme Brahman,
because it is the source of all beings and so forth.
For those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest, the affliction is indeed greater;
for the goal that is the Unmanifest—the mental state directed toward the Unmanifest—is attained with difficulty by embodied beings who possess the conceit of identifying the body with the Self.
For those who possess bodies consider the body itself to be the Self. (BhG 12.3–5)
The Lord has clearly stated that those who sit near Him are the most disciplined:
"But those who, having renounced all actions in Me and being intent on Me, worship Me, meditating upon Me with an undivided yoga... (BhG 12.6).
I am the deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence for those whose minds are absorbed in me; I become so, O Pārtha, before long.
But those who, having renounced all worldly actions— such as eating and so forth which are necessary for the maintenance of the body and for its sustenance—
as well as all Vedic rites such as sacrifice, giving, oblation, and austerity, together with their causes and their intended objects, into Me with a mind directed toward the inner self;

"Devoted to Me" (matparāḥ) means having Me as their sole goal; "by means of yoga that is indeed without another" (ananyenaiva yogena) means by means of yoga that has no other purpose. The meaning is that they worship Me while meditating upon Me, performing meditation, worship, prostration, praise, glorification, and so forth—acts which are themselves exceedingly dear to them and equal to the attainment of the goal itself.
Because they are opposed to attaining Me, I shall, in a very short time, deliver them from the ocean called saṃsāra, which is like death itself.
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me.
Thereafter you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, because it is the supreme human goal, because it is easily attainable, and because it is obtainable without delay, fix your mind on Me alone; concentrate your mind upon Me.
Establish your intellect in Me; form the firm conviction that I alone am the supreme goal to be attained. Hereafter, you shall dwell in Me alone.
The meaning is: immediately after fixing the mind with the firm resolve that "I alone am the supreme goal to be attained," you shall dwell within Me.
But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me,
then seek to reach me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of practice.
Now, if you are unable to fix your mind steadily upon me all at once,
then desire to attain me through the yoga of practice,

[meditating] upon me as an ocean of countless virtues— such as natural, limitless, and unsurpassed beauty, good character, friendliness, affection, compassion, sweetness, profundity, magnanimity, heroism, valor, omniscience, the state of having true desires, the state of having true resolves, universal lordship, and being the cause of all things.

Having attained a firm concentration of the mind through the yoga of repeated practice of remembrance imbued with unsurpassed love for me— who am the adversary of all that is to be abandoned— desire to attain me.
If you are unable even to practice, become one who is intent upon My work;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.
Now, if you are unable even to practice mindfulness in this manner,

be intent upon my work. My works consist of building temples, clearing away weeds, lighting lamps, sweeping, sprinkling water, smearing with cow dung, gathering flowers, performing worship, chanting my names, circumambulating, offering praise, prostrating, and so forth.
Perform those actions with extreme devotion;

even while performing actions for my sake with extreme devotion, you will soon attain a firm state of mind fixed upon me through the practice of yoga, and thereby achieve the perfection consisting in attaining me.
Or, if you are unable to do even this, take refuge in my yoga.
Then, with self-restraint, practice the renunciation of the fruits of all actions.

Now, if you are unable to perform even this [meditation] by relying on My yoga— that is, if you cannot perform even this work for Me, which takes the form of exclusive devotion produced by contemplating My qualities—

then, having relied upon the yoga of the Imperishable (akṣara-yoga), which consists of contemplating one's own true nature, generates supreme devotion, and was taught in the first six chapters, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions as a means to that end.
For the realization that I am the sole object of attainment arises only in one whose sins have been entirely destroyed;

such a person is self-controlled, meaning one whose mind is restrained. Then, through action performed as worship of me without aiming for its fruits, and through the perfected meditation upon the Self—

When the inner self (pratyagātman)— whose sole nature is to have me as its remainder— is directly realized, with all obscurations such as ignorance having ceased, supreme devotion to me arises spontaneously.
And so it will be stated:
“By worshipping Him through his own duty, a person attains perfection,” beginning thus, [it continues]:
“Freed from possessiveness and tranquil, he is fit for becoming Brahman;
having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires.”
“Being equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me. (BhG 12.11)
Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation, peace follows immediately.

From the practice of mindfulness—which is devoid of excessive attachment and is of a firm nature—there arises the direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*) of that [Self] preceded by an investigation into the true nature of the imperishable; this alone is distinguished as being for the welfare of the Self.
Even from the direct realization of the Self, which is yet unperfected in form, meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the Self as its means is distinguished as being for the welfare of the Self.
And even from that meditation, which is yet unperfected in form, action (*karman*) performed by abandoning the fruits as its means is distinguished.
From the performance of action without regard for its fruit, tranquility of mind will arise immediately through the removal of sin;
when the mind is tranquil, meditation on the Self will be perfected;
and from meditation, there will follow the direct realization of that [Self].
Because supreme devotion arises from direct realization, for one who is unable to practice the yoga of devotion, steadfastness in the Self alone is better.

The meaning is that even for one steadfast in the Self, if the mind is not yet tranquil, steadfastness in the performance of action—whose fruit is not sought and which contains within it the knowledge of the Self—is better for the attainment of that steadfastness. (BhG 12.12)
He describes the qualities to be adopted by one who is devoted to action performed without regard for its fruit:
"One who is not a hater of any beings, but friendly and compassionate,
free from the sense of 'mine' and free from egoism, equal in pleasure and pain, and patient" (BhG 12.13).
The yogi who is ever contented, self-controlled, and firm in resolve, whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. (BhG 12.14)

One who is "non-hostile toward all beings"— that is, non-hostile toward all beings, even those who are hostile or harmful— reflecting that "these beings hate and do harm in accordance with my own faults and impelled by the Lord"; such a person, maintaining a friendly disposition toward all those beings who hate and do harm, is "friendly" (*maitra*).

Feeling compassion for those very beings who are suffering, he is compassionate; being free from the sense of "mine" regarding the body, the senses, and their related objects, he is without possessiveness;
and being devoid of the conceit that the body is the self, he is without egoism.
Therefore, he is equal in pain and pleasure, free from elation and dejection when pleasure and pain arise from his own volition;
he is patient, remaining unmodified even by those two which are unavoidable and produced by physical contact;
and he is contented, being satisfied with whatever means for sustaining the body comes to him by chance.
The constant yogi is one who is perpetually intent on the contemplation of the Self as distinct from primordial nature; he is self-controlled, having restrained the fluctuations of the mind,
and possesses firm conviction regarding the truths proclaimed in the scriptures of the supreme Self.

"Having dedicated mind and intellect to Me" means that the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone is worshipped through action performed without regard for its fruit, with the thought, "When He is worshipped, He will bring about my direct realization of the Self.
Thus, one whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me is My devotee; such a person, who worships Me in this manner through the yoga of action—[for him...]
He is dear to me.
He by whom the world is not agitated and who is not agitated by the world, and who is free from joy, envy, fear, and anxiety—he, too, is dear to Me. (BhG 12.15)
Because the world is not agitated by the person who is established in action and serves as its cause— meaning he does not perform even the slightest action that causes agitation to the world—
and because he is not agitated by the world serving as its cause— meaning that the entire world performs actions that do not cause him agitation,
due to his certainty in being non-opposed to all.
For this very reason, [one acts] toward someone with joy, toward someone with indignation, and toward someone with fear.
He who is liberated from agitation toward anything whatsoever— one who has become thus— he too is dear to me.
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress, and has renounced all undertakings—he who is my devotee is dear to me. (BhG 12.16)
Indifferent, meaning indifferent toward all things other than the Self; pure, meaning having a body nourished by substances prescribed by the scriptures;
and skillful, meaning capable of undertaking the actions enjoined by the scriptures.
One who is indifferent to other matters, free from distress when scriptural duties are completed, devoid of pain regarding unavoidable sufferings such as cold, heat, and contact with people,
and one who has abandoned all undertakings— that is, one who has renounced the commencement of all actions other than those prescribed by scripture.
He who is such a devotee of mine is dear to me.
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires,
who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to Me.
He who does not rejoice when he encounters that which is dear to men— a source of joy—
and he who, being a practitioner of action (*karmayogin*), does not rejoice upon obtaining it;
and [likewise] that which is unpleasant—
Having attained that, he does not feel aversion;
and having encountered that which is a cause of grief for human beings— such as the loss of wife, children, or wealth— he does not grieve.
Nor does he long for such [states] as he has not yet attained;
being a renouncer of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he abandons both because there is no difference in their being causes of bondage, just as evil is.
Such a person is one who possesses devotion.
He is dear to me.
He who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and who is free from attachment—[he is a yogi].
A man who is equal in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes,
homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion— such a person is dear to Me.
By the verse beginning with "one who is not hateful toward any being," freedom from hatred and other such emotions toward enemies, friends, and others has been stated;
here, however, an even greater distinction is expressed: equanimity of mind toward them even when they are present.
Furthermore, one who is unattached to dwellings and the like due to having a steady mind fixed on the Self is called "homeless" (aniketa).
For that very reason, he is also equanimous toward honor, dishonor, and so forth;
one who is thus devoted is dear to Me.
Establishing the superiority of one who is steadfast in devotion over one who is steadfast in the self, He concludes in accordance with the beginning:
"But those who worship this nectar of dharma as it has been described, full of faith, regarding Me as the Supreme Goal—they, the devotees, are exceedingly dear to Me. (BhG 12.20)

"Dharmyāmṛta" means that which is both righteous and immortal; those, however, who worship the yoga of devotion— which is the means of attainment equal to the goal itself— in the manner described in such passages as "those who, fixing their minds on Me," and so forth;
Those devotees are exceedingly dear to me.

In the first hexad, it was stated that the vision of the true nature of the individual self (pratyagātman)— which is the means for attaining the Supreme Brahman, the Lord Vāsudeva, who is the ultimate goal to be reached— is accomplished through the two-fold steadfastness characterized by the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action, and which constitutes an ancillary to the worship of the Lord in the form of devotion.

In the middle hexad, the steadfastness in the yoga of exclusive and absolute devotion was expounded, preceded by the knowledge of the true nature and the majesty of the reality of the Lord, who is the supreme object of attainment.

It has been stated that for those who desire preeminent sovereignty and for those who desire only the absolute liberation of the self (*ātma-kaivalya*), the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) is the means for attaining their respective goals.

Now, in the subsequent six chapters (*ṣaṭka*), the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and their conjunction; the Lord (*īśvara*) and His true nature; action (*karman*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and devotion (*bhakti*); as well as the essential forms and methods of their attainment, which were set forth in the two preceding six-chapter sections, are further clarified.
Among these, first, in the thirteenth chapter, the essential natures of the body and the self are presented.
The purification of the true nature of the body, the means for attaining the Self dissociated from the body,
and the thorough purification of the nature of the isolated Self.
The cause of the connection between such a self and non-conscious matter, as well as the method for the contemplation of their distinction, is stated.
The Blessed Lord said:
This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the "field" (kṣetra).
Those who know this call him who understands it the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). (BhG 13.1)
"This body is 'I am a god,' 'I am a human,' 'I am fat'."

The perception "I am emaciated," which occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the self as the enjoyer, is described by those who know the true nature of the body as the field of experience belonging to the enjoyer— the self— which is a distinct entity from that [body].
This [body] exists both in its individual parts and as a composite whole.

"He who knows, 'I know this'— those who know the truth of the Self (ātmayāthātmyavidaḥ) call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), as he is a distinct entity from that which has become the object of knowledge by virtue of being the knower."

Even though at the time of reflecting on objects such as a jar—which are distinct from the body—one reflects upon the self as the knower in grammatical coreferentiality with the body, thinking, "I am a god," "I am a human," or "I know the jar" and so forth;

nevertheless, at the time of experiencing the body, one experiences the body itself as an object of knowledge, just like a jar or other things, in the form "I know this. Thus, the body is also [an object] for the self, the knower, by way of being an object of knowledge.
Like a jar or other such objects, it is a distinct entity.
Likewise, just as with a jar or similar things, the knower—the *kṣetrajña*—is a distinct entity from the body, which is the object of cognition.

As for the perception [of them] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), this is logically established because, in reality, the body—like "cowness" and so forth—is of a nature whose sole essence is to serve as a qualification of the Self, and is thus not established apart from it.

In that regard, because the uncommon form of the knower is not an object of the instruments such as the eyes, and because it is an object of the mind refined by yoga, the deluded perceive the knower as having only the form of *prakṛti* simply due to the proximity of *prakṛti*;
and thus he will say:
"Whether departing, or staying, or even enjoying, [the self] is associated with the qualities (*guṇas*)."
"The deluded do not perceive it; those with the eye of knowledge see it. (BhG 13.1)
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bharata;
the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field—that, in My view, is true knowledge. (BhG 13.2)
Know Me as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who possesses the aspect of being the knower in all fields such as those of gods and humans; know Me as having that as My very self.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "and also the Knower of the Field," it is understood that one should also know the Field itself to be Me.

Just as the Field must be designated through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the Knower of the Field—since its sole nature is to be a qualification of the Knower and it is not established independently of Him—so too [is the Knower of the Field designated].

Likewise, know that the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are to be designated through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Me alone, because they are established as non-different from Me, having My specific attributes as their sole nature.

The Śrutis declare that the field—which consists of the aggregate of earth and the other elements—and the knower of the field have the Lord as their very self, since their essential nature is solely to be the body of the Lord:

"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3)

“He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller (antaryāmin), the immortal. Such passages as these [establish this].

This very state of the Blessed One’s abiding as the self of all knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) by way of being their inner controller is the reason for designating Him through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with them:
“I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings.”

Having stated previously and subsequently— "There is nothing, whether moving or unmoving, that exists without Me"— and "Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but one part," He designates [Himself] in the middle by means of grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
By the words "Of the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu," and so forth,
that knowledge which has been declared regarding the discrimination between the field and the knower of the field, and regarding their having Me as their Self—
that alone is the knowledge to be accepted; this is My opinion.
Some say: "Know me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)"—from this grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), oneness is understood.
Consequently, it must be accepted that although the Lord alone exists, He appears as if He were the Knower of the Field due to ignorance;
and this teaching of oneness is intended for the cessation of that [ignorance].

And by this most authoritative instruction of the Blessed One—just as the delusion of being a snake is removed by the authoritative instruction, "This is a rope, not a snake"—the delusion of being a *kṣetrajña* (individual soul) is likewise removed.
They should be asked: Is this teacher, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord, one whose ignorance has been removed through the direct realization of the true nature of the Self, or not?
If ignorance has ceased, then—
given that it is impossible for any other form to be superimposed upon the Self, whose sole nature is non-dual pure consciousness— the perception of distinctions such as "son of Kuntī" and so forth,
as well as activities such as teaching directed toward them, would not be possible.

Now, if one's ignorance has not been removed because of the absence of the direct realization of the Self, then, precisely because of that state of ignorance, the teaching of the knowledge of the Self would be impossible;
for it has been said: "The knowers of reality, who see the truth, will instruct you in that knowledge."

Therefore, these aforementioned doctrines, which were promulgated by the ignorant for the sake of deluding the world and which contradict the Vedas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, logic, and their own words, are to be disregarded.
In this regard, the truth is as follows:

certain Śrutis declare the distinction between the essential natures of the non-sentient entity (acidvastu), the sentient entity (cidvastu), and the Supreme Brahman, characterized respectively as the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the Lord.
“The Illusionist creates all this universe, and another, distinct from him, is bound by that illusion”; “One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial matter) and the Great Lord as the Illusionist”;

“The perishable is Pradhāna, the imperishable and immortal is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self. By the phrase “the imperishable and immortal Hara,” the enjoyer is indicated.

He is Hara because he seizes the *pradhāna* as an object of experience for the self; [as it is said]: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him";
"The Lord of *pradhāna* and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the master of the *guṇas*";
"The Lord of the universe, the sovereign of the self, the eternal, the auspicious, the infallible."
“The two, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord”;
“The eternal among eternals, the consciousness among conscious beings, the one who fulfills the desires of the many”;
“Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller.”
“Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one then attains immortality”;
“One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other looks on without eating”;
“The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring similar to herself.”

“For one unborn, indeed, rejoicing [in her], lies along with her; another unborn one abandons her once her enjoyments have been experienced. And so forth. Here too [it is said]: “This eightfold nature of mine is called ‘ego’ (ahaṅkāra).
Know this to be my lower nature; but other than this, know my higher nature.”
"O Kaunteya, at the end of a kalpa, all beings go to my own material nature;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth."
Taking hold of my own nature, I project forth this entire multitude of beings again and again, which is powerless under the sway of nature.
"Under my supervision, Nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world indeed revolves."
“Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless,” and, “The Great Brahman is my womb; in it I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs.”

I unite the embryo known as consciousness with that which is the source of the world— the Great Brahman belonging to me, called primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the subtle essence of beings and an insentient entity; then, from that union of the sentient and the insentient brought about by my volition, [the world arises].
The meaning is that in this way the origin of all beings—whether conscious, unconscious, or a mixture of both, ranging from gods down to stationary objects—takes place.

Thus, certain Śrutis declare that since the sentient and the insentient, which exist in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed and persist in all states, constitute the body of the Supreme Person, they abide not separately from Him as being governed by Him; and they declare the Supreme Person to be their Self.
“[He] who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within”—beginning thus, and continuing until:

“[He] who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Likewise:
“[He] who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know”—beginning thus.
“He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know;
he who moves within Death (mṛtyu), whose body is Death, whom Death does not know—this is Nārāyaṇa, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God.
Here, by the word "Death," the subtle state of insentient matter denoted by the word "Darkness" (tamas) is expressed.

In this very Upaniṣad, because of the statement, "The unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable; the imperishable dissolves into darkness," and also because of the statement, "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all," the Supreme Person alone—

having the conscious and unconscious entities existing in all states as His body— is the one who exists in the form of the world, both in its causal and effected states, as that which is manifested by Him.
To make this point known, certain scriptural passages state that the world—both in its state as effect and in its state as cause—is that very same [Brahman]:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second";
and "It thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate.'"

Beginning with “It created fire,” and continuing through, “All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support,” and “All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; that art thou, Śvetaketu.”
Likewise: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate.
He performed austerity."
Beginning with, "Having performed austerity, he created all this," it concludes with,
"The real and the immortal became the Real."
Here too, the distinction between the essential natures of the conscious and the unconscious and the Supreme Person, established by another scriptural passage, is recalled:
"Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms";
and, "Having created that..."
"It entered into that very thing;

having entered it, it became both the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat) ... both consciousness (vijñāna) and the unconscious, both the true (satya) and the untrue (anṛta), and it became the true. Thus [it is said].
The differentiation of name-and-form is exactly of this nature;
for it has also been stated in this regard: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by means of name and form."

Therefore, since the Supreme Person alone possesses the gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities as His body—both in His state as the effect and His state as the cause—it is most appropriately established that through the knowledge of the cause, the effect is known; thus, the intended "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is logically consistent.
This is evidenced by the scriptural passage: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form."
Having indicated all insentient matter by the words “three deities,” the scripture speaks of the differentiation of names and forms through the entry of the individual soul, which is His own self;

therefore, all expressive words denote the Supreme Self alone as qualified by the insentient and the individual soul. Consequently, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of a word denoting the effect with a word denoting the Supreme Self in His causal state is primary (*mukhyavṛtta*).

Therefore, since Brahman alone— consisting of the gross and subtle aspects of the sentient and the insentient— is both the effect and the cause, the world has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*).

Although the world has Brahman as its material cause because Brahman itself possesses the subtle sentient and insentient entities as its body, it is even more appropriately established that there is no confusion of the natures of the sentient, the insentient, and Brahman, because the composite whole functions as the material cause.

Just as a multicolored cloth, although originating from a collection of white, black, and red threads, possesses its connection with whiteness and so forth only in the specific regions of those respective threads— so that even in its state as an effect there is no confusion of colors everywhere— in the same way, although the world originates from a collection of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, even in its state as an effect there is no confusion between the states of being an enjoyer, an object of enjoyment, and a controller.
In the case of threads, which are capable of existing separately, they possess the status of being both cause and effect only when they are occasionally conjoined by the will of a person;

however, in this context, since both the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit) in all their states constitute categories of existence only as modes (*prakāra*) of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*)—being His body—the Supreme Person Himself, as that mode, is both the cause and the effect.
He alone is always denotable by every word; this is the distinction.
The distinction of intrinsic natures and their non-confusion are equal both there [in the cause] and here [in the effect].
This being so, even when the supreme Brahman enters into the state of an effect, its lack of modification is more convincingly established because there is no change in its essential nature.

Furthermore, its status as an effect is also established because it exists as the self of the conscious and unconscious reality that is in a gross state and differentiated by the division of name and form.
For being an effect consists precisely in the attainment of a different state.
And the declarations that the supreme Brahman is devoid of qualities are justified because of its lack of connection with any qualities to be abandoned, as it is said:
"He is free from evil, ageless, and deathless."

Having negated the qualities to be abandoned by stating, "free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst," and having established the multitude of auspicious qualities by stating, "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true," this very Śruti restricts the general negation of qualities understood elsewhere to those qualities that are to be abandoned.

Furthermore, the doctrine that Brahman is pure consciousness in essence [is consistent] with [the fact that it is] omniscient, omnipotent, and the source of all auspicious qualities which are the opposite of everything to be abandoned.
This is more logically consistent because it is accepted that the nature of Brahman is definable solely through knowledge, and that its essence is knowledge itself by virtue of being self-luminous—
as in the scriptural passages: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action."
Passages such as “By what, O Maitreyi, would one know the knower? declare its nature as a knower;

while passages such as “Truth, Knowledge... declare its nature as pure consciousness, both by virtue of being definable solely as knowledge and by its self-luminosity. Furthermore, [the text] states: “He desired, ‘May I become many.’”

“‘It thought: May I be many’; ‘It was differentiated by name and form alone’—thus, it is Brahman itself that, through its own volition, exists in various ways as the manifold forms of diverse moving and stationary beings.
Therefore, the multiplicity of entities that are not of the nature of Brahman, which is opposed to that [Brahman], is denied as being unreal.”

“He who perceives here [in this world] as if there were diversity goes from death to death... for there is not the slightest diversity here,” and “For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another;
but where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the manifold nature of Brahman—consisting in its assuming various names and forms through its own volition, as established by such scriptural passages as "May I be many, may I procreate"—is also being negated.
Indeed, that [manifold nature] was established at the very commencement of the negative statement: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him," and it is stated:
"Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self."

"From that great Being, this [world] is breathed forth—namely, the Rig Veda," and so forth. Thus, for all the Śrutis—which declare the distinction in essential nature and the distinction in inherent character between the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, and which declare the relationship of cause and effect as well as the non-difference between cause and effect—the conscious and the unconscious are always in a body-soul relationship with the Supreme Self; and when existing as bodies, they reach a subtle state in the causal condition that is unfit for the differentiation of name and form.

Furthermore, since this is known from the Śrutis themselves— which declare that during the state of being an effect [Brahman] attains a gross state appropriate to that— it is seen that there is no room whatsoever for the doctrine of Brahman’s ignorance (*brahmājñānavāda*), the doctrine of the distinction in Brahman due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikabrahmabheda-vāda*),
or any other doctrine rooted in fallacious reasoning that contradicts all the Śrutis; therefore, enough with excessive prolixity.
That field—what it is, of what nature, what its modifications are, and from whence it arises;
and who He is, and what His powers are—hear that from me in brief.
That field is that which it is, that substance it is, of what nature it is as the basis for various beings, what its modifications are, and what those modifications themselves are.
From what and by what cause this has arisen;
the meaning is: for what purpose it has arisen, and what its essential nature is.
And who he is, and who that Knower of the Field is, what his essential nature is, what his power is, and what his powers are—
all that.
Listen from me in brief, that is, in summary.
It has been sung in many ways by the seers, in various distinct Vedic meters,
and also in the form of the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are reasoned and definitive.

This very reality of the field and the knower of the field has been sung in many ways and by many methods by seers such as Parāśara and others: "O King, I, you, and likewise others, are carried away by the elements;
even this aggregate of elements, having fallen into the flow of the qualities (guṇas), goes along."
O Lord of the Earth, these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are indeed subject to karma;
and that karma, accumulated through ignorance, exists in all living beings without exception.
The Self is pure, imperishable, peaceful, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature.
Likewise: "Since the body, characterized by the head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the person, for what reason, O King, do I apply this notion of 'I' to it? And similarly:
"Is this the head? Or is this your chest, or likewise your belly?"
How much more so your feet and other limbs? O lord of the earth, how can this truly belong to you?
Having become distinct from all your constituent parts and remaining separate, O King, reflect with great precision upon the question: "Who am I?"
BhG 13.
Thus they speak of the two distinct [principles] as having Vāsudeva as their essence:
"The senses, mind, intellect, being, radiance, strength, and fortitude..."
They say that both the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) have Vāsudeva as their essence.
BhG 13.

Thus, by means of various meters and distinct types of meters—namely the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas—the essential natures of the body and the self are sung separately: "From that very Self, indeed, space was produced."
From space comes air;
from air, fire; from fire, water.
From water comes earth; from earth come plants;
from plants comes food.

Having described the nature of the body with the words, "From food [comes] the person; this very person consists of the essence of food," and having described the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) as internal to that, and the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) as internal to that,
[the text] describes the nature of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) with the words, "Different from this one consisting of mind is the inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*)."

"Therefore, different from this self consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya) is another inner self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). Thus, the supreme Self is declared to be the one consisting of bliss by virtue of being the inner self even of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). In this way, in the Ṛg, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the distinctness of the field and the knower of the field, as well as their nature as Brahman, is clearly sung in various places. And by the words of the Brahma-sūtras—that is, by the words known as the aphorisms for establishing Brahman, namely the Śārīraka-sūtras—[this is further confirmed].
"Reasoned" means accompanied by logical arguments;
"ascertained" means concluding with a definitive determination.
Starting from the aphorism "Space is not [produced], because it is not so heard [in scripture]," the determination of the nature of the field (kṣetra) has been stated.

Beginning with the words, “The Self [is] not [the body], because of the Veda and because of its eternity from those [scriptures],” the determination of the true nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has been stated.
And by the words, “But [it is] from the Supreme, for that is heard,” its identity with the Blessed Lord has been stated through the fact that it is impelled by Him.
Thus, listen to the true nature of the Field and the Knower of the Field, which has been sung in many ways by Me, now being stated very clearly and concisely—this is the meaning. (BhG 13.4)
The great elements, ego-sense, intellect, and the unmanifest;
the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the physical aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—
this is declared to be the field in brief, together with its modifications.
The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest are the substances that initiate the field.
The great elements are earth, water, fire, air, and space;
ego-consciousness is the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
Intellect is the Great One (mahat),
the unmanifest is primordial nature (prakṛti);
the ten senses and the one [mind], along with the five objects of the senses— these are the principles (tattvas) dependent upon the field (kṣetra).
The five organs of cognition are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose;
the five organs of action are speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals— these are the ten—
and "one" refers to the mind.
The five objects of the senses are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
desire, aversion, pleasure, and pain are called the functions of the field (kṣetra) and the transformations of the field,
even though desire, aversion, pleasure, and pain are attributes of the self (ātman).
Nevertheless, because they are produced by the Self’s connection with the field (*kṣetra*), they are called modifications of the field by virtue of being the effects of the field.
Their status as attributes of the Person (*puruṣadharman*) will be stated later: "The Person is said to be the cause of being the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) of pleasures and pains."

The *saṃghāta* (aggregate) is the support for consciousness (*cetanā*). "Support" (*ādhṛti*) means a substratum (*ādhāra*). It is the aggregate of elements (*bhūtasamghāta*) that arises as the substratum for consciousness—which experiences pleasure and pain and accomplishes enjoyment and liberation.

Composed of substances beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with earth, it serves as the locus for the sense organs; it is subject to modifications such as desire, aversion, pleasure, and pain; it consists of the form of the aggregate of elements; and its purpose is to serve as the substratum for the experience of pleasure and pain by consciousness.
It has been called the "field";
this field has been declared in brief, in summary, along with its modifications and its effects.
Now, those qualities which are to be adopted as means for attaining self-knowledge regarding the duties pertaining to the field are declared:
humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint. (BhG 13.7)

Humility (*amānitva*) is the state of being free from contempt toward superior persons. Freedom from hypocrisy (*adambhitva*) is the absence of hypocrisy, which consists in performing religious duties for the sake of gaining a reputation for piety.
Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the state of being free from causing pain to others through speech, mind, or body;
patience (*kṣānti*) is the state of having an unaltered mind even when being harmed by others;
and straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the uniformity of one's speech, mind, body, and so forth toward others.

Service to the teacher (*ācāryopāsana*) is the state of being devoted to prostration, inquiry, and attendance toward the teacher who bestows the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). Purity (*śauca*) is the fitness of mind, speech, and body for the knowledge of the Self and its means, as established by the scriptures.
Steadfastness (*stairya*) is immovability regarding the meaning taught in the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātmaśāstra*).
Self-restraint is the withdrawal of the mind from objects other than the true nature of the self.
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism, and the constant perception of the evils of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering; BhG 13.8.
Detachment from the objects of the senses is the agitation [of the mind] through the contemplation of the defects in objects that are distinct from the Self;
non-egoism is the absence of the conceit of being the Self in the body, which is not the Self;
this is mentioned for the sake of illustration.

And what is intended is the absence of the conceit of "mine" regarding that which is not one's own. Regarding the observation of the defects of birth, death, old age, and disease: it is the contemplation of the inevitability of the defect consisting of the suffering of birth, death, old age, and disease as long as one possesses a body. (BhG 13.8)
Non-attachment and absence of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (BhG 13.9)
Non-attachment (*asakti*) is the state of being free from clinging toward possessions that are distinct from the self;

non-possessiveness (*anabhiṣvaṅga*) is the state of being free from attachment toward children, wife, home, and so forth, beyond their status as instruments for performing actions prescribed by the scriptures; and it is the state of being free from joy and agitation when encountering desirable or undesirable events arising from one's own mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*). (BhG 13.9)
And unwavering devotion to me through the yoga of exclusive concentration;
resorting to solitary places; and a lack of delight in the assembly of men. (BhG 13.10)
Steadfast devotion through the yoga of single-mindedness toward me, the Lord of all;
dwelling in places devoid of people;
and a lack of delight in the assembly of men. (BhG 13.10)
Constancy in the knowledge of the Self, reflection on the meaning of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
that which is contrary to this is ignorance. (BhG 13.11)
Knowledge concerning the self is *adhyātmajñāna*; its steadfastness (*niṣṭhatva*) means being intent upon that.
The meaning is: reflection on the purpose of the knowledge of reality—that is, reflection whose aim is the knowledge of reality—is what constitutes such steadfastness.
It is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because by means of it the Self is known.
The meaning is that it is the means for the knowledge of the Self.
Humility and the other qualities mentioned as belonging to the person associated with the field are indeed a collection of attributes conducive to the knowledge of the Self;
everything other than these is an action of the field that is opposed to the knowledge of the Self, and thus constitutes ignorance. (BhG 13.11)
Now, the true nature of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who was described by the characteristic of being a knower in the verse beginning "he who knows this," is clarified:
"I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality.
It is the beginningless Brahman, beyond me; it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent. (BhG 13.12)
By means of the disciplines such as humility and the rest, I shall declare that which is to be known and attained— the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman)—
knowing which one attains the immortal Self that is free from natural attributes such as birth, old age, and death;
that of which no beginning is found.
That [Self] is beginningless; for this inner self (pratyagātman) has no origin, and consequently, it has no end.
And the Śruti says: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die."
"Mat-para" means one for whom I am the supreme;
as it has been said: "But know My other nature, the higher one, which is the soul (jīva)."
For the nature of the Self has as its sole essence being a remnant of the Blessed One by virtue of being the Blessed One’s body;
and thus says the Śruti:
"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who controls the self from within."

Likewise, there are such passages as: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; he has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him," and "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas."

*Brahman* means that which possesses the quality of vastness (*bṛhattva*), being an entity distinct from the body and so forth; the meaning is the principle of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña-tattva*) which is by its own nature devoid of limitation by the body and other such things.
For it is heard in scripture: "And that [self] is capable of infinity";
its limitation by the body and its atomicity are caused by karma;
for one liberated from the bondage of karma, there is infinity.
The word "Brahman" is also applied to the Self:
"Having transcended these qualities, he becomes fit for Brahman-hood;
for I am the foundation of the immortal and the imperishable Brahman."
“Having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me.”

BhG 13. “Thus,” it is said: that which is neither existent nor non-existent is not described by the words "existent" or "non-existent" because its own essential nature is devoid of the two states consisting of cause and effect.
For in the state of being an effect, it is called "existent" due to its participation in the names and forms of gods and so forth.
Its state of unfitness [to be perceived] is said to be "non-existent" during the causal stage;
and thus says the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent."
There are such [scriptural passages] as: "From that, indeed, Being was born," and "In the beginning, this was undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form.
However, the soul's persistence in these two states of cause and effect is brought about by its being enveloped by ignorance in the form of karma.
The phrase "not produced by its own nature" means that the essential nature of the Self is not denoted by the words "existent" or "non-existent.

Even though the Supreme Brahman in its causal state is referred to in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it nevertheless possesses as its body the subtle sentient and insentient entities that are incapable of being divided into name and form.

The Supreme Brahman exists in the state of being the cause; thus, even the essential nature of the field and the knower of the field (kṣetra-kṣetrajña) in that causal state is denoted by the word "non-existent" (asat).
Since that state of the knower of the field is produced by karma, its perfectly pure essential nature cannot be designated by the terms "existent" or "non-existent."
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands pervading everything. (BhG 13.13)

That pure nature of the Self has hands and feet everywhere, being capable of the functions of hands and feet in all places; likewise, it has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and ears everywhere, performing the functions of the eyes and other senses in all directions. As it is heard in scripture regarding the Supreme Brahman, which is without hands or feet: "He moves swiftly though handless, He grasps though footless; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears. Thus, although the Supreme Brahman is without hands and feet, its performance of the functions of hands, feet, and so forth is everywhere proclaimed.

Even for the inner self (pratyagātman), which is inherently pure, the capacity to perform all functions—such as having hands and feet everywhere—is established by scripture through its attainment of identity with That (Brahman).

For it is heard in scripture: "Then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains supreme equality. And it will be said: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature."

It stands pervading everything in the world; that is to say, it remains having permeated the entire multitude of things in the world, its perfectly pure nature being omnipresent because it is devoid of limitations such as space and so forth. (BhG 13.13)
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is beyond the gunas, yet the experiencer of the gunas.
"Sarvendriyaguṇābhāsam" means that which has the appearance of the qualities of all the senses;
"indriyaguṇāḥ" refers to the functions of the senses.
The meaning is that it is capable of cognizing objects even through the functions of the senses.
The meaning is that, by its very nature, it is devoid of all sense organs; even without the functions of the senses, it knows everything by itself.

It is unattached, being by nature free from association with bodies such as those of gods and others, and it is the sustainer of all, being capable of supporting all bodies, including those of gods and others.
"According to the Vedic scripture, 'He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold,' and so forth;

[the Self] is likewise devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) by its very nature, being free from the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, yet it is also the experiencer of qualities (*guṇabhoktṛ*), possessing the capacity to experience the qualities such as *sattva*. (BhG 13.14)
It is outside and within all beings; it is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away and yet it is near.
Having abandoned the elements such as earth and the rest, it exists externally without a body,
and it also exists within them— in those states of independent activity established by such scriptural passages as, "eating, playing, and rejoicing with women or with vehicles."

It is both active and yet non-active by its very nature; though it is active within embodied existence, it is unknowable due to its subtlety. Thus, that reality of the Self, endowed with all powers and omniscient, although existing in this field, is not perceived as distinct from the body by worldly beings because of its extreme subtlety.
That [Self] is both far away and near; for men who are devoid of qualities such as humility and possess contrary qualities, it remains extremely distant even while residing within their own bodies.
Likewise, for those endowed with qualities such as humility, that very same Self resides nearby.
That which is undivided, yet appears as if divided among all beings;
that which is to be known as the sustainer of beings, and as both the devourer and the source of creation.
The reality of the Self (ātman-vastu), which exists everywhere among all beings such as gods and humans, is undivided by virtue of its single form as the cognizer.

To the ignorant, however, it appears as if divided according to the forms of gods and so forth, as in the thought, "This is a god" or "This is a human. Although it is associated with the body through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such thoughts as "I am a god" or "I am a human," it has already been stated at the outset that it can be known as something distinct from the body by virtue of being the cognizer.
Regarding the phrase "he who knows this," [the author] now states "and the sustainer of beings" (*bhūtabhartṛ*) to show that it can also be known through other modes.
It is the sustainer of the beings— earth and the rest— which are aggregated in the form of the body.
That [Self] should be known as distinct from the beings who are to be sustained; "distinct" (arthāntaram) means that it is capable of being known as something other [than them].
Likewise, it is "devouring" (grasiṣṇu), meaning it devours material things such as food.
It can be understood that it exists as something distinct from the beings being consumed, by virtue of its being the consumer;
and it is both the sovereign and the cause of manifestation—
the cause of manifestation for food and other things that have been consumed and transformed into different forms.
The meaning is that it can be known as something distinct from those [elements];
since swallowing, birth, and so forth are not observed in a dead body, it is determined that the field, which is a mere aggregate of elements, is not the cause of swallowing, birth, and sustenance.
That is said to be the light of even the lights, beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of every being.

Even for lights such as lamps, the sun, and gems, that very [Self] is the illuminator; for even in the case of lamps, the sun, and so forth, it is knowledge alone, in the form of the light of the Self, that is the illuminator.
Lamps and the like, however, perform only the removal of dense darkness which obstructs the contact between the object and the sense faculty;
it is by that much alone that they possess the quality of being illuminators. Beyond that, [the nature of] darkness is described.
The word "tamas" refers to primordial nature (prakṛti) in its subtle state;
the meaning is that [the Self] is said to be beyond that primordial nature.
Therefore, knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the single form of knowledge—this is what is to be known.
And that [Self] is to be reached through knowledge; the meaning is that it is attainable by means of the instruments of knowledge previously mentioned, such as humility (amānitva) and so forth.
It is "established in the heart of all," meaning it is present, abiding specifically within the hearts of all beings, beginning with human beings. (BhG 13.17)
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been briefly described.
Having understood this, my devotee attains to my own state of being. (BhG 13.18)
Thus, from the words "the great elements, the ego," etc., up to "the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude," the reality of the field (*kṣetra*) has been stated in brief.

From the words "humility," etc., up to "reflection on the meaning of the knowledge of reality," the means for knowing the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is that which is to be known, has been stated.

And from the words "without beginning, having Me as the supreme," etc., up to "seated in the heart of all," the true nature of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who is the object of knowledge, has also been stated in summary.
My devotee, having realized the true nature of this field,
the true nature of the means for attaining the self-nature which is distinct from the field, and the true nature of the knower of the field,
becomes fit for My state of being.
The meaning is that whatever is my state or intrinsic nature— namely, the state of being beyond saṃsāra— is attained for the sake of reaching that very state beyond saṃsāra.

Now, regarding the beginninglessness of the association between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the self (puruṣa), whose natures are absolutely distinct, as well as the differentiation of effects from these two when associated, and the cause of that association, it is said: "Know both primordial nature and the person to be indeed beginningless;
know also the transformations and the qualities to have their origin in primordial nature. (BhG 13.19)
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are mutually conjoined and beginningless;

know that the modifications such as desire and aversion, which are the causes of bondage, as well as the qualities such as humility and so forth, which are the causes of liberation, arise from Prakṛti.

This *prakṛti*, which has been evolving since beginningless time and has transformed into the form of the field (*kṣetra*), becomes the cause of bondage for the *puruṣa* through its own modifications such as desire and aversion when it is conjoined with him;
the meaning is that the very same [prakṛti] becomes the cause of liberation for the *puruṣa* through its own modifications such as humility (*amānitva*) and so forth.
Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause in the agency of action and its instruments;
the person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.
The effect is the body;
the causes are the sense organs together with the mind, consisting of knowledge and action.
Regarding their capacity for activity, the cause is primordial nature (prakṛti) itself as presided over by the person (puruṣa).
The meaning is that these are actions which serve as the means for experience, having their basis in *prakṛti* transformed into the form of the field (*kṣetra*) presided over by the *puruṣa*.
The *puruṣa*'s status as a presider is precisely in relation to that [transformation].

It has been stated [in the Sūtras], beginning with "The Self is the agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless"; for the agency of the person consists precisely in being the cause of effort directed toward the governance of the body.
The person, when conjoined with primordial nature (prakṛti), is the cause of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains.
The meaning is that it is the substratum for the experience of pleasure and pain.
Thus, the distinction between the functions of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, which are mutually intertwined, has been stated.
Now, he explains the cause for the Puruṣa—who by his very nature consists solely of the bliss of self-experience—to experience worldly pleasure and pain:
"For the Puruṣa, situated in Prakṛti, experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti."
The word "guṇa" (quality) is used figuratively with respect to its own effects.

By nature, the Puruṣa has the singular happiness of self-experience; yet, while abiding in Prakṛti—that is, being in contact with Prakṛti—he experiences the "guṇas" born of Prakṛti, which have their limiting adjuncts in contact with Prakṛti, and which consist of the effects of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, namely pleasure, pain, and so forth.
He enjoys, that is, he experiences.
He states the cause for the connection with material nature:
"Attachment to the qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs" (BhG 13.21).

Abiding in various specific wombs such as those of gods and humans—which are themselves transformations of preceding material natures—this person becomes attached to pleasures, pains, and the like, which consist of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* associated with those respective wombs; he then engages in meritorious and sinful actions that serve as the means for those experiences.
Consequently, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of those merits and sins, he is born into good or bad wombs, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.
And from that, one undertakes action;
from that, one is born;
until one cultivates qualities such as humility and the like, which serve as the means for attaining the Self.
To that same extent he wanders in saṃsāra.
Thus it has been said: "Attachment to the qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs" (BhG 13.21).
The supreme person within this body is called the witness, the consenter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the great lord,
and also the supreme self.
Abiding in this body, this person becomes the overseer and the consenter of the body by way of volitions and other functions that conform to the body's activity;
likewise, he becomes its sustainer; and likewise, he becomes the experiencer of the pleasure and pain produced by the body's activity.
Thus, by means of governing the body, sustaining the body, and presiding over the body, Maheśvara becomes the master with respect to the body, the senses, and the mind.
And so it will be said:
"Whatever body the Lord (īśvara) acquires and whatever [body] he departs from,
he goes taking these with him, like the wind carrying fragrances from their source."
Thus it is said:
"In this body, he is called the Supreme Self (paramātman) in relation to the body, the senses, and the mind.
Furthermore, the word *ātman* is used immediately thereafter for both the body and the mind.
"By means of meditation, some perceive the Self by the self within the self";
from the use of the word "also," it is understood that Maheśvara is also mentioned [therein];

this Supreme Person—whose power of knowledge is unlimited, as described in such passages as "I am the beginningless Supreme"—[is bound] due to attachment to the qualities produced by the connection with beginningless *prakṛti*.
Thus he becomes the Great Lord (Maheśvara) consisting of the body alone, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) consisting of the body alone.
He who knows this Person and Nature along with its qualities,
in whatever way he may live, is not born again.

He who knows— discerns according to reality with discrimination— this Puruṣa of the aforementioned nature, and this Prakṛti of the aforementioned nature, together with the qualities such as *sattva* whose natures are to be described hereafter; |||
Even though he exists in every way within the bodies of gods, humans, and others in an exceedingly afflicted manner, he is not born again; he does not deserve further association with *prakṛti*.
The meaning is that at the time of the end of that body, he attains the Self, which is characterized by unlimited knowledge and is free from all evil.
Some perceive the Self by means of the self through meditation;
others by the yoga of Sāṅkhya, and still others by the yoga of action. (BhG 13.24)

Some who have perfected yoga perceive the self situated within their own body by means of the self— that is, by means of the mind, through meditation, and through yoga. Others, however, whose yoga is not yet perfected, perceive the self after making the mind fit for yoga by means of Sāṃkhya-yoga and the yoga of knowledge.
Others, who are not qualified for the yoga of knowledge, and those who are so qualified but are attached to easier means,
as well as those who are outwardly designated [as practitioners], perceive the Self by attaining fitness of mind through the yoga of action which contains within it knowledge.
But others, not knowing thus, worship having heard it from others;
they too certainly cross over death, being devoted to what they have heard.

But others, who are not qualified for the means of perceiving the Self such as the yoga of action (karmayoga) and so forth, worship the Self through karma-yoga and other practices after hearing about it from others—those wise ones who perceive reality; they too transcend death by means of the vision of the Self. This applies to those who are devoted to sacred revelation (śruti), whose steadfastness consists solely in hearing.
And these, being devoted to hearing [the teachings] and purified of sin, certainly transcend death by gradually undertaking karma-yoga and the other stages;
and from the word "api" (even/also), it is understood that there is a distinction from those mentioned previously.

Now, in order to explain the method of investigating the Self as distinct from its association with primordial nature (prakṛti), [the Lord] states that all beings, whether stationary or moving, are born from the conjunction of consciousness and the unconscious:
"Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull among the Bharatas, to be from the union of the field and the Knower of the field" (BhG 13.26).
As long as any being is born, whether stationary or moving,
it is born solely through the mutual conjunction of the field and the knower of the field; it is born already conjoined,
not separated from one another— this is the meaning.
He who sees the Supreme Lord dwelling equally in all beings,
remaining undecaying when they perish— he truly sees.

Thus, he who perceives the Self—which, though joined with all beings in mutual association, is devoid of the diverse forms such as gods and so forth; which exists there in each instance as the Supreme Lord in relation to their respective bodies, senses, and minds; which is uniform in its nature as the knower; and which, while those bodies and other factors perish, does not perish because its essential nature is indestructible—[he sees truly].
