He sees; he sees the self as it truly exists.

However, the intention is that he who perceives even the self as having a distorted form—such as that of a god or other beings—and as being subject to birth, destruction, and so forth, wanders perpetually in saṃsāra.
For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy the self by means of the self; therefore, one attains the supreme goal. (BhG 13.28)

Seeing the Lord— the Self— who exists everywhere within the bodies of gods and others as their presiding ruler, support, and controller, and who is equal because He is devoid of the diverse forms of gods and others and consists solely of the form of knowledge;
seeing Him thus with the mind (ātmanā),
one does not harm, but rather protects, one's own Self.
He liberates [beings] from saṃsāra.
Consequently, because he perceives a uniform nature everywhere through his state of being the knower, he attains the supreme goal (parāṃ gatim);
it is called a "goal" (gati) because it is that which is gone toward.
One attains the Self as it truly exists, which is the supreme goal to be reached;

however, by perceiving the Self as something diverse everywhere due to its association with the forms of gods and other beings, one destroys oneself and casts oneself into the midst of the ocean of existence.
And he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone,
and likewise sees the Self as the non-doer, he truly sees.

He who perceives that all actions are performed by *prakṛti*— in accordance with the previously stated principle that "prakṛti is said to be the cause in the state of being the effect, the instrument, and the agent"—
and likewise perceives the Self as having the nature of knowledge and as being non-agents; [he sees correctly].
He who perceives that its conjunction with primordial nature, its locus therein, and the experience of pleasure and pain produced thereby are all caused by ignorance in the form of karma—
he sees the Self as it truly exists.
When one perceives the diversity of beings as abiding in the One,
and likewise perceives their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman.

When one perceives that the distinct states of all beings— whether gods or others— who consist of the two principles of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, such as their divinity, humanity, shortness, or tallness, are situated in one place, namely situated in a single principle (*ekatatva*),
which is situated in *prakṛti* and not situated in the Self (*ātman*).

When he perceives from that very source—namely, from primordial nature (prakṛti) itself—the progressive expansion through the distinctions of sons, grandsons, and so forth, at that very moment he attains Brahman; the meaning is that he reaches the Self, which is uninterrupted and has the single form of pure knowledge.
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this supreme Self is immutable;
O son of Kuntī, even though dwelling in the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.
This Supreme Self, having been extracted from the bodies and defined by its own essential nature,
is imperishable— meaning devoid of decay— even while residing in the body; because it is beginningless and uncreated,
and because it is devoid of qualities, being free from the attributes of *sattva* and the rest, it does not act.
It is not defiled by the inherent nature of the body; it is not defiled.
Even if [the Self] does not act because it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), how is it that, being eternally conjoined with the nature of the body, it is not defiled? To this, he says:
"Just as space, though all-pervading, is not defiled because of its subtlety."
Likewise, the Self, though situated everywhere within the body, is not tainted.
Just as space, although omnipresent and in contact with all things, is not defiled by the inherent natures of those things due to its subtlety,
so too the Self, because of its extreme subtlety, is not defiled by the inherent natures of this or that body, even though it abides in every body, whether divine or human.
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field.
Just as the one sun illuminates this entire world by its own radiance,

so too does the Knower of the Field illuminate the entire field— both internally and externally, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head— with his own knowledge, thinking, "This is my field, and it is such."

Therefore, the meaning is that this Self, characterized as described, is absolutely distinct from this field—which is the object of knowledge—just as the sun, the illuminator, is distinct from the world illuminated by it, because [the Self] exists as the knower while [the field] has become the known.

Those who, by means of the eye of knowledge, thus understand the distinction between the field and the Knower of the field, as well as the liberation from the material nature of beings, go to the Supreme.

In the manner thus described, those who perceive the difference— the distinction— between the field and the Knower of the field by means of the eye known as discriminative knowledge, and who [perceive] the liberation from the material nature of the elements, they go to the Supreme; they attain the Self which is freed from bondage.
"Liberation" (mokṣa) means that by which one is liberated;
the meaning is that humility and so forth are the means to liberation.

Having understood the distinction between the field and the knower of the field through the knowledge described concerning their discrimination, and having attained humility and so forth—the means to liberation from primordial matter (prakṛti) as it has transformed into the form of the elements—those who practice them [attain liberation].
The meaning is that, their bonds being released, they attain the Self which abides in its own nature and is characterized by unconditioned knowledge.

In the thirteenth chapter, it was stated that having realized the true nature of the essential being of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which are distinct from one another, one is released from bondage through qualities such as humility (*amānitva*) when these are graced by devotion to the Blessed One.
Furthermore, it was declared therein that the cause of bondage is attachment to pleasure and so forth, which consist of the successive qualities of *sattva* and the rest:
"The cause of this [bondage] is attachment to the qualities, resulting in births in good and evil wombs."
Now, the manner in which the *guṇas* are the cause of bondage and the manner of their cessation are being described.
The Blessed Lord said:
Furthermore, I shall again declare the supreme knowledge among all forms of knowledge,
knowing which all the sages have attained the highest perfection beyond this world.

Furthermore, I shall speak again of another knowledge—distinct from what was previously mentioned—which concerns the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and which is contained within the very nature of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

That knowledge is the highest of all knowledges concerning *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Having known that knowledge, all the sages—those whose nature is reflection—have attained the supreme perfection beyond this bondage of *saṃsāra*; they have achieved the supreme perfection consisting in the attainment of the nature of the utterly pure Self.
Furthermore, he distinguishes that knowledge by its fruit:
"Having resorted to this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
they are not born even at creation, nor do they suffer at dissolution" (BhG 14.2).

Having resorted to this knowledge which is about to be declared, they have attained my own nature; having reached equality with me, they are not born even at the time of creation, nor do they undergo the state of being objects of creation;
and at the time of dissolution, they do not suffer, nor do they undergo the state of being objects of destruction.

Now, in order to explain the manner in which the material qualities (*guṇas*) act as the cause of bondage, the Blessed One stated by Himself that the entire multitude of beings is born from the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* through the words "whatever is born" (*yāvat saṃjāyate kiñcit*). He says: "The Great Brahman is My womb; in it I place the seed."
From that, O Bhārata, the origin of all beings occurs.
I place the embryo within that Great Brahman, which is the source of the entire universe—
namely, earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect.
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.

The insentient primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which was indicated by the phrase "this other [nature]," is called the "Great Brahman" (*mahadbrahma*) because it is the cause of the transformations such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*).
Even in the *Śruti*, primordial nature is sometimes designated as Brahman, as in:
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge..."
"Therefore, from this [Brahman] are born name, form, and food";
and "But know my other nature, higher than this,
which has become the individual soul (jīva)"— thus is that supreme nature indicated which consists of a multitude of conscious beings.

Because it is the seed of all living beings, it is called by the word "womb" (*garbha*). Into that great, insentient Brahman which serves as the womb, I place the embryo consisting of an aggregate of consciousness;
the meaning is that I unite the aggregate of conscious nature, which constitutes the class of enjoyers, with the insentient primordial matter (*prakṛti*), which has become the field of experience.
Therefore, from that conjunction of the two natures brought about by my will, there arises the manifestation of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Even the state of being an effect is brought about by me alone through the conjunction of the conscious and unconscious natures; thus he says:
"O son of Kuntī, whatever forms are produced in all wombs, their great source is Brahman, and I am the father who provides the seed. (BhG 14.4)

In all wombs— whether those of gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, humans, cattle, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth— the various forms that come into being and are born have Brahman as their great womb, their cause. The meaning is that Prakṛti (Nature), in which the group of conscious beings has been joined by Me, and which exists in states ranging from Mahat down to the specific elements, is the cause.
The meaning is this: I am the seed-giving father, and in each respective case, I am the one who joins the multitude of conscious beings with their corresponding karma.

Thus, at the beginning of creation, for those born in the wombs of gods and others through contact with insentient matter by the force of past karma, [the Lord] states the cause of their repeated birth in the form of gods and so forth:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of Prakṛti, O mighty-armed one, bind the immutable embodied self within the body. (BhG 14.5)

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities (guṇas) which are inherent to the nature of Prakṛti; they are specific modifications whose existence is determined solely by their effects, such as illumination and so forth. While unmanifest in the state of Prakṛti, they become manifest in its transformations, such as Mahat and the rest. [These qualities] belong to this embodied being (dehin), who is connected to bodies such as those of gods and humans, which are composed of the specific evolutes beginning with Mahat and ending with the gross elements.

The meaning is that they bind the immutable one—which by its own nature is unworthy of connection with the qualities—while it abides in the body; that is, they bind it through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of its abiding in the body.

He describes the nature and the manner of bondage of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*: "Therein, O sinless one, *sattva*, because of its purity, is illuminating and free from affliction; it binds by attachment to happiness and by attachment to knowledge. (BhG 14.6)
In this context, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* [are the constituents]; the nature of *sattva* is as follows: because of its purity (*nirmalatva*), it is illuminating (*prakāśaka*).
Purity is the state of being devoid of the inherent nature of obscuring light and pleasure.
The meaning is that, by virtue of having an exclusive nature in producing light and pleasure, it serves as the cause of light and pleasure.
*Prakāśa* is the comprehension of the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmyāvabodha*).
*Anāmaya* means that no effect known as *āmaya* (affliction) exists;
the meaning is that it is the cause of freedom from disease.

This quality called *sattva* binds this embodied being through attachment to pleasure and attachment to knowledge; the meaning is that it produces in the person an attachment to pleasure and an attachment to knowledge.

For when attachment to knowledge and pleasure arises, one engages in their means—both worldly and Vedic—and consequently, one is born into wombs that serve as the means for experiencing their fruits. Thus, *sattva* binds the person by way of attachment to pleasure and knowledge.
Furthermore, it is said that *sattva* is that which generates knowledge and bliss, as well as the generation of attachment for those two.
Know that *rajas* is of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action. (BhG 14.7)
*Rajaḥ* consists of passion (*rāga*) and serves as the cause of passion;
*rāga* is the mutual longing between a woman and a man.
*Tṛṇāsaṅgasamudbhavam* means the place of origin for thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) and attachment (*asaṅga*), that is to say, it is the cause of thirst and attachment.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the longing for all objects of sense, such as sound and the rest;
attachment (*saṅga*) is the desire for union with relatives, such as sons, friends, and so forth.
That *rajas* binds the embodied being by means of generating a longing for actions and activities.

For whatever actions an embodied being undertakes out of longing for ritual acts, those acts take the form of merit and demerit; thus, they become the causes of birth in wombs that serve as the means for experiencing their fruits.
Therefore, through the gateway of attachment to action, passion binds the embodied being.
Thus, it has been stated that passion (rajas) is the cause of attachment to craving and the cause of attachment to karma.
But know that *tamas* is born of ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep.
In this context, ignorance is intended to be something other than knowledge.
Knowledge is the comprehension of the true nature of reality; that which is other than it is the cognition that is its opposite.
Tamas, however, arises from knowledge whose object is contrary to the true nature of things;
it deludes all embodied beings.
Delusion (moha) is erroneous knowledge.
The meaning is that it is the cause of erroneous knowledge (*viparyayajñāna*).
That darkness (*tamas*) binds the embodied soul by means of its being the cause of negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*ālasya*), and sleep (*nidrā*).
Negligence is a lack of attentiveness that serves as the cause for engaging in activities other than those duties that ought to be performed.
Laziness is the nature of not undertaking actions,
which is to say, a state of rigidity.
Sleep is the cessation of the activity of all the sense-faculties due to the exhaustion of the person's effort in activating those faculties.
In that regard, the cessation of the activity of the external senses is dream;
the cessation of the mind as well is deep sleep.
He states the primary factors among sattva and the others that serve as gateways to bondage:
"Sattva attaches one to happiness, O Bharata; rajas to action;
but tamas, veiling knowledge, attaches one to negligence. (BhG 14.9)
Sattva is characterized primarily by attachment to happiness; rajas is characterized primarily by attachment to action;

but tamas, having veiled the knowledge of the true nature of things, is characterized primarily by attachment to activity contrary to what ought to be done, by virtue of being the cause of erroneous cognition. (BhG 14.9)
The qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the others, are inherent to the very nature of primordial matter (prakṛti) when it has transformed into the form of the body;
and since they all exist at all times due to that inherent nature, how do they produce mutually contradictory effects? To this, he says:
"O Bhārata, sattva prevails by overpowering rajas and tamas."
Rajas, sattva, and tamas; likewise, tamas, sattva, and rajas.
Although the three qualities— sattva and the others— are inherently linked to the nature of the self as it is conjoined with primordial matter (prakṛti),
nevertheless, due to the force of past karma and the irregularity of food that serves as the sustenance for the body, sattva and the others function by way of mutual emergence and suppression.
At times, having suppressed rajas and tamas, sattva exists in a state of predominance.
Likewise, sometimes rajas overcomes tamas when sattva is present, and at other times tamas overcomes rajas when sattva is present.
And one should understand that [state] only by perceiving its effect; thus he says:
"When light arises through all the gates in this body—that is, knowledge—then one should know that *sattva* has increased. (BhG 14.11)

When knowledge arises through all the gateways of cognition, such as the eyes and so forth, illuminating the true nature of things, then one should know that *sattva* has increased in that body. (BhG 14.11)
Greed, worldly activity, the undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—
these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas.
Greed is the disposition of not relinquishing one's own possessions;
activity is the nature of being in motion even without aiming for a specific purpose;
and undertaking is the commencement of actions that serve as means to achieve results.
Lack of tranquility is attachment to the senses;
longing is the desire for sense objects.
These arise when rajas has increased.
The meaning is that when greed and the like prevail, one should know that rajas has increased.
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—
these arise when Tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus.
Lack of illumination is the non-arising of knowledge; lack of engagement is rigidity;
and negligence is inattention resulting from the inclination toward what should not be done.
Delusion is erroneous knowledge;
these arise when darkness has increased. One should know that by these, darkness has increased. (BhG 14.13)
But when the embodied soul meets its dissolution while sattva is predominant,
then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Highest.

When goodness (sattva) has increased, if the embodied one meets with dissolution— that is, death— while goodness is thus predominant, he attains stainless worlds, which are free from impurity and devoid of ignorance, belonging to those who know the highest, namely those who know the supreme reality and the true nature of the Self.
He attains [the goal]; that is, he reaches it.

But when his goodness has increased, having died, he is born into families of those who know the Self; thus it is said that he becomes qualified for meritorious deeds which are the means for attaining knowledge of the true nature of the Self. (BhG 14.14)
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action.
When rajas has increased, having met death, one is born into families of those performing actions for the sake of results;
the meaning is that, having been born there, one becomes qualified for actions that are the means to achieve results such as heaven.
Likewise, one who has merged into darkness is born in the wombs of the deluded.
Likewise, when darkness has increased, one who has died is born in deluded wombs—such as the wombs of dogs, pigs, and so forth;
the meaning is that one is born unfit for the undertaking of any human goals.
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by goodness (sattva);
the fruit of passion (rajas) is suffering, and the fruit of darkness (tamas) is ignorance.

Thus, those who know the transformation of the qualities of *sattva* say that when one’s *sattva* has increased, even after undergoing death, the fruit of the well-performed action— performed by one born into a family of self-knowers (*ātmavit*), free from desire for rewards, and consisting of service to Me— becomes once again even more abundant in *sattva*, stainless, and devoid of even the scent of suffering.

Those who know the true nature of the *guṇas* say that the fruit of *rajas* increased at the final moment consists essentially of the sufferings of saṃsāra, taking the form of a succession of undertakings of actions preceded by attachment to the means of attaining fruits, birth in a family, and the desire for results; and the undertaking of further actions preceded by the desire for the fruits of those results, which in turn leads to the increase of *rajas* and further rebirth.
Likewise, ignorance is the fruit of *tamas*; thus, the fruit of *tamas* increased at the final moment takes the form of a succession of ignorances.
Regarding what kind of fruit—such as the stainless state—is produced by an excess of *sattva* and the other qualities, he says here:
"From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas*, greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance. (BhG 14.17)
Thus, from sattva increased through such a succession, knowledge arises in the form of direct realization of the true nature of the self.
Likewise, from increased rajas, greed for fruits such as heaven arises.
And likewise, from increased tamas, negligence arises—the engagement in improper action caused by a lack of attentiveness.
And from that arises delusion, which is erroneous cognition;
from that, a greater darkness; and from that, ignorance, which is the absence of knowledge.
Those established in *sattva* go upward; those characterized by *rajas* remain in the middle;
and those of the nature of *tamas*, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward.
In the manner thus described, those established in *sattva* go upward; they gradually proceed from the bonds of *saṃsāra* toward liberation.

Because *rajas* produces the desire for fruits such as heaven, those characterized by *rajas* perform actions that serve as the means to those fruits; having experienced the fruit, they are born again and perform those very same actions, and thus they "stay in the middle."
Because it is characterized by the nature of returning [to rebirth], that state is essentially nothing but suffering.

Those belonging to the *tāmasa* class, however, abiding in the functions of the lowest quality (*guṇa*), descend further and further through increasingly degraded functions of the *tamas* quality: first to the state of being an outcaste, and from there to the state of an animal.
From that follows birth as worms, insects, and so forth; then the state of being stationary; and from that, the state of being shrubs or creepers.
And thus, the meaning is that they become like stone, wood, clods of earth, grass, and so forth.

He describes the manner of ascending upwards by way of transcending the qualities (*guṇas*) for those whose being has been successively developed through specific foods and specific meritorious deeds performed without desire for fruits:
"When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities, and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains My state. (BhG 14.19)
Thus, by resorting to sattvic food and by performing actions in the form of worship of the Lord without any desire for fruits,
one completely overcomes rajas and tamas. Established in the preeminent quality of sattva, when this person no longer perceives any agent other than the gunas,
but perceives that the gunas themselves are the agents in their respective activities according to their own nature;

When one knows that which is beyond the qualities (*guṇa*) and knows the Self (*ātman*) as other than the qualities and the agents—that is, as the non-agent—he attains My state; he attains that which is My state.
This is what is meant: "The agency of the Self, whose nature is inherently pure, in various actions is caused by attachment to the qualities rooted in its own prior karma;
but the Self is in itself a non-agent, having the single form of undivided knowledge. When one perceives the Self in this way, [he attains My state].
Then he attains my state of being. (BhG 14.19)
It has been stated that by perceiving the Self as the non-agent, distinct from the agents that are the *guṇas*, one attains the state of the Blessed Lord;
as to what that state of the Blessed Lord is like, he says:
"Having transcended these three *guṇas* which arise from the body, the embodied one..."
Freed from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, one partakes of the immortal.

This embodied soul, having transcended these three qualities— sattva and the others— which arise from the body and originate from primordial nature (prakṛti) transformed into the form of the body, perceives the Self as distinct from them and consisting solely of the nature of knowledge; thus liberated from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, he experiences the immortal Self.
The meaning is: "This is my true nature. (BhG 14.20)
Then Arjuna, inquiring about the nature and conduct of one who has transcended the qualities (guṇas), as well as the cause for such transcendence, said:
Arjuna said:
By what marks, O Lord, does one become transcendent over these three qualities?
What is his conduct, and how does he transcend these three qualities?
By what signs and by what characteristics is one who has transcended these three qualities—sattva and the others—recognized?
What is his conduct, and with what kind of conduct is he endowed?
The meaning is: what is the nature of his conduct, which serves as a sign for understanding his true nature?
And how, by what means, does one transcend these three qualities, beginning with sattva? // BhGR 14.21 //
The Blessed One said:
O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they have arisen, nor does he long for them when they have ceased.
He who does not hate the effects of sattva, rajas, and tamas—known as illumination, activity, and delusion—which have arisen toward objects other than the Self that are undesirable;
and likewise, he who does not crave those same effects when they have ceased in regard to objects other than the Self that are desirable.
He who sits like one indifferent, not shaken by the qualities (guṇas), and remains steadfast,
thinking only that "the qualities are moving," does not waver.
"Sitting like one indifferent" means sitting elsewhere as if indifferent, satisfied by the contemplation of the Self as distinct from the qualities (*guṇas*);

he who is not shaken by the qualities through the medium of aversion or desire, but remains silent after reflecting that "the qualities are engaged in their own functions, such as illumination," does not move— that is,
he does not exert effort in accordance with the effects of the qualities.
Equanimous in pain and pleasure, established in self, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
the wise man is the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and views blame and self-praise as equal.
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the factions of friend and foe,
and has renounced all undertakings— he is said to have transcended the qualities.
He is equal in suffering and happiness, possessing an even mind toward both pleasure and pain; he is self-abiding, established in himself.

The meaning is that, because his own self alone is dear to him, he maintains an even mind toward the birth, death, and other such experiences of pleasure and pain belonging to others—such as sons and so forth—who are distinct from that self.
For that very reason, he regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
for that very reason, he is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, having an attitude of equanimity toward objects that are either pleasant or unpleasant;
and he is steadfast, being by nature skilled in the discernment of the self.

For that very reason, he is equal-minded regarding self-praise and blame from others; that is, by reflecting upon his own lack of connection [to the qualities], he maintains an even mind toward praise and blame caused by the presence or absence of virtues and vices based on the human conceit (abhimāna) regarding the self. Likewise, he is equal-minded toward honor and dishonor resulting from those [qualities], as well as toward the factions of friends and enemies produced by them, precisely because of the absence of any personal connection to them.
Similarly, he is one who has renounced all undertakings (ārambha) occasioned by being an embodied being.
He who is thus constituted is said to have transcended the qualities.
Now, regarding the transcendence of these qualities of such a nature, he states the primary cause:
"And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion, having transcended these qualities, becomes fit for the state of Brahman. (BhG 14.26)

The transcendence of the *guṇas* will not be accomplished merely by the contemplation of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and the Self, as stated in the passage beginning with "There is no agent other than the *guṇas*"; for that [discrimination] is liable to be sublated by contrary latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have been active since beginningless time.
[One must instead take refuge in] Me, whose resolve is ever-true, who am supremely compassionate, and an ocean of affection for those who seek refuge.
He who serves by means of devotional yoga (*bhaktiyoga*) characterized by non-deviation and single-mindedness,
transcends these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which are difficult to overcome, and becomes fit for becoming Brahman—
that is, he becomes capable of attaining the state of Brahman.
The meaning is that one attains the self as it truly is—immortal and imperishable.
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable,
of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
The word "hi" indicates the reason:
because I, when served by means of unswerving devotion, am the foundation of the immortal and imperishable Brahman,
as well as of the eternal Dharma— that is, of that sovereignty which is eternally unsurpassed.
And regarding "absolute bliss," the meaning is the bliss to be attained by the knower, which is indicated by such passages as "Vāsudeva is everything.
Although the term *śāśvatadharma* (eternal dharma) denotes the means of attainment,
nevertheless, because it occurs in conjunction with the two preceding and following terms— which are of the nature of that which is to be attained— this term also indicates the object of attainment.

This is what is meant: since in the preceding section—beginning with "For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome; those who take refuge in Me alone [cross over]"—it has been established that the transcendence of the *guṇas* and the attainment of the Imperishable preceded by that transcendence have as their sole means of accomplishment taking refuge in the Lord alone, the transcendence of the *guṇas* has as its sole means the exclusive taking of refuge in the Lord.
And the state of Brahman preceded by that. // BhG 14.27 //

In the Chapter on the Field (*kṣetrādhyāya*), having clarified the essential natures of the field and the knower of the field— the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*— it was stated that for the *puruṣa*, who is pure and whose sole form is unlimited knowledge, the connection with *prakṛti* (which has transformed into the forms of gods and so forth) is caused by the continuous flow of attachment to the qualities of *prakṛti*, and is thus beginningless. In the immediately following chapter, it was taught that the *puruṣa*'s connection with *prakṛti*— which exists in both causal and effected states— is rooted in attachment to the qualities (*guṇas*).

Having stated that [the world] was created by the Blessed Lord alone, and having explained in detail the manner of attachment to the gunas, it was declared that the attainment of the true nature of the Self— preceded by the cessation of attachment to the gunas— is rooted in devotion to the Blessed Lord. Now, [the text describes] the state of the worshipful Blessed Lord as possessing the manifestations (vibhūti) of both the perishable and the imperishable, consisting of the bound and the liberated.

He begins to describe the state of the Blessed Lord as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who is of a different nature from the two types of persons—the perishable and the imperishable—due to His being the sole repository of all auspicious qualities that are the opposites of everything to be abandoned, and because of His absolute excellence.

In this regard, he first describes the manifestation known as the Imperishable (*akṣara*), whose bonds have been severed by the weapon of the form of non-attachment; and he describes the specific transformation of the insentient (*acit*) which, spread out in the form of bonds that are themselves objects to be cut, takes the shape of the *aśvattha* tree.
The Blessed Lord said:
They speak of the imperishable Ashvattha tree as having its roots above and its branches below; the Vedas are its leaves—he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas. (BhG 15.1)
Regarding that which is called *saṃsāra*, the eternal *aśvattha* tree with its roots above and branches below, the Vedas declare:
"This eternal *aśvattha* has its roots above and its branches below," and "He who knows this tree with its roots above and branches below," and so forth.
Its roots are directed upward because it is established above the seven worlds with the four-faced Brahmā and others at its summit;
its branches extend downward because they reach down to all humans, beasts, deer, worms, insects, moths, and stationary beings dwelling upon the earth;
and it is imperishable because, due to the arising of perfect knowledge which serves as the cause for non-attachment, it cannot be severed in the form of its continuous flow.
And regarding that *aśvattha* tree, they say its leaves are the *chandas*;
the *chandas* are the revealed scriptures (*śruti*), such as: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu."

"This tree of worldly existence increases through those optional rites (kāmyakarman) prescribed in Vedic texts such as, ‘One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni’; therefore, the Vedas themselves are its leaves, for by means of leaves a tree grows. He who knows this Aśvattha tree in such a manner is a knower of the Vedas.”
For the Veda declares the means for cutting down the tree of saṃsāra;
one who possesses the knowledge of the nature of the tree to be cut—which is useful for knowing the means of cutting—is called a "knower of the Veda" (vedavit). (BhG 15.1)
Its branches extend downward and upward, nourished by the *guṇas* and having sense-objects as their sprouts.
From that tree whose branches consist of humans and so forth, other branches produced by various actions extend further downward in the form of humans, animals, and the like;
and upward they extend in the form of *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, gods, and so forth.
And these [trees] are "increased by qualities," meaning increased by the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
they have "sprouts that are objects," meaning shoots consisting of objects such as sound and so forth.
To the question "How so? he says:
And its roots extend downward, reaching into the world of men, bound by karma.

Of this tree, which has its root in the Brahma-world and its crown in the human realm, the roots extend downward into the human world; the meaning is that those roots are the very actions (karman) bound to [rebirth], and they exist as roots in the human world below.
For by means of the actions performed while in the human state, one becomes lower beings such as humans and animals,
or higher beings such as gods and so forth.
Its form is not perceived here in that way; it has no end, no beginning, and no fixed foundation.
This tree has its roots above by virtue of being the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and so forth, and its branches below by virtue of being the foremost among humans through the succession of its lineage.

Just as this form has been described—whereby, through the root-actions performed in the human state, there is again the state of having branches spreading both downward and upward—it is not perceived by those in saṃsāra in that way.
They perceive only this much: "I am a human, the son of Devadatta, the father of Yajñadatta, and possessed of a body corresponding to that."
Likewise, the destruction of this tree, caused by non-attachment to enjoyments consisting of the *guṇas*, is not perceived;
likewise, its beginning, which is attachment to the *guṇas* itself, is not perceived;
and its foundation, which is ignorance in the form of the conceit of self in that which is not-self, is not perceived.
For it is in this very ignorance that he is established; indeed, ignorance itself is his foundation.
Having cut down this *aśvattha* tree, whose roots are firmly grown, with the firm weapon of non-attachment; // BhG 15.3 //
Therefore, that state should be sought after, reaching which they do not return again.
Having cut down this *aśvattha* tree— which has grown roots deeply and in many ways— with the firm weapon of right knowledge called non-attachment to the enjoyments consisting of the *guṇas*,
one must then seek after and search for that state by means of detachment from sense objects.
Having gone to which, they do not return again.

How can attachment to enjoyments consisting of the gunas, which has proceeded from beginningless time, and its root, perverted knowledge, be brought to an end? To this he says: "One should take refuge in that very same Primal Person from whom this ancient course of worldly existence has issued forth" (BhG 15.4).
And for the sake of removing ignorance and the like, [one should seek refuge] in Him alone—the primordial one who is the source of the entire universe—as it is said:
"By Me as the supervisor, nature produces the moving and the unmoving," and "I am the origin of all; from Me everything proceeds."
One should take refuge in that very Primal Person alone, whom [the Lord] has described in such passages as, "O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me.
One should take refuge in Him alone because this activity of attachment to enjoyment consisting of the *guṇas*— which belongs to the Creator of the entire universe—
is ancient, being from of old and ever-expanding.
For I have already said this before:
"This divine illusion of mine, consisting of the qualities, is indeed difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion."

Alternatively, there is the reading "prapadyeyataḥ pravṛttiḥ"; having approached— that is, having gone for refuge to— that very same primordial Person, the ancient (purāṇī), time-honored activity which is the means for all this, beginning with the cessation of ignorance, has been set in motion.
The activity of the ancient seekers of liberation is ancient;
for the meaning is that the ancient seekers of liberation, having approached me alone as their refuge, became liberated from bondage.
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.

Thus, having come to me for refuge, they are free from pride and delusion—meaning they have emerged from the delusion consisting of the ego and the conceit of "I" regarding the self; they have conquered the fault of attachment, meaning they have overcome the fault known as attachment to enjoyments composed of the gunas;
and they are constantly devoted to the inner self—that which is knowledge of the Self is "adhyātma."
They are devoted to the knowledge of the self;
their desires have ceased, as have all other desires; they are liberated from the pairs of opposites such as the notions of pleasure and pain;
they are undeluded, knowing the nature of both the self and the non-self.
They go to that imperishable state; they attain the Self as it truly exists, whose form is uninterrupted knowledge.
The meaning is that for those who have come to Me for refuge, all these activities—beginning with grace from Me alone—become easily accomplished and culminate in perfection.
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, reaching which they do not return.
That light of the Self is not illumined by the sun, nor by the moon, nor by fire.
For knowledge alone is the illuminator of everything;
external lights, however, are auxiliary by means of dispelling the darkness that obstructs the connection between the objects and the senses.
And yoga is the illuminator of this [knowledge].
And its opposite is beginningless karma;
the cessation of that is said to have its root in taking refuge in the Blessed One, characterized by non-attachment and so forth—
that state having gone to which they do not return again.
That supreme abode, the supreme light, is mine— meaning it is my own, existing as my manifestation and being a portion of me.
Its supremacy consists in its being the illuminator even of the sun and other luminaries.
For the luminaries such as the sun do not illuminate the light of knowledge;
knowledge alone is the illuminator of everything.
An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul in the world of the living,
draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature.
Thus described, the eternal one, being indeed a portion of My own self, becomes a living soul (jīva) when enveloped by beginningless ignorance in the form of karma;

existing in the world of living beings, he draws toward himself the senses—with the mind as the sixth—situated within bodies that are specific transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti), such as gods, humans, and others.
And some, liberated from this ignorance by the path previously mentioned, abide in their own true nature.

But as the individual soul (*jīvabhūta*), its knowledge and sovereignty being extremely contracted, it is the lord of the senses—with the mind as the sixth—which consist of specific transformations of *prakṛti* obtained through karma; it draws them hither and thither according to karma.
Whatever body the Lord acquires and whatever [body] he departs from,
he goes taking these with him, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
Regarding that body which it attains and from which body it departs,
there this lord of the senses goes forth, taking these senses along with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.

The meaning is that just as the wind, taking up fragrances from a source such as a garland, sandalwood, or musk along with their subtle particles from that location, moves elsewhere, so it is in this case.
What, then, are those senses? To this he says:
"Having presided over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose, as well as the mind, this [Self] experiences the objects of the senses" (BhG 15.9).

Having presided over these six sense organs, with the mind as the sixth, and having directed them toward their respective functions, he resorts to— that is, enjoys— those objects such as sound and the rest.
Whether it is departing, or staying, or even enjoying experiences endowed with the qualities, the deluded do not perceive it; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive it.

Thus, though endowed with such qualities— being conjoined with a physical aggregate (piṇḍa) consisting of human form and so forth, which is a particular transformation of *prakṛti* composed of the qualities (*guṇas*) like *sattva* and the rest; whether departing from that specific aggregate, or abiding within that specific aggregate,

or at any time experiencing objects made of the *guṇas*— the deluded do not perceive [the Self] as distinct from the aggregate of human form and so forth, which is a particular transformation of *prakṛti*, but rather [perceive it] as having the single form of knowledge alone.
The deluded are those who possess the conceit of identifying with the physical body, such as the human form;
however, those with the eye of knowledge—who possess the wisdom whose object is the discrimination between the Self and the body—behold this [Self] in every state as having only a distinct nature.
Striving yogis perceive Him established within themselves;
yet those of unrefined soul, though striving, do not perceive Him, being devoid of discernment.

Those yogis who, preceded by surrender to Me, strive in karma-yoga and other disciplines, become pure in their inner selves; with the eye called yoga, they behold Him—though situated within the self (the body)—as distinct from the body and established in His own nature.
But those of unrefined self, even though striving, being devoid of surrender to Me, have for that very reason unconsecrated minds.
For that very reason, the mindless—those devoid of the consciousness capable of beholding the Self—do not see it.

Thus, it has been stated that even among the luminaries— the sun, the moon, and fire— which illuminate by way of dispelling the thick darkness that obstructs the contact between the senses and their objects, the light of knowledge (*jñāna-jyotis*) is the illuminator; this is the glory (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed One, existing both in the state of liberation and in the state of the individual soul (*jīva*).
“That is My supreme abode,” and “An eternal portion of Myself alone becomes a living being in the world of the living.
Now, He declares that even the light of luminous bodies such as the sun— which is a specific transformation of the non-sentient (acit)— is a manifestation (vibhūti) of the Blessed Lord.
That splendor which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world,
and that which is in the moon and in the fire— know that splendor to be mine.
Know that the splendor which illuminates this entire world— the splendor of these [deities] beginning with the sun— is my own splendor, granted by me to them when I am propitiated by each of them.
And [the Lord] says that the power of supporting the earth, which is the sustainer of beings, belongs to me: "And entering the earth, I support all beings by my vital energy."
And becoming the sapid Soma, I nourish all herbs.
Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my power—that is, by my unimpeded capacity.
Likewise, becoming the moon consisting of the essence of nectar, I nourish all herbs.
Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire and taking refuge in the bodies of living beings, I,
conjoined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, digest the four kinds of food.

Becoming Vaiśvānara, the digestive fire within the stomach, and having entered the bodies of all living beings, I—joined with the various functions of the prāṇa and apāna breaths—digest the fourfold food consisting of what is chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk. (BhG 15.14)

In this context, Soma and Vaiśvānara, who are manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Supreme Person, are indicated through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Him in the phrases "I, having become Soma" and "having become Vaiśvānara.
And He states the reason for indicating both of them, as well as the entire collection of beings, through coordination with the Supreme Person:
And I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
By all the Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas as well.

In the heart—the locus where arises the knowledge that is the root of all activity and cessation for those two, Soma and Vaiśvānara, as well as for the entire multitude of beings—I am seated as the Self, restraining everything by my own volition.
Thus say the Śrutis:
"He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all."
“He who dwells in the earth,” “He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self... and controls it,” and “The heart, resembling the interior of a lotus bud, is indeed turned downward.”
“Now, that which is this small lotus-like dwelling in this city of Brahman,” and so forth; and the Smṛtis as well:
“Viṣṇu is the teacher of the entire world, he who consists of the world.”
“[He is] the ruler of all, subtler than the subtlest,” and “King Yama, son of Vivasvat, who dwells here within your heart,” and so forth.
Therefore, memory arises for all beings from me alone.
Memory is a cognition arising solely from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, directed toward an object previously experienced.
Cognition is the ascertainment of a real entity produced by the senses, inferential signs, scripture, or yoga;
that too comes from me.
And there is exclusion (*apohana*).
Exclusion is the cessation of cognition,
or it is the act of excluding (*ūhana*).
*Ūhana* means *ūha*.

*Ūha* is a cognition that assists the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which is produced by the investigation of the totality of causal factors (*sāmagrī*) and so forth, and has as its object the fitness of a means of valid knowledge to function in a particular manner—namely, the thought, "This means of valid knowledge ought to proceed in this way.
And that *ūha* arises from me alone.
"I alone am to be known by all the Vedas.

Therefore, because Agni, Sūrya, Vāyu, Soma, Indra, and the others have Me as their inner controller and are thus of My nature, I alone am to be known even by all the Vedas whose purpose is to expound them;
just as the words "god," "man," and so forth, refer only to the individual soul (jīvātman).

The author of the Vedāntas is the one who establishes the "end" (anta)— that is, the fruit— of the Vedas, such as [the injunctions] "one should sacrifice to Indra," "one should sacrifice to Varuṇa," and so forth;
for all those Vedas culminate in that fruit.
I am the maker of the end and the maker of the fruit; the meaning is that I alone am the bestower of the fruit declared by the Vedas.
This has indeed been stated previously.

Beginning with, "Whichever embodied being, devoted, desires to worship with faith whatever form [he chooses]," and continuing with, "And from that he obtains his desires, for they are indeed ordained by Me alone," and also,
"For I am the enjoyer and likewise the Lord of all sacrifices," [it is shown that] I alone am the knower of the Vedas, and I alone am the knower of the Vedas.
The intention is this: "I alone know this Veda which speaks of Me in such a way; he who explains the meaning of the Veda otherwise than this is not a knower of the Veda. BhG 15.15.
Therefore, hear from me alone the meaning that constitutes the essence of all the Vedas:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are the perishable; the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable. (BhG 15.16)
"There are these two persons renowned in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.

Among them, the person designated by the term "perishable" refers to all beings—from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass—consisting of consciousness mixed with the perishable nature [of matter], which is denoted by the word *jīva*.
Here, the designation as a single "person" (*puruṣa*) is made by means of the single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the association with non-consciousness.

The liberated self (muktātmā), designated by the word "syllable" (akṣara), is immutable (kūṭastha), free from contact with the insentient (acit), and abides in its own essential nature. Because it lacks contact with the insentient, it does not possess the specific transformations of the insentient—such as the bodies of Brahmā and others—which are unique to that [contact]; thus it is called "immutable. Here too, the designation of oneness is expressed by means of the single limiting adjunct consisting of the dissociation from the insentient.
For since time without beginning, not even one has been liberated prior to this;
as it has been said: "Many, purified by knowledge and austerity, have attained My state," and "They are not born even at creation, nor are they disturbed at dissolution. (BhG 15.16)
But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.

But the Supreme Person (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ) is distinct from those two—the bound and the liberated persons designated by the terms "the Perishable" (kṣara) and "the Imperishable" (akṣara); He is a different entity, declared in all the Śrutis as the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Indeed, from the very designation "Supreme Self," it is understood that the Supreme Person is a different entity from the bound and liberated persons. How so? Because He, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
That which is perceived is the world (*loka*);
these three constitute the "three worlds.

This triad—namely, the insentient, the sentient conjoined with it, and the liberated sentient being—is that which He, having entered as the Self, sustains, as is known through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
He is distinct from that which is pervaded and from that which is to be supported;
and he is distinct from the three worlds mentioned above,
because he is imperishable.

And He is the Lord (Īśvara); for the Lord, whose nature is imperishable, is indeed distinct from the unconscious which is perishable by nature, as well as from the conscious which follows that [unconscious] through its connection with it, and from the liberated soul who was previously connected [to matter] due to its fitness for such a connection. Likewise, He is the Lord of these three worlds.
Therefore, it is an entity distinct from that which is to be ruled.
Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

Since, by the natures thus described, I have transcended the perishable person (kṣara-puruṣa), and for the reasons stated, I am superior even to the liberated imperishable (akṣara), therefore I am celebrated as Puruṣottama in the world and in the Veda.
The term "loka" here refers to the Smṛti because it illuminates the meaning of the Vedas;
that is to say, it refers to both Śruti and Smṛti.
First, regarding Śruti:
In such passages as, "Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own form; he is the highest person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3),
and also in the Smṛti, such as, "The partial incarnation of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, who is unborn and without beginning, middle, or end" (Bhagavadgītā 4.7).
O Bhārata, he who knows me thus as the Supreme Person without delusion, being all-knowing, worships me with his whole being.

He who, being undeluded, knows Me— the Supreme Person— in the manner thus described, knowing Me to be of a different nature from both the perishable and the imperishable persons by virtue of My immutable essence and My possession of sovereignty such as pervasion and sustenance—
he, the all-knowing, knows everything that is to be known as the means for attaining Me.
He worships me with his whole being; and by all those modes of worship that have been prescribed as means for attaining me, he worships me.
[He experiences] whatever joy I feel toward all feelings directed toward me, and whatever joy I feel through all forms of worship directed toward me.
Both kinds of joy arise for me through this feeling.
Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me; it honors this realization of the state of being the Supreme Person.
Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled all duties.
Thus, this teaching, which establishes my status as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), is the most secret of all secrets;
I have spoken it to you because you are the most worthy recipient due to your sinlessness.
By understanding this, one becomes wise and has accomplished their purpose. For one who seeks me, whatever wisdom is to be acquired would all be attained through this.
The meaning is that everything which was to be done by him would have been accomplished.
By this verse, [this is shown].

It is stated that this aforementioned knowledge concerning the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), which is produced solely by the scripture, accomplishes all this; it does not consist of direct realization (sākṣātkāra).

By means of the three preceding chapters, the true nature of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—both in their separated and conjoined states—and the fact that their conjunction and disjunction are caused by attachment to the *guṇas* and its opposite [dispassion], have been established.
Furthermore, it has been shown that *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, in all their various modes of existence, constitute the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Blessed Lord;

and that the Blessed Lord, who possesses these manifestations, is distinct from the insentient entity (the manifestation) and from the sentient entity (which exists in the three forms of bound, liberated, and both), and is therefore the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) by virtue of His imperishability, pervasiveness, sustenance, and lordship.
And the true nature [of the self] has been described.

Immediately following that, in order to establish the stability of the entire subject matter thus declared, the Blessed Lord spoke of the division between the divine and demoniacal creations— those who are subject to the scriptures and those who are their opposites— in order to explain the necessity of being governed by the scriptures.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; BhG 16.1.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice, compassion for all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (BhG 16.2)
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with divine fortune.
Fear is the suffering born from perceiving the causes of suffering, which consists of the separation from the desired and the union with the undesired;

the absence of fear (*abhaya*) is the cessation of that. Purity of being (*sattva-saṃśuddhi*) is the state of the inner organ (*sattva*), the mind, being untouched by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*).
The establishment in the yoga of knowledge is steadfastness in the discernment of the true nature of the self as distinct from primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
Generosity (*dāna*) is the bestowing of wealth acquired by righteous means upon a worthy recipient.
Self-restraint (*dama*) is the constant practice of turning the mind away from its inclination toward sense objects.
Sacrifice (*yajña*) is the performance of the great sacrifices and other rites consisting of the worship of the Lord, free from any desire for fruits.
Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the dedication to the practice of the Vedas with the realization that the entire Veda teaches the Lord along with His manifestations and the methods of worshipping Him.
Austerity (*tapas*) is the practice of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, fasting on the twelfth lunar day, and so forth, which serves to produce fitness for performing actions that please the Lord.
Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the single-minded orientation of the activities of mind, speech, and body toward others.
Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the avoidance of harming others. Truthfulness (*satya*) is speech that is beneficial and corresponds to the reality of things as they have been perceived.
Non-anger is the state of being free from mental agitation that results in harming others. Renunciation is the relinquishing of attachments that are contrary to one's own welfare.
Tranquility is the cultivation of restraining the senses from their tendency toward sense objects.

Absence of backbiting is the refraining from reporting words that cause harm to others. Compassion toward beings is the inability to endure the suffering of all living creatures. Absence of greed is the state of being free from covetousness.
Alternatively, the reading is *alolutvam*;
the meaning is the absence of longing for sense objects.
*Mārdavam* means softness, the absence of hardness.
The meaning is that she is worthy of association with virtuous people.
*Hrī* is shame regarding the performance of improper acts;
*acāpala* is steadiness in the presence of desirable objects.
*Tejas* is the state of being unassailable by wicked people.
*Kṣamā* is the absence of mental agitation toward others even when experiencing pain caused by them.
*Dhṛti* is the determination to perform one's duty even in the face of great adversity.
Purity (*śauca*) is the fitness for performing what is prescribed by the scriptures, pertaining to both the external and internal organs.
Non-malice (*adroha*) is non-obstruction toward others; the meaning is the state of being free from obstructing the natural activities of others.
Absence of excessive pride means the absence of arrogance in an improper place; it is the state of being free from that.
These qualities belong to one born into the divine nature.
The divine fortune (*daivī saṃpat*) is that which pertains to the gods; the gods are those whose nature is to follow the command of the Blessed One; it is their fortune.
And that [practice] is indeed the following of the Lord’s command; the meaning is that it occurs for one who is born into that [lineage], for one who has been directed toward that,
and for one who is born to turn away from that.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness,
and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.
Hypocrisy (*dambha*) is the performance of religious duties for the sake of proclaiming one's own righteousness.
Arrogance (*darpa*) is the joy arising from the experience of sense objects that causes a lack of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
And excessive pride (*atimāna*) is a conceit consistent with one's own learning and lineage.
Anger is a transformation of the mind whose fruit is the infliction of pain upon others; harshness is a disposition that causes distress to the virtuous;
ignorance is the lack of discrimination regarding the reality of the higher and the lower, and between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
These dispositions belong to one born into the demonic endowment;
the *asuras* are those whose nature is to transgress the commands of the Blessed One. (BhG 16.4)
The divine nature is considered to lead to liberation, while the demoniacal leads to bondage.
The divine nature consists in compliance with my command; it leads to liberation—that is, to release from bondage—and by degrees leads to the attainment of Me. This is the meaning.
The demoniacal nature, which consists of pride and the transgression of scriptural injunctions, leads to bondage; that is to say, it results in the attainment of a downward state of existence.
Having heard this, Arjuna was overcome with extreme fear because he had not yet ascertained his own true nature; to him, [the Lord] spoke thus:
"Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born endowed with divine nature. (BhG 16.5)
Do not grieve;
for you, O Pāṇḍava, have been born with a divine nature.
For the intention is this: "You are indeed the son of Pāṇḍu, the foremost of the righteous."
There are two types of creation of beings in this world: the divine and the demoniac.
The divine has been described at length; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demoniac.
In this world of action, the creation of beings who perform actions is twofold: divine (*daiva*) and demonic (*āsura*).
"Creation" (*sarga*) means origination;

the meaning is that, by the power of past actions consisting of merit and demerit, beings are produced at the very time of their birth in distinct categories for the purpose of either following the command of the Lord or acting contrary to it.
In that regard, the divine creation has been described in detail—the birth of the gods, whose nature is to follow my command, for the purpose of performing specific conduct;

and that conduct, consisting of the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion, has been described in detail. Also described is the creation of the asuras, which serves the purpose of [defining] their conduct.
Listen to that conduct from me; hear it from my presence.
Asuras do not understand the path of engagement nor the path of withdrawal;
in them there is neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth.

The asuras do not know— that is, they do not understand— the Vedic dharma consisting of both worldly engagement (pravṛtti) and renunciation (nivṛtti), as well as the means for attaining prosperity (abhyudaya) and the means for attaining liberation (mokṣa).
Purity (śauca)— the fitness for performing Vedic rites established by the scriptures,
whether external or internal— is not found among the asuras.

Nor is there that conduct by which internal and external purity is produced—namely, the conduct consisting of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) and so forth—for such conduct is not found among them.
As it has been said: "One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts."
Likewise, truth does not exist among them, insofar as speech that expresses the welfare of beings according to their actual state is not found among them.
Moreover, they say that this world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord;
that it arises from mutual union, and what else, save for desire as its cause? (BhG 16.8)

They do not say that this world is unreal; rather, because it is the effect of Brahman designated by the word "Real," they declare it to have Brahman as its self. Likewise, they do not say that it is without support;
for it is supported by Brahman, since the earth, upheld by the infinite Brahman, sustains all the worlds.

As it has been said: "This earth, supported on its head by that best of Nāgas, ever bears the garland of the worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans. Thus, [the world] is without a Lord (anīśvara).
Nor do they say, "This has been ordained by me, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of all, whose resolve is truth.
For it has been said: "I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
And yet they speak thus: "Arising from one another"—what else could this mean?
This world of humans, animals, and so forth is perceived as having arisen through the mutual relationship between woman and man;
what else is perceived that is not of this nature? The meaning is that nothing at all is perceived [that is not so].
Therefore, this entire world has desire as its cause. // BhGR 16.8 //
Holding fast to this view, their souls ruined and their intellects small,
these evil-doers of fierce deeds arise for the destruction of the world.
Holding fast to this view and relying upon it,
those of ruined souls— who do not perceive a self distinct from the body—
and of small intellect— being unskilled in discrimination, thinking that the self is perceived as a knower within the body which is itself an object of knowledge like a jar— [fall into error].
Those of fierce deeds, who are harmful to all, prevail for the destruction of the world.
Taking recourse in insatiable desire, possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance,
they act with impure vows, having grasped false notions through delusion.

Relying on desire—which is difficult to satisfy and whose objects are hard to attain—and out of delusion and ignorance, they grasp at improper attachments and possessions acquired through unjust means; possessed by hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, they engage in impure observances, being devoted to vows not ordained by the scriptures. (BhG 16.10)
Resorting to immeasurable anxiety that lasts until the end of their dissolution,
they are devoted solely to the enjoyment of desires, convinced that this is all there is.

Desiring to die today or tomorrow, they have resorted to immeasurable and indefinable anxiety concerning objects to be accomplished within a time limit ending at the dissolution of the material world—that is, until the final cosmic dissolution.
Likewise, being devoted solely to the enjoyment of desires, they consider the enjoyment of desires alone to be the supreme human goal;
they are convinced that "this is all," having reached the firm conclusion that no human goal exists beyond this.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment to accumulate wealth by unjust means.
Bound by hundreds of snares of desire— by those hundreds of bonds called longing— and devoted solely to lust and anger,
they strive for the accumulation of wealth through unjust means for the sake of sensual enjoyment. (BhG 16.12)
"Today this has been gained by me; I shall attain this desire;
this is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again. (BhG 16.13)
All this, such as fields, sons, and so forth, has been obtained by me solely through my own power,
and not through unseen forces (adṛṣṭa) or the like;
and I alone shall attain this desire.
It is not accompanied by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. [One thinks:
"This wealth has been obtained through my own power; it is mine, and this too shall again belong to me solely through my own power. (BhG 16.13)
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well.
"This enemy has been slain by me, who am powerful;
I, being a hero and steadfast, shall slay other enemies as well."
What is the use here of this unseen auxiliary imagined by those of weak intellect?
And thus:
"I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (BhG 16.14)
"I am the lord, I am independent;
I alone am the controller of others.
I am an enjoyer; by my own nature, I am an enjoyer."
Not by means of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth.
I am established; I am self-established;
not from anything such as the unseen force.
Likewise, one is strong by oneself alone;
one is happy by oneself alone.
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance. (BhG 16.15)
I am wealthy by my own right; I possess noble lineage, for I was born from a preeminent family by my own merit;
in this world, what other person exists who is my equal, having acquired all prosperity through my own power?

"I myself shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice"—thus deluded by ignorance, they believe that sacrificial rites, giving, and so forth can be performed by themselves alone, independent of the grace of the Lord; thus they are deluded by ignorance. (BhG 16.15)
Perplexed by manifold thoughts, enveloped in the net of delusion,
and addicted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, they fall into impure hell.
Thinking that everything can be accomplished by oneself alone, without depending on unseen forces such as Īśvara and others, one might resolve:
"I shall act in this way," and "I shall do that."
Furthermore, they are distracted by many thoughts such as "I shall do this," being enveloped by such a net of delusion and intensely attached to sensual enjoyments.
Those who die midway fall into the impure hell.
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride,
they perform sacrifices under the guise of religion, yet out of hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions.
"Esteemed by themselves alone" means they esteem themselves by themselves.
"Arrogant" means considering themselves complete, performing no [virtuous] actions whatsoever.

How so? Possessed by the intoxication of wealth and pride—meaning, filled with the arrogance produced by wealth, learning, and noble birth—they perform sacrifices through "name-sacrifices," that is, sacrifices whose sole purpose is the name itself, such as "I am a sacrificer. Even that is done for the motive of hypocrisy, in order to proclaim their status as performers of sacrifice.
They perform sacrifices without following the prescribed rules and contrary to the injunctions.

"Those who sacrifice while being such as these," he says, "are possessed by egoism, power, arrogance, desire, and wrath; hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, they are envious. (BhG 16.18)

They rely on such egoism as "I alone act for everything, independent of anything else," as well as on power, thinking "my strength alone is sufficient for the performance of all things," and on pride, thinking "there is no one at all who is my equal."
Thinking, "For me who have become thus, everything will be accomplished by mere wish," they resort to desire; and thinking, "I shall slay all those who do me harm," they resort to anger.
Thus they are dependent upon these two.

Those who are envious and hostile toward Me—the Supreme Person who dwells within their own bodies and those of others, and who is the director of all—reveal faults in My abiding state through fallacious arguments; being unable to endure Me, they rely on egoism and the like, performing all ritual acts such as sacrifices [thinking them to be the cause]. This is the meaning. (BhG 16.18)
Those hateful, cruel, and most base of men, who are inauspicious, I perpetually hurl into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence.

Those cruel and lowest of men who hate Me in this way— I cast them perpetually into transmigrations, which consist of the continuous succession of births, old age, death, and so forth; therein, moreover, I cast them specifically into demonic wombs, into births that are entirely opposed to My favor.
The meaning is that I alone join [the soul] with those cruel intellects which serve as the cause for activities conducive to attaining various births.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth, they do not reach Me, O son of Kuntī, but from there go to the lowest state. (BhG 16.20)

Having attained births that are contrary to my favor, those deluded ones, possessing knowledge opposed to mine, fail to reach me; indeed, failing to attain the knowledge that "the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Lord of All, exists," they go from one birth to another toward only the lowest state. 20.
He states the root cause of this destruction of the self, which possesses the nature of an asura:
"This threefold gate of hell, which leads to the ruin of the self—namely, lust, anger, and greed—one should therefore abandon these three. (BhG 16.21)
This triple gate of that hell, which consists of the nature of the asuras,
is the destruction of the self; the essential nature of these three— lust, anger, and greed— has already been explained previously.
The door is the path; that is to say, the cause.
Therefore, one should abandon these three.
Therefore, because desire, anger, and greed are the causes of most terrible hells,
one should abandon this triad from afar.
O son of Kuntī, a person liberated from these three gates to darkness practices what is beneficial for the self and thereby attains the supreme goal.

A man liberated from these—desire, anger, and greed, which are gateways to darkness and causes of knowledge contrary to Me—practices what is for his own highest good; having attained knowledge of My domain, he strives for conformity with Me, and thereby attains Me alone as the supreme goal. (BhG 16.22)
Disregard for the scriptures is the primary cause of this hell; thus he says:
"He who, casting aside the injunction of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims, attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. (BhG 16.23)
The scripture is the Vedas;
the injunction is the instruction.
He who, having cast aside my instruction known as the Vedas, acts according to his own will—that is, proceeds by a path conforming to his own desires—[is a transgressor].
He does not attain accomplishment; he does not attain any accomplishment pertaining to the next world; he does not attain any happiness, nor the supreme goal.
The meaning is: from what [cause] does one attain the supreme goal? BhG 16.23.
Therefore, the scripture is your authority for determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having ascertained what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.

Therefore, regarding the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done—that is, the determination of what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected—the scripture alone is your authority.

The Vedas, augmented by the treatises on Dharma, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and so forth, teach that very action which consists of pleasing the Supreme Reality known as Puruṣottama and which serves as the means for attaining Him.
Having understood that reality and that action as prescribed by the scriptural injunctions, and having discerned them correctly without deficiency or excess—
You ought to do that; you ought to take up that very thing.

It has been stated that the knowledge of the reality to be attained and the knowledge of the means for attaining it, as expressed through the description of the division between gods and demons, have the Veda as their sole source.
Now, [the text describes] how that which is not prescribed by scripture is fruitless because it belongs to the demonic nature,
and how that which is prescribed by scripture is threefold according to its constituent qualities (guṇas).
The definition established by the scriptures is now stated.

In this regard, Arjuna—unaware that what is not prescribed by the scriptures is fruitless—questions [the Lord] out of a desire to understand the distinctions in fruits caused by the qualities such as *sattva* with respect to sacrifices and other rites performed with faith, though not ordained by the scriptures. Thus, Arjuna said:
Those who, discarding the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifice endowed with faith—what, O Kṛṣṇa, is their firm basis? Is it goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)?
For those who, abandoning the injunctions of the scriptures, worship endowed with faith—
what is their standing?
What is their nature?
Or is it passion? Or is it darkness?
The conclusion is the state of stability.
That in which something abides is called its "state" (sthiti); thus, sattva and the other qualities themselves are said to be the final goal (niṣṭhā). Is their state in sattva, or rather in rajas?
Or rather, the meaning is "in darkness. (BhG 17.1)
Thus questioned, the Blessed One, keeping in mind that faith not enjoined by the scriptures and the sacrifices and other rites preceded by such faith are fruitless,
first stated the threefold nature of scriptural faith in order to demonstrate the threefold nature of scriptural sacrifices and other rites according to their qualities.
The Blessed Lord said: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature;
it is sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic—listen to that. BhG 17.2.
