For all embodied beings, faith is threefold. It is born of one's own nature— nature being one's own unique disposition— and is caused by past latencies, manifesting as specific inclinations toward various things.
Where there is inclination (*ruci*), there faith (*śraddhā*) arises.
For faith is a haste toward a means of accomplishment preceded by the conviction that "this indeed accomplishes what is desired by oneself.
Inclination, faith, and latent impression (*vāsanā*) are attributes of the self (*ātman-dharma*), produced through contact with the qualities (*guṇa*).

The producers of those impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth of the self and its attributes are the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which reside in the body, the senses, the internal organ, and their objects, and which are to be defined solely through their effects; that is to say, they arise from the experience of the body and other factors endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and the rest.
Consequently, this faith (*śraddhā*) is of three kinds: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.
Listen to this very faith;
the meaning is: listen to that nature which is the nature of that faith.
The faith of every being conforms to their own nature, O Bhārata;
this person is made of faith—whatever one's faith is, that indeed one is.
*Sattva* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For every person, faith (*śraddhā*) conforms to their internal organ; whatever qualities the internal organ possesses, [so does the faith].
The meaning is that faith arises with respect to that object.
The word *sattva* is intended to indicate the previously mentioned body, senses, and so forth.
This person consists of faith (*śraddhāmaya*).
"Consisting of faith" means a transformation of faith.
Whatever one's faith is— whatever kind of faith a person is endowed with— that very person is a transformation of that very kind of faith.
If one is endowed with faith regarding meritorious action, one becomes joined with the fruit of meritorious action; thus it is said that the attainment of the fruit is primarily dependent on faith.
He explains that very point:

"Those characterized by sattva worship the gods; those characterized by rajas, the yakṣas and rākṣasas; and other people, characterized by tamas, worship the spirits of the dead and hosts of elemental beings. (BhG 17.4)
Those in whom the quality of *sattva* predominates, being endowed with *sāttvika* faith, worship the gods;

that is to say, their *sāttvika* faith has as its object the sacrifice to the gods, which is the cause of supreme happiness unmixed with suffering. Those characterized by *rajas* worship the *yakṣas* and *rakṣasas*.
But other people, who are characterized by darkness (tāmasa), worship the spirits (pretas) and hosts of elemental beings (bhūtagaṇas).
The meaning is that the faith belonging to passion (rājasī śraddhā) produces little happiness intermingled with suffering,
while that belonging to darkness (tāmasī) consists mostly of suffering and produces very little happiness.

Thus, in the case of sacrifices and other rites prescribed by the scriptures when performed with faith, there is a specific excellence of fruit according to their qualities. However, in non-scriptural practices such as asceticism and sacrifice—which are contrary to my instruction—there is not even a trace of happiness, but rather only misfortune. Revealing this which is held in his heart, he says: "Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures..."
Endowed with hypocrisy and egoism, and possessed by the force of desire and passion.
Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements within the body,
and likewise Me who dwell within the body— know them to be of demonic resolve.
This is for the purpose of illustration: those people who perform even extremely severe penance not ordained by the scriptures;
likewise, those who perform sacrifices and other rites involving great exertion that are not ordained by the scriptures.
Those who, joined with hypocrisy and egoism and impelled by the force of desire and passion, emaciate the aggregate of elements such as earth residing within the body,
and likewise emaciate the individual soul (jīva) which is a portion of Me and resides within the body,
perform penances and carry out sacrifices and other rites.
Know those to be the demonic resolves;
the resolve of the asuras is a demonic resolve;
for asuras are those who act contrary to my command.
Because they act contrary to my command, no connection with even a fraction of happiness exists for them;
rather, as was stated previously, they fall into a multitude of calamities:
"They fall into the blazing hell" (BhG 16.16).
Now, the text elaborates upon the specific distinctions among the ritual sacrifices and other practices taught in the scriptures according to their constituent qualities (*guṇas*).
In that regard, since the increase of *sattva* and the other qualities is rooted in food, the threefold nature of food is stated first:
"For the mind, my dear, consists of food (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*)."
For it is heard in scripture: "From purity of food comes purity of being.
Indeed, for everyone, food is dear in three ways;
likewise, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—listen now to this distinction between them. (BhG 17.7)
Just as food is dear to every class of living beings in three ways according to their possession of the three qualities such as goodness (sattva) and the rest,
so too sacrifice, austerity, and charity are each of three kinds.

Listen to this distinction among them: listen to this distinction being described according to the differentiation of the beings [into the three qualities] regarding those sacrifices of food, austerity, and charity. BhG 17.7.

Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy, which are savory, succulent, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—such foods are dear to those of sattvic nature. (BhG 17.8)
For one endowed with the quality of *sattva*, foods consisting of *sattva* become dear;
and foods consisting of *sattva* increase longevity and further increase one's *sattva*.
*Sattva* is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); here, knowledge, which is the effect of the internal organ, is denoted by the word *sattva*.
This is because, as in the statement "from *sattva* knowledge arises," *sattva* is the cause for the increase of knowledge.
Food, too, consists of the essence of living beings and is a cause for the increase of knowledge;
likewise, it promotes the growth of strength and health,
the increase of happiness and joy, and at the time of digestion, it itself increases one's well-being.
Likewise, they increase joy by means of undertaking actions that serve as causes for joy;
they are savory, being endowed with a sweet taste;
and they are smooth, being possessed of oiliness.

Stable foods are those that have a stable transformation; pleasant foods are those with a beautiful appearance. Such foods, consisting of *sattva*, are dear to a person of *sattvic* nature. (BhG 17.8)
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are desired by those of the *rajas* nature; they bring about pain, grief, and disease. (BhG 17.9)
Bitter tastes, sour tastes, those pungent with salt,
and those that are excessively hot.
Excessively sharp, parched, and burning—
these are the pungent, sour, salty, very hot, sharp, parched, and burning [qualities].
Those that are difficult to apply due to excessive coldness, excessive sharpness, and so forth, are *tīkṣṇa* (sharp);
those that cause desiccation are *rūkṣa* (dry);
those that cause heat or burning are *vidāhin* (caustic).
Such foods as these are favored by those of the passionate nature (rājasa);
because they consist of passion (rajas), they increase suffering, grief, and disease, and they increase passion itself. (BhG 17.9)
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and long kept, as well as that which is leavings or impure—such food is dear to those of tamasic nature. (BhG 17.10)
Stale, meaning having remained for a long time; sapless, meaning its natural flavor has been lost;
and putrid, meaning possessed of a foul odor.
"Stale" means that which has changed its flavor due to the lapse of time;
"leftover" means what remains after others, such as one's teacher, have eaten;
"impure" means unfit for sacrifice.
The meaning is "that which remains from what is not offered in sacrifice.
Such food, consisting of darkness (tamas), is dear to those characterized by tamas. It is called "bhojana" because it is that which is eaten; thus, "bhojana" is simply food.
Furthermore, it increases darkness (*tamas*);
therefore, those who desire the welfare [of others] should consume only *sāttvika* food for the sake of increasing the essence (*sattva*) of sentient beings.
That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits,
having settled the mind with the thought "sacrifice must indeed be performed," is characterized by goodness (sāttvika).

That sacrifice which is performed by persons free from desire for fruit, according to the injunctions seen in the scriptures, endowed with mantras, materials, rituals, and so forth, and which is offered with the mental resolve that "it must indeed be sacrificed"— that is, as an act of worshiping the Blessed One for its own sake—
is *sāttvika*. (BhG 17.11)
But that sacrifice which is performed with a view toward fruit, or even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be rajasic.
Know that sacrifice to be rajasic which is performed with an intent for rewards, characterized by hypocrisy, and having fame as its fruit. (BhG 17.12)
A sacrifice devoid of prescribed rules, lacking the distribution of food, bereft of mantras and priestly fees,
and destitute of faith, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

"Devoid of ritual" means lacking the injunctions prescribed by the Brāhmaṇas; "devoid of the speech of the Brāhmaṇas" means lacking the declaration "Sacrifice! made by learned Brāhmaṇas endowed with good conduct; "without prepared food" means lacking the materials not [otherwise] enjoined.
They declare that sacrifice to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa) which is devoid of mantras, lacks sacrificial fees, and is bereft of faith.
Now, in order to explain the threefold nature of austerity according to its qualities, he first describes its classification based on its accomplishment through body, speech, and mind:
"Reverence for the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity. (BhG 17.14)
Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise;
purity, such as bathing at sacred fords and the like; and straightforwardness, which is the conduct of mind and body in accordance with one's nature.
Celibacy is the absence of looking at women with the thought of them as objects of enjoyment and so forth;
non-violence is the absence of harming living beings.
This is called austerity of the body. (BhG 17.14)
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, as well as the practice of reciting one's own sacred texts—this is said to be austerity consisting of speech. (BhG 17.15)
Speech that causes no agitation to others, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, as well as the practice of Vedic recitation—this is called austerity consisting of speech.
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint,
and purity of being— this is called mental austerity.
Clarity of mind (manaḥprasāda) is the state of the mind being free from anger and other such afflictions; gentleness (saumyatva) is the mind's inclination toward the prosperity of others;
and silence (mauna) is the restraint of the activity of speech by means of the mind.
Self-restraint is the fixing of the mental faculty upon the object of meditation;
purity of being is the state of being free from thoughts concerning objects other than the Self;
this is austerity of the mind. (BhG 17.16)
That threefold austerity which is performed by men with supreme faith,
by those who are disciplined and free from desire for fruits, is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

That threefold austerity which is performed with the body, speech, and mind by men who are free from desire for fruit, who are disciplined— meaning endowed with the thought that "this is the means of propitiating the Supreme Person"— and who possess supreme faith, is declared to be *sāttvika*. (BhG 17.17)
That austerity which is performed for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, and which is done with hypocrisy, is declared here to be rajasic; it is unstable and impermanent. (BhG 17.18)
Reverence is respect through the mind;
honor is praise and esteem through speech; and worship consists of physical acts such as prostration.
That austerity which is performed with the motive of attaining rewards, for the sake of honor and the like, and out of hypocrisy as its cause—
that is declared here to be rajasic; because it is a means to fruits such as heaven, it is unstable and transient.
Mobility is the state of being subject to falling; the cause of movement is the fear of falling; and instability is the quality of being perishable.
That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself or for the sake of destroying another, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

The deluded are those lacking discrimination; by means of a deluded grasp— that is, through the stubborn attachment created by the deluded— they perform austerity that causes self-torment without examining their own strength and so forth,
as well as that which is performed for the purpose of destroying another.
That is declared to be tāmasa.
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given," to one who does not return the favor,
at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient— that gift is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

That gift which is given at the proper place and time to a worthy recipient— even one who has not rendered assistance— and which is free from any expectation of reward, is declared to be *sāttvika* (of the nature of goodness).
But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit,
and which is given with a sense of distress— that is declared to be rajasic.
That gift which is given with the expectation of a return favor or a reward in mind, and which is acquired through hardship or consists of impure substances,
is declared to be "royal" (rājasam).
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients,
without respect and with contempt, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients; that which is given disrespectfully, devoid of honor such as washing the feet and so forth; and that which is given with contempt, accompanied by disdain, and lacking in proper etiquette.
That is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). //22//
Thus, the distinction among Vedic sacrifices, austerities, and gifts has been stated according to the differentiation of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
now, the definition of that very same Vedic sacrifice and so forth—by means of its conjunction with the *praṇava* and its designation by the word *sat*—is being stated:
"The designation of Brahman is traditionally remembered as threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*."
By him, in ancient times, the Brahmins, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were established.
"Oṃ tat sat"—this threefold designation is recorded as the word of Brahman; it is coextensive with Brahman. And Brahman is the Veda.
By the word "Veda," Vedic ritual action is meant.
The Vedic [practice] consists of sacrifices and the like.
Ritual action such as sacrifice is accompanied by the words "Oṃ Tat Sat.
The accompaniment of the word "Oṃ" occurs because it is employed at the beginning of the performance as an integral part of Vedic ritual.
The connection between those two words, "that" (tat) and "existent" (sat), serves to express venerability by way of denotation.

Thus, the Brāhmaṇas—meaning those belonging to the three higher castes who are connected with the Vedas—are conjoined with that threefold word; and the Vedas and sacrifices were ordained in the past, meaning they were created by me alone in the beginning.
The manner of the connection of the three words "Oṃ," "Tat," and "Sat" is now described.
First, he explains the manner of the connection of the word "Oṃ":
"Therefore, having uttered 'Oṃ,' [one should perform] the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity."
These are constantly practiced by those who discourse on Brahman, as prescribed by the ordinances.

Therefore, for the proponents of Brahman—the members of the three twice-born classes who follow the Vedas—the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity, as prescribed by rule and declared in the Vedas, always proceed at all times after first uttering "Om"; likewise, the Vedas themselves are commenced by uttering "Om.
Thus, the connection of the word "Om" with the Vedas and with Vedic rites such as sacrifices has been described.

Because they uphold the Vedas accompanied by the word "Om" and because they perform sacrificial and other rites accompanied by that same word, the connection with the word "Om" has been described for the three social classes who are designated by the term "Brāhmaṇa. Now, he explains the manner in which these [other classes] are connected with the word "Tat":
"Without aiming for a fruit, [performing] acts of sacrifice and austerity... (BhG 17.25).
And various acts of giving are performed by those who desire liberation.

The actions of Vedic study, sacrifice, austerity, charity, and ritual performance which are performed by members of the three twice-born classes seeking liberation, without aiming for their fruits, are to be designated by the word *tat*—which denotes Brahman—as being the means for attaining Brahman;
for the word *tat* is well known as a term for Brahman, as in the passage: "That which is yours, what, and which—that unsurpassed state."

Thus, it has been stated that the connection with the word "That" (tat) applies to the study of the Vedas, sacrifices, and so forth—which serve as means to liberation—by virtue of their being denotable by that term.
Likewise, for members of the three twice-born classes, the connection with the word "That" is logically established precisely through the performance of such activities as the study of the Vedas.

Now, in order to explain the manner in which the word *sat* applies to these [three types of sacrifices], he describes the manner in which the word *sat* is derived in common usage: "The word *sat* is employed in the sense of existence (*sadbhāva*) and in the sense of goodness (*sādhubhāva*);
likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is applied to a praiseworthy action. (BhG 17.26)
The word *sat* is employed in both worldly and Vedic usage to denote existence (*sadbhāva*), presence (*vidyamānatā*), and goodness or auspiciousness (*sādhubhāva*, *kalyāṇabhāva*) in all things.

Likewise, when a praiseworthy and auspicious worldly action has been performed by some person, the word *sat* is applied—meaning it is used—in the sense that "this is a good deed" (*satkarma*). (BhG 17.26)
Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "good" (sat);
and action performed for their sake is likewise designated as "good."
Therefore, the steadfastness of the Vedic people—the members of the three higher castes—in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "Good" (sat) because of its auspicious nature.
And the action intended for that purpose—that is, intended for the sake of the three castes, such as sacrifice, charity, and so forth—is likewise designated as "Good.

Consequently, the Vedas, the Vedic rites, the members of the three castes indicated by the term *brāhmaṇa*, and [the syllable] *oṃ*—all these are distinguished from non-Vedic things and non-Vedic practices by the defining characteristic of their connection with the words *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*.
These are to be understood. BhGR 17.27.
Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is called "unreal"; it is of no account either after death or here in this world.
Even that which is performed according to the scriptures, such as the *homa* and other rites, if done without faith, is said to be non-existent (*asat*).
Why? Because "it does not lead to the hereafter, nor to this world, nor to liberation."
Nor for the sake of worldly fruits. // BhGR_17.28 //

In the two preceding chapters, it was established that only Vedic action—consisting of sacrifice, austerity, charity, and so forth—is the means for attaining both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and not any other; furthermore, the general characteristic of Vedic action is its connection with the syllable *praṇava* (Om);
and therein lies the distinction between the means for liberation and the means for prosperity, which is indicated by the respective application of the terms *tat* and *sat*.
And the means for attaining liberation is action such as sacrifice performed without attachment to its fruits;
the undertaking of such action arises from the predominance of *sattva*; and the increase of *sattva* occurs through the practice of *sāttvika* food—so it has been stated.
Next, the identity of renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*) as taught as the means to liberation, the essential nature of renunciation,
and the contemplation of the agency of all actions in the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of All.
By means of describing the effects of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the necessity of adopting the quality of *sattva* is established;

the manner in which the performance of duties appropriate to one's own caste—which constitute the supreme worship of the Supreme Person—brings about the attainment of that Supreme Person is explained;
and it is demonstrated that the essential meaning of the entire Gītā scripture is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). These are the subjects set forth.

In this regard, Arjuna asks for the sake of determining the distinctness or identity of renunciation (*tyāga*) and relinquishment (*saṃnyāsa*), as well as for the sake of determining their essential nature:
Arjuna said:
"O mighty-armed one, I desire to know the true nature of relinquishment."
And of renunciation, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin, tell me the difference. (BhG 18.1)
For renunciation (*tyāga*) and asceticism (*saṃnyāsa*) are prescribed as means for liberation:

"By action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality; those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the realization of Vedānta, being self-controlled ascetics of pure being through the yoga of renunciation—they all, at the time of their final end in the world of Brahman, are liberated through supreme immortality. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)
In these and other such passages, I desire to know separately the reality—that is, the true nature—of this renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and abandonment (*tyāga*).
This is the intention: are these two words, "renunciation" and "abandonment," distinct in meaning?
Or, if they indeed have a single meaning while appearing as two separate meanings, then I wish to know their essential nature through their distinction;
even if they are one, that essential nature must be explained. (BhG 18.1)
Now, in order to determine that these two have indeed a single essential nature— which is as follows— the Blessed Lord, demonstrating the disagreement among disputants,
said: the Blessed Lord said.
The wise understand *saṃnyāsa* to be the renunciation of actions performed for the sake of desire;
the discerning call the abandonment of the fruits of all actions *tyāga*. (BhG 18.2)
Some scholars understand *saṃnyāsa* as the renunciation of desirable actions, that is, the abandonment of their very performance.

However, other discerning ones declare that in the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*), the meaning of the word "renunciation" refers solely to the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions—whether obligatory, occasional, or desirable.
Among these views, scriptural renunciation concerns the nature of desirable actions themselves.
Demonstrating a dispute regarding the scope of the fruits of all actions, [the Lord] employed the word *saṃnyāsa* in one instance and the word *tyāga* in the other.
From this, it is understood that the identity of meaning between the words *tyāga* and *saṃnyāsa* is accepted.
Likewise, because the definitive statement is made using the word *tyāga* itself in the passage: "Hear from Me the certainty regarding that renunciation (*tyāga*), O best of the Bharatas."
“However, the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate;
its abandonment through delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).”
“‘The threefold fruit of action—unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.
From this observation that these two terms are used interchangeably, it is certain that their meaning is accepted as being identical. (BhG 18.2)
Some wise men have said that action should be abandoned as being full of evil;
others, however, have said that the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.

Some wise men—the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas) and the Vaidikas who follow their doctrine—declare that all action, such as sacrifice and the like, must be renounced by one seeking liberation because it binds due to possessing defects such as passion; other scholars declare that action, such as sacrifice and the like, is not to be renounced.
Listen to my definitive conclusion regarding renunciation, O best of the Bharatas;
for renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds. (BhG 18.4)
In this regard, since there is such disagreement among disputants, hear from me the definitive conclusion concerning renunciation;
renunciation consists in [the relinquishing of] the fruit and the action itself while the Vedic rites are indeed being performed.
Indeed, I have already previously proclaimed that [action] as threefold with reference to the agent:
"Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Self,
being free from desire and the sense of 'mine,' fight, free from fever."
The renunciation of the fruit is the thought, "May the fruit of this action, such as heaven and the like, not be mine.
The renunciation regarding the action is the abandonment of the sense of "mine-ness" toward the action, thinking, "This action is mine because it is the means to my fruit.
The renunciation regarding agency is the abandonment of one's own agency by reflecting on the Lord of All as the true agent. // BhG 18.4 //
Acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed.

Ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas, such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity, should never be abandoned by one seeking liberation; rather, they must be performed daily until the moment of death. (BhG 18.4)
Why?
Because sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise. (BhG 18.5)

Rituals such as sacrifice, charity, and austerity, pertaining to the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas), are purifiers for the wise—those whose nature is contemplation. "Contemplation" here means meditative worship (upāsanā);
the meaning is that for those seeking liberation who practice worship throughout their lives, these acts destroy prior karma that would otherwise obstruct the perfection of that worship. (BhG 18.5)
Moreover, O Pārtha, it is my firm and supreme conviction that even these actions must be performed, having abandoned attachment and the fruits thereof. (BhG 18.6)
Since for the wise, sacrifices, charity, austerity, and so forth are purifying,
therefore— just like meditation— these actions such as sacrifice and the rest, being forms of worship to Me,

must be performed day after day until death by one seeking liberation, having abandoned attachment to action, the sense of "mine," and the fruits thereof, for the sake of perfecting that meditation; this is My settled and supreme opinion.
But the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate;
its abandonment through delusion is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
The renunciation or abandonment of obligatory and occasional duties, such as the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and so forth, is not tenable;
for, as it is said, "even the maintenance of the body would not be accomplished by one who performs no action," the very maintenance of the body would remain unachieved.
Indeed, when the maintenance of the body is fulfilled through the consumption of what remains from the sacrifice, it leads to right knowledge; otherwise, [it does not].

The statement, "But those wicked ones consume sin," implies that the nourishment of the mind by consuming what remains from non-sacrificial acts—which is of the nature of sin—leads to perverted knowledge.

For it is said, "The mind, my dear, consists of food," meaning that the mind is indeed nourished by food. As it is taught: "When the food is pure, the inner being (sattva) becomes pure; when the inner being is pure, mindfulness becomes firm."
Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the complete liberation from all knots.
Thus, it is heard in scripture that knowledge, which consists of the direct realization of Brahman, depends upon the purity of one’s food and other factors.

Therefore, the daily and occasional rites such as the great sacrifices (mahāyajña) must be undertaken until death for the very sake of attaining knowledge of Brahman; hence, their abandonment is not justified.
Thus, the abandonment of action—which generates knowledge—out of a delusion regarding its binding nature is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Renunciation rooted in darkness is *tāmasa*.
Renunciation is rooted in darkness because it has ignorance, which is the effect of darkness, as its root;
for darkness is indeed the root of ignorance.
"Negligence and delusion arise from darkness, as well as ignorance itself"—this has been stated here.
Ignorance, moreover, is the opposite of knowledge, being a perverted cognition; and so it will be explained further on.
“That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and all things in a perverted manner— that, O Pārtha, is tāmasī. Therefore,
the meaning is that the abandonment of obligatory and occasional rites is rooted solely in perverted knowledge.
He who, out of fear of bodily affliction, abandons action simply because it is painful,
performs a passionate renunciation and shall never obtain the fruit of renunciation.
Although action is an indirect means to liberation, nevertheless,

because it must be accomplished through the acquisition of material goods— which are themselves of the nature of suffering— and because it involves great exertion and causes physical exhaustion, it brings about despondency of the mind. Out of fear of this, one should strive for the practice of knowledge alone in order to achieve yoga.

He who abandons the duties of the stages of life, such as the great sacrifices, performs a renunciation rooted in *rajas*—a *rājasa* renunciation—and thus does not obtain the fruit of renunciation, which consists in the arising of knowledge that the meaning of the scriptures is established as it truly is. For it will be said: "That intellect by which one perceives things incorrectly, O Pārtha, is *rājasī*."
For action is not a cause for mental clarity by way of its visible result;
rather, it is so by way of generating faith in the Blessed One.
When prescribed action is performed simply because it ought to be done, O Arjuna,
having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit,
that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

Action prescribed for the various social classes and stages of life— such as the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and great sacrifices (mahāyajña)— should be performed as a form of worship unto Me, considering it to be its own inherent purpose. When such action is performed after abandoning attachment to the work, the sense of "mine-ness," and the fruit thereof,
that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
It has its root in *sattva*;
that is to say, its root is the knowledge of the meaning of the treatise as it truly exists.
For it has been stated that *sattva* produces the knowledge of things as they truly exist.
“From sattva, knowledge arises. And it will be said:
“Engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness,”
“O Pārtha, that intellect which understands both bondage and liberation is sāttvika. Thus [it is said].
He does not hate unwholesome action nor does he cling to wholesome action;
he is renounced, filled with compassion for all beings, wise, and one whose doubts have been severed.
Thus possessed by the [divine] being, the wise man, knowing reality as it truly is, has his doubts severed by that very knowledge;
he renounces attachment to action, its fruits, and the sense of agency.
He does not hate unwholesome karma, nor does he become attached to wholesome karma. Unwholesome karma has an undesirable fruit.
Wholesome action has as its fruit desirable forms, heaven, sons, cattle, food, and so forth;
this is because one is free from the sense of "mine" regarding all action,
and because one has renounced all fruits other than Brahman.

And because they have abandoned the sense of agency, one does not harbor attachment or aversion toward those two while they are being performed. Here, "sinful action" (pāpakarma) is intended to mean that which arises from negligence (*prāmādika*); as it is said: "Neither one who has not desisted from misconduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated [attains the goal]."
Nor can one whose mind is not tranquil attain this through mere intellectual knowledge.
Thus, because it is heard that the non-cessation of misconduct is an obstacle to the arising of knowledge,
the scriptural renunciation consists in the relinquishing of agency, attachment, and fruit with regard to action,
not the relinquishing of the essential nature of the action itself. (BhG 18.10)
Regarding this, it is said:
"Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to renounce actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a renouncer. (BhG 18.11)
For one who bears a body—that is, while maintaining a physical form—it is not possible to renounce actions entirely;
because eating, drinking, and so forth, which are for the sake of sustaining the body, as well as the activities associated with them, are unavoidable.
And for that purpose, the performance of the great sacrifices and other rites is likewise unavoidable.

But he who, among those great sacrifices and other rites, renounces the fruit— that very person is designated as a "renouncer" in such scriptural passages as, "By renunciation some have attained immortality.
The term "renouncer of the fruit" is used for the purpose of illustration, implying a renouncer of the fruit, the sense of agency, and attachment to action.
“...is proclaimed to be threefold,” because of the context [of the preceding verse].

Now, it may be objected that ritual actions such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the Jyotiṣṭoma, as well as the Great Sacrifices (mahāyajña) and others, are enjoined by the scriptures as being connected with fruits such as heaven;
for even the obligatory and occasional rites are indeed prescribed with a connection to results, such as in the injunction: "The Prājāpatya [penance] is for householders."
Therefore, when performing those actions understood to have the nature of being means for their respective fruits,
a connection with results— whether desired or undesired— is unavoidable even for one who does not intend such results, just as it is with the sowing of seeds and so forth.

Therefore, since action results in fruits that are opposed to liberation, one who desires liberation should not perform ritual action; to this he replies: "The threefold fruit of action—unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced. (BhG 18.12)
The undesirable is the fruit of hell and so forth;
the desirable is heaven and so forth; the mixed is that which is interspersed with the undesirable, such as children, cattle, food, and the like.
This threefold fruit of action belongs to those who do not renounce— those who lack the renunciation of agency, possessiveness, and results— after death;
that is to say, after the time following the performance of the action.
But for renunciants—those who have abandoned agency and the like—there is never anywhere any fruit that is opposed to liberation.

This is what is meant: although the Agnihotra, the Great Sacrifices (mahāyajña), and so forth are indeed those very same rites, nevertheless, just as in the case of the qualifications of livelihood and desire, they are resolved through a distinction in application (viniyoga) regarding the qualification for liberation.

And there is the application [of karma] to liberation, as stated in such passages as: "The Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting.
Thus, while these very actions are being performed...
The renunciation of agency and so forth, which is the accomplishment of the scriptures, is *saṃnyāsa*; that very same thing is called *tyāga*.
Now, by contemplating the Lord, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and the agent, he describes the manner of contemplating the self as non-agent;
for it is precisely through this that the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*) regarding both the fruit and the action is abandoned.
Indeed, the Supreme Person initiates actions for the purpose of His own divine play (*līlā*) by means of His own individual soul (*jīvātman*), as well as His own instruments, body, and vital breaths.
Therefore, even results such as the cessation of hunger residing in the individual soul (jīvātman),
and the action that serves as their means, belong to the Supreme Person alone.
"O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes."
These have been declared in the Sāṃkhya doctrine and in the Kṛtānta for the successful accomplishment of all actions.

"Sāṃkhya" means intelligence; in the Sāṃkhya and in the Kṛtānta—that is, in the determination accompanied by Vedic intelligence concerning the reality of things as they truly exist—for the sake of the success, that is, the origination, of all actions.
These five causes have been declared; understand them from me and reflect upon them.

For the Vedic intellect determines that the Supreme Self alone is the agent, regarding the body, senses, vital breaths, and the individual self (jīvātman) as merely instruments, according to the text:
"He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."
“In the Teacher who has entered within, the Self of all beings,” and so forth.
Regarding this, it is said: "The locus, likewise the agent, and the various instruments,
as well as the diverse and distinct activities— fate is the fifth among these."
Whatever action a person undertakes with body, speech, and mind—
whether it be righteous or its opposite— these five are its causes.
In every action— whether physical or verbal— that is either right and established by scripture, or its opposite and prohibited; or even in the body itself.
And these five are the causes in the mental [realm]: the substratum is the body;
it is called the substratum because the individual self (jīvātman) presides over it—that is, the body, which consists of an aggregate of the great elements (mahābhūta).

Likewise, the agent is the individual soul (jīvātman); this individual soul possesses both the quality of being a knower and the quality of being an agent, as stated in the sūtra: "He is a knower for that very reason."
And this has been established by the sūtra: "There is an agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless.

Furthermore, the instruments are of various kinds; the fivefold group of organs beginning with speech, hands, and feet, together with the mind, constitutes the organs of action, which are distinct and perform separate functions for the accomplishment of action.
And their activities are manifold and distinct.
By the word "activity" (*ceṣṭā*), the fivefold wind is denoted, as it expresses its specific functions.
The various activities and various functions of the fivefold wind—which sustains the body and the senses and is divided into the distinctions of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth—are meant.

And "the divine" (*daiva*) is the fifth here; in this collection of causes for action, the divine is the fifth, meaning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is the primary cause in the accomplishment of action.
For it has been said: "And I am seated within the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
And He will say: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings."
Causing all beings to revolve, as if mounted on a machine, by means of his illusory power.
Thus,

the agency of the individual self (jīvātman) is dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātman), as established in such passages as, "But [agency belongs] to the other, for so scripture declares" (Brahmasūtra 2.3.40).

But surely, if the agency of the individual self (jīvātman) were thus dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātman), the individual self would not be subject to injunctions regarding actions; consequently, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would become purposeless.

This objection, too, has been answered by the author of the Sūtras with the words: "But [the Self] depends on the effort exerted, because otherwise prescribed and prohibited injunctions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth.
What is meant is this: by means of the instruments, the body, and so forth, which are bestowed by the Supreme Self, which serve as its substrates, and which possess powers imparted by Him...

The individual soul (jīvātman) itself, being the substratum of that [body] and possessing the power deposited therein, initiates effort in the form of presiding over the instruments by its own will for the accomplishment of action; the Supreme Self (paramātman), residing within it, impels it by granting His consent. Thus, the individual soul also possesses the status of being the cause of its own activity through its own intellect.

Just as in the performance of actions such as moving a very heavy rock or a tree, which require many men to accomplish, many individuals possess causality and are subject to injunctions and prohibitions—
so it being thus, he who, due to unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the sole agent, that person of dull wit does not see.
Thus, since the agency of the individual self (jīvātman) actually exists by the permission of the Supreme Self (paramātman),

he who perceives the Self alone as the sole agent in that action is of perverted intellect (durmati); because his understanding is unrefined— that is, because his cognition of things as they truly are has not been perfected— he does not see, he does not perceive the agent as it truly is.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, and whose intellect is not tainted—
even by slaying these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
The disposition of one who contemplates the Supreme Person as the agent—that specific mental modification whose object is agency—is not produced by the ego;
that is to say, the knowledge "I am doing" does not exist for him.
His intellect is not smeared [by the action], because since he lacks the sense of agency in this work, he thinks, "This fruit does not attach to me."
The meaning is that he for whom the realization arises, "This is not my action," even after killing these people in battle, he does not kill them—
not only Bhīṣma and the others, is the sense.
Therefore, by that action called fighting, one is not bound;
the meaning is that one does not experience its fruit.

Since all this reflection on the absence of agency and so forth occurs only through the increase of the quality of *sattva*, the Lord— desiring to make known the worthiness of *sattva* as something to be adopted and intending to elaborate upon the diversity in actions caused by the qualities of *sattva* and the others—
first states the manner in which action is impelled:
"Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower constitute the threefold impulse to action."
The cause, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold summary of action.
Knowledge is knowledge regarding the action to be performed; the object of knowledge is the action to be performed;
and the knower is the one who understands it—thus, the impulsion toward action is threefold.
The meaning is that the injunction for rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma is joined with the awakening, the object to be awakened, and the awakener.
In that context, the ritual action, which is the form of the object to be awakened, is subsumed under three categories: the instrument, the object, and the agent.
The instrument consists of the means of accomplishment, such as substances and so forth.
Action consists of sacrifices and the like;
the agent is the performer. (BhG 18.18)
Knowledge, action, and the agent—these three are indeed described according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas) in the enumeration of the qualities; hear about them also exactly as they are.
Knowledge concerning the duties to be performed, the action being performed,

and the performer of that action— these are declared to be of exactly three kinds according to the distinctions of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, in the enumeration of the qualities (*guṇasaṃkhyāna*), that is, in the calculation of the effects of the qualities.
Listen correctly to those [qualities] as well—knowledge and the rest—which are distinguished according to their specific attributes; listen to them exactly as they are.
Know that knowledge to be *sāttvika* by which one perceives the one undecaying reality, undivided within the divided, existing in all beings. (BhG 18.20)

Among all beings who are divided according to their forms as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, students, householders, and so forth, and who are entitled to perform ritual action—that knowledge by which one perceives the single reality called the Self, which is undivided even therein;
which, although these beings possess various forms such as Brahminhood and are subject to distinctions such as white or long, is itself devoid of division within its own nature as consciousness;

which is imperishable, remaining unchanging and unaffected even amidst the perishable bodies of Brahmins and others, and which is unfit for attachment to results at the time of eligibility for action—[one perceives this].
Know that knowledge to be of the nature of sattva.
But that knowledge which perceives various distinct entities as separate from one another among all beings— know that knowledge to be rajasic.

Know that knowledge to be rajasic which, at the time of eligibility for action, perceives all beings— beginning with Brahmins— as diverse entities called "selves" through their distinct forms as Brahmins and so forth, and as variously differentiated by distinctions such as white or long, and as fit for connection with fruits [of action] and the like. (BhG 18.21)
But that which is attached to a single task as if it were the whole, which is without cause,
devoid of the true goal, and trivial— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

But that knowledge which is attached—as if it possessed the entirety of its fruit—to a single effect, a single task, or a ritual act such as the propitiation of hosts of spirits and ghosts, which yields a very meager result;

which is causeless, yet in reality lacks such a cause for attachment because it does not possess the entirety of its fruit; and which, being devoid of the true object, has as its domain false objects just as before, by way of conceiving the Self as possessing separateness and so forth—[that is the knowledge of the ignorant].
And because it has as its object the propitiation of spirits such as ghosts and demons, that knowledge is of very little fruit and is small; therefore, it is declared to be tamasic.

Having thus described the threefold nature of the knowledge regarding the duties to be performed—according to their qualities—at the time of qualification through the aspect of the qualified person, [the Lord] now states the threefold nature of the action to be performed according to its qualities:
"Action that is obligatory, free from attachment, performed without passion or hatred, by one who does not desire its fruit—that is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). (BhG 18.23)
It is performed as prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*),
free from attachment— that is, free from attachment to agency and the like— and performed without passion or hatred, meaning it is not done out of passion for fame or hatred of ill-repute.
The meaning is that it is performed without hypocrisy;
that action which is done by one who does not desire fruit—that is, without the intention for a result—and is performed simply because it ought to be done, is said to be *sāttvika*. (BhG 18.23)
But that action which is performed with a desire for rewards, or again with egoism,
and involves great exertion— that is declared to be rajasic.

Furthermore, that action which is performed with great effort by one who desires objects of pleasure, who seeks fruits, or who possesses egoism— the word "vā" being used in the sense of "and"— and who is joined with the conceit of agency; that is,
the action performed by one endowed with such a conceit as "this laborious work is being done by me alone," is of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That, therefore, is of the nature of *rajas*; such is the meaning. (BhG 18.24)
Action that is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity, is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
The "consequence" (anubandha) is the suffering that follows once an action has been performed;
"destruction" (kṣaya) is the loss of wealth while the action is being carried out;
and "harm" (hiṃsā) is the injury to living beings therein.
Personal effort is one's own capacity for completing an action;
that action which is undertaken out of delusion— without regard for or reflection upon these [factors]— due to ignorance of the Supreme Person as the agent;
That is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
One who is free from attachment, devoid of egoism, endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm,
and remains unchanged in success or failure— such an agent is said to be characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
Free from attachment means being devoid of attachment to the fruits of action; free from egoistic speech means being devoid of the conceit of agency.
Endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm: fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the endurance of unavoidable suffering until the completion of an undertaken task;
enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is the state of having a mind that is resolutely engaged.
Endowed with those two,

remaining unchanging in success or failure— whether in action such as battle or in the acquisition of materials required for it— one whose mind is unperturbed by success or failure is called a Sāttvika agent.
One who is passionate, desiring the fruit of action, greedy, violent by nature, and impure...
The agent who is possessed by joy and sorrow is proclaimed to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
One who is passionate seeks fame;
one who desires the fruits of action seeks the results of that action;
and one who is greedy is devoid of the disposition to spend wealth required for the performance of action.
One who is violent, performing actions by causing pain to others;
who is impure, lacking the purity required for action;
and who is possessed by joy and sorrow—being filled with joy at success such as victory and with sorrow at failure in actions like war—is proclaimed to be a Rajasic agent. (BhG 18.27)
One who is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, lazy,
despondent, and procrastinating is said to be a doer of tamasic nature.
Unfit means unqualified for the performance of scriptural duties; engaged in improper acts; and vulgar, meaning one who has not acquired knowledge.
Stabdha is one who is stubborn and lacks the habit of undertaking tasks; śaṭha is one who delights in malevolent rites such as sorcery;
naikṛtika is one who is intent on deception.

The lazy person is one whose activity is sluggish even toward undertakings that have already been commenced; the despondent is one whose nature is characterized by excessive dejection; the procrastinator is one who, while performing rites such as malevolent magic (abhicāra), habitually considers the long-term harm to others—such a person is the agent [described].
That is characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
Thus, the threefold division according to the gunas has been stated regarding the knowledge of the objects of action to be performed, the action itself to be performed, and the performer;
now, he speaks of the threefold division according to the gunas of the intellect (buddhi) and fortitude (dhṛti), which consist of the determination of all principles and all human goals:
"Listen to the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to the gunas."
It shall be declared in its entirety and in detail, O Dhanañjaya.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is knowledge in the form of certainty preceded by discrimination;
fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the sustaining of an action already commenced even when obstacles arise.
Listen as I describe to you correctly their threefold distinction according to the qualities of *sattva* and the others. (BhG 18.29)

O Pārtha, that intellect which understands both engagement and withdrawal, what should be done and what should not be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation— that intellect is sāttvika.
*Pravṛtti* is dharma that serves as the means for worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*),
while *nivṛtti* is that which serves as the means for liberation (*mokṣa*);
the intellect that knows both of these as they truly exist— [that is the intellect].

[He] is one who knows, in specific places, times, and circumstances, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done for all social classes—those established in either the dharma of engagement or the dharma of withdrawal—thinking, "This is to be done;
this is not to be done";
and [he knows] fear and fearlessness: transgression of the scripture is the ground of fear, while conformity to it is the ground of fearlessness.
That intellect which understands bondage and liberation, the true nature of worldly existence and the true nature of its cessation, is sattvic.
O Pārtha, that intellect which understands dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, is rajasic.

That which does not correctly know, as previously described, the two kinds of dharma and their opposite, nor what is to be done and what is not to be done by those intent upon them in terms of place, time, and circumstance—that is the rājasic intellect. (BhG 18.31)
That intellect which, enveloped by darkness, O Pārtha, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and all things in a perverted manner— that intellect is tāmasī.
But the intellect characterized by darkness (tāmasī buddhiḥ), being enveloped by darkness, perceives all objects erroneously: it regards unrighteousness as righteousness,
and righteousness as unrighteousness.
One perceives an existing object as non-existent, a non-existing object as existent,
and the supreme reality as the inferior.
Furthermore, the supreme reality is thus; the meaning is that everything else is considered to be the opposite. // BhGR 18.32 //
That fortitude by which one sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths,
and the senses through unwavering yoga— that, O Pārtha, is sattvic fortitude.
By means of that fortitude (*dhṛti*) which is unfailing in yoga, a person sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses.
Yoga is the worship of the Lord, which serves as the means to liberation.

By means of that fortitude—which is unfailing because it is directed toward yoga as its purpose and consists of the activities of the mind and so forth that serve as the means to that [yoga]—he sustains them.
The meaning is that it is characterized by *sattva*. (BhG 18.33)
But that resolve by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna, while desiring the fruits through attachment—that resolve, O Pārtha, is rajasic. (BhG 18.34)
The fortitude by which a man desiring rewards, through intense attachment, maintains virtue, pleasure, and wealth—that is *rājasī* (passionate).
By the words "virtue, pleasure, and wealth," their means—the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses—are indicated.
Here too, in the phrase "desiring rewards," the word "reward" intends precisely virtue, pleasure, and wealth, because they are of the nature of passion (*rājasa*).
Therefore, it is said that the mental activity by which one maintains the mind and the other senses with regard to dharma, pleasure, and wealth is of the nature of passion (rājasī).
O Pārtha, that resolve by which the dull-witted man does not abandon sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and even intoxication— that is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
By means of that steadfastness (dhṛti):
sleep (svapna), which is drowsiness;
and intoxication (mada), the pride born from the experience of sense objects.
The dull-witted person does not relinquish, but rather maintains, the activities of the mind, vital breath, and so forth, which are directed toward dreams and intoxication;

and likewise, he maintains those activities of the mind, vital breath, and so forth, which are directed toward objects that produce fear, grief, and despondency, as well as the sounds associated with them. These [activities] serve as the means for those [states].
That resolve is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī).
Now, O bull among the Bharatas, hear from me about the threefold happiness.
All those previously mentioned—the knowledge, action, agent, and so forth—are subordinate to it; hear now how that happiness is threefold according to the gunas.
Through practice, one finds delight therein and reaches the end of suffering.
That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result, born from the clarity of one's own intellect, is declared to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika). BhG 18.37.
In that happiness, through long-term practice, one gradually attains unsurpassed delight and reaches the end of suffering— that is, one reaches the end of all worldly suffering.

He specifies that very [bliss]: that bliss which, at the outset—at the time of beginning yoga—is like poison or like suffering because it is to be accomplished through great effort and because its distinct nature has not yet been experienced; yet, in its final transformation, it is comparable to nectar.
In its transformation and maturation, through the power of practice, when the nature of the isolated Self is manifested, it becomes like nectar;

and that [nectar] is born from the clarity of the intellect regarding the Self— the "intellect regarding the Self" (ātmabuddhi) being the intellect whose object is the Self— and its "clarity" (prasāda) is the state of having all other objects withdrawn from it.
The happiness born from the experience of the self, whose nature is isolated by means of a consciousness from which all other objects have ceased, becomes like nectar;
that happiness is declared to be *sāttvika*. (BhG 18.37)
That pleasure which, arising from the contact of the senses with their objects, is like nectar at first but turns out to be like poison in its consequence, is declared to be rajasic.

That pleasure which, at the time of its initial experience through the contact of the sense organs with their objects, is like nectar, but which in its final transformation—when the hunger and other causes for the objects' pleasantness have ceased—is like poison drunk because that pleasure becomes a cause for hell and the like; that pleasure is remembered as *rājasa*. (BhG 18.38)
That pleasure which, both at the beginning and in its consequence, deludes the self and arises from sleep,
laziness, and negligence, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
That pleasure which, both at the outset and in its consequence, at the time of experience and in its ripening, causes delusion of the self—that is, becomes a cause of delusion;
here, "delusion" (moha) is intended as the non-manifestation of things as they truly are;
it arises from sleep, laziness, and negligence, being produced by sleep, laziness, and negligence.
For sleep and the like are causes of delusion even at the time of experience;
the fact that sleep is a cause of delusion has already been touched upon.
Indolence is the sluggishness of the activity of the sense faculties.
When there is dullness in the functioning of the sense faculties, cognition itself becomes dull.
Since negligence consists in a lack of attention to what is to be done, cognition also becomes dull in that case as well.
Consequently, both of these are causes of delusion (*moha*).
That happiness is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Therefore, it is implied that one who desires liberation should overcome rajas and tamas and cultivate goodness (sattva) alone. BhG 18.39.
There is no being on earth, nor again among the gods in heaven,
that is free from these three qualities born of nature.

On earth among humans and others, in heaven among the gods, or among those joined with primordial nature— from Brahmā down to the stationary objects— there is no being whatsoever that is liberated from these three qualities born of nature.
The renunciation (tyāga) indicated as a means to liberation in such passages as, "Some have attained immortality through renunciation," is not different from the meaning of the word *saṃnyāsa*.
And that [renunciation] is the abandonment of both fruit and action, rooted in the abandonment of the sense of agency (*kartṛtva*) even while actions are being performed.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the abandonment of agency consists in the contemplation of the Supreme Person as the agent.

All of this has been elaborated as the distinct functions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* in order to demonstrate that they serve to increase the qualities of *sattva*, thereby making known the worthiness of *sattva*. Now, in order to establish that action performed as a means to liberation takes the form of worshiping the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*),
and that the fruit of such performed action is the attainment of Him, [the Lord speaks] to those qualified for it, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others.
He describes the nature of the duties to be performed, distinguished by the various qualities such as sattva which are inherent in one's own nature, along with their application:
"O scorcher of foes, the duties of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras are distributed according to the qualities born of their own natures. (BhG 18.41)

The "own nature" (*svabhāva*) of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas refers to their inherent disposition, which means the past karma that serves as the cause for birth as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth; from that [karma] arise the qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the rest.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the quality of *sattva* arises from his own nature through the suppression of *rajas* and *tamas*.

The quality of passion (rajas) arising from the nature of the Kṣatriya is manifested through the predominance of darkness (tamas) over goodness (sattva); the quality of darkness (tamas) arising from the nature of the Vaiśya is slightly intensified through the predominance of goodness (sattva) over passion (rajas); whereas the quality of darkness (tamas) arising from the nature of the Śūdra is excessively intensified through the predominance of passion (rajas) over goodness (sattva).
By means of these qualities arising from their own nature, the respective duties have been set forth in the scriptures;
those such as the Brāhmaṇas possess these very qualities, and these are their specific duties.
For the scriptures establish this by distinguishing that these are indeed the fluctuations (vṛttayaḥ).
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness,
as well as knowledge, realization, and faith in the Vedas— this is the action pertaining to Brahman, born of one's own nature.
Tranquility (*śama*) is the restraint of the external senses; self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the internal organ;
austerity (*tapas*) is bodily affliction established by the scriptures, consisting in the restraint of enjoyments.
Purity is fitness for performing the actions prescribed by the scriptures;
forbearance is the state of an unaltered mind even when being oppressed by others;
and straightforwardness is the manifestation of external conduct that corresponds to one's internal thoughts toward others.
*Jñāna* is the knowledge of the true nature of the higher and lower principles; *vijñāna* is the knowledge whose object is the uncommon, specific attributes residing in the higher principle;
and *āstikya* is the preeminent certainty regarding the truth of the entire Veda.
The meaning is that he cannot be moved by any cause whatsoever.

The Blessed One, the Supreme Person, Vāsudeva, who is denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman," from whom every trace of defect has been removed, and who possesses an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities such as innate, unsurpassed, and excessive knowledge and power— he alone is the sole cause of the entire universe and the substratum of the entire universe.
He alone is the impeller of everything,

and all Vedic ritual action is a means of propitiating Him; when propitiated by various such acts, He bestows the fruits known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— this certainty regarding the truth of this matter is *āstikya* (faith).
“I alone am to be known by all the Vedas”;
“I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds”;
“all this is strung upon me.”
“Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities... one attains peace”; “There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya”;
“From whom proceeds the activity of beings, by whom all this is pervaded.”
“By worshipping Him through his own duty, a human being attains perfection”;
for it is said, “He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds.
This, indeed, is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa born of his own nature. (BhG 18.42)
Prowess, majesty, fortitude, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle, as well as generosity and lordliness—this is the duty of a kṣatriya, born of his own nature. (BhG 18.43)
Valor (*śaurya*) is the capacity for entering a battle without fear;
brilliance (*tejas*) is the state of being unassailable by others;
and fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the capacity to complete an undertaking even when obstacles arise during its execution.
Skill (*dākṣyam*) is the capacity for the successful accomplishment of all actions; non-retreat even in battle is the refusal to turn back even when certain of one's own death in combat;

generosity (*dānam*) is the relinquishment of one's own wealth culminating in the transfer of ownership to another; and lordship (*īśvarabhāvaḥ*) is the capacity to govern all people other than oneself.
This is the action born of the very nature of a Kṣatriya.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature.
"Agriculture" (kṛṣi) means the production of crops through plowing;
"cattle-rearing" (gorakṣya) means the tending of livestock—this is the meaning.
Trade, consisting of buying and selling for the purpose of accumulating wealth,
is the action born of the very nature of the Vaiśya.
Action consisting of service is also the duty born of one's own nature for the Śūdra.

The service of the three preceding castes is the innate duty (*svabhāvaja-karma*) of the Śūdra. This has been stated for the purpose of illustrating the duties prescribed by the scriptures that must be performed by the four castes along with their respective livelihoods;
for sacrifices and the like are common to the three [upper] castes.
Peace (*śama*) and the other qualities are common to the three castes who seek liberation.

However, because a Brāhmaṇa possesses an abundance of *sattva* by nature, peace, self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth are easily acquired; therefore, it is said that for him, peace and the rest are duties born of his own nature (*svabhāvajam karma*).

On the other hand, because the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are by nature dominated by *rajas* and *tamas*, peace, self-restraint, and so forth are difficult to acquire; therefore, it is said that those are not their [inherent] duties.
The livelihood of a Brahmin consists of officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts;
that of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the realm; and that of a Vaiśya consists of agriculture and the other duties as previously described.
But for a Śūdra, his duty and livelihood consist solely in service to the three preceding castes.
Devoted to his own respective duty, a man attains perfection;
hear how one who is intent on his own work finds success. (BhG 18.45)
A person who is devoted to his own respective duty as it has been prescribed attains perfection, which is the attainment of the supreme state.
Listen now to how one who is intent on his own work finds success and reaches the supreme state. (BhG 18.45)
Since from Him proceeds the activity of all beings and by Him all this is pervaded,
a human being attains perfection by worshipping Him through his own prescribed duty.

Having worshipped Me— who am established as the inner self within Indra and others— by means of My own action, through which the activity of beings such as their birth and so forth proceeds, and by which all this is pervaded, a human being attains perfection in the form of reaching Me through My grace.
It has already been stated by me that everything arises from Me alone and that all this is pervaded by Me: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world."
"Nothing else exists that is higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya";
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded"; "Under My supervision, Nature produces the moving and the unmoving."
"In me all things have their origin; from me everything proceeds," and so forth. (BhG 18.46)
"One's own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed.
Thus, one's own duty consists of the form of worshiping Me, having abandoned the sense of agency and so forth;
it is the duty that is fit to be undertaken by oneself alone.

For when the *puruṣa* is conjoined with *prakṛti*, the dharma consisting of *karmayoga*— which takes the form of the activity of the senses— is easy to perform. Therefore, one's own duty (*svadharma*), known as *karmayoga*, is superior even if it is deficient in quality, compared to the duty of another (*paradharma*)— namely *jñānayoga*, which consists of the mastery of the senses and is practiced by a person skilled in subduing them— because the latter involves negligence due to its nature of restraining all the senses, whereas the former may sometimes be well-performed.
He establishes that very point:
"One who performs action determined by one's own nature incurs no sin. (BhG 18.47)

Since action is necessarily determined by its very nature as the activity of the senses for the person (puruṣa) who is conjoined with primordial matter (prakṛti), one who performs action does not incur sin— that is, does not undergo transmigratory existence— because that action is performed without negligence.
Since the yoga of knowledge is subject to negligence because it must be accomplished through the restraint of all the senses, one who is devoted to it might indeed incur sin through negligence.
Therefore, he recalls what was stated in the third chapter—that devotion to action alone is superior:
"O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon one's innate duty even if it is flawed;
for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, as fire is by smoke. (BhG 18.48)
Therefore, because it is easy through its innate nature and because it entails vigilance, one should not abandon action even if it is accompanied by defects and suffering;
the meaning is that even one who is fit for the yoga of knowledge should perform only the yoga of action.
All undertakings—
For undertakings of action and undertakings of knowledge are both shrouded by defect and suffering, like fire by smoke;
however, this is the distinction: the yoga of action is easy to perform and free from negligence, whereas the yoga of knowledge is the opposite.
With an intellect unattached everywhere, self-conquered, and free from longing,
he attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of actionlessness.
With an intellect unattached to all fruits and the like, having conquered the self— that is, having mastered the mind—
one is free from longing for personal agency through the contemplation of the Supreme Person as the true agent.

Thus, one who is endowed with renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which has been determined to be non-different from relinquishment (tyāga), attains the supreme perfection of freedom from action (naiṣkarmya-siddhi) while performing action; the meaning is that he attains the supreme steadfastness in meditation (dhyāna-niṣṭhā), which is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga). He attains the aforementioned attainment of the yoga of meditation, characterized by the cessation of the activities of all the senses.
Understand from me, O son of Kuntī, how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman; I shall describe in brief that which is the supreme culmination of knowledge.
Having attained perfection— having attained the perfection of meditation produced by the yoga of action performed day after day until death—
listen from me in brief as to how, in what manner, one who exists [in that state] attains Brahman.
That very Brahman is specified as "that which is the supreme consummation of knowledge.
The meaning is that it is the supreme goal, the ultimate attainment, of knowledge consisting of meditation.
Endowed with purified intellect and having restrained the self through fortitude,
one should abandon the objects of the senses such as sound and cast off attachment and aversion.
Frequenting solitary places, eating sparingly, with speech, body, and mind restrained,
he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken refuge in dispassion.
Having abandoned egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness,
and being free from the sense of "mine" and tranquil, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Endowed with a purified intellect whose object is the reality of the Self as it truly exists,
and having restrained the self through fortitude by turning the mind away from sense-objects so as to make it fit for yoga,
one should abandon sound and other objects, rendering them absent.
Having eliminated passion and hatred caused by those [objects],
he dwells in a secluded place, avoiding all things that are antagonistic to meditation; he eats moderately, being free from both overeating and fasting.
Restraining speech, body, and mind, with the activities of his body, speech, and mind directed toward meditation,

being constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation, and remaining thus until the end of life, he is daily intent on the yoga of meditation; relying upon detachment, he increases his dispassion toward various objects by reflecting on the defects inherent in all things other than the reality that is the object of meditation.

Having abandoned egoism— the conceit of self in that which is not the self— strength, meaning the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that causes its increase, and the pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness caused by them;
Free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama), being devoid of the notion of ownership toward all things that do not belong to the self;

peaceful (śānta), finding joy solely in the experience of the Self—one who is thus constituted and practices the yoga of meditation is fit for becoming Brahman (brahmabhūyāya). This means that, liberated from all bonds, he experiences the Self as it truly exists. // BhG 18.51–53 //
Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion unto Me. (BhG 18.54)

"Become Brahman" means one whose essential nature is a self that has manifested as having the sole form of unlimited knowledge and whose singular essence is being the absolute remainder (of all things).
For it has been stated [in the Gītā]: "But know My other nature, higher than this," thus declaring that He is the remainder of all.
With a serene self—meaning one whose essential nature is unpolluted by afflictions, karma, and so forth—one does not grieve for any particular being whatsoever apart from Me.
He desires nothing; rather,

regarding all beings other than myself as equally unworthy of regard, and considering the entire multitude of things as mere straw, he attains supreme devotion toward me, the Lord of all, whose play consists in the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe.

In his own Lord— the glorious, lotus-eyed one, who is an ocean of the nectar of beauty, who is solely intent upon a multitude of countless, unsurpassed, and excellent auspicious qualities, and from whom every trace of all that is to be abandoned has been cast away— one attains supreme devotion, which consists in the experience of what is exceedingly dear.
He states the fruit of that:
"By devotion he comes to know Me in truth—how great I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter. (BhG 18.55)
He truly knows Me as I am— in My essential nature and My inherent being, as well as in My qualities and My manifestations— by means of such devotion.
Having known Me in truth, immediately thereafter—following that knowledge of reality—one enters Me through devotion (*bhakti*).
The meaning is that one attains Me by means of a devotion of infinitely increasing intensity, which arises subsequent to the vision of My essential nature, attributes, and manifestations.
Here, the word "thereafter" (*tataḥ*) indicates the cause of that attainment.

Devotion alone is what is being specified; for it is stated [in the verse] that "by means of undivided devotion He can be known," since that very devotion is declared to be the cause for entering into Him in reality. (BhG 18.55)
