Thus, the fruition of the obligatory and occasional duties (nitya-naimittika-karma) appropriate to one's caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), when performed as worship of the Supreme Person with their fruits and other rewards renounced, has been described.
Now, he states that even for optional rites (kāmya-karma), when performed in the very same manner, the fruition is that same [liberation]:
"Even while always performing all actions, one who takes refuge in Me..."
Through my grace, one attains the eternal, imperishable state.
Not only the obligatory and occasional rites,
but even all rites performed with desire,
one who acts with me as his refuge— having surrendered to me the sense of agency and so forth— attains through my grace the eternal, imperishable, and perfect state.
It is called a "pada" because it is reached or gone to;
the meaning is that one attains me.
Since this is so, therefore,
having surrendered all actions to Me with your mind, regarding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of discernment, keep your mind constantly fixed on Me. (BhG 18.57)
"With the mind" means with the thought of one's own belonging to Me and being subject to My control.
For it has been said: "Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind directed toward the Self.
Having renounced all actions—along with their agents and objects of worship—in Me, [one should act].

With Me as the supreme goal—meaning, perceiving Me alone as the fruit to be attained—perform actions while constantly resting upon this very yoga of wisdom and remain with your mind ever fixed on Me. (BhG 18.57)
With your mind fixed on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace;
but if, out of egoism, you do not listen to Me, you shall perish.
Thus, with your mind fixed on Me, while performing all actions, you shall cross over all the difficulties of worldly existence solely through My grace.

But if, out of egoism, you think "I alone know everything regarding what ought and ought not to be done," and do not listen to what I have said because of such an attitude, you will perish; you will be ruined.
For indeed, there is no one other than myself who is the knower or the ruler of all that is to be done and not to be done among the entire multitude of living beings.
If, relying on the ego, you think "I will not fight," this resolve of yours is in vain; your own nature will compel you.
If, relying on the conceit of independence in the knowledge of what is beneficial and harmful for yourself, you think "I will not fight" by disregarding my command,
this resolve of yours toward independence shall prove false; for nature will compel you to battle— it is nature that will drive you, an ignorant man agitated by my sovereignty, to engage in war.
He explains this:
"Bound by your own karma born of your nature, O son of Kuntī, you shall do that very thing which you do not wish to do out of delusion, even against your will. (BhG 18.60)
For valor is the action of a kṣatriya born of his own nature;
bound by his own action called valor which is born of his nature, he is indeed rendered powerless.
Unable to endure being insulted by others, you yourself shall engage in that battle which you now, out of delusion and ignorance, do not wish to undertake.
Indeed, I, the Lord of all, have ordained every class of beings to follow their material nature in accordance with their past actions; hear that:
"The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine. (BhG 18.61)
The Lord Vāsudeva, whose nature is the governance of all, dwells in the region of the hearts of all beings—that place where knowledge arises as the root of all activity.
How, and doing what, does He dwell there?
Causing all beings, mounted upon a machine, to revolve by means of His illusory power (māyā).

The meaning is that all beings, mounted upon the machine called *prakṛti*— which consists of the body and senses created by Him alone— remain as He causes them to function according to their respective qualities (*guṇas*) by means of His own *māyā*, which is composed of the qualities such as *sattva*.
This has also been stated previously:
“I am seated within the heart of all, and from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss”; “Everything proceeds from Me”;
and the Śruti passage beginning with, “He who dwells in the self,” and so forth. (BhG 18.61)
He states this as the cause for the cessation of illusion:
"Seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. (BhG 18.62)
Since this is so,
therefore, that very one who is the ruler of all,
stationed in the role of your charioteer out of affection for those who have sought refuge in him—
And go for refuge with your whole being and your entire self to the Instructor who says, "Do it thus";
follow him with your whole soul.
Otherwise, even against your will, you would have been compelled to engage in battle and other such acts by the ignorant one impelled by his *māyā*.
If that were so, you would be lost;
therefore, the meaning is that you should perform battle and other such duties in the manner prescribed by Him.
By acting thus, through His grace, you will attain supreme peace—the cessation of the bondage of all karma—and the eternal state.
As it is declared by hundreds of scriptural passages:
"The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," and "Those great ones attain the heavenly world where the ancient Sādhyas and gods abide."
“Wherein the seers, the first-born, who are ancient,” “beyond the firmament, placed in the secret cave,” and “he who is its supervisor in the highest heaven.”
“Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven,” and “He reaches the end of the path, that highest step of Viṣṇu,” and so forth.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared to you by Me;
having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.
Thus, this knowledge—dearer than all secrets, concerning the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion—must be understood by those seeking liberation.
Having reflected upon all of this in its entirety, act as you wish according to your own qualification;
the meaning is: "Practice whichever you prefer—whether the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, or the yoga of devotion."
Listen again to my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets;
because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.

Among all these secrets, because the yoga of devotion is the most excellent, it was previously described as the "greatest secret" in such passages as: "But this greatest secret I shall declare to you, who are free from cavil.
Listen again to my supreme word concerning that same subject;
since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone. I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me.
In the Vedāntas, in such passages as, "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness;

knowing him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey," the knowledge enjoined—expressed by terms such as *dhyāna* (meditation) and *upāsana* (worship)—is a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-saṃtāna*) that has the same form as direct perception (*darśana-samānākāra*) and is exceedingly dear.
In this context, it is enjoined: "Be intent on Me.
"My devotee" means one who is exceedingly dear to Me.
By being exceedingly dear to Me, the meaning is: "Establish an uninterrupted flow of remembrance that is unsurpassed in its dearness."
"One who sacrifices to me" (madyājī);
here too, the phrase "my devotee" (madbhaktaḥ) is to be supplied.
"Sacrificing" (yajana) means worshiping (pūjana).
Be intent on propitiating me with the utmost love;
for propitiation consists in the complete fulfillment of all remaining duties.
Pay homage to me.
"Salutation" means bowing down; the meaning is: "Act with excessive humility toward me, making yourself exceedingly dear to me.
Conducting yourself in this manner, you shall come to Me alone.
I promise this truth to you; I make this vow to you,
and it is not merely a form of persuasion,
because you are dear to me.
"For he who knows Me is exceedingly dear to Me, and he is dear to Me," as has been stated previously.
For one in whom there exists an excessive love for Me, there likewise arises in Me an excessive love for him; thus, unable to endure separation from him, I cause him to attain Me.
Therefore, my promise has been proven true: "You shall come to Me alone. (BhG 18.65)
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins, do not grieve.

While performing all duties— consisting of the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion— which serve as the means for attaining the supreme goal of liberation, with extreme love by regarding them as service to Me according to one's qualification,
one should renounce them by abandoning the sense of agency regarding the fruit, the action, and the performer, in the manner described.
Devote yourself to Me alone as the sole agent, the one to be propitiated, the goal to be attained, and the means;
this indeed is the renunciation of all duties that accords with the scriptures.
"Hear from Me the certainty regarding that renunciation, O best of the Bharatas."
For renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Beginning with [the verse] "BhG 18.9" and continuing up to:
"Having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika)."
For it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is called a "renouncer."
Thus, it was firmly established at the beginning of the chapter:

"I shall liberate you from all sins"— that is, as you proceed in this manner, I shall liberate you from all sins consisting of the non-performance of what ought to be done and the performance of what ought not to be done, which have been accumulated since beginningless time and are obstacles to attaining Me.

"Do not grieve; do not give way to sorrow. Or rather, because the yoga of devotion is accomplished by a person who is utterly dear to the Blessed One and liberated from all sins, and because the sins that obstruct its commencement are infinite, [it cannot be removed] by religious duties of atonement performed within a limited time.

Observing that those [duties] were difficult to traverse and considering his own unfitness to undertake the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), the Blessed Lord spoke to dispel the grief of the sorrowing Arjuna: "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone. [He spoke thus] regarding the various and infinite sins accumulated since time immemorial—which are contrary to the commencement of the yoga of devotion and correspond to their respective atonements—[and which require] specific forms of expiation.

Abandoning all the various and infinite religious duties— such as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *kūśmāṇḍa*, *vaiśvānara*, *vrātapatīṣṭi*, *pavitreṣṭi*, *trivṛt-agniṣṭoma*, and others— which are difficult to perform and exist only for limited periods of time, take refuge in me alone, who am supremely compassionate, whose protection is sought by the entire world without distinction, and who am an ocean of affection for those who seek shelter, in order to achieve success in the practice of the yoga of devotion.
I shall liberate you from all evils—from all those sins which are opposed to the undertaking of devotion according to the nature described above; do not grieve.
This should never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is devoid of devotion,
nor to one who is unwilling to listen, nor to one who finds fault with Me.
This supreme secret teaching has been declared by me to you; it must not be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who has not practiced fervent penance.
While you are the speaker, it must never be spoken to one who possesses no devotion toward me.
The meaning is that it should not be told to one who has performed penance but lacks devotion,
nor to one who does not desire to hear;
even if he is devoted, it should not be told to one who does not wish to listen.
And it should not be spoken to one who is envious of me— that is, to one who, when my true nature, my sovereignty, and my qualities are described, points out faults in them.
The use of a non-identical case ending is intended to make known that it must be absolutely avoided.
He who shall declare this supreme secret among my devotees, having offered supreme devotion to me, will come to me alone; of this there is no doubt.
He who shall proclaim this supreme secret among My devotees and explain it, having offered supreme devotion to Me, shall come to Me alone; there is no doubt in this. (BhG 18.68)
And among human beings, there shall be no one who does more for me than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he.
Among all human beings, no other person has ever before been so exceedingly dear to me as this one, nor shall there be anyone so in the future.
For, although the unworthy were first mentioned, the worthy were not mentioned because speaking of them would have been most undesirable.
And whoever shall study this dialogue of ours concerning Dharma, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction.

"He who shall study this dialogue of ours concerning dharma, by him I shall be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. The meaning is: "By means of this sacrifice of knowledge which is being described here, I shall be worshipped by that person merely through the act of studying this [text]."
Even that man who, possessing faith and free from malice, should merely listen to this,
shall be liberated and attain the auspicious worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.

Even that man who, endowed with faith and free from malice, should merely hear this— by that hearing alone, he too shall be liberated from sins that oppose devotion and attain the worlds of my devotees who perform meritorious deeds.
O Pārtha, has any part of this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind?
Has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed within you, O Dhanañjaya?
"O Pārtha, has this which was spoken by me been heard by you with an attentive mind?
Has the delusion born of your ignorance been destroyed—that ignorance through which, being bewildered, you said, 'I will not fight'? (BhG 18.72)
Arjuna said:
"The delusion is destroyed, and memory has been regained by me through Your grace, O Acyuta.
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled; I shall do as You command."
Delusion is erroneous cognition;
by your grace, that has been destroyed in me.
Memory is the knowledge of reality as it actually exists.
And that [liberation] has been obtained solely through your grace: namely,

the delusion consisting of the conceit of selfhood regarding the non-self, which is primordial nature (prakṛti), and the delusion consisting of the conceit of not having that as one's self regarding the entire aggregate of conscious and unconscious entities, which have that [nature] as their essence because they constitute the body of the Supreme Person.

All notions of bondage regarding ritual action—whether of the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) kind—which is the means for attaining the Supreme Person because it is His worship, have been destroyed.

Furthermore, there has arisen the knowledge that the Self is distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), devoid of its inherent qualities, whose sole nature is that of a knower, who exists solely as a subordinate to the Supreme Person, and whose very essence is to be governed by Him.

The knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Person—the Supreme Brahman, who is designated by the term *parabrahma*, who is the great ocean of the multitude of all auspicious qualities such as natural, infinite, and unsurpassed excellence of knowledge, strength, sovereignty, heroism, power, and splendor, and whose very essence is the sole auspiciousness that is the opposite of all defects, and who performs the play of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe.

Thus, I have attained the knowledge that "You are Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, who is to be known through the Vedāntas and is attainable solely through the worship of the Supreme Person—a worship which takes the form of devotion brought about by the qualities of self-restraint, tranquility, and so forth; which consists in the performance of obligatory and occasional rites and the avoidance of prohibited acts, all of which have as their sole fruit the daily accumulation of pleasure for the Supreme Person preceded by the realization and practice of the true nature of such higher and lower principles.
Furthermore, being freed from all despondency rooted in bondage, attachment, compassion, and erroneous knowledge, I now stand firm, self-composed, and free from doubt.

The meaning is that he will act upon your words regarding the duty of engaging in battle and so forth this very moment; that is to say, he will perform the battle and other such tasks as you have described.
To Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who asked what his own sons and the Pāṇḍavas would do in battle,
Sañjaya said:
"Thus I [have related] the conversation between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha."
I have heard this wonderful dialogue, which causes the hair to stand on end.

Thus have I heard this hair-raising and wonderful dialogue, exactly as it was spoken, between Vāsudeva, the son of Vasudeva, and the high-souled Pārtha, the son of his paternal aunt, who is possessed of great intelligence and has taken refuge at his two feet. (BhG 18.74)
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret Yoga directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as he himself was speaking it.

By the grace of Vyāsa, through the favor of Vyāsa, having obtained divine sight and hearing, I have heard this supreme secret called Yoga directly from the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself as he spoke it— the Lord who is the storehouse of knowledge, strength, sovereignty, heroism, power, and splendor, and the master of yoga.
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over.
Remembering this holy and wonderful dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, which I heard directly, I rejoice again and again.
And as I recall again and again that most wonderful form of Hari,
O King, great is my amazement, and I rejoice again and again.
As I repeatedly recall that most wonderful divine form of Hari revealed to Arjuna, which was directly perceived by me, great amazement arises within me, and I rejoice again and again. (BhG 18.77)
What need is there for much speaking here?
Wherever Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, is, and wherever Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, is, there will be fortune, victory, prosperity, and unfailing policy; this is my conviction.
In whom the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara) resides— the Lord of all yogas, that is, of all inherent natures belonging to every conscious and unconscious entity existing in high and low forms;
He whose differentiation of the nature, subsistence, and activity of Himself and all other things is dependent solely upon His own volition.

"Kṛṣṇa is the son of Vasudeva, and where Pārtha—the son of his paternal aunt and a wielder of the bow—has his feet as his sole refuge, there prosperity, victory, fortune, and statesmanship are certain and immovable; such is my conviction. (BhG 18.78)
